title: Module 7: Applications & Capstone
text:
Case Study: ML Training

Training a large model means repeatedly running the forward pass (Dec 2’s territory) and computing gradients (autograd, briefly introduced Module 6) across enormous datasets, for many GPUs, for days or weeks
The core operation, repeated billions of times, is still the matrix multiply — Module 6’s @/cuBLAS, at a scale where even small per-operation inefficiencies compound into real time and cost
Multi-GPU training adds a new problem this course hasn’t covered: GPUs must periodically synchronize their results with each other over a network — a much slower and more complex version of Module 2’s host↔︎device transfer, now between multiple devices instead of one


~2 min. This connects directly to Module 1’s “a single training run can use thousands of GPUs for weeks” slide and Dec 2’s LLM content — training is the other half of that picture, generation (inference) being the half already covered.

title: Module 7: Applications & Capstone
text:
Case Study: Rendering

Real-time ray tracing and path tracing (how modern game and film rendering works) is fundamentally a massively parallel, per-pixel or per-ray computation — the same “one thread, one independent unit of work” shape from Module 2, applied to light rays instead of array elements
Rendering workloads are often extremely divergent (Module 2’s Sep 30 content): different rays can bounce very different numbers of times before terminating, meaning different threads in the same warp frequently disagree on how much work remains
This is precisely why divergence-handling (predication, the cost of mismatched branches) matters so much in graphics-focused GPU work — it’s not just an exam topic, it’s the daily reality of writing a renderer


~2 min. Good moment to note that this course’s CUDA-focused, compute-only framing deliberately skipped graphics-specific GPU features (rasterization, texture units) — rendering workloads use the same underlying hardware and many of the same programming concepts, just with a different problem shape and additional graphics-specific hardware in play.

title: Module 7: Applications & Capstone
text:
Case Study: Genomics

DNA/protein sequence alignment — finding where a short sequence matches within a much longer reference — has the same shape as Module 5’s parallel patterns: many independent comparisons that can run simultaneously, sometimes combined via a reduction to find the best-scoring match
Protein structure prediction (the class of problem AlphaFold addresses) relies heavily on large matrix operations and neural-network inference — Module 6’s @ and PyTorch content, at a much larger and more specialized scale
Genomics datasets are enormous (a single human genome is billions of base pairs) — exactly the kind of scale where Module 1’s “GPU wins when there’s enough work to amortize overhead” reasoning applies cleanly


~2 min. If time allows, ask whether anyone has used or heard of AlphaFold — it’s a widely-known example that makes “neural network inference, GPU-accelerated, at genomics scale” concrete rather than abstract.

title: Module 7: Applications & Capstone
text:
Case Study: Finance

Monte Carlo simulation (running a random model millions of times to estimate a risk or a price) is embarrassingly parallel in the exact sense Module 1 defined it — each simulated trial is fully independent of every other one
Module 5’s random-number generation and reduction patterns (CuPy’s GPU-side RNG, tree reduction to aggregate results) map directly onto this: generate millions of random scenarios on the GPU, then reduce them down to a summary statistic (an average price, a risk estimate)
High-frequency trading systems care intensely about latency, not just throughput — a reminder that Module 1’s latency-vs-throughput framing isn’t just “GPU vs. CPU,” it’s a real design axis within GPU-accelerated systems too, echoing Dec 2’s batching-strategy discussion


~2 min. Nice closing case study for the module — it reuses nearly every major concept from the semester (embarrassingly parallel, RNG, reduction, latency-vs-throughput) in one recognizable real-world context.

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
Today’s Plan

Why some problems can’t use the “every thread independent” pattern from Modules 2-4
Tree reduction: combining N values down to one, in log(N) parallel rounds instead of N sequential steps
The reduction kernel, applied to sum, max, and (conceptually) dot product
A warp-level optimization for the final few rounds


~1 min. Full 50-min session — no quiz today (Quiz 5 opens at the start of Lab 10, Nov 6, not this lecture). This session is the conceptual pivot of the module: everything since Module 2 has been “one thread, one independent output” — today breaks that assumption for the first time.

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
Beyond Embarrassingly Parallel

So far, every kernel has followed the same shape: thread i computes output i, using only input i (or a small fixed neighborhood, for stencils) — no thread needs any other thread’s result
Some problems don’t fit that shape at all:

Sum all elements → the answer requires combining every input; no single thread can know the total on its own
Find the maximum → same problem, different combining operation
Running total (prefix sum) → each output depends on all prior inputs (Nov 9)

These problems need threads to communicate and combine partial results — a genuinely different kind of parallel pattern from anything so far this semester


~3 min. These two patterns (reduction, and Nov 9’s prefix scan) appear constantly outside this course too — databases, compression, sorting, and nearly every non-trivial GPU algorithm use one or both. The capstone’s cp.argpartition internally relies on a reduction-like operation.

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
The Serial Approach, for Contrast
def serial_sum(arr):
    total = 0.0
    for x in arr:       # N steps, strictly sequential
        total += x
    return total

O(N) time, O(1) memory — simple, and completely sequential: step 2 can’t start until step 1’s result is known
Naively porting this to the GPU doesn’t help: one thread would do all N additions while thousands of others sit idle
The question this session answers: can we restructure the computation itself — not just throw more threads at the same sequential recipe — so that work happens in parallel rounds?


~2 min. Emphasize “restructure,” not “parallelize as-is” — a common early misconception is that any serial loop can just run on more threads. This one specifically can’t, without changing the algorithm’s shape.

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
Tree Reduction: The Idea
[DIAGRAM] — 8 elements in a row: [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]. Three rounds drawn as successive rows beneath, each with arrows connecting pairs from the row above into a single combined value below. Round 1 (stride 4): arrows connect position 0↔︎4, 1↔︎5, 2↔︎6, 3↔︎7, producing [8, 10, 6, 7]. Round 2 (stride 2): arrows connect position 0↔︎2, 1↔︎3 of that new row, producing [14, 17]. Round 3 (stride 1): one arrow connects the remaining pair, producing [31]. Caption: “3 rounds for 8 elements = log₂(8).”

Instead of adding elements one at a time, pair them up and add all pairs simultaneously — one round of parallel work replaces many sequential additions
Each round halves the number of “active” values remaining, so N elements reduce to one in log₂(N) rounds, not N
For N = 1,000,000: a serial sum takes 1,000,000 sequential steps; tree reduction takes about 20 parallel rounds


~4 min. Walk the diagram’s three rounds out loud, stride value by stride value — students trace this exact 8-element example by hand in Lab 10 before writing any code.

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
The Stride-Halving Kernel
@cuda.jit
def block_sum(arr, out):
    s = cuda.shared.array(shape=256, dtype=numba.float32)
    ti = cuda.threadIdx.x
    i  = cuda.grid(1)

    s[ti] = arr[i] if i < arr.shape[0] else 0.0
    cuda.syncthreads()

    stride = 128         # blockDim.x // 2
    while stride > 0:
        if ti < stride:
            s[ti] += s[ti + stride]
        cuda.syncthreads()
        stride //= 2      # halve each round
    if ti == 0:
        out[cuda.blockIdx.x] = s[0]   # this block's sum, in one element

Each thread loads one element into shared memory (Module 4), padding out-of-range threads with the additive identity (0.0) so they don’t corrupt the sum
Every round, only the threads with ti < stride do work — that’s exactly half as many active threads as the previous round, matching the diagram above
syncthreads() after every round is required: a thread reading s[ti + stride] must wait until whichever thread wrote it in the previous round has finished (Module 4’s shared-memory rules apply here directly)


~3 min. This is the exact kernel Lab 10 has students build up piece by piece. Walk through it in the same order as the code: load-to-shared, the stride loop, the single-thread final write. Emphasize only thread 0 writes the result — every other thread in the block does useful work during the loop but writes nothing at the end.

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
Multi-Level Reduction

One kernel launch gives you one sum per block, not one sum for the whole array — out[blockIdx.x] holds that block’s partial result
For N = 1,000,000 with 256-thread blocks: (1,000,000 + 255) // 256 = 3,907 blocks, so 3,907 partial sums remain after one kernel launch, not the single total you actually want
Getting the final answer needs a second pass: either launch the same reduction kernel again on the array of partial sums (repeating until one value remains), or — since 3,907 values is small — just copy them to the host and let NumPy finish the job

block_sums_gpu = cuda.device_array(n_blocks, dtype=np.float32)
block_sum[n_blocks, BLOCK](arr_gpu, block_sums_gpu)
cuda.synchronize()

block_sums_cpu = block_sums_gpu.copy_to_host()
total = block_sums_cpu.sum()   # finish the last, small reduction on the CPU

~3 min. This two-pass (or GPU-then-CPU) pattern is ubiquitous in real GPU reduction code — it’s exactly what cp.sum() (Module 6) does internally, optimized further than a hand-written version. That’s why the capstone uses CuPy’s built-in reductions rather than a hand-rolled kernel: this pattern, done well, is genuinely fiddly to get optimal.

O(N)
O(log N)




Both algorithms do the same total amount of work — tree reduction doesn’t do fewer additions overall, it does the same additions arranged so many happen simultaneously
The speedup comes entirely from parallelism (many operations at once), not from an algorithmically “smarter” computation
This is a recurring theme in parallel algorithms: sometimes the total work even goes up compared to the serial version, and that’s still a win if it converts into far fewer sequential steps — wall-clock time is what matters, not operation count


~2 min. Worth stating explicitly since it cuts against a common intuition: “parallel” doesn’t automatically mean “does less work” — it means “does the same (or more) work in fewer sequential rounds, using more processors at once.”

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
section: Different Combiners: Max and Dot Product
text:
Different Combiners: Max and Dot Product

The tree-reduction shape doesn’t care what operation combines two values — swap += for a different associative operation and the exact same stride-halving pattern still works
Maximum: replace s[ti] += s[ti + stride] with s[ti] = max(s[ti], s[ti + stride]), and pad out-of-range threads with a very negative identity value (-1e9) instead of 0.0 — this is Lab 10 Exercise 3
Dot product: compute a[i] * b[i] per thread first, then reduce those products with += exactly as in block_sum — this is the same “multiply then reduce” shape as the capstone’s similarity computation, just done with a hand-written kernel instead of CuPy’s Q @ D.T
The requirement is associativity: (a ⊕ b) ⊕ c == a ⊕ (b ⊕ c), so it doesn’t matter which order pairs get combined in — addition, max, and min all qualify; subtraction does not


~3 min. The associativity requirement is worth naming explicitly and briefly testing student intuition on — ask “would this trick work for subtraction?” and let them reason out why not (order-dependence breaks the tree’s freedom to combine pairs in any order).

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
Warp-Level Tricks

Once a reduction’s stride drops to 32 or below, every remaining active thread belongs to a single warp (Sep 30) — and a warp already executes in lock-step, one instruction at a time, across all its lanes
Modern CUDA offers warp shuffle instructions (cuda.shfl_down_sync in Numba) that let threads within one warp exchange values directly, register-to-register, without ever touching shared memory at all
Using shuffle for a reduction’s final few rounds skips the shared-memory read/write and the syncthreads() call entirely for that portion — a real, measurable speedup on the “small stride” tail of the reduction
A word of caution: an older, informal trick claims you can also just skip syncthreads() once stride ≤ 32 while still using shared memory, reasoning that “the warp is lock-step anyway.” This is no longer reliably safe on modern GPU architectures (Volta and later independently schedule threads within a warp) — the shuffle-instruction approach above is the correct, current way to get this optimization


~3 min. This slide is intentionally awareness-level, not a skill this course’s labs or checkpoints require — Lab 10’s block_sum uses syncthreads() for every round, which is always correct, just not maximally fast. Flag explicitly that this is here so students recognize the pattern in production CUDA code, not because it’s required for CK-10.

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
Today’s Plan

A second cooperative pattern: every output depends on all prior inputs, not just a combined total
Inclusive vs. exclusive scan, and why the exclusive version is usually more useful
The Blelloch algorithm: up-sweep and down-sweep, traced by hand before any code
Real applications: stream compaction, histograms, sorting


~1 min. Full 50-min session, no quiz. This is a genuinely harder algorithm than reduction — budget extra time for the two hand-traced diagrams, don’t rush them.

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
What Is a Prefix Sum?
Input:              [2, 5, 1, 8, 3, 7, 4, 6]
Exclusive scan out: [0, 2, 7, 8, 16, 19, 26, 30]

output[i] = the sum of every input strictly before index i — output[0] is always 0 (nothing comes before the first element)
Contrast with inclusive scan, where output[i] = sum of input[0..i] (index i included): [2, 7, 8, 16, 19, 26, 30, 36] for the same input
The exclusive version is usually the more directly useful one in parallel algorithms — it gives each element a ready-made “slot” or “offset” to write into, which is exactly what stream compaction (below) needs


~3 min. Have students verify the first few outputs by hand from the input list before revealing the diagram — this cements “strictly before” (exclusive) vs. “up to and including” (inclusive) far better than the definition alone.

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
Why Prefix Scan Matters

Stream compaction: given a boolean mask of which elements survive, exclusive scan of the mask gives each surviving element its exact output position — you built and used exactly this in Lab 11’s bonus exercise
Histogram computation: converting per-bin counts into cumulative offsets (where does each bin’s data start, in a combined output array) is a prefix scan
Sorting: radix sort — a fast, non-comparison-based sorting algorithm — uses prefix scan internally at every digit pass
Dynamic allocation: when many threads each need a variable-size chunk of a shared output buffer, exclusive scan of the requested sizes gives every thread its own non-overlapping starting offset
You are not expected to implement all of these applications — the point is that prefix scan is a primitive: one algorithm that shows up, often invisibly, inside many others


~2 min. Stream compaction is the one application students actually build (Lab 11’s bonus) — the others are here so the pattern is recognizable by name later, not because they’re separately assessed.

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
The Serial Algorithm
def exclusive_scan_seq(arr):
    out = [0] * len(arr)
    running = 0
    for i in range(len(arr)):
        out[i] = running
        running += arr[i]
    return out

Straightforward and O(N) sequential — each output depends on the running total built up from everything before it, which is exactly what makes this look hard to parallelize at first glance
Lab 11 Exercise 1 has you write this exact function — understanding this version thoroughly is what makes the parallel version (next) legible, rather than a magic trick
The whole rest of this session is answering one question: how do you compute something that looks inherently sequential using O(log N) parallel rounds instead?


~2 min. Deliberately start here rather than jumping straight to Blelloch — the serial version being trivial is what makes the parallel version’s cleverness visible by contrast.

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
Blelloch Scan: Two Phases
The Blelloch exclusive scan solves this in two phases, both O(log N) rounds:

Up-sweep (reduce): build partial sums bottom-up — the exact same tree shape as Nov 2’s reduction
Down-sweep: propagate those partial sums back down top-to-bottom, converting them into prefix values

Total: O(N) work, O(log N) steps — same complexity class as tree reduction, for a harder problem.

~2 min. Point out explicitly: up-sweep is literally the reduction algorithm from Nov 2, run for its side effects (the partial sums left behind at each level) rather than just its final total. Students who understood Nov 2 already understand half of this algorithm.

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
Up-Sweep on [2, 5, 1, 8]
[DIAGRAM] — Four boxes in a row holding 2, 5, 1, 8, with two rounds drawn beneath as tree-reduction-style arrows. Round 1 (stride 1): an arrow from box 0 into box 1 (box 1 becomes 2+5=7), and an arrow from box 2 into box 3 (box 3 becomes 1+8=9) — boxes now read 2, 7, 1, 9. Round 2 (stride 2): an arrow from box 1 into box 3 (box 3 becomes 7+9=16) — boxes now read 2, 7, 1, 16. Caption: “s[3] = 16 = the total sum of all four elements — same result the Nov 2 reduction tree would produce, but the intermediate partial sums (7, 9) are kept, not discarded.”
Initial:  [2, 5, 1, 8]
stride=1: s[1] += s[0] → [2, 7, 1, 8]
          s[3] += s[2] → [2, 7, 1, 9]
stride=2: s[3] += s[1] → [2, 7, 1, 16]
Result:   [2, 7, 1, 16]   ← s[3] = total sum

~4 min. Lab 11 Exercise 2 has students trace this on the full 8-element array from the “What Is a Prefix Sum” slide. Walk through this simpler 4-element version here first to establish the index pattern before scaling up.

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
Down-Sweep
[DIAGRAM] — The same four boxes, starting from the up-sweep’s final state [2, 7, 1, 16], with the last box first reset to 0: [2, 7, 1, 0]. Round 1 (stride 2): an arrow shows box 1’s value (7) moving into box 3, while box 1 simultaneously receives box 3’s old value (0) — resulting in box 3 = 7 + 0 = 7, box 1 = 0: state becomes [2, 0, 1, 7]. Round 2 (stride 1): two simultaneous swap-and-add operations, box 0↔︎1 and box 2↔︎3, following the same swap pattern — final state [0, 2, 1, 7] then combined to [0, 2, 7, 8]. Caption: “Each step: the left partner’s old value moves right and gets added; the left partner receives the right partner’s old value.”
Set s[3] = 0:              [2, 7, 1, 0]

stride=2:
  tmp = s[1] = 7
  s[1] = s[3] = 0
  s[3] = tmp + s[3] = 7+0 = 7    → [2, 0, 1, 7]

stride=1:
  tmp=s[0]=2; s[0]=s[1]=0; s[1]=0+2=2   → [0, 2, 1, 7]
  tmp=s[2]=1; s[2]=s[3]=7; s[3]=7+1=8   → [0, 2, 7, 8]

Final: [0, 2, 7, 8]  ✓ matches the exclusive scan definition

~5 min. This is the module’s hardest diagram — budget the full five minutes, don’t compress it. The pattern to emphasize: at each swap-and-add step, the left position’s old value is what moves to the right (and gets added there); the left position then receives whatever the right position used to hold. Students who trace both phases by hand in Lab 11 report this is what finally makes the GPU kernel (next slide) legible.

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
The GPU Version
BLOCK = 16

@cuda.jit
def exclusive_scan_gpu(arr, out):
    s   = cuda.shared.array(shape=BLOCK, dtype=numba.float32)
    ti  = cuda.threadIdx.x
    i   = cuda.grid(1)

    s[ti] = arr[i] if i < arr.shape[0] else 0.0
    cuda.syncthreads()

    # Up-sweep
    stride = 1
    while stride < BLOCK:
        if (ti + 1) % (stride * 2) == 0:
            s[ti] += s[ti - stride]
        cuda.syncthreads()
        stride *= 2

    # Clear root — this is the single most-forgotten step
    if ti == BLOCK - 1:
        s[ti] = 0.0
    cuda.syncthreads()

    # Down-sweep
    stride = BLOCK // 2
    while stride > 0:
        if (ti + 1) % (stride * 2) == 0:
            tmp            = s[ti - stride]
            s[ti - stride] = s[ti]
            s[ti]          = tmp + s[ti]
        cuda.syncthreads()
        stride //= 2

    if i < out.shape[0]:
        out[i] = s[ti]

Every line here is one of the two hand-traced diagrams above, translated directly into indexing arithmetic — the (ti + 1) % (stride * 2) == 0 condition is just “which positions are active at this stride,” the same positions the diagrams marked with arrows
Lab 11 Part 4 gives you this kernel pre-written and asks you to verify it against your own hand trace — the goal is confirming understanding, not re-deriving the indexing from scratch under time pressure


~3 min. Point at the “clear root” line specifically — Lab 11’s own instructor notes flag this as the single most-forgotten step by students attempting this from memory. It’s the one line that has no analogue in the up-sweep and is easy to skip if you’re pattern-matching rather than reasoning through the algorithm.

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
Today’s Plan

A third cooperative pattern: many threads that might all want to update the same memory location, at a location not known until runtime
Why the naive version of this is a race condition — reduction and scan don’t have this problem, and this pattern shows why they were special cases
Atomic operations: the hardware-guaranteed fix
A worked example: computing a histogram


~1 min. Full 50-min session, no quiz. This closes out Module 5’s three cooperative patterns: combine-to-one (reduction), propagate-outward (scan), and now many-to-one-of-several (atomics/histograms).

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
A New Kind of Conflict

Reduction and scan both have a property that made them tractable: at every step, the set of memory locations being written is known in advance and non-overlapping — no two threads in the same round ever write the same address
A histogram breaks that property: given a stream of values, each thread looks at one value, decides which “bin” it belongs to, and increments that bin’s counter — but which bin depends on the data itself, not on the thread’s index
Two different threads can easily land on the same bin at the same time — say, two threads both processing a value that falls in bin 5 — and both need to increment counts[5]
This is a fundamentally different problem: unpredictable, data-dependent collisions, not the clean tree structure of reduction or scan


~3 min. Frame this explicitly as “the third pattern” completing the module — students should leave recognizing reduction (combine to one), scan (propagate to all), and atomics (handle unpredictable collisions) as three distinct answers to “how do threads cooperate,” not one topic that happens to have three examples.

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
The Race Condition, Concretely
@cuda.jit
def histogram_broken(values, counts):
    i = cuda.grid(1)
    if i < values.shape[0]:
        bin_idx = values[i]           # which bin does this value belong to?
        counts[bin_idx] += 1          # BROKEN — see below

counts[bin_idx] += 1 looks like one operation, but the hardware executes it as three: read counts[bin_idx], add 1 to that value, write the result back
If two threads both target the same bin_idx at nearly the same time, both can read the same starting value before either has written their update back — both then write back old_value + 1, and one of the two increments is silently lost
With enough threads and enough collisions, a histogram built this way undercounts — every run potentially giving a slightly different (wrong) answer, since the exact interleaving of threads is not deterministic


~3 min. This is the same read-modify-write race condition idea introduced very briefly for shared memory in Module 4 — here it’s global memory, and the collision is data-dependent rather than a missing syncthreads(). Worth drawing the two-thread interleaving out explicitly: Thread A reads 5, Thread B reads 5 (before A writes), A writes 6, B writes 6 — the count should be 7, but ends at 6.

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
Atomic Operations: The Fix
from numba import cuda

@cuda.jit
def histogram_correct(values, counts):
    i = cuda.grid(1)
    if i < values.shape[0]:
        bin_idx = values[i]
        cuda.atomic.add(counts, bin_idx, 1)   # read-modify-write, guaranteed indivisible

cuda.atomic.add(array, index, value) performs the entire read-modify-write as one indivisible hardware operation — no other thread can observe or interfere with it partway through
If two threads call atomic.add on the same address at the same moment, the hardware serializes them: one fully completes, then the other — never an interleaved, lost update
This is the general fix for exactly the race condition on the previous slide — replace the naive += with the atomic version whenever multiple threads might write the same address


~3 min. Emphasize “indivisible,” not “fast” — atomics fix correctness, they don’t inherently make the operation cheap (next-to-last slide covers the cost). The syntax itself is simple; the concept (why it’s needed, what “indivisible” guarantees) is the real content here.

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
A Complete Histogram Kernel
NUM_BINS = 10

@cuda.jit
def histogram(values, counts):
    i = cuda.grid(1)
    if i < values.shape[0]:
        bin_idx = min(int(values[i] * NUM_BINS), NUM_BINS - 1)   # clamp to valid range
        cuda.atomic.add(counts, bin_idx, 1)

# Launch
counts_gpu = cuda.to_device(np.zeros(NUM_BINS, dtype=np.int32))
histogram[blocks, threads](values_gpu, counts_gpu)
cuda.synchronize()

Each of potentially millions of threads independently computes which bin its value belongs to, then atomically increments that bin — no coordination between threads needed beyond the atomic operation itself
counts_gpu must be zero-initialized before the kernel runs — atomics increment whatever is already there, they don’t reset it
Notice the bin-index computation clamps into [0, NUM_BINS-1] — same “handle the edge case explicitly” habit as Module 3’s stencil boundary conditions, just for a different kind of edge case


~2 min. This is a complete, runnable pattern — worth a live demo if time allows, generating random data and confirming the GPU histogram matches np.histogram on the same data.

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
Atomics Beyond Addition

cuda.atomic.add is the most common atomic, but Numba provides others for the same indivisible-read-modify-write guarantee with different combining operations:

cuda.atomic.max(array, index, value) / cuda.atomic.min(...) — atomic maximum/minimum, useful whenever many threads might all want to update a shared “best so far” value
cuda.atomic.compare_and_swap(array, old, new) — the building block many other atomics (and lock-free algorithms generally) are built from: “update this value only if it still equals what I expect”

Anywhere multiple threads might write to the same, data-dependent location — not a fixed, thread-indexed location like every kernel before this session — an atomic operation (or a redesign to avoid the collision entirely) is required for correctness


~2 min. Keep this at the level of “these exist and follow the same pattern as atomic.add” — no worked example needed for each; the histogram example already carries the core idea.

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
The Cost of Atomics

Atomics guarantee correctness by serializing conflicting operations — which means heavy contention (many threads atomically writing the same address at the same time) can become a real bottleneck, similar in spirit to Module 4’s bank conflicts
A histogram with very few bins and a huge number of threads (e.g. 10 bins, a million threads) will see enormous contention — most threads end up waiting in line for the same handful of addresses
A histogram with many bins relative to thread count sees far less contention, since collisions become statistically rare
This is a genuine performance/correctness tradeoff: atomics are always correct, but not always fast — the naive version from two slides ago was fast (no serialization) and wrong; the atomic version is always right, and its speed depends on how much actual contention your specific data causes


~2 min. Good closing thought for the module: this is the last of three techniques (bounds guards, syncthreads, atomics) that all trade a small amount of overhead for correctness — worth naming that pattern explicitly as something students have now seen three times.

title: Module 5: Parallel Patterns
text:
Module 5 Wrap-Up

Nov 2 — Reduction: combine N values into 1, in O(log N) rounds, via a binary tree of associative operations (sum, max, dot product all fit)
Nov 9 — Prefix scan: compute a running total at every position, also in O(log N) rounds, via the two-phase Blelloch up-sweep/down-sweep
Nov 11 — Atomics: handle unpredictable, data-dependent collisions between threads with hardware-guaranteed indivisible operations, at the cost of serializing genuine contention
Three different answers to the same underlying question this whole module asked: what do threads do when they can’t stay fully independent?


~1 min. Good slide to revisit before Quiz 6 (Nov 16), which covers this whole module.

title: Module 3: Kernel Development & Profiling
section: From “Does It Run” to “Does It Run Well”
text:
From “Does It Run” to “Does It Run Well”

Every kernel you’ve written so far (Labs 4-5) follows one pattern: one thread computes one output element, checked by one bounds guard
That pattern is correct, and it’s the right default — but it’s not the only shape a kernel can take, and getting it running is only the first bar to clear
The rest of this module is about two things: designing kernels deliberately rather than by habit, and measuring whether they’re actually fast


~2 min. Framing slide — sets up why “design patterns” and “debugging” belong in the same session as a matched pair: patterns are how you write a kernel well the first time, debugging is what you do when it isn’t.

title: Module 3: Kernel Development & Profiling
section: Pattern: One Thread, One Output Element

title: Module 3: Kernel Development & Profiling
text:
Pattern: The Grid-Stride Loop
@cuda.jit
def scale_grid_stride(arr, factor):
    start  = cuda.grid(1)
    stride = cuda.gridsize(1)          # total threads launched
    for i in range(start, arr.shape[0], stride):
        arr[i] = arr[i] * factor

A different shape: launch a fixed, modest number of threads, and have each one loop over multiple elements, striding by the total thread count
Useful when N is unknown at launch time, or so large that launching one thread per element isn’t practical, or when you want the same kernel to run efficiently across a wide range of N without recomputing launch config each time
You won’t be asked to write this pattern in a lab or checkpoint this semester — it’s here so you recognize it when you see it in real-world CUDA code, which uses it constantly


~2 min. Explicitly flag this as awareness-level, not tested — students should not walk away thinking they need to memorize cuda.gridsize() syntax for a checkpoint. The goal is purely “don’t be confused when you see this shape later in your career.”

title: Module 3: Kernel Development & Profiling
text:
Choosing a Launch Configuration

So far, launch configuration (THREADS, computed BLOCKS) has mostly been handed to you or fixed at a round number like 256
In practice, there is rarely one obviously-correct block size — it depends on the kernel’s resource usage (registers, shared memory) and the GPU’s occupancy limits (Sep 30)
A few reliable heuristics: prefer multiples of 32 (whole warps, no wasted lanes — Sep 30); common starting points are 128, 256, or 512 threads per block; extremes (very small or very large blocks) are rarely optimal
Beyond those heuristics, the honest answer is: measure it. Lab 6 (this Friday) has you sweep several block sizes on a real kernel and find the fastest empirically — that’s Oct 7’s subject in full


~3 min. Resist the temptation to give a definitive “always use 256” rule — the entire point of Oct 7’s profiling session is that this has to be measured per-kernel. This slide should leave students slightly unsatisfied with “it depends,” which Oct 7 then resolves with a concrete method.

title: Module 3: Kernel Development & Profiling
text:
Debugging Numba CUDA Kernels

GPU kernels run outside the normal Python debugger — you can’t drop a breakpoint inside a @cuda.jit function the way you would in ordinary Python
Common failure modes you’ll hit this semester:

Silent wrong answers — almost always a missing or incorrect bounds guard (Module 2)
TypingError at compile time — Numba’s CUDA compiler only supports a restricted subset of Python/NumPy; an unsupported operation (e.g. Python lists, string formatting, most NumPy functions) inside a kernel fails to compile with a (sometimes cryptic) type error
Shape mismatches — passing an array of the wrong shape or dtype to a kernel that assumes a specific layout



~3 min. Ask the room if anyone has already hit a TypingError in Lab 4 or 5 — normalize it as a routine part of the workflow, not a sign something has gone deeply wrong.

title: Module 3: Kernel Development & Profiling
section: Debugging Technique: Shrink N and Verify by Hand
text:
Debugging Technique: Shrink N and Verify by Hand
N_DEBUG = 8   # instead of 1,000,000 — small enough to eyeball
arr = np.arange(N_DEBUG, dtype=np.float32)
arr_gpu = cuda.to_device(arr)

my_kernel[1, N_DEBUG](arr_gpu)     # one block, exactly enough threads
cuda.synchronize()

print(arr_gpu.copy_to_host())      # small enough to read directly

Before trusting a kernel at N = 1,000,000, run it at N = 8 (or similar) and check every value by hand or against a tiny NumPy reference
Launching one block with exactly N threads (no ceiling division needed) removes launch-configuration bugs from the picture while you debug the kernel body itself
Every lab’s Completion cell does a version of this at full scale — this technique is how you get there with confidence, one step earlier


~2 min. This is the single most useful habit to instill this session — most kernel bugs are far easier to spot in 8 printed numbers than in a checksum computed over a million.

title: Module 3: Kernel Development & Profiling
text:
Debugging Technique: The CUDA Simulator
import os
os.environ["NUMBA_ENABLE_CUDASIM"] = "1"   # set BEFORE importing numba.cuda

from numba import cuda

@cuda.jit
def my_kernel(arr):
    i = cuda.grid(1)
    print("thread", i, "sees", arr[i])   # print() now actually works!
    if i < arr.shape[0]:
        arr[i] = arr[i] * 2.0

Setting NUMBA_ENABLE_CUDASIM=1 runs your @cuda.jit kernel in pure Python, on the CPU, one simulated thread at a time — no GPU required
Inside the simulator, ordinary Python print() and even pdb breakpoints work exactly as they would in any Python function — neither works reliably in a real GPU kernel
Trade-off: the simulator is much slower and doesn’t reflect real GPU timing — use it to debug logic, then switch back to a real GPU to debug and measure performance


~2 min. This is a genuinely useful Numba feature many students won’t discover on their own — worth a live demo if time allows, showing a kernel with a deliberate bug caught via a print() that would be silent (or crash unhelpfully) on real hardware.

text:
Today’s Plan

The most common — and most deceptive — mistake in timing GPU code
Timing correctly, and what a time-vs-problem-size curve tells you
Reading a profiler-style table: which configuration is fastest, and why
Amdahl’s Law — the theoretical ceiling on any speedup, no matter how good your kernel is


~1 min. Full 50-min session, no quiz. Two distinct halves: measurement technique (first ~20 min), then the theoretical ceiling that measurement is ultimately in service of (Amdahl, last ~20 min).

title: Module 3: Kernel Development & Profiling
section: The Wrong Way to Time a GPU Kernel
text:
The Wrong Way to Time a GPU Kernel
import time

start = time.perf_counter()
my_kernel[blocks, threads](arr_gpu)
end = time.perf_counter()

print(f"{(end - start)*1000:.2f} ms")  # WRONG

A GPU kernel launch is asynchronous — the CPU issues the launch and immediately continues to the next line, without waiting for the GPU to actually finish
time.perf_counter() here measures how long it took to launch the kernel, not how long the kernel took to run
The result: a suspiciously, impossibly fast number — this is the bug, not a real measurement


~3 min. This is Lab 06’s critical demo. Let the wrong number sit for a moment before revealing why it’s wrong — the surprise is the point, it makes the fix memorable.

title: Module 3: Kernel Development & Profiling
text:
The Right Way: cuda.synchronize()
import time
from numba import cuda

start = time.perf_counter()
my_kernel[blocks, threads](arr_gpu)
cuda.synchronize()              # wait for the GPU to actually finish
end = time.perf_counter()

print(f"{(end - start)*1000:.2f} ms")  # CORRECT

cuda.synchronize() blocks the CPU until every previously-launched GPU operation has completed
Without it, you are timing a function call that returns almost instantly, not a computation
This is not a beginner mistake to be embarrassed about — the same bug appears in published papers and shipped industry code. Professional GPU code-review checklists explicitly call it out


~2 min. Reiterate: the fact that the wrong code runs, produces a plausible-looking (if suspiciously small) number, and never raises an error is exactly what makes this trap dangerous. There is no crash to alert you.

title: Module 3: Kernel Development & Profiling
text:
Timing Across Problem Sizes
sizes = [10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000, 5_000_000, 20_000_000]

for N in sizes:
    arr = cp.random.randn(N, dtype=cp.float32)

    start = time.perf_counter()
    result = cp.sum(arr ** 2)
    cp.cuda.Stream.null.synchronize()   # CuPy's equivalent of cuda.synchronize()
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start

    print(f"N={N:>10,}  time={elapsed*1000:.2f} ms")

Running the same computation across a range of N reveals whether GPU overhead (kernel launch, PCIe transfer — Module 2) is dominating small problems
At small N, expect the GPU to look slow — fixed overhead dominates. At large N, that overhead is amortized and the GPU’s raw throughput wins
Lab 6 has you find this crossover point directly — it’s a concrete answer to Module 1’s “when does the GPU actually win?” question


~2 min. Tie explicitly back to Module 1’s “when does the GPU win/lose” slide — this timing sweep is that question, answered empirically instead of just in principle.

title: Module 3: Kernel Development & Profiling
text:
Reading a Profiler-Style Table
Lab 6 has you sweep the naive matmul kernel across three block sizes and record the results:
     Block |  Time (ms) | Threads/block
------------------------------------------
       8x8 |      14.82 |             64
     16x16 |       6.31 |            256
     32x32 |       8.94 |           1024

Reading this table is itself a skill: scan the “Time” column for the minimum, then ask why that configuration won — this is exactly what CK-06 tests
Here, 16×16 is fastest — not the smallest block (8×8, too few threads to keep the SM busy) and not the largest (32×32, resource limits reduce how many blocks can be resident at once — Sep 30’s occupancy content)
A profiler-style table like this is a compressed record of an experiment — reading it well means reconstructing the “why,” not just picking out the smallest number


~3 min. Numbers shown are representative, not guaranteed — actual Lab 6 results vary by Colab’s assigned T4 and current load. The shape (middle value wins) is the teachable pattern, not these exact milliseconds.

title: Module 3: Kernel Development & Profiling
text:
Compute-Bound or Memory-Bound?

The naive matmul kernel reads a full row of A and a full column of B from global memory for every single output element it computes — with zero reuse between threads
That’s a lot of global-memory traffic relative to the arithmetic done per byte fetched (low arithmetic intensity — Module 1’s preview of this idea)
Diagnosis: this kernel is memory-bound, not compute-bound — its ALUs are very often waiting on data, not the limiting factor
This diagnosis is exactly why Module 4’s tiled matmul (reusing data via shared memory) gets such a large speedup over this naive version — it directly attacks the memory-bound bottleneck identified here


~3 min. This is CK-06’s Q1 in worked-example form — plant the reasoning pattern here (describe the access pattern → count reuse → conclude bound type) so students can reproduce it on a different kernel in the checkpoint.

title: Module 3: Kernel Development & Profiling
section: Why a Middle Block Size Often Wins
text:
Why a Middle Block Size Often Wins

Very small blocks (8×8 = 64 threads = 2 warps): too few resident warps for the scheduler to hide memory latency well (Sep 30) — the SM often has nothing else ready to run while one warp waits
Very large blocks (32×32 = 1024 threads): each block claims a large share of the SM’s fixed register/thread budget, so fewer blocks fit resident at once — occupancy can drop even though each individual block is “big”
The middle ground (16×16 = 256 threads = 8 warps) is often the sweet spot: enough warps to hide latency, without claiming so much of the SM’s budget that fewer blocks fit
“Often” is doing real work in that sentence — this is a heuristic, not a law. The only way to know for a specific kernel is to measure, exactly as Lab 6 does


~2 min. This is CK-06’s Q2 in worked-example form. Emphasize this is reasoning from the occupancy concept (Sep 30), not a new independent rule to memorize.

title: Module 3: Kernel Development & Profiling
section: Amdahl’s Law: The Serial Fraction Problem
text:
Amdahl’s Law: The Serial Fraction Problem
Every program has two parts:

Parallel part (fraction \(p\)): can run on all GPU cores simultaneously
Serial part (fraction \(1-p\)): must run sequentially — no amount of parallel hardware helps

\[\text{Speedup}(n) = \frac{1}{(1-p) + \frac{p}{n}}\]
where \(n\) is the number of parallel processors applied to the parallel part.

~4 min. Derive from first principles: if total serial-equivalent work is 1 unit, the serial part takes time \((1-p)\) regardless of \(n\), and the parallel part takes time \(p/n\). Total time is the sum; speedup is 1 divided by that. This is the formal version of Module 1’s informal preview.

title: Module 3: Kernel Development & Profiling
text:
The Ceiling
As \(n \to \infty\) (infinitely many processors):
\[\text{Speedup} \to \frac{1}{1-p}\]

A 5% serial fraction caps total speedup at 20× — forever, no matter how many GPU cores you add
A 1% serial fraction caps it at 100×. Even a tiny serial fraction becomes the binding constraint once \(n\) is large enough

[DIAGRAM] — Line chart, x-axis “number of processors n” (log scale, 1 to 10,000), y-axis “speedup.” Four curves for p = 0.5, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99. All four curves rise initially, then flatten into a horizontal asymptote — the p=0.5 curve flattens near speedup=2 almost immediately, while the p=0.99 curve keeps climbing much further before flattening near speedup=100. Dashed horizontal lines mark each curve’s ceiling value.

~2 min. The diagram is the “aha” — a static formula is less convincing than watching four curves all hit a wall at different heights. EL-03 has students apply this exact ceiling to the capstone’s estimated 5% serial fraction.

title: Module 3: Kernel Development & Profiling
text:
The Uncomfortable Implication

Your GPU kernel is 50× faster than the CPU version. The serial part of your program is completely unchanged.
If the serial fraction is 5%, the end-to-end speedup of your whole program is still capped at 20×, no matter how fast that kernel gets
Cutting the serial fraction from 5% to 2.5% buys more end-to-end speedup than doubling the GPU kernel’s raw performance
Practical consequence: sometimes the highest-value optimization isn’t the kernel at all — it’s the data loading, the preprocessing step, or a serial aggregation on the host


~3 min. This is the punchline students should carry into the capstone: profiling (this session’s first half) tells you where time goes; Amdahl tells you the ceiling on how much any one piece of optimization can help.

title: Module 3: Kernel Development & Profiling
text:
Applying Amdahl to the Capstone
In the capstone’s similarity-search pipeline:

Serial: data loading, host↔︎device PCIe transfer, cp.argpartition for top-K — estimated at roughly 5% of total time
Parallel: the Q @ D.T similarity computation itself — roughly 95%

\[\text{Max possible speedup} = \frac{1}{0.05} = 20\times\]

EL-03 (due Sun, Oct 18 — the day before the midterm) has you read Herb Sutter’s “The Free Lunch Is Over” essay and apply this exact calculation to the capstone yourself
At CK-14 (end of semester), you’ll measure your actual speedup and compare it against this theoretical ceiling


~2 min. EL-03’s timing is deliberate — Amdahl’s Law is squarely midterm material, and finishing the reading/calculation the day before the exam is meant to cement it, not just check a box.

title: Module 3: Kernel Development & Profiling
section: Beyond Element-wise: What Is a Stencil?
text:
Beyond Element-wise: What Is a Stencil?

Every kernel so far has been element-wise: output i depends only on input i (or input (row, col)) — no thread needs to look at its neighbors
A stencil breaks that pattern: output i depends on a small neighborhood of nearby inputs, not just the one at the same position
Classic examples: a moving average (each output = average of nearby inputs), image blur (each output pixel = weighted average of nearby pixels), numerical derivatives (each output = a weighted combination of neighboring values)
The “one thread, one output” launch pattern (Oct 5) still applies — what changes is what each thread reads, not how many threads you launch


~3 min. Frame this explicitly as “the launch pattern you already know, applied to a kernel body that reads more than one input” — students shouldn’t feel like they’re learning an entirely new launch mechanic, just a new kernel-body shape.

title: Module 3: Kernel Development & Profiling
text:
The Boundary Problem
[DIAGRAM] — A 1D array of 10 cells, indices 0-9, drawn in a row. Above index 0, dashed “ghost” cells at positions -2 and -1 are shown with question marks, labeled “neighbors that don’t exist.” Above index 9, the same for positions 10 and 11 on the right. A caption: “Every interior cell has real neighbors on both sides. Cells near the edges do not.”

A stencil reads a neighborhood around each position — but positions near the edge of the array have neighbors that fall outside the array entirely
Every stencil kernel needs an explicit policy for what to do at the boundary — there is no “correct” default, only different reasonable choices with different tradeoffs
Three common policies: clamp (reuse the nearest valid edge value), zero-pad (treat out-of-range neighbors as zero), wrap (treat the array as circular, wrapping around to the other side)


~3 min. Don’t rush past “there is no correct default” — this is a genuine design decision, not a fact to memorize. Different applications legitimately prefer different policies (image processing usually clamps or wraps; some signal-processing contexts zero-pad).

title: Module 3: Kernel Development & Profiling
text:
Our Policy: Clamping
def clamp(x, lo, hi):
    return min(max(x, lo), hi)

clamp(-1, 0, 9)   # -1 is out of range  → snaps to 0
clamp(5, 0, 9)    #  5 is in range     → unchanged
clamp(15, 0, 9)   # 15 is out of range → snaps to 9

This course uses clamping (also called edge-replication) throughout: any neighbor index that falls outside the valid range is snapped to the nearest valid edge index instead
Effect: edge pixels/values get their “missing” neighbors filled in with a repeat of the nearest real value, rather than a fabricated zero or a wraparound from the opposite edge
Every stencil kernel this semester (Lab 7, CK-07) uses this exact clamp() helper — implemented inline inside the kernel, since Numba CUDA kernels can’t call arbitrary Python helper functions


~2 min. Flag the “can’t call arbitrary helper functions” constraint explicitly — students will need to inline the clamp logic (min(max(idx, 0), n-1)) directly in the kernel body rather than calling a separate clamp() function, which is a real Numba CUDA limitation worth knowing about before Lab 7.

title: Module 3: Kernel Development & Profiling
text:
A 1D Warm-up: Moving Average
@cuda.jit
def moving_average_1d(arr, out, n, radius):
    i = cuda.grid(1)
    if i < n:
        total = 0.0
        for d in range(-radius, radius + 1):
            j = min(max(i + d, 0), n - 1)   # clamp inline
            total += arr[j]
        out[i] = total / (2 * radius + 1)

Each output i averages 2*radius + 1 neighboring inputs — radius 2 means a 5-wide window (2 before, the center, 2 after)
The min(max(...)) clamp appears inside the loop, once per neighbor read — this is CK-07’s exact pattern
Near the edges, clamping means some neighbor positions repeat (e.g. near index 0, j clamps to 0 for every out-of-range neighbor) — that’s the clamping policy visibly at work, not a bug


~3 min. This is Lab 07 Part 3’s warm-up, shown here as a worked example before the lab. Have students trace through i=0, radius=2 by hand: d ranges over -2,-1,0,1,2; j clamps to 0,0,0,1,2 — three of the five taps are the same repeated value.

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
text:
Today’s Plan


Why serial CPU performance stopped improving for free
Three physical walls: clock speed, power, memory
Why the industry’s answer was “more cores,” and why GPUs are the extreme end of that answer


~1 min. Pure housekeeping — say it, move on. Today’s lecture time is ~35 min after the quiz, so pacing is tighter than a normal 50-min session.

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
text:
20 Years of Free Performance

From roughly 1980 to 2004, CPU clock speed doubled about every 18 months (a corollary of Moore’s Law, below)
Every year, the exact same program ran faster on new hardware — with zero code changes
Developers could treat performance as someone else’s problem: just wait for next year’s chip


~2 min. Ask the room: “When did you last upgrade a device and notice your code/apps ran faster just from the hardware?” The honest answer today is: rarely, unless the workload is GPU-accelerated. That gap is the subject of this module.

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
text:
Moore’s Law, Precisely

“The number of transistors on an integrated circuit doubles roughly every two years, at roughly constant cost.” — Gordon Moore, 1965


Moore’s Law is about transistor count, not clock speed directly
For ~40 years, more transistors did translate into higher clock speed, because of a companion effect: Dennard scaling
Dennard scaling (1974): as transistors shrink by a factor, you can also lower their voltage by that same factor — so power density stays roughly constant even as clock speed rises
Transistor count kept doubling. Clock speed did not — Dennard scaling broke first (next slide)


~3 min. Common misconception to correct explicitly: many students conflate “Moore’s Law” with “clock speeds double every 2 years.” Moore’s Law (transistor count) is alive-ish today; the clock-speed corollary died around 2005 specifically because Dennard scaling died, not because Moore’s Law did.

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
text:
Clock Speed Stagnation
 

Single-core clock speed has been stuck at ~3–4 GHz for two decades
Single-thread performance still creeps up (better branch prediction, bigger caches, deeper pipelines) — but those are diminishing returns, not doubling every 18 months
Something had to replace “just run it at a higher frequency”


~3 min. Source a current chart (CPU-DB, Karl Rupp’s “42 Years of Microprocessor Trend Data” is the canonical one instructors use) before drawing this. Students are often surprised the plateau has lasted this long — it predates most of them being alive.

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
text:
The Power Wall


Dynamic power draw of a chip is approximately \(P \approx C \cdot V^2 \cdot f\) (capacitance × voltage² × frequency)
Under Dennard scaling, shrinking transistors let you lower \(V\) every generation — so raising \(f\) didn’t raise power density
Around 2005 (~90 nm), \(V\) hit a floor: drop it further and transistors leak current even when “off,” wasting power and generating heat with no benefit
Without falling \(V\), raising \(f\) directly raises power density — past what air cooling (and eventually any practical cooling) can remove from a chip the size of a fingernail


~3 min. This is the physical reason behind the previous slide’s plateau. Keep the formula but don’t derive it — the takeaway is “voltage stopped shrinking, so frequency stopped rising, or the chip melts.” EL-03’s Sutter essay covers this from the software-consequences angle; this slide covers the hardware cause.

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
text:
The Memory Wall


CPU compute throughput improved dramatically for decades; DRAM latency (time to fetch one value) improved only modestly over the same period
A single memory fetch has taken roughly 100 ns for a long time — during which a modern CPU core could execute hundreds of instructions
Consequence: a core that issues one memory request and then waits idles for hundreds of cycles unless something else fills that time
CPUs hide this with large caches and speculative prefetching; GPUs hide it differently — by keeping thousands of other threads ready to run while one thread waits (Module 2)


~3 min. Term coined by Wulf & McKee (1994). This is the setup for why occupancy/warp-scheduling (Module 2) and coalesced memory access (Module 4) matter so much for GPU performance — plant the vocabulary “hiding latency” now, it recurs constantly for the rest of the course.

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
text:
The Industry’s Answer: More Cores

Clock speed capped by the power wall. Memory latency capped by physics. Single-core performance alone could no longer 10× every few years
The industry’s pivot (mid-2000s onward): stop making one core faster, put more cores on the chip instead
Consumer CPUs went from 1 core (pre-2005) → 2 → 4 → 8 → today’s 16–32+ core desktop chips
A GPU is the same idea taken to its logical extreme: instead of tens of powerful cores, thousands of small, simple ones


~2 min. This is the bridge sentence for the whole module: multicore CPUs and GPUs are answers to the same problem (the walls above), differing only in degree. Session 2 makes that “degree” concrete with real numbers.

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
text:
One Expert vs. a Crowd
[DIAGRAM] — Two side-by-side scenes (same visual language as Module 0’s cashier diagram). Left: one highly-skilled cashier serving customers one at a time from a long line, labeled “CPU core: minimize time per customer.” Right: many ordinary cashiers, each serving one customer simultaneously from short lines, labeled “GPU cores: maximize customers served per minute.” A stopwatch icon on the left, a “customers/min” throughput gauge on the right.

A CPU core is built to finish one task as fast as possible — deep pipelines, branch prediction, large caches, all in service of low latency
A GPU core is built to keep as many tasks moving simultaneously as possible, even if each one individually is slower — high throughput
Neither is “better” in general — they’re optimized for different jobs. Session 2 puts real numbers on this comparison


~3 min. Callback to Module 0’s cashier analogy — reuse the same visual language deliberately so it reads as a continuation, not a new idea. Attach the vocabulary words “latency” and “throughput” precisely here; Module 0 introduced the picture without the terms.

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
text:
Amdahl’s Law — A First Look
Even if you accelerate 95% of a program perfectly on parallel hardware, the unaccelerated 5% caps your total speedup:
\[\text{Speedup} \leq \frac{1}{1 - 0.95} = \frac{1}{0.05} = 20\times\]

No matter how many cores (or GPU threads) you throw at the parallel 95%, the serial 5% eventually dominates the wall-clock time
This is why “just add more cores” has diminishing returns, and why which part of a problem you parallelize matters as much as how well
We derive and apply this formally in Module 3 — for now, just the intuition: serial code is a ceiling on parallel speedup


~3 min. Full derivation and the general formula (with \(p\) = parallel fraction, \(s\) = speedup of that fraction) is Module 3. Here, one concrete worked number is enough — don’t derive the general form yet.

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
text:
This Week

Lab 03 (Fri, Sep 18): Benchmark a loop vs. a vectorized NumPy call; measure the actual speedup ratio and compute GFLOP/s

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
text:
Today’s Plan

Put real numbers on “latency-optimized vs. throughput-optimized”
Three metrics that quantify the difference: FLOPS, memory bandwidth, SIMD width
When a GPU actually wins — and when it loses
Where GPUs came from (GPGPU/CUDA), and where the field is now
Checkpoint CK-03 preview, and what’s due before Lab 3


~1 min. Full 50-minute session — no quiz today. Sixteen slides at roughly 3 min each; keep moving, this is a dense but mostly-conceptual session.

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
text:
Two Design Philosophies, Defined

Latency-optimized (CPU): minimize the time to finish one task, even if that costs silicon area and power that a hundred smaller cores could have used instead
Throughput-optimized (GPU): maximize the number of tasks finished per second, even if any single task takes longer than it would on a CPU
Every architectural difference on the next few slides is a consequence of one of these two design goals


~2 min. This slide is the thesis statement for the whole session — the rest is evidence. Consider writing “latency” and “throughput” on the board and returning to these two words explicitly at the end of the session.

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
section: Anatomy of a CPU Core vs. a GPU Core
text:
Anatomy of a CPU Core vs. a GPU Core



CPU cores spend most of their transistor budget on control: predicting branches, reordering instructions, caching data — all to keep one instruction stream fast


GPU cores spend most of their transistor budget on arithmetic: many small, simple ALUs with minimal control logic each


Removing branch prediction and out-of-order execution is a deliberate trade: a GPU core is “dumber” per-core, but you get thousands of them for the same silicon



~3 min. This is the physical justification for every number on the next slide’s table. Students sometimes ask “why doesn’t NVIDIA just make GPU cores as smart as CPU cores” — the answer is area: a CPU-grade core with branch prediction and OOO execution is roughly an order of magnitude larger than a GPU core.

Neither number alone tells you which chip is faster for your problem — that depends on whether your problem can use thousands of simultaneous, independent cores (next few slides)


~3 min. Numbers are representative of a high-end 2025-era CPU (e.g. desktop/workstation-class) vs. a data-center GPU (e.g. A100/H100-class) and a Colab T4 will be noticeably smaller than the GPU column here — flag that Lab 3 onward runs on a T4, so measured numbers in lab will be well below these headline figures.

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
text:
FLOPS: Measuring Raw Compute

FLOPS = floating-point operations per second — one add or one multiply on a floating-point number counts as one FLOP
GFLOPS = \(10^9\) FLOPS, TFLOPS = \(10^{12}\) FLOPS
A “multiply-then-add” (fused multiply-add, FMA) is often counted as 2 FLOPs, since it does both operations in one hardware step
Achieved GFLOP/s for a program = (total FLOPs the program performs) ÷ (measured wall-clock time) — this is exactly what Lab 3 asks you to compute


~3 min. Worked example if time allows: a length-\(N\) dot product does \(N\) multiplies + \(N\) adds = \(2N\) FLOPs; if it runs in \(t\) seconds, achieved rate is \(2N/t\) FLOP/s. Students will reuse this exact formula in Lab 3.

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
section: Memory Bandwidth: The Other Half of the Story
text:
Memory Bandwidth: The Other Half of the Story

FLOPS tells you how fast the ALUs can compute — but they can’t compute on data that hasn’t arrived yet
Memory bandwidth = bytes per second the chip can move between memory and its compute units
Arithmetic intensity = FLOPs performed per byte of data moved — the ratio that determines whether compute or memory is your bottleneck
Low arithmetic intensity → memory-bound: ALUs sit idle waiting on data, no matter how fast they are
High arithmetic intensity → compute-bound: memory keeps up, so raw FLOPS is what limits you


~3 min. Don’t derive the roofline model here — that’s Module 4’s job, and it explicitly says so on its own slide. This is only the vocabulary preview: “arithmetic intensity,” “memory-bound,” “compute-bound.” Students will recognize these terms when Module 4 formalizes them.

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
text:
SIMD: One Instruction, Many Data



SIMD = Single Instruction, Multiple Data: one instruction, dispatched once, applied to many data elements in lock-step


CPUs have narrow SIMD units (e.g. AVX processes 8 float32s at once) as an add-on to their mainly-scalar design


GPU cores execute in wide lock-step groups by default — NVIDIA calls a group of 32 threads executing the same instruction together a warp (SIMT — Single Instruction, Multiple Threads — the GPU-specific variant; full mechanics in Module 2)


SIMD/SIMT is why “same operation on every element” (like NumPy vectorization) maps so naturally onto GPU hardware



~3 min. Deliberately foreshadow “warp” without teaching it — Module 2’s execution-model lecture (Sep 23) is where thread/warp/block/grid gets taught properly (C2.2). Here it’s just enough vocabulary to explain why SIMD-shaped problems are the GPU’s home turf.

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
text:
When Does the GPU Win?
The GPU wins when a problem has:

Many independent operations — no data dependencies between them, so they can run in any order or simultaneously
The same operation on every element — one instruction can serve millions of threads (SIMD/SIMT, previous slide)
Enough arithmetic per byte moved — high arithmetic intensity, so the ALUs aren’t left waiting on memory (previous-previous slide)


NumPy’s vectorized array operations are a preview of exactly this shape — which is why Module 0’s “why loops are slow” lesson is really a GPU-suitability lesson in disguise


~3 min. Tie explicitly back to Module 0 Session 3’s NumPy vectorization content — same underlying reason, different hardware. Students should start recognizing “is this vectorizable?” and “would this benefit from a GPU?” as close to the same question.

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
text:
When Does the GPU Lose?
The GPU loses (or the CPU wins) when:

Serial dependencies dominate — each step needs the previous step’s result, so there’s nothing to run in parallel (Amdahl’s Law from Session 1 sets the ceiling)
The problem is too small — launching thousands of GPU threads has fixed overhead; if the work doesn’t fill the device, that overhead isn’t amortized
Data transfer costs more than the speedup — moving data to and from the GPU takes time; if the computation itself is cheap, the round trip can cost more than it saves


~2 min. Students will hit all three of these failure modes empirically in labs (especially #2 and #3 — a common early-semester mistake is “my GPU code was slower,” which is almost always one of these). Naming them now gives students the vocabulary to self-diagnose later.

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
text:
From Graphics to General Purpose

GPUs were originally built to shade millions of pixels in parallel — each pixel computed by the same shader program, independent of its neighbors
Around 2006, researchers noticed: “shading a pixel” and “processing one element of a large independent array” are the same computational shape
Any “embarrassingly parallel” problem (independent, identical per-element work) could, in principle, be reframed as a graphics-shader-style workload
NVIDIA formalized this with CUDA (released 2007) — a way to write general-purpose parallel code for the GPU without pretending it’s a graphics shader


~2 min. Brief history slide — the point is the conceptual leap (fixed-function graphics chip → general-purpose parallel computer), not a detailed timeline.

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
text:
NVIDIA’s CUDA Model

The programmer writes a kernel — the code for what one thread does
The programmer specifies how many threads to launch (the grid); the hardware creates and schedules all of them
The same kernel code runs on every thread, simultaneously, each operating on a different piece of data (SIMT, from earlier this session)

# Conceptually — not real syntax yet, that's Module 2:
# "Run compute_similarity for every (query, database_item) pair — simultaneously"
sim_kernel[grid, threads](Q_gpu, D_gpu, sim_gpu)

The programmer declares the parallelism; the hardware executes it — you never write a loop that says “now do item 2”


~3 min. We are not writing CUDA syntax yet — Module 2 (starting Sep 21) teaches @cuda.jit, thread indexing, and launch configuration in full. This slide is purely the mental model: kernel = one thread’s code, grid = how many copies.

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
section: The Scale of Modern GPU Computing
text:
The Scale of Modern GPU Computing

A single high-end datacenter GPU (H100-class): on the order of 2,000 TFLOPS at reduced precision (FP16) — roughly 1,000× a high-end CPU’s FLOPS
A single training run for a large AI model can use thousands of GPUs, continuously, for weeks
Serving inference (e.g. a chatbot) to millions of users means continuous, ongoing GPU demand, not a one-time cost
This scale is why GPU programming skill is in high demand — the compute budget of modern computing runs through chips like the ones in this table


~2 min. EL-05 (energy and ethics, later in the course) reads the Strubell paper on the energy cost of training large NLP models. Plant the question here without answering it: this throughput is not free, environmentally or economically.

title: Module 1: The Case for GPUs
section: The Organizing Question of This Course
text:
The Organizing Question of This Course

Given a problem and a GPU with thousands of cores, how do you structure the code so that all of them are doing useful work simultaneously, and waiting as little as possible?


Every module this semester answers one piece of this question:

Module 2: how to launch and index threads correctly
Module 3–4: how to keep memory from being the bottleneck
Module 5: how threads cooperate when the answer isn’t purely independent per-element
Module 6+: when to use a library instead of writing the kernel yourself



~2 min. Return to this slide’s question explicitly at the start of each subsequent module — it’s the thread (pun intended) that ties the whole course together.
