title: The End of Free Lunch
text:
Today’s Plan


Why serial CPU performance stopped improving for free
Three physical walls: clock speed, power, memory
Why the industry’s answer was “more cores,” and why GPUs are the extreme end of that answer


~1 min. Pure housekeeping — say it, move on. Today’s lecture time is ~35 min after the quiz, so pacing is tighter than a normal 50-min session.

title: The End of Free Lunch
text:
20 Years of Free Performance

From roughly 1980 to 2004, CPU clock speed doubled about every 18 months (a corollary of Moore’s Law, below)
Every year, the exact same program ran faster on new hardware — with zero code changes
Developers could treat performance as someone else’s problem: just wait for next year’s chip


~2 min. Ask the room: “When did you last upgrade a device and notice your code/apps ran faster just from the hardware?” The honest answer today is: rarely, unless the workload is GPU-accelerated. That gap is the subject of this module.

title: The End of Free Lunch
text:
Moore’s Law, Precisely

“The number of transistors on an integrated circuit doubles roughly every two years, at roughly constant cost.” — Gordon Moore, 1965


Moore’s Law is about transistor count, not clock speed directly
For ~40 years, more transistors did translate into higher clock speed, because of a companion effect: Dennard scaling
Dennard scaling (1974): as transistors shrink by a factor, you can also lower their voltage by that same factor — so power density stays roughly constant even as clock speed rises
Transistor count kept doubling. Clock speed did not — Dennard scaling broke first (next slide)


~3 min. Common misconception to correct explicitly: many students conflate “Moore’s Law” with “clock speeds double every 2 years.” Moore’s Law (transistor count) is alive-ish today; the clock-speed corollary died around 2005 specifically because Dennard scaling died, not because Moore’s Law did.

title: The End of Free Lunch
text:
Clock Speed Stagnation
 

Single-core clock speed has been stuck at ~3–4 GHz for two decades
Single-thread performance still creeps up (better branch prediction, bigger caches, deeper pipelines) — but those are diminishing returns, not doubling every 18 months
Something had to replace “just run it at a higher frequency”


~3 min. Source a current chart (CPU-DB, Karl Rupp’s “42 Years of Microprocessor Trend Data” is the canonical one instructors use) before drawing this. Students are often surprised the plateau has lasted this long — it predates most of them being alive.

title: The End of Free Lunch
text: The Power Wall

title: The End of Free Lunch
text:
The Power Wall

Dynamic power draw of a chip is approximately \(P \approx C \cdot V^2 \cdot f\) (capacitance × voltage² × frequency)
Under Dennard scaling, shrinking transistors let you lower \(V\) every generation — so raising \(f\) didn’t raise power density
Around 2005 (~90 nm), \(V\) hit a floor: drop it further and transistors leak current even when “off,” wasting power and generating heat with no benefit
Without falling \(V\), raising \(f\) directly raises power density — past what air cooling (and eventually any practical cooling) can remove from a chip the size of a fingernail


~3 min. This is the physical reason behind the previous slide’s plateau. Keep the formula but don’t derive it — the takeaway is “voltage stopped shrinking, so frequency stopped rising, or the chip melts.” EL-03’s Sutter essay covers this from the software-consequences angle; this slide covers the hardware cause.

title: The End of Free Lunch
text: The Memory Wall

title: The End of Free Lunch
text:
The Memory Wall

CPU compute throughput improved dramatically for decades; DRAM latency (time to fetch one value) improved only modestly over the same period
A single memory fetch has taken roughly 100 ns for a long time — during which a modern CPU core could execute hundreds of instructions
Consequence: a core that issues one memory request and then waits idles for hundreds of cycles unless something else fills that time
CPUs hide this with large caches and speculative prefetching; GPUs hide it differently — by keeping thousands of other threads ready to run while one thread waits (Module 2)


~3 min. Term coined by Wulf & McKee (1994). This is the setup for why occupancy/warp-scheduling (Module 2) and coalesced memory access (Module 4) matter so much for GPU performance — plant the vocabulary “hiding latency” now, it recurs constantly for the rest of the course.

title: The End of Free Lunch
text:
The Industry’s Answer: More Cores

Clock speed capped by the power wall. Memory latency capped by physics. Single-core performance alone could no longer 10× every few years
The industry’s pivot (mid-2000s onward): stop making one core faster, put more cores on the chip instead
Consumer CPUs went from 1 core (pre-2005) → 2 → 4 → 8 → today’s 16–32+ core desktop chips
A GPU is the same idea taken to its logical extreme: instead of tens of powerful cores, thousands of small, simple ones


~2 min. This is the bridge sentence for the whole module: multicore CPUs and GPUs are answers to the same problem (the walls above), differing only in degree. Session 2 makes that “degree” concrete with real numbers.

title: The End of Free Lunch
text:
One Expert vs. a Crowd
 

A CPU core is built to finish one task as fast as possible — deep pipelines, branch prediction, large caches, all in service of low latency
A GPU core is built to keep as many tasks moving simultaneously as possible, even if each one individually is slower — high throughput
Neither is “better” in general — they’re optimized for different jobs. Session 2 puts real numbers on this comparison


~3 min. Callback to Module 0’s cashier analogy — reuse the same visual language deliberately so it reads as a continuation, not a new idea. Attach the vocabulary words “latency” and “throughput” precisely here; Module 0 introduced the picture without the terms.

title: The End of Free Lunch
text:
Amdahl’s Law — A First Look
Even if you accelerate 95% of a program perfectly on parallel hardware, the unaccelerated 5% caps your total speedup:
\[\text{Speedup} \leq \frac{1}{1 - 0.95} = \frac{1}{0.05} = 20\times\]

No matter how many cores (or GPU threads) you throw at the parallel 95%, the serial 5% eventually dominates the wall-clock time
This is why “just add more cores” has diminishing returns, and why which part of a problem you parallelize matters as much as how well
We derive and apply this formally in Module 3 — for now, just the intuition: serial code is a ceiling on parallel speedup


~3 min. Full derivation and the general formula (with \(p\) = parallel fraction, \(s\) = speedup of that fraction) is Module 3. Here, one concrete worked number is enough — don’t derive the general form yet.

title: The End of Free Lunch
text:
This Week

Session 2 (Wed, Sep 16): CPU vs. GPU design philosophy, with real numbers — FLOPS, memory bandwidth, SIMD
Lab 03 (Fri, Sep 18): Benchmark a loop vs. a vectorized NumPy call; measure the actual speedup ratio and compute GFLOP/s 


~1 min. Quick pointer slide, not a deep dive — just orient students to what’s next.

title: Python for Java Developers
text:
Same Logic, Different Grammar

You already know how to program: variables, loops, conditionals, functions — that thinking transfers completely
What’s different is syntax — the words and punctuation Python expects instead of Java’s
Today is a translation exercise, not a “learn programming from scratch” lecture
Goal by the end of class: read any short Python snippet and know what it does, even before you’ve memorized every keyword


~2 min. Reassure the room explicitly — many students hearing “new language” panic unnecessarily. Frame this as vocabulary, not new concepts.

title: Python for Java Developers
text:
No More Type Declarations


Java
int count = 5;
double price = 9.99;
String name = "Ada";
boolean done = false;

Python
count = 5
price = 9.99
name = "Ada"
done = False


Python infers the type from the value — you never write int, double, or String before a variable
The variable can even change type later (usually a bad idea, but Python allows it — Java does not)
Capitalization matters: Python’s True/False/None, not Java’s true/false/null


~3 min. Live-type this in a Colab cell rather than just showing it — run type(count), then reassign count = "five" and run type(count) again to make the “types are not fixed” point concrete.

title: Python for Java Developers
text:
Dynamic Typing: The Grammar-Teacher Analogy

Java is a strict grammar teacher: before you say a sentence, you must announce what part of speech every word is going to be — noun, verb, adjective — and the teacher checks you announced correctly before you’re allowed to speak
Python assumes you know what you mean, and figures out the parts of speech from context as you go
Trade-off: Java catches certain mistakes before the program ever runs (compile-time). Python only discovers a mismatch when that line actually executes (run-time) — so Python programs can fail later and more unexpectedly than Java ones
This is why Python code tends to look shorter — but it also means you need to test what you write more carefully


~3 min. This analogy is worth landing well — it explains why Python looks so sparse compared to Java without requiring any compiler-theory vocabulary the students don’t have.

title: Python for Java Developers
Python for Java Developers
Python for Java Developers
Python for Java Developers
Python for Java Developers
Python for Java Developers
text:
Lists: Java’s ArrayList, Python’s list


Java
ArrayList<Integer> nums =
    new ArrayList<>();
nums.add(10);
nums.add(20);
nums.get(0);
nums.size();

Python
nums = [10, 20]
nums.append(30)
nums[0]
len(nums)


Python’s list is built into the language — no import, no <Integer> type parameter
A single Python list can hold mixed types ([1, "two", 3.0]) — Java’s ArrayList<Integer> cannot
len(nums) is a function call, not a method — this is a common early typo (nums.len() does not exist)


~3 min. The “mixed types allowed” point is worth a live demo — it looks alarming to a Java developer at first. Note explicitly that NumPy arrays (Session 3) are not like this — they go back to Java’s “one type only” discipline, for reasons we’ll cover then.

title: Python for Java Developers
text:
List Slicing
nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

nums[1:3]     # [20, 30]   — index 1 up to (not including) index 3
nums[:2]      # [10, 20]   — from the start up to index 2
nums[3:]      # [40, 50]   — from index 3 to the end
nums[-1]      # 50         — negative index counts from the end
nums[::2]     # [10, 30, 50] — every 2nd element

Slicing has no Java equivalent — closest is manually looping and copying into a new array
The pattern [start:stop:step] — memorize this now, because NumPy array slicing (Session 3) uses exactly the same syntax


~3 min. Emphasize the last bullet strongly — this slide is deliberately positioned as direct setup for Session 3. Have students predict nums[1:-1] before revealing the answer.

title: Python for Java Developers
text:
None vs. null, and Truthiness
result = None          # Python's "no value" — like Java's null

if result:              # careful: 0, "", [], and None are all "falsy"
    print("has a value")
else:
    print("nothing here")

None is Python’s null — same idea, different capitalization and spelling
Java only treats null itself as special in an if. Python additionally treats 0, 0.0, "" (empty string), and [] (empty list) as “falsy” in an if — this has no Java parallel and causes real bugs
Rule of thumb: if you mean “is this specifically None,” write if result is None:, not just if result:


~2 min. This is a genuine gotcha, not a style note — an empty list silently behaving like “false” surprises every Java developer at least once. Worth a quick live example: if []:  print("shown"); else: print("not shown").

title: Python for Java Developers
text:
List Comprehensions: Thinking in Expressions


The loop way
squares = []
for x in range(10):
    squares.append(x ** 2)

The Pythonic way
squares = [x ** 2 for x in range(10)]


Both produce the exact same list — the second is Python’s idiomatic shorthand for “build a new list from a rule”
Read it right-to-left: “for x in range(10),” “compute x squared,” “collect into a list”
You’ll see this pattern constantly in other people’s Python code this semester — recognize it even if you don’t write it yet


~3 min. Don’t require fluency writing these yet — just reading comprehension. This slide is also a deliberate bridge: next session, NumPy will replace both versions above with x ** 2 on a whole array, no loop or comprehension at all.

title: Python for Java Developers
text:
Common Gotchas for Java Developers








Habit from Java
What happens in Python
Fix




5 / 2 expecting 2
Returns 2.5 (true division)
Use 5 // 2 for integer division


Forgetting : after if/for/def
SyntaxError
Every block header ends in :


Mixing tabs and spaces
IndentationError, sometimes silent
Let Colab auto-indent; don’t hand-fix


nums.length
AttributeError
Lists use len(nums), not .length




Keep this table — every row on it will bite someone in Lab 1


~3 min. Deliberately positioned near the end so students leave with a concrete “watch out for these” list fresh in mind before Friday’s lab.

title: Python for Java Developers
section: Why This Matters for GPU Programming
text:
Why This Matters for GPU Programming

Python’s flexibility (no type declarations, quick to write) is exactly why we prototype in it
But that same flexibility has a cost: a Python for loop is checking and re-checking types on every single iteration — work a compiled Java loop never has to do
Next session, we’ll measure that cost, and meet the tool (NumPy) that removes it — which is also the first step toward the GPU way of thinking


~2 min. This is the bridge slide into Session 3 — plant “loops are secretly expensive” as a question, don’t answer it yet. Session 3 answers it with a real analogy and (in Lab 2/CK-2) real numbers.

title: COSC 435 - Acceleration
text:
Course Description
Official catalog description:

This course will study the tools, techniques and architectures to provide hardware acceleration of software. Topics include: high-level synthesis, register transfer level descriptions and synthesis, gate and transistor level descriptions, finite state machines, systolic arrays and pipeline architectures. Both Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) and custom integrated circuit approaches will be covered. In addition to the application of Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tools, the algorithms they use will be described.

Course focus, Fall 2026:
This course introduces the architectures and programming models behind modern General-Purpose Graphics Processing Unit (GPGPU) computing. As the demand for computational throughput has outpaced what traditional single-core processors can deliver, GPUs have become the engine behind machine learning, scientific simulation, and real-time graphics. Acceleration teaches you to think and program in parallel - shifting from the “one instruction at a time” model of introductory programming to orchestrating thousands of threads working simultaneously on the same problem. The course uses Python and industry-relevant GPU frameworks (Numba CUDA, CuPy, PyTorch) throughout, delivered via Google Colab, so no prior experience with systems languages is required.

Upon completion of the course, students will be able to:

Design accelerators for algorithms as demonstrated by creating an accelerator using high-level synthesis and FPGAs.

Create an opinion on a technical subject using appropriate sources as demonstrated by researching an analysis of a classic paper on hardware architecture on electronic design automation.

title: Module 6: Cloud Computing & Microservices
section: Recap: You’ve Already Used the Cloud
text:
Recap: You’ve Already Used the Cloud
Before defining anything: you’ve already relied on a cloud provider without thinking of it that way. MongoDB Atlas, since Lab 9 — you never installed a database server, never provisioned a machine. You made an account, clicked a button, and had a running, replicated MongoDB cluster within minutes.
That’s cloud computing. Today: precise vocabulary for what you were actually doing.

Timing: 3 min. Anchor immediately in something concrete and already-experienced, rather than opening with an abstract definition.

title: Module 6: Cloud Computing & Microservices
text:
What Is Cloud Computing?
Cloud computing means renting computing resources — servers, storage, databases, machine learning services — over the internet, on demand, paying only for what you actually use.

You never own or physically touch the hardware; the provider does, somewhere in one of their data centers.
Before cloud: a startup had to buy and rack physical servers — real upfront cost, real lead time — before writing a single line of application code.
With cloud: you can start with $0, write code today, and scale to millions of users later, on the same code, just by renting more.


Timing: 5 min. The “same code, just renting more” line is worth landing explicitly — it’s Week 1’s “the code doesn’t change, only the scale does” idea, now applied to infrastructure instead of data volume.

title: Module 6: Cloud Computing & Microservices
section: The Apartment Analogy: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
text:
The Apartment Analogy: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
Cloud providers offer different amounts of “already done for you”:

IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): renting an empty apartment. Four walls, plumbing, electricity — no furniture. You install your own operating system and runtime, everything above the bare hardware.
PaaS (Platform as a Service): renting a furnished apartment. Utilities and maintenance are handled — you just move in your own belongings (your code and data). The provider manages the OS, the runtime, the scaling.
SaaS (Software as a Service): a hotel room. Everything is provided and maintained for you — you just use it. You never think about plumbing or furniture at all.

Concretely: Google Colab is PaaS-like (you write code, Google manages the runtime underneath it). MongoDB Atlas is SaaS-like (you never configure a database server at all — you just use the database).






Think about it


A startup wants to deploy a Python web app without managing servers, operating systems, or runtime environments — just write code and deploy it. Which of the three fits?




Timing: 5 min. Callout answer: PaaS — this is close to Quiz 8 Q3’s own scenario shape (Heroku/App Engine), so it’s good rehearsal without spoiling the quiz’s exact wording.

Cloud computing takes that same idea and hands the “adding machines” part to the provider: click a button (or, as Nov 30 covers, let it happen automatically) and more capacity appears, without you racking a single physical server yourself.
Same vocabulary, same idea — now something you rent, not something you build.

title: Module 6: Cloud Computing & Microservices
section: EL5 Preview: When the Cloud Breaks
text:
EL5 Preview: When the Cloud Breaks
(EL5 — assigned today, due Nov 30): read a real cloud outage post-mortem and reflect on which distributed-systems concepts explain the failure.
Recall Module 2 Session 3’s GitHub case study — a network partition lasting seconds caused an outage lasting a day. Real cloud outages follow the same pattern:

Single-region risk — many services quietly depend on the same one region; if it goes down, everything built on it goes down together.
Cascading failures — one service slows down, its queues fill up, callers time out, and the failure spreads to services that were never directly affected.
The “retry storm” — the moment a recovering service comes back online, every client that was failing retries at once, instantly overwhelming it again.


Timing: 4 min. This slide anchors EL5, it doesn’t teach new content in depth — point back to Module 2 Session 3’s GitHub incident explicitly as the model students should apply to whatever outage post-mortem they choose to read.

title: Module 6: Cloud Computing & Microservices
section: Autoscaling: Extra Cooks During the Dinner Rush
text:
Autoscaling: Extra Cooks During the Dinner Rush
Autoscaling means a cloud service automatically adds capacity when demand rises, and removes it again when demand falls — with no human deciding when.

Kitchen picture: a branch calls in extra cooks the moment a dinner rush starts, and sends them home once things quiet down — not a fixed staff sized for the busiest night of the year, sitting idle every other night.
Concretely: a web service might normally run on 2 machines, automatically scale to 20 during a traffic spike (a product launch, a viral post), then scale back down to 2 once traffic drops.
This is scaling out from Module 3 — but automatic, and elastic in both directions, scaling out and back in, based on real-time demand rather than a human’s decision.







Important


Without autoscaling, you face two bad choices: provision for peak load and pay for idle capacity almost all the time, or provision for average load and fall over during a spike. Autoscaling is the industry’s answer to not having to choose.




Timing: 4 min. Keep this brief but don’t skip it — it’s promised syllabus content for today even though it isn’t separately quiz-tested.

title: Module 6: Cloud Computing & Microservices
section: Serverless: You Never See a Machine at All
text:
Serverless: You Never See a Machine at All
Serverless computing goes one step further than renting a machine — you don’t manage a machine at all, not even a rented one.

You write a single function. The provider runs it only when triggered — an HTTP request, a file upload, a scheduled time — on infrastructure you never provision, see, or manage.
You pay only for the time your function actually runs, not for an idle server waiting for the next request.
Recall Nov 23’s Cloud-Native Data Services table: “Our Flask API → AWS Lambda + API Gateway, Cloud Run” was left unexplained on purpose. That’s exactly this — a serverless Flask deployment doesn’t run on a machine you provisioned; it runs only when a request actually arrives.







Think about it


Our classroom Flask API (Wed Dec 2) runs on one machine the whole time class is happening, whether or not anyone is hitting it. What would change, in cost and in behavior, if it ran serverless instead?




Timing: 4 min. Closes the loop on the deliberate plant from Nov 23 — say explicitly “this is the answer to the row I left unexplained last session.”

title: Module 6: Cloud Computing & Microservices
section: Bridge: One Kitchen vs. Many Kitchen Branches
text:
Bridge: One Kitchen vs. Many Kitchen Branches
Since Module 1, one running picture has covered how work gets organized: one kitchen, many cooks (a single program); many kitchen branches, coordinating over the phone (distributed machines). Today’s last topic asks the same question one level up: should your application itself be built as one kitchen doing everything, or as many specialized branches?

Timing: 3 min. Explicit bridge slide — make the “one level up” framing clear before the next two slides apply it.

title: Module 6: Cloud Computing & Microservices
text:
Monolith: One Big Kitchen
Monolith: the entire application — every function — is built and deployed as a single unit.
┌──────────────────────────────────┐
│           Monolith               │
│  ┌────────┐ ┌───────┐ ┌───────┐ │
│  │  Auth  │ │Orders │ │Payment│ │  ← all in one kitchen
│  └────────┘ └───────┘ └───────┘ │
│              Database            │
└──────────────────────────────────┘

Kitchen picture: one kitchen, one staff, cooking the auth dish, the orders dish, and the payment dish, all in the same space — deployed (opened for business) as one unit.
✅ Simple to develop and test — everything lives in one codebase, one process.
✅ Easy deployment — one thing to build, one thing to deploy.
❌ One bug anywhere can crash the entire kitchen, not just the dish it was in.
❌ Fixing a typo in the payment logic means rebuilding and redeploying the entire application — auth and orders included, even though neither changed.


Timing: 4 min. Checkpoint 8’s key distinguishing question is “can you update one part without redeploying everything” — the last bullet here is the direct answer for a monolith: no.

title: Module 6: Cloud Computing & Microservices
text:
Microservices: Separate Kitchen Branches
Microservices: each function is built and deployed as an independent service, communicating with the others the same way Module 2 taught you any two machines communicate — over REST APIs.
Client
  ↓
API Gateway
  ├── Auth Branch         (own DB, own deployment)
  ├── Order Branch        (own DB, own deployment)
  ├── Payment Branch      (own DB, own deployment)
  └── Notification Branch (own DB, own deployment)

Kitchen picture: an Auth branch, an Order branch, a Payment branch — each its own kitchen, its own staff, its own inventory — calling each other on the phone (a REST request) whenever one needs something from another.
✅ Each branch scales independently — today’s autoscaling can add capacity to just the Payment branch during a sale, without touching the others.
✅ Different teams can deploy their own branch independently — no coordinating one giant release.
❌ Every call between branches is now a network call — Module 2’s entire catalogue of failure modes (lost messages, timeouts, partial failures) applies to every one of these calls, where a monolith’s internal function calls never fail that way.
❌ Distributed tracing, service discovery, keeping data consistent across many separate databases — all genuinely new problems a monolith never had.


Timing: 5 min. The “every call is now a network call” bullet is worth dwelling on — it’s the direct payoff of Module 2 Session 1’s entire catalogue (lost/delayed/reordered messages, partial failures, the timeout problem), now shown to apply inside a single application’s own architecture, not just between two different companies’ servers.

New product, small team, fast iteration

Microservices

Microservices

Monolith (simpler transactions)









Note


Many companies start with a monolith and break it into microservices as they scale. Netflix, Uber, and Amazon all did this — it’s a normal evolution, not a sign the monolith was a mistake.




Timing: 3 min. Resist framing microservices as strictly “better” — Checkpoint 8’s own sample solution credits the monolith with real, legitimate advantages for its scenario.

Flask: Module 2’s REST Vocabulary, in Code
Everything Flask does is Module 2’s REST anatomy, written as code instead of read off the wire:







Module 2 concept
Flask’s version




A URL identifies a resource
@app.route("/users/<id>")


An HTTP verb says what to do
methods=["GET"], methods=["POST"], …


A response has a status code
return jsonify(...), 201


A JSON body
jsonify({...}) builds one for you



Flask is a lightweight Python web framework — small enough that a full REST API is often under 50 lines of code.

Timing: 4 min. Walk this table before showing any code — the goal is “you already know all of this conceptually, Flask is just the syntax,” not introducing REST as new material.

title: Module 6: Cloud Computing & Microservices
Module 6: Cloud Computing & Microservices
text:
Flask Route Patterns
# Query parameters: GET /search?q=python&limit=10
from flask import request

@app.route("/search")
def search():
    q     = request.args.get("q", "")
    limit = int(request.args.get("limit", 10))
    return jsonify({"query": q, "results": []})

# POST with a JSON body
@app.route("/users", methods=["POST"])
def create_user():
    data = request.get_json()
    name = data["name"]
    return jsonify({"created": name}), 201

request.args.get(...) reads a query parameter — the part of the URL after ?.
methods=["POST"] is Module 2’s POST verb, named explicitly — without it, this route only accepts GET by default.
request.get_json() reads the request’s JSON body — the counterpart to jsonify() on the way out.
, 201 returns HTTP status 201 (“Created”) — Module 2’s status-code vocabulary, chosen deliberately instead of the default 200.


Timing: 4 min. Point at each line and name which Module 2 concept it’s implementing — the whole point of this slide is “no new ideas, just syntax for old ones.”

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
Recap: From Hadoop to Spark
Module 3 ended with MapReduce’s biggest weakness: every job writes its intermediate results to disk, even between steps of the same pipeline. For a job that only runs once, that’s fine. For anything iterative — trying 100 variations of a machine-learning model, or chaining ten transformations together — writing to disk every single step is slow.
Apache Spark was built to fix exactly this.

Timing: 3 min. Just re-anchor: MapReduce’s map→shuffle→reduce→disk cycle from Module 3 is the thing Spark is reacting against. Don’t re-teach MapReduce, just point at the pain point.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
What Is Apache Spark?
Apache Spark is a distributed data-processing engine — the successor to Hadoop MapReduce for most large-scale data work today.

Key idea: keep intermediate data in memory across steps of a pipeline, instead of writing every step to disk the way MapReduce does.
Result: 10–100× faster for workloads that reuse the same data across multiple steps (iterative algorithms, interactive queries, multi-stage pipelines).
Written in Scala, but has full APIs in Python (PySpark — what we use), Java, R, and SQL.
Beyond the batch DataFrame work this course focuses on, Spark also has Spark SQL (write actual SQL queries against a DataFrame), Structured Streaming (process data as it arrives, not just in batches), and MLlib (distributed machine learning) — all part of the same engine, not separate tools. We only use the batch/DataFrame piece this semester.
In our classroom cluster, Spark jobs happen to read from HDFS and get scheduled by YARN, both from Module 3 — but that’s a choice about our setup, not a requirement of Spark itself. Spark can just as easily read from S3, local files, a database, or a Kafka stream; it isn’t tied to HDFS the way MapReduce, in practice, always was.


Timing: 4 min. Emphasize continuity, not replacement: HDFS and YARN don’t go away in our setup. Spark is a new way to compute, sitting on the same storage and scheduling layer already taught — but say explicitly that this is our classroom’s configuration, not a general Spark requirement (Final Q17 tests this distinction directly: Spark is not tied to HDFS). The SQL/ streaming/MLlib bullet is Quiz 5 Q9’s multi-select — keep it to one sentence each, this course never touches any of the three.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
Why Spark Improves on MapReduce
Picture a pipeline with three steps: filter, then group, then sort.

MapReduce: step 1 writes its full output to disk. Step 2 reads it back from disk, computes, writes its output to disk. Step 3 does the same. Three disk round-trips for one pipeline.
Spark: step 1’s output stays in memory. Step 2 reads it from memory, computes, keeps its result in memory. Step 3 does the same. Disk is only touched if you explicitly ask Spark to save something, or if data is too big to fit in memory.







Important


This matters most for iterative workloads — anything that reuses the same data repeatedly, like training a machine-learning model over many passes. A single MapReduce-style batch job that runs once and finishes isn’t dramatically slower in MapReduce; it’s repeated work over the same data where Spark’s in-memory model wins big.




Timing: 4 min. This is Quiz 5’s Q1 almost verbatim — spend real time here. The wrong-but- tempting answer is “Spark just has better algorithms”; the right answer is specifically about avoiding repeated disk I/O across steps.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
RDDs vs. DataFrames
Spark actually has two ways to represent distributed data. You need to know both exist, even though we will work almost entirely with the second one.









RDD (Resilient Distributed Dataset)
DataFrame




What it is
A low-level, distributed collection of arbitrary Python objects
A distributed table — named columns, with a schema


Structure
None enforced — Spark doesn’t know what’s inside
Spark knows every column’s name and type


Optimization
None — you write exactly what runs
Spark’s optimizer can rewrite your query to run faster


Feels like
A distributed Python list
A distributed spreadsheet




RDDs came first (Spark’s original data structure) and are still there underneath everything.
DataFrames were added later, and are what virtually everyone uses for tabular data today — including everything in this course, the labs, and the capstone.







Think about it


If Spark doesn’t know what’s inside an RDD, what can’t it do that it can do with a DataFrame? (Hint: think about what “optimizing a query” requires knowing about the data first.)




Timing: 5 min. This slide exists specifically because Quiz 5’s Q2 asks students to distinguish RDD from DataFrame directly — don’t let this be a one-line footnote. The answer to the callout: without column names/types, Spark can’t reorder operations, push filters down, or pick an efficient join strategy — it just has to run your code as literally written.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
Spark Architecture
┌──────────────────────────────────┐
│         Driver Program           │  ← your Python script
│  SparkContext / SparkSession     │
└──────────────┬───────────────────┘
               │ task distribution
    ┌──────────┼──────────┐
┌───▼───┐  ┌──▼────┐  ┌──▼────┐
│Exec 1 │  │Exec 2 │  │Exec 3 │  ← workers (run tasks)
└───────┘  └───────┘  └───────┘
    ↑           ↑          ↑
    └───────────┴──────────┘
         Cluster Manager
              (YARN)

Driver: coordinates the whole computation — your code runs here, and it decides what work to hand out. Plays the same role Module 3’s ApplicationMaster played for a MapReduce job: one coordinator, dispatched for this one application.
Executor: a worker process that actually runs tasks and holds a slice of the data in memory — the same role Module 3’s NodeManager-run tasks played, just for Spark tasks instead of Map/Reduce tasks.
Cluster manager: allocates machines/resources to your job — in our classroom cluster, that’s YARN, the exact same resource manager Module 3 used for MapReduce jobs. Spark doesn’t bring its own scheduler here; it asks YARN for workers, the same way a MapReduce job did.







Diagram to add later (Excalidraw / pyxcd / draw.io)


A “Driver” box at the top (drawn like a small laptop/script icon, since it’s literally “your Python code”), with a downward arrow labeled “task distribution” fanning out to three “Executor” icons (worker/gear icons, each shown holding a small stack of data-block icons to represent “holds a slice of the data in memory”). Below all three, one “Cluster Manager (YARN)” icon with upward arrows from each Executor back into it, visually matching Module 3’s YARN diagram’s ResourceManager/NodeManager icon style so students recognize it as the same underlying system. Caption: “Same YARN as Module 3 — just handing out Spark tasks instead of Map/Reduce tasks.”




Timing: 4 min. The payoff line: “you already learned what YARN does in Module 3 — Spark just hands YARN a different kind of job to schedule.” Don’t re-explain YARN from scratch.

text:
SparkSession — Your Entry Point
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

# Create (or reuse) a SparkSession
spark = SparkSession.builder \
    .appName("MyFirstSparkJob") \
    .getOrCreate()

print(spark.version)

Every PySpark program starts by creating (or reusing) exactly one SparkSession.
.getOrCreate() — if a session already exists, reuse it; otherwise, create a new one.
In our classroom setup: every %%spark notebook cell (via sparkmagic, from Lab 6) already has a spark object ready to use — you skip the SparkSession.builder step entirely in Labs 7 and 8 and the capstone. You’ll still write it by hand for Checkpoint 4, since checkpoints are graded as standalone code.


Timing: 3 min. Flag the discrepancy explicitly: checkpoints want the full SparkSession.builder... line (Quiz 5 Q3 tests this exact syntax); the labs’ %%spark cells already have spark built for you. Both are correct, in their own context — this is not a contradiction.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
Creating and Inspecting a DataFrame
data = [
    ("Alice", "Engineering", 95000),
    ("Bob",   "Marketing",   62000),
]
columns = ["name", "department", "salary"]

df = spark.createDataFrame(data, columns)

df.printSchema()   # show column names and inferred types
df.show()           # print the rows

printSchema() shows you the column names and the types Spark inferred for each.
show() prints rows to the screen — and, importantly, it’s the first thing on this slide that actually runs anything (more on why that distinction matters in a few slides).
You can also read a DataFrame straight from a file — covered in full next session.


Timing: 4 min. This mirrors Lab 7 Task 1 almost exactly — flag that connection so students recognize the lab as “the same two commands you just saw, applied to your own data.”

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
DataFrames Are Immutable
Every PySpark DataFrame, once created, never changes. Every operation returns a brand-new DataFrame — the original is always left untouched.
filtered = df.filter(df["salary"] > 70000)

# df itself is completely unchanged here — still has all rows
# filtered is a NEW DataFrame with only the matching rows






Important


This trips up almost everyone coming from pandas or spreadsheets, where you’re used to modifying data in place. In PySpark, if you don’t assign the result of an operation to a variable, the result is thrown away and nothing changes. df.filter(...) on its own line, with no =, does nothing useful.




Timing: 3 min. Quiz 5’s Q6 asks this directly (true/false, “does filter() modify df in place?”). Say the rule out loud, plainly, more than once — it’s one of the most-missed ideas in this whole module.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
Lazy Evaluation — The Core Idea
# These lines define a PLAN — nothing runs yet
filtered   = df.filter(df["salary"] > 70000)
selected   = filtered.select("name", "salary")
sorted_df  = selected.orderBy("salary", ascending=False)

# THIS triggers computation — Spark executes the whole plan at once
sorted_df.show()

Nothing above sorted_df.show() actually touches the data. Spark just records each step as part of a plan — this is called lazy evaluation.
That recorded plan has a name: a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) — a chain of steps that only ever flows forward, never loops back on itself. Each transformation you chain adds one more step to the DAG; nothing runs until an action triggers the whole thing at once.
Only when you call an action (show(), count(), …) does Spark look at the entire DAG you built, optimize it, and run it all at once.
Why bother? Because seeing the whole plan first lets Spark skip unnecessary work — for example, if you filter() then select() two columns, Spark can avoid ever reading the columns you didn’t ask for.


Timing: 5 min. Quiz 5’s Q8 tests this definition directly. The “why bother” bullet is the part students usually skip — don’t let this be just “Spark waits to run things,” make sure they leave with why waiting is useful. The DAG bullet is here specifically because Lab 7 Task 2 asks “What is a DAG in Spark? When does Spark build it and when does it execute it?” as a graded question — without this bullet, that question would be untaught.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
Transformations vs. Actions







Transformations (lazy — build the plan)
Actions (trigger execution)




filter()
show()


select()
count()


groupBy()
collect()


orderBy()
write.csv()


withColumn()
first()


join()
take(n)









Tip


If a line of PySpark code returns a DataFrame, it’s a transformation. If it returns data or writes a file, it’s an action.




Timing: 4 min. This table is the single most quiz-relevant slide in the session — Quiz 5 Q10 and Quiz 6 Q2 both hinge on this exact distinction. Have students apply the rule-of-thumb callout to two or three examples out loud before moving on.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
Recap: Transformations, Actions, Laziness
Three ideas from Monday, quickly:

Transformations (filter, select, …) build a plan but don’t run anything.
Actions (show, count, …) trigger Spark to actually execute that plan.
DataFrames are immutable — every transformation returns a new DataFrame; you must assign the result or it’s discarded.

Today: turning real files into DataFrames, and the two most common transformations you’ll use on almost every dataset — filtering rows and selecting columns.

Timing: 3 min. Fast recap only — the point is to have the vocabulary ready, not re-teach it.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
Loading Data into Spark
# CSV with a header row
df = spark.read.csv("path/to/file.csv", header=True, inferSchema=True)

# TSV (tab-separated) with no header
df = spark.read.csv("path/to/file.tsv", sep="\t", header=False, inferSchema=True)

# JSON
df = spark.read.json("path/to/file.json")

# From HDFS — always your own username, never a shared placeholder
df = spark.read.csv("hdfs:///user/<your-username>/data.csv", header=True, inferSchema=True)

header=True tells Spark the first row is column names, not data.
inferSchema=True tells Spark to scan the file and guess each column’s type (integer, string, double, …) rather than treating every value as text.
Reading hdfs://... paths works exactly the same as reading a local path — Spark doesn’t care where the file lives, as long as it can reach it.


Timing: 4 min. Quiz 5 Q4 tests this exact syntax verbatim (spark.read.csv(..., header=True, inferSchema=True)) — make sure students see and can reproduce it, not just recognize it.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
A Word on Schemas

Without inferSchema=True, Spark treats every column as a string — even columns that are clearly numbers. Filtering df["salary"] > 70000 on a string column silently does the wrong thing (string comparison, not numeric).
inferSchema=True costs a little extra time (Spark has to scan the file first), but for anything you’ll filter or aggregate numerically, it’s worth it.
df.printSchema() is your first move on any new dataset — confirm the types are what you expect before writing a single transformation.







Think about it


You load a CSV and printSchema() shows a price column typed as string, not double. What’s the most likely cause — and what’s the first thing you’d check in the raw file?




Timing: 3 min. The intended answer to the callout: either inferSchema was left off, or the column has some non-numeric values mixed in (e.g. "N/A") that forced Spark to fall back to string for the whole column.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
Filtering Rows
from pyspark.sql.functions import col

# Filter rows — both forms below are equivalent
high_earners = df.filter(df["salary"] > 70000)
high_earners = df.filter(col("salary") > 70000)

# You can also pass a filter as a plain SQL-style string
high_earners = df.filter("salary > 70000")

# .where() is just another name for the same thing
high_earners = df.where(df["salary"] > 70000)

df["salary"] and col("salary") are two ways of referring to the same column — use whichever reads more clearly in context.
filter() and where() are exact synonyms — pick one and be consistent.
Remember: this returns a new DataFrame. high_earners is new; df still has every row.


Timing: 4 min. Quiz 6 Q10 lists several of these forms as “select all that apply” — students need to recognize all of them as valid, not just the one they memorize.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
Selecting and Renaming Columns
# Select specific columns
result = df.select("name", "department", "salary")

# Add a new computed column
df = df.withColumn("salary_k", col("salary") / 1000)

# Rename a column
df = df.withColumnRenamed("salary", "annual_salary")

select() keeps only the columns you name, in the order you name them, dropping the rest.
withColumn(name, expression) adds a new column computed from existing ones — or overwrites an existing column if you reuse its name.
withColumnRenamed(old, new) changes a column’s name without touching its values.


Timing: 4 min. Quiz 5 Q7 tests select() directly. Point out the parallel with the earlier filter-forms slide: these are all just “transformation in, new DataFrame out,” same pattern every time.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
Adding a Computed Column
from pyspark.sql.functions import col

# Wrong — this is pandas syntax, and it doesn't work in Spark
df["new_col"] = df["col1"] * 2

# Right — Spark syntax
df = df.withColumn("new_col", col("col1") * 2)
The pandas-style assignment on the first line above doesn’t raise an error that’s obviously about this mistake — it just fails, because PySpark DataFrames don’t support item assignment the way pandas DataFrames do. withColumn is the only correct way to add or replace a column.

Timing: 3 min. This is worth its own slide (not folded into “common mistakes”) because it’s the single most common first bug students hit in Lab 7 — the error message is unhelpful, so seeing the correct pattern before hitting the bug saves real debugging time.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
Avoiding Common PySpark Mistakes
# ❌ Wrong — using a Python list comprehension on a Spark DataFrame
result = [row for row in df if row["salary"] > 70000]  # doesn't use Spark at all

# ✅ Right — use Spark's own filter
result = df.filter(col("salary") > 70000)

# ❌ Wrong — forgetting that filter() doesn't modify df in place
df.filter(col("salary") > 70000)   # result thrown away — df is unchanged
high_earners = df.filter(col("salary") > 70000)  # correct — result is captured

A Python for loop over a DataFrame technically works, but it pulls everything to a single machine and processes it one row at a time in plain Python — throwing away everything Spark is for.
The second mistake is the immutability rule from Session 1, showing up again in real code — if your DataFrame “isn’t changing,” check whether you forgot to assign the result.


Timing: 5 min. Both of these are genuinely common — if time is short, prioritize the second one, since it’s the more frequent real bug in student code across every lab this module.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
Worked Example: Filter → Select
Given a DataFrame employees with columns name, department, salary:
# Goal: names and salaries of everyone in Marketing earning over $60,000

marketing_high_earners = employees \
    .filter(col("department") == "Marketing") \
    .filter(col("salary") > 60000) \
    .select("name", "salary")

marketing_high_earners.show()

Multiple .filter() calls chain naturally — each one narrows the DataFrame further.
Order between the two filters here doesn’t change the result, but select() must come after both filters — once you select() away a column, you can no longer filter on it.


Timing: 4 min. This example deliberately uses a different scenario from Checkpoint 4’s own movies.csv example (below) so it doesn’t spoil the checkpoint — but it’s the exact same filter→select shape students are about to be graded on.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
section: Recap + Why Today Matters for Lab 8
text:
Recap + Why Today Matters for Lab 8
So far: create/load a DataFrame, filter rows, select columns. Today adds the two operations that turn “look at some rows” into “answer an actual analytical question”: grouping data together and combining two datasets.
This is also exactly what Friday’s Lab 8 needs — real MovieLens rating data, joined with movie titles, grouped by movie, to find the highest-rated films. Everything today is in direct service of that lab.

Timing: 3 min. Say the Lab 8 connection explicitly and early — it gives today’s content an obvious “why,” which matters since this is the last lecture day before that lab.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
GroupBy and Aggregation
from pyspark.sql.functions import avg, count, round as spark_round, desc

# Average salary and headcount by department
df.groupBy("department") \
  .agg(
      spark_round(avg("salary"), 2).alias("avg_salary"),
      count("name").alias("num_employees")
  ) \
  .orderBy(desc("avg_salary")) \
  .show()

groupBy("column") — a transformation; it doesn’t compute anything on its own, it just says “gather rows into groups by this column’s value.”
.agg(...) — applies one or more aggregation functions (avg, count, sum, …) to each group, producing one output row per group.
.alias("name") — renames the resulting column to something readable.


Timing: 4 min. Quiz 6 Q1 and Q5 both test reading/predicting groupBy().agg() / groupBy().sum() output directly — walk through what the output shape looks like (one row per distinct group value), not just the syntax.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
Aggregation Functions Reference
from pyspark.sql.functions import (
    avg, count, sum as spark_sum, min, max, countDistinct
)

df.groupBy("category").agg(
    count("*").alias("total_rows"),
    avg("price").alias("avg_price"),
    spark_sum("revenue").alias("total_revenue"),
    min("price").alias("cheapest"),
    max("price").alias("most_expensive")
)







Function
What it computes




count()
Number of rows (per group, or count("*") for all rows)


avg()
Mean of a numeric column


sum()
Total of a numeric column — note the as spark_sum import alias, since sum is also a Python built-in


min() / max()
Smallest / largest value


countDistinct()
Number of unique values




Timing: 3 min. The sum as spark_sum import quirk is worth calling out explicitly — students who skip it and just write sum(...) get confusing errors from Python’s built-in sum() shadowing the Spark one.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
orderBy and the Top-N Pattern
# The "top N by some metric" pattern — you'll use this constantly
top_5 = df.groupBy("department") \
          .agg(spark_round(avg("salary"), 2).alias("avg_salary")) \
          .orderBy("avg_salary", ascending=False) \
          .limit(5)

top_5.show()

orderBy(column, ascending=False) sorts descending; ascending=True (or omitting it) sorts ascending.
.limit(n) keeps only the first n rows after sorting.
.show(n) — a shortcut that sorts-then-limits-then-prints in one call, when you don’t need the limited DataFrame for anything else afterward.







Tip


This exact pattern — groupBy → agg → orderBy → limit/show(n) — is precisely what Checkpoint 5 asks you to do, and it’s the core of Lab 8’s “top 10 highest-rated movies” task.




Timing: 4 min. Quiz 6 Q4 tests orderBy(..., ascending=False) syntax directly. Flag the Checkpoint 5 connection out loud — this slide is deliberately the most directly test-relevant one in the session.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
section: Actions, Revisited: The Risk of collect()
text:
Actions, Revisited: The Risk of collect()
Session 1 introduced actions as “the things that trigger execution.” One of them deserves a warning of its own.
# ⚠️ Dangerous on a large DataFrame
all_rows = df.collect()   # pulls EVERY row to the driver machine, as a Python list

# ✅ Safer — limit first
sample = df.limit(100).collect()

collect() brings all matching rows back to the driver program, as ordinary Python objects — not distributed anymore.
If the DataFrame is large, this can crash the driver — the driver has one machine’s worth of memory, not the whole cluster’s.
count() and show(n) don’t have this problem: count() returns a single number, and show(n) only ever prints n rows without collecting the rest.


Timing: 5 min. Quiz 6 Q7 tests this risk directly (“main risk of collect() on a very large DataFrame”) — this is a real, industry-relevant footgun, not a trivia fact, so it’s worth the full 5 minutes.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
Writing DataFrame Output
# Write as CSV — creates a folder, not a single file
df.write.csv("output/path", header=True, mode="overwrite")

# Write as JSON
df.write.json("output/path", mode="overwrite")

df.write.csv(...) is an action — like show() or count(), it triggers Spark to execute the full pending plan, this time saving the result to storage instead of printing it.
mode="overwrite" replaces existing data at that path; mode="error" (the default) fails if the path already exists, to prevent accidentally destroying previous output.
The capstone’s spark_job.py uses this same write pattern — except writing to MongoDB instead of a CSV folder, which Module 5 covers.


Timing: 3 min. Quiz 6 Q8 and Q9 both test that write.csv() is an action, not a transformation — reinforce that classification explicitly, since “write” sounds like it should just be setup, not execution.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
text:
Joins in PySpark
# Inner join: only rows with matching keys in both DataFrames
result = ratings.join(movies, on="movieId")

# Left join: all rows from the left DataFrame, matched rows (or nulls) from the right
result = ratings.join(movies, on="movieId", how="left")

# Joining on differently-named columns
result = df1.join(df2, df1["user_id"] == df2["id"])

A join combines two DataFrames into one, matching rows where a key column agrees.
Inner join (the default): keep only rows that have a match in both DataFrames — rows with no match on either side are dropped.
Left join: keep every row from the left DataFrame; unmatched rows get null for the right DataFrame’s columns instead of being dropped.







Think about it


ratings has a movieId for every rating. movies has a movieId and title for every film. If you inner-join them, could you ever end up with fewer rows than ratings had originally? What would that mean about the data?




Timing: 5 min. The callout’s answer: yes — if some movieId in ratings has no matching row in movies (a deleted or mislabeled film), the inner join silently drops those ratings. This is exactly the kind of thing Lab 8’s Task 2 depends on getting right.

title: Module 4: Apache Spark & PySpark
section: Worked Example: A Full Multi-Step Query
text:
Worked Example: A Full Multi-Step Query
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, avg, count, round as spark_round, desc

top_movies = ratings \
    .groupBy("movieId") \
    .agg(spark_round(avg("rating"), 2).alias("avg_rating"),
         count("rating").alias("num_ratings")) \
    .filter(col("num_ratings") >= 50) \
    .join(movies, on="movieId") \
    .select("title", "avg_rating", "num_ratings") \
    .orderBy(desc("avg_rating"))

top_movies.show(10, truncate=False)
Reading this top to bottom: group ratings by film, compute each film’s average and count, keep only films with enough ratings to be meaningful, join in the title, keep just the columns we want, sort by rating, show the top 10.

Timing: 4 min. This is deliberately close to Lab 8 Task 2’s actual solution shape — walk through it step by step rather than all at once, since chaining six operations together is a lot to take in as a single block the first time.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Recap: One Kitchen, Many Kitchens
Module 1 ended on this picture: parallel = one kitchen, many cooks sharing the same counters. Distributed = many separate kitchens, coordinating over the phone, sharing nothing directly.
Module 2 is entirely about that second picture — and about one hard truth: the phone line between kitchens is not reliable.

Each kitchen (a node) has its own memory, its own state, its own clock on the wall.
The only way one kitchen learns anything about another is by sending a message — a phone call, a courier — across a network that can be slow, or drop the call, or deliver things out of order.
Everything in this session is a consequence of that one fact.


Timing: 3 min. Just re-anchor the picture from Module 1’s last slide — don’t re-derive it. This slide’s whole job is continuity.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
What Is a Distributed System?
A distributed system is multiple independent computers that communicate over a network and present themselves to a user as a single, coherent system.

Google Search — your query is answered by coordinating across thousands of machines, but it looks like one search box to you.
Netflix — video encoding, recommendations, billing, and streaming all run on physically separate machines, often in different countries, working together to serve one app.
Your bank’s ATM network — every ATM is a separate machine, but they all need to agree on your account balance.







Think about it


Name one app or service you used this morning that you’d guess is a distributed system. What tipped you off — was it the scale, or something about how it behaved?




Timing: 4 min. Let 2–3 students answer the callout question out loud before moving on — email, maps, any app with a login are all fair answers, and hearing several examples cements the definition better than the definition alone.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Why Distribute?
Three genuine reasons, not just “because it’s trendy”:

Scale — one machine has a ceiling (recall Module 1, Session 1: one machine can’t hold 80 billion rows). A distributed system grows by adding more machines, not by buying an impossibly bigger one.
Availability — if one server goes down, others can keep serving requests. A single machine has no backup; if it fails, the whole service fails with it.
Geography — serving a user in Tokyo from a datacenter in Tokyo is faster than serving them from Virginia. Distributing lets you put copies of your system physically close to your users.


Timing: 4 min. Keep this brisk and positive — it’s the sales pitch. The very next slide is the catch, and the contrast lands better if this slide doesn’t undercut itself early.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
The Catch
Every benefit on the last slide comes at a cost: you now have more than one machine that has to agree with itself.

Networks are unreliable — messages get lost, delayed, or corrupted.
Machines fail independently — one kitchen can go dark while the others keep cooking.
Clocks drift — there is no single, shared notion of “now” across separate machines.







Important


None of this is a bug you can fix once. It’s a permanent property of having more than one computer. The rest of this module — CAP, replication, consistency — is the industry’s answer to “given that these problems never fully go away, how do we build systems that are still useful?”




Timing: 3 min. This is a framing slide — its only job is to set up the next four slides as elaborations of these three bullets, in order.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: Messages Get Lost, Delayed, or Reordered
text:
Messages Get Lost, Delayed, or Reordered
Picture one kitchen calling another to relay three orders, one after another. On a single machine, “one after another” is guaranteed. Across a network, it is not.

A message can be lost entirely — the call drops, nobody at either end knows for sure it happened.
A message can be delayed — it arrives seconds, or minutes, later than sent, for reasons neither side controls.
Messages can arrive out of order — the second order can reach the kitchen before the first one, even though they were sent in sequence.







Diagram to add later (Excalidraw / pyxcd / draw.io)


Two vertical timelines side by side, “Kitchen A” (sender) on the left and “Kitchen B” (receiver) on the right, time flowing downward. Draw three arrows from A to B labeled “Order 1,” “Order 2,” “Order 3” leaving A top-to-bottom in that order, but arriving at B in a scrambled order (e.g., Order 2 arrives first, then Order 1, then Order 3 — draw the arrows crossing each other). Caption: “Sent in order. Arrived out of order.”









Think about it


If Kitchen A sends “start Order 1” and then “cancel Order 1” a second later, and Kitchen B receives them in the wrong order, what goes wrong? What would you need to add to the messages themselves to prevent it?




Timing: 5 min. Let students actually attempt an answer to the callout before revealing that the usual fix is attaching a sequence number or timestamp to each message — don’t give it away immediately, the point is to let them discover why ordering info has to travel with the message.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Partial Failures

On a single machine, if the CPU fails, everything fails together — one clean, total failure.
In a distributed system, some machines can fail while others keep running perfectly. The system is never simply “up” or “down” — it can be up for some users and down for others, at the same instant.
This asymmetry is what makes distributed systems fundamentally harder to reason about than single-machine programs: you can no longer assume “the program” is in one consistent state.







Think about it


Three of a bank’s ten ATMs go offline for an hour. Is the ATM network “working” or “broken”? Who gets to decide — the bank, or each individual customer trying to use it?




Timing: 4 min. There’s no clean right answer to the callout — that’s the point. “Working for some, broken for others” is a genuinely uncomfortable middle ground that single-machine thinking doesn’t prepare you for.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: The Timeout Problem: Dead or Just Slow?
text:
The Timeout Problem: Dead or Just Slow?
Here is the single hardest consequence of network unreliability: from the outside, a crashed node and a slow node look identical.

Kitchen A calls Kitchen B and gets no answer. Is Kitchen B’s phone line down? Is the kitchen on fire? Or is Kitchen B just extremely busy and will answer in ten more seconds?
Kitchen A cannot tell the difference. All it knows is: no response yet.
The only tool available is a timeout — waiting some fixed amount of time, then assuming failure. But there’s no “correct” amount of time to wait: too short, and you declare a merely-slow node dead; too long, and you waste time waiting on a node that’s truly gone.







Think about it


You’re designing the timeout for a payment system. What happens if you set it too short? What happens if you set it too long? Which mistake would you rather make, and why?




Timing: 5 min. This is a genuinely famous, unsolved-in-general problem in distributed systems — resist the urge to present a “correct” timeout value, because there isn’t one; the tradeoff itself is the content.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
No Global Clock
Every kitchen has a wall clock. None of them are perfectly synchronized — each one drifts a little, faster or slower, for entirely mundane reasons (temperature, manufacturing tolerance, when it was last set).

On a single machine, “what time is it” has one unambiguous answer, from one clock.
Across machines, each one has its own clock, and they disagree — usually by milliseconds, but disagree nonetheless. This is called clock drift.
Worse: even the rate at which each clock runs is slightly different, so the disagreement keeps changing over time, not staying fixed.







Important


This means you cannot simply timestamp two events on two different machines and trust the timestamps to tell you which one happened first. A “later” timestamp might actually describe an earlier event, if that machine’s clock is running fast.




Timing: 5 min. This is likely the most surprising idea in the session for students — most have never had reason to doubt that “5:00:03pm” means the same instant everywhere. Give it room; don’t rush past the callout.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Ordering Without a Shared Clock
If you can’t trust timestamps to order events, how do you know which of two things happened first?

The puzzle: Kitchen A and Kitchen B both claim they received the same customer’s order “first.” Neither trusts the other’s wall clock. How do you settle it?
A partial answer: instead of asking “what time did this happen,” ask “what did this event depend on knowing about?” If Kitchen B’s order explicitly referenced information from Kitchen A’s order (e.g., “adding to the order Kitchen A just confirmed”), then A’s event must have happened first — regardless of what either clock says.
This idea — ordering by cause-and-effect instead of by clock — is called a logical clock, and it’s a real, used solution to exactly this problem. We won’t build one in this course, but the puzzle itself is worth sitting with.







Think about it


Two students submit an assignment through two different servers, one second apart by each server’s own clock — but the servers’ clocks are known to disagree by up to five seconds. Can you say for certain who submitted first? What evidence would settle it?




Timing: 5 min. Keep the logical-clocks mention brief and conceptual — the goal is “this is a real, solvable problem with real solutions,” not to teach vector clocks in a 50-minute session. The callout question is the actual payload of this slide.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: Four Ways a Node Can Fail
text:
Four Ways a Node Can Fail
Not all failures look the same. It’s worth naming the shapes:








Failure type
What it looks like
Kitchen picture




Crash
The node stops entirely — cleanest and easiest to detect (eventually)
The kitchen goes completely dark, no lights, no phone


Omission
The node is alive but drops some messages — receives but doesn’t respond, or vice versa
The phone rings but nobody picks up some of the time


Timing
The node responds, but too slowly to be useful
The kitchen answers the order an hour after it was needed


Byzantine
The node responds with incorrect data — hardware fault, corruption, or a malicious actor
The kitchen confirms an order it never actually received



Most real systems are designed to tolerate crash and omission failures. Byzantine failures — where a node actively lies — are far harder to defend against, and are mostly a concern in specialized settings (e.g., systems that must tolerate malicious participants).

Timing: 5 min. Byzantine failures are the one row worth pausing on — ask “why would this be so much harder to detect than a crash?” A crashed node is silent; a Byzantine node looks completely normal while being wrong, which is what makes it dangerous.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
The Fallacies of Distributed Computing
In the 1990s, engineers at Sun Microsystems (Peter Deutsch and colleagues) wrote down eight assumptions that programmers new to distributed systems make — and every one of them is false:

The network is reliable
Latency is zero
Bandwidth is infinite
The network is secure
Topology doesn’t change
There is one administrator
Transport cost is zero
The network is homogeneous







Think about it


Pick one of the eight. Describe a concrete way a program would break if a developer believed it was true. (Fallacy 2 — zero latency — is a good one to start with: what breaks if your code assumes a network call returns instantly?)




Timing: 4 min. You don’t need to cover all eight in equal depth — 1 (reliability) and 2 (zero latency) are the two most directly relevant to everything else in this session, so weight discussion toward those if time is short.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: Bridge: These Problems Don’t Go Away
text:
Bridge: These Problems Don’t Go Away
Everything in this session — lost messages, partial failures, the timeout problem, clock drift — is permanent. No clever engineering makes any of it disappear.
What engineering can do is make explicit, principled choices about which problems to tolerate and how. Next session: the most famous framework for making exactly that choice — the CAP theorem.

Timing: 3 min. End on this forward-reference. Don’t preview CAP’s content, just the fact that it’s coming and why it matters given everything just covered.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: Recap: Last Time We Broke Everything
text:
Recap: Last Time We Broke Everything
Session 1’s punchline: networks are unreliable, nodes fail independently, and there’s no shared clock. None of that is fixable.
Given all of that is permanently true, a real system still has to make some promise to its users. The CAP theorem is a precise statement about exactly which promises you can make at the same time — and which you can’t.

Timing: 3 min. Brief bridge — the whole session is really “here’s the formal shape of the tradeoff Session 1 kept gesturing at.”

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: Three Things You’d Want From Any System
text:
Three Things You’d Want From Any System
Before the acronym, the plain-language wants:

“Give me correct, up-to-date data.” — you don’t want a system that tells you your bank balance is $500 when it’s actually $0.
“Always give me an answer.” — you don’t want a system that just hangs, refusing to respond at all.
“Keep working even when part of the network breaks.” — you don’t want the whole system to go down just because two datacenters temporarily can’t talk to each other.







Think about it


Before you see the formal theorem: do you think a system could realistically promise all three of these, all the time? What would have to be true for that to work?




Timing: 4 min. Let students guess. Most will say “why not?” — that’s exactly the intuition the theorem is going to correct.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Consistency, Defined Precisely
Consistency (in CAP): every read returns the most recent successfully written value — or an error. No client ever sees stale or conflicting data.

Picture every kitchen branch sharing one single, authoritative order book. The instant one branch writes an update, every other branch reading that book sees the update too — instantly, with no lag.
This is a strong guarantee. It is not “eventually correct” — it is “correct right now, every single time you look.”


Timing: 4 min. Emphasize “or an error” — a consistent system is allowed to refuse to answer rather than answer with stale data; that detail is exactly what makes consistency-favoring systems (two slides ahead) make sense.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Availability, Defined Precisely
Availability (in CAP): every request to a working node receives a response — the system never simply times out or refuses. That response is not guaranteed to reflect the most recent write.

Picture every kitchen branch always answering the phone and giving some answer to “what’s in my order” — even if that branch hasn’t heard about a change another branch just made.
This is a weaker promise than it sounds: “always answers” is not the same as “always answers correctly.” An available system can be wrong and still be available, as long as it responds.







Important


This precise wording matters for the quiz: Availability means a response happens, not that the response is up to date. Confusing “available” with “correct” is the single most common mistake with this definition.




Timing: 4 min. The callout is worth reading verbatim — this exact confusion (available = correct) is the wrong answer on the quiz’s Availability question.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Partition Tolerance, Defined Precisely
Partition tolerance: the system continues to operate even when the network splits it into groups that cannot communicate with each other.

A network partition is what happens when the phone lines between two groups of kitchen branches go dead — branches within a group can still talk to each other, but the two groups are cut off from one another.
“Tolerating” a partition doesn’t mean the partition doesn’t happen — it means the system keeps doing something useful on both sides of the split, rather than simply freezing entirely.







Diagram to add later (Excalidraw / pyxcd / draw.io)


Two clusters of 2–3 kitchen-branch icons each, with a jagged lightning-bolt break drawn across a dashed line separating the two clusters, labeled “Network Partition.” Within each cluster, branches are still connected to each other by solid lines (they can talk internally); no lines cross the break. Caption: “Both sides are still alive. Neither side can hear the other.”




Timing: 4 min. Get the diagram description across verbally even without the drawn version yet — “two groups, each internally fine, cut off from each other” is the exact picture the CAP theorem’s “P” is about.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: The Theorem: Pick Two, Not Three
text:
The Theorem: Pick Two, Not Three
The CAP theorem: when a network partition occurs, a distributed system must choose between Consistency and Availability. It cannot have both, at the same time, during the partition.







Consistency
Every read gets the latest write, or an error


Availability
Every request gets a response


Partition tolerance
The system keeps working despite a network split









Important


Why can’t you have all three? During a partition, one side of the split cannot reach the other. If it wants to stay available (answer requests), it must answer using only what it locally knows — which might be stale, violating consistency. If it wants to stay consistent, it must refuse to answer until it can confirm it has the latest data — violating availability. There is no third option once the partition has actually happened.




Timing: 5 min. Walk the callout’s logic slowly, out loud — this is the actual proof sketch of the theorem in plain language, and it’s worth more time than the table itself.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Why “CA” Isn’t Really an Option
The theorem is often summarized as “pick two of three” — implying CA (Consistency + Availability, no Partition tolerance) is a valid third choice. In practice, it mostly isn’t.

Choosing “no partition tolerance” means promising the network will never split. At internet scale — many machines, many datacenters, the public internet in between — that promise will be broken eventually.
When it is, a CA system has no principled answer: it wasn’t designed to handle the partition at all.
In practice, you choose to favor consistency or favor availability — the real design decision is what happens during a partition, not whether you can avoid partitions altogether.







Think about it


Can you think of any real system, at any scale, where you’d be confident a network partition will never happen? What would have to be true about it?




Timing: 5 min. This directly matches Quiz 2’s true/false question on CA systems — make sure “networks partition eventually, at scale” is stated as plainly as it is here.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Worked Scenario: A Partition Happens
A distributed order-tracking system has two datacenters, East and West, normally kept in sync. The network between them just went down — a partition.
A customer in the East datacenter’s region asks: “What’s the status of my order?”

Option 1 (favor Consistency): East checks whether it can confirm its data matches West’s latest state. It can’t — West is unreachable. East returns an error: “Unable to confirm latest status, try again later.”
Option 2 (favor Availability): East answers immediately with whatever it has locally — which might be a minute out of date if West processed an update East hasn’t heard about yet.







Think about it


Which option would you choose if this were a hospital’s patient-monitoring system? Which would you choose for a social media “like” counter? What’s actually different about these two cases?




Timing: 6 min. This is the session’s centerpiece — let students actually argue both sides before revealing that “it depends on the cost of being wrong,” which is exactly what the next three slides formalize.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: Consistency-Favoring Systems: When in Doubt, Refuse to Answer
text:
Consistency-Favoring Systems: When in Doubt, Refuse to Answer
Consistency-favoring systems sacrifice availability during a partition — they’d rather give no answer than a possibly-wrong one.

Traditional relational databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, in their typical single-primary configurations)
HBase, ZooKeeper
Anywhere being wrong is worse than being unavailable — financial transactions, inventory counts that must never oversell, coordination systems other services depend on for correctness


Timing: 4 min. Tie directly back to the hospital half of the previous slide’s callout — “refuse to answer” is the right instinct exactly when a wrong answer could cause real harm.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: Availability-Favoring Systems: When in Doubt, Answer Anyway
text:
Availability-Favoring Systems: When in Doubt, Answer Anyway
Availability-favoring systems sacrifice strict consistency during a partition — they’d rather give a possibly-stale answer than no answer at all.

Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB
DNS — described further in Session 4
Anywhere being unavailable is worse than being briefly out of date — a shopping cart, a social media feed, a “likes” counter


Timing: 4 min. Tie back to the social-media half of the previous slide’s callout — nobody is harmed if a like count is off by a few for a minute, but a shopping cart that refuses to load loses the sale outright.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Choosing Consistency vs. Availability
There is no universally “correct” choice — it depends entirely on which failure mode costs you more.









Scenario
Cost of stale data
Cost of no answer
Likely choice




Bank balance
High — could overdraw an account
Moderate — customer waits
Consistency-favoring


Shopping cart
Low — item count off by one, briefly
High — lost sale
Availability-favoring


Airline seat booking
High — double-booked seat
Moderate — customer retries
Consistency-favoring


Social media like count
Very low — nobody notices
Low-moderate — feels broken
Availability-favoring









Think about it


Pick a system you use often. Would you guess it favors consistency or availability — and what evidence from how it behaves when things go wrong would tell you which one it actually is?




Timing: 4 min. Encourage genuinely varied answers to the callout — the point isn’t a single correct system to name, it’s the reasoning process of inferring a design choice from observed behavior.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: Wrap: Bridge to the Case Study
text:
Wrap: Bridge to the Case Study
You now have the vocabulary to analyze a real distributed system failure precisely: was it a Consistency problem, an Availability problem, or the moment a partition forced a choice between them?
Friday: we apply exactly this to a real, documented outage.

Timing: 3 min. Close with the forward-reference. No new content — just make sure the consistency-favoring/availability-favoring vocabulary feels ready to use before Friday.
