Instructor note: the case study below is a real, publicly documented incident (GitHub’s database infrastructure, October 2018), summarized here for teaching purposes with approximate figures. Before presenting, pull up GitHub’s own public incident-analysis blog post to confirm exact numbers and, ideally, project it live during the “setting the scene” slide — reading from the primary source adds credibility that a paraphrase can’t.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Framing: No New Concepts Today
Today, no new theory — we take everything from Sessions 1 and 2 (partial failure, network partitions, CAP, the timeout problem) and apply it to something that actually happened to a real company, on real infrastructure.
Your job for the next 45 minutes: think like the engineers who had to make these decisions in real time, without knowing the ending in advance.

Timing: 2 min. Set the tone: this is discussion, not lecture. Resist the urge to over-explain before the class has had a chance to guess.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
The Incident: Setting the Scene
In October 2018, GitHub — a service used by millions of developers daily — experienced a major outage affecting the accuracy and availability of data for roughly 24 hours.

GitHub’s database infrastructure spans multiple physical datacenters on the US East and West coasts, kept in sync so that any datacenter can serve requests with up-to-date data.
The trigger was small: a routine piece of network maintenance caused a brief network partition — on the order of tens of seconds — between two of their East Coast facilities.
A partition lasting under a minute ended up causing a day-long incident. That gap between cause and consequence is exactly what today is about.


Timing: 4 min. Don’t reveal the split-brain mechanism yet — the whole point of the next few slides is to have students reason toward it themselves.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: The Trigger: A Brief Network Partition
text:
The Trigger: A Brief Network Partition
For those tens of seconds, part of GitHub’s database cluster on the East Coast could not communicate with the rest of the cluster.

GitHub’s database system is designed with automatic failover: if the primary database (the one accepting writes) becomes unreachable, the system can automatically promote a different copy to become the new primary.
That’s a reasonable design — it’s meant to preserve availability during exactly this kind of network hiccup.
But automatic failover during a partition is precisely the scenario Session 2 warned about: both sides of a partition might independently believe they are now in charge.


Timing: 4 min. Let this slide’s last line sit — it’s a direct setup for the next discussion prompt.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Discussion: Predict What Should Happen






Think about it — discuss in pairs (2 min), then share


Given everything from Session 2: if a network partition briefly separates a database’s primary copy from the rest of the cluster, and the rest of the cluster automatically promotes a new primary to keep serving requests — what happens when the partition heals a few seconds later and both copies think they’re the real primary?



Write down your prediction before the next slide reveals what actually happened.

Timing: 5 min including discussion. Circulate and listen for the phrase “which one is right” or “conflicting data” — that’s the answer the class needs to arrive at collectively before the reveal.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
What Actually Happened: Split-Brain
This exact scenario is called split-brain: two nodes, each convinced it is the sole authority, both accepting writes independently.

During those tens of seconds, a small number of writes were accepted by both the original primary and the newly promoted one — each unaware of the other’s writes.
When the partition healed, GitHub’s systems had two divergent versions of recent data, and no automatic way to know which write in each conflicting pair was the “real” one.
This is Session 1’s “no global clock, no reliable ordering” problem, made concrete: there was no trustworthy way to say which of two conflicting writes happened first.







Diagram to add later (Excalidraw / pyxcd / draw.io)


Two database-cylinder icons labeled “Original Primary” and “Newly Promoted Primary,” side by side with a jagged break between them (reuse the partition-break style from Session 2’s diagram). Under each cylinder, draw a small stack of write-icons flowing in — different writes on each side — to show both accepting writes independently during the split. Below, a merge arrow pointing from both cylinders down into one box labeled “Reconciliation (~24 hours)” with a question mark on the two divergent write-stacks feeding into it. Caption: “Both sides kept working. That’s the problem.”




Timing: 5 min. If a group’s earlier prediction named “conflicting data” or similar, credit it explicitly before revealing this slide’s framing — it reinforces that the reasoning, not just the fact, is the point.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: Discussion: Consistency Problem, Availability Problem, or Both?
text:
Discussion: Consistency Problem, Availability Problem, or Both?






Think about it — discuss in pairs (3 min), then share


Using Session 2’s precise definitions: was the root cause of this incident a Consistency failure, an Availability failure, or something else entirely? (Hint: was the system actually unavailable during those tens of seconds — or did trying too hard to stay available cause the real damage?)




Timing: 6 min including discussion. The intended insight: the partition itself briefly threatened availability, but the automatic-failover mechanism’s attempt to preserve availability is what created the consistency violation. It’s a case where optimizing for one side of CAP directly caused the failure on the other side — a subtler lesson than “pick consistency or availability” makes it sound.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
The Recovery: Choosing Consistency
Once GitHub discovered the divergent data, they faced the same fork in the road as Session 2’s worked scenario — except now with real, already-written, conflicting data.

They chose consistency over availability for the recovery: rather than guess which conflicting writes were correct (or serve stale/wrong data), they took the affected systems partially offline and manually reconciled the data.
This is why a network issue lasting under a minute produced an outage lasting around 24 hours — the partition itself was brief, but restoring a trustworthy, consistent state took far longer than the failure that caused the mess.


Timing: 5 min. Emphasize the asymmetry: the trigger was seconds, the consequence was a day. That gap is the single most important fact of the whole case study to remember.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: Discussion: Was That the Right Call?
text:
Discussion: Was That the Right Call?






Think about it — small groups (3–4 students), 4 min, then share


GitHub chose to go partially unavailable for ~24 hours rather than risk serving incorrect data. Do you agree with that choice, for a code-hosting platform specifically? Would your answer change for a different kind of service — say, a live sports-scores app, or an air-traffic control system? What’s the actual variable that should decide this, in general?




Timing: 6 min including discussion. Push groups toward naming “the cost of being wrong vs. the cost of being unavailable” explicitly — that’s the same axis from Session 2’s consistency-vs-availability table, now applied to a real, harder case where the “right” answer is genuinely debatable.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Connecting to the Fallacies
Look back at Session 1’s eight fallacies of distributed computing. Which ones does this incident illustrate?

“The network is reliable” — a routine maintenance operation caused a partition; the network broke exactly when it wasn’t expected to.
“Topology doesn’t change” — the automatic failover mechanism existed because the system’s designers already knew topology (which node is primary) needs to be able to change — and that flexibility is exactly what created the split-brain risk.







Think about it


Can you connect a third fallacy from Session 1’s list to some part of this incident?




Timing: 4 min. Leave the third fallacy genuinely open — several are defensible (e.g., “there is one administrator” relates to coordinating a fix across a large engineering org during an active incident).

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: Small-Group Exercise: Diagnose Your Own Scenario
text:
Small-Group Exercise: Diagnose Your Own Scenario
In groups of 3–4, pick one of the following scenarios. In 5 minutes, decide: favor consistency or favor availability, and what would you tell users while recovering?

A ride-sharing app’s driver-location service loses connection between two regional servers for 30 seconds.
A university’s course-registration system briefly can’t confirm seat counts are in sync across two servers during peak registration.
A multiplayer game’s leaderboard can’t sync scores between two regions for a few minutes during a network blip.

Be ready to defend your choice to the class — including what you’d do differently from GitHub’s approach, if anything.

Timing: 7 min, including a couple of groups reporting back. If time is short, cut to 2 scenarios rather than rushing all 3 — depth of discussion matters more than covering everything.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Wrap-Up
Today’s takeaway isn’t “GitHub made a mistake” — their recovery choice was defensible and matches the consistency-favoring reasoning from Session 2. The real lesson is narrower and more useful:
A partition lasting seconds can create a consequence lasting a day, and the choice of how to respond to it is a design decision made in advance, not improvised during the incident.
Monday: back to new material — the client-server model, and what actually happens when you type a URL into a browser.

Timing: 2 min. Close on the forward-reference to keep momentum into Session 4.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: Recap: From Failures to How Things Talk
text:
Recap: From Failures to How Things Talk
Sessions 1–3 were about what goes wrong: lost messages, partitions, split-brain. Today, before going further, we need the basics of how machines talk to each other when things go right — the client-server model and HTTP.

Timing: 3 min. Brief tonal shift — signal explicitly that today is foundational/mechanical rather than failure-focused, so students recalibrate expectations.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
The Client-Server Model
The most common shape of communication between two machines: one asks, one answers.

The client initiates a request. Your laptop’s browser, your phone’s app — these are clients.
The server receives the request, does whatever work is needed, and sends back a response. A kitchen branch answering the phone is the server; the customer calling in is the client.
Crucially: the client always initiates. A server doesn’t call you out of the blue to tell you your order is ready — you have to ask.







Think about it


Name three client-server interactions you had this morning — before you even opened this course’s slides. (Hint: your phone checking for notifications counts.)




Timing: 4 min. Let several students answer — email, weather app, any login screen, a map loading — the goal is making them notice how constant and invisible this pattern already is in their daily life.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: Not Every Server Is Only a Server
text:
Not Every Server Is Only a Server
Real systems are rarely just “one client, one server” — they’re chains.

When your browser asks a web server for a page, that web server might itself act as a client to a database server, asking it for the data needed to build the page.
Distributed systems are often long chains of client-server relationships: browser → web server → application server → database — each link in the chain plays “client” to the one after it, and “server” to the one before it.
This is why “client” and “server” describe a role in a specific interaction, not a permanent label on a machine.


Timing: 4 min. Worth a quick concrete trace: “when you load Netflix’s homepage, how many client-server hops do you think happen before you see a single thumbnail?” — no need for a precise answer, just to loosen the assumption that it’s always exactly one hop.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: The Journey of a URL — Step 1: The Address Book (DNS)
text:
The Journey of a URL — Step 1: The Address Book (DNS)
You type www.example.com into your browser. The very first problem: that’s a name, not an address. Computers on a network find each other using numeric addresses (IP addresses), not human-friendly names.

DNS (Domain Name System) is the internet’s address book — it translates a human-readable name like www.example.com into a numeric address like 93.184.216.34.
Kitchen picture: you know the name of a restaurant branch, not its phone number. DNS is the phone directory you look the name up in before you can actually call.
This lookup happens automatically, in milliseconds, before your browser can even attempt to contact the server.


Timing: 5 min. No need to go deep into DNS internals (recursive resolvers, caching, etc.) — the one idea to land is “names have to be translated to addresses before anything else can happen.”

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Step 2: Opening the Line (TCP Connection)
With the numeric address in hand, your browser opens a connection to that machine.

This is like the phone actually starting to ring at the other end — a connection is established between your machine and the server, over which data can now flow in both directions.
We won’t go deep into how this connection is established (that’s networking-course territory) — the one thing to know is that it happens before any actual request is sent, and it can itself fail (recall Session 1: the line can be slow to open, or fail to open at all).


Timing: 4 min. Deliberately light-touch — no TCP handshake details, no OS/networking vocabulary. The goal is just to have a named step between “found the address” and “sent the request,” not to teach networking.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Step 3: Sending the Request
With the line open, your browser sends an actual request — a structured message asking for something specific.

The request names what’s being asked for (which page, which resource) and how (more on this in a moment).
Kitchen picture: the call has connected, and now you actually place your order — not just “hello,” but “I’d like the Tuesday special, extra large.”
The request travels across the network to the server — and, as Session 1 established, that trip is not instant and not guaranteed.


Timing: 5 min. This is the natural moment to plant “the request has a format” without fully teaching HTTP yet — that’s two slides away, after the response side of the story is told first.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: Step 4: The Server Does the Work
text:
Step 4: The Server Does the Work
The server receives the request and does whatever is needed to fulfill it.

This might be as simple as reading a file off disk, or as complex as querying a database, running a computation, or — per the previous slide’s chain idea — becoming a client itself to another server.
How long this takes varies enormously: a cached, simple page might take milliseconds; a page that requires a complex database query might take much longer.
Kitchen picture: the branch has your order, and is now actually cooking it — this is the part of the phone call where you’re on hold.


Timing: 4 min. Brief — the mechanics of server-side processing aren’t this course’s focus; the point is just naming this as a distinct step with its own variable duration.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Step 5: The Response Comes Back
Once the work is done, the server sends a response back across the same connection — the requested data, plus information about whether the request succeeded.

Kitchen picture: the branch calls back with your order — “here it is,” or “sorry, we’re out of that.”
Your browser receives the response and renders it — turning the raw data into the page you actually see.
This is also a point where things can go wrong per Session 1: the response itself can be lost, delayed, or the connection can drop before it fully arrives.


Timing: 4 min. Keep the failure-mode callback brief — one sentence — since the tone of this session is meant to be mechanical/foundational, not a return to Session 1’s failure catalogue.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: The Whole Journey, Start to Finish
text:
The Whole Journey, Start to Finish
1. You type www.example.com
        ↓
2. DNS lookup: name → numeric address     (the address book)
        ↓
3. Connection opens to that address        (the phone line connects)
        ↓
4. Browser sends a request                 (you place your order)
        ↓
5. Server does the work                    (the kitchen cooks)
        ↓
6. Server sends a response                 (the callback: "here it is")
        ↓
7. Browser renders the response            (you see the page)
Every one of these seven steps takes real time, and every one of them can fail independently — this single, everyday action is itself a small distributed system, with all the properties Sessions 1–3 described.






Diagram to add later (Excalidraw / pyxcd / draw.io)


A horizontal 7-step flow, browser icon on the left, server icon on the right, DNS depicted as a small “address book” icon above the line between them (queried before the main connection line is drawn). Number each step 1–7 matching the list above, with small icons: a magnifying glass for DNS lookup, a phone/plug icon for the connection, an envelope for the request, a gear/pot icon for server processing, a return envelope for the response, and an eye icon for rendering.




Timing: 5 min. This is the payoff slide of the session — walk it top to bottom, and explicitly connect back: “this is why loading a single web page is not instantaneous, and why it sometimes fails partway through.”

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
HTTP: The Standard Order Form
Step 4 (sending a request) and step 6 (sending a response) both need to happen in a format both sides agree on — otherwise the server couldn’t understand the request, or the browser couldn’t understand the response.

HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is that agreed-upon format. It’s a set of rules both client and server follow for how requests and responses are structured.
Kitchen picture: HTTP is like a standardized order form every branch in the chain uses — no matter which branch you call, the form has the same fields in the same places, so anyone can read it.







Think about it


Why does everyone need to agree on the same request/response format, rather than each server inventing its own? What would break if they didn’t?




Timing: 4 min. The callout’s answer is really “interoperability” — any client can talk to any HTTP server, precisely because the format is standardized rather than server-specific. Let students arrive at that themselves before naming it.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
HTTP Verbs
An HTTP request always names an action it wants performed — the verb:








Verb
Operation
Kitchen picture




GET
Read a resource
“What’s in order #42?”


POST
Create a new resource
“Start a brand-new order”


PUT
Replace a resource entirely
“Throw out order #42, replace it with this”


PATCH
Partially update a resource
“Just change the drink on order #42”


DELETE
Remove a resource
“Cancel order #42”




Timing: 5 min. These five verbs, and being able to pick the right one for a scenario, are directly tested (Quiz 2’s HTTP methods question) — worth a quick “which verb?” cold-call for a couple of scenarios before moving on.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Wrap: Bridge to REST
Today gave you the mechanics: client, server, DNS, connections, and HTTP as the shared format both sides speak.
Wednesday: REST — the specific style of using HTTP that almost the entire industry has converged on, and the format Checkpoint 2 will test you on directly.

Timing: 3 min. Close on the forward-reference — Session 5 builds directly and immediately on today’s HTTP-verbs slide.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: Recap: HTTP Is the Protocol, REST Is the Style
text:
Recap: HTTP Is the Protocol, REST Is the Style
Session 4 gave you HTTP: the shared format for requests and responses. HTTP itself is fairly general — it can be used in many ways.
REST (Representational State Transfer) is a specific, disciplined style of using HTTP that the industry has largely standardized on for building APIs. Today: what makes an API count as RESTful, and how to read one.

Timing: 3 min. Brief — just draw the HTTP-vs-REST distinction (protocol vs. a style of using it) before the rest of the session builds on it.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
What Makes an API “RESTful”?

Resources have URLs. Every “thing” the API exposes — a user, an order, a book — is identified by a URL, e.g. /users/42 or /orders/17.
The verb says what to do; the URL says what to do it to. GET /users/42 reads user 42. DELETE /orders/17 removes order 17. Same verbs from Session 4, now paired with specific resource URLs.
One API, many endpoints. A single REST API commonly exposes many different URLs for different resources — /users, /orders, /products might all live under the same API.


Timing: 4 min. This slide directly matches Quiz 2’s REST-structure question — “identified by a URL and an HTTP method” and “a single API can expose multiple endpoints” are both verbatim-testable ideas here.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Statelessness
REST is stateless: each request must contain everything the server needs to understand and fulfill it. The server does not remember anything about you between requests.

Kitchen picture: every single phone call to a branch has to restate your full order from scratch — the branch keeps no memory of your last call. If you called yesterday and ordered a pizza, that fact is gone; today’s call must include everything relevant again.
This sounds inefficient, but it’s a deliberate design choice: a stateless server can hand your next request to a completely different machine (recall replication and scaling motivations) without that machine needing to know anything about your previous requests.







Think about it


If a server had to remember every client’s conversation history, what would that make harder when you’re trying to scale the service across many machines?




Timing: 4 min. The callout’s intended answer connects directly back to Module 1/Session 1’s scaling motivation — remembering per-client state ties a client to a specific machine, which fights against the “add more machines” scaling story.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Anatomy of a Request
GET /users/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Accept: application/json

Verb + path: GET /users/42 — read the resource at this URL.
Headers: metadata about the request — here, which host to talk to, and what response format is acceptable.
Some requests (like POST or PUT) also include a body — the actual data being sent, e.g. the details of a new order to create.


Timing: 4 min. Keep headers light — Host and Accept are enough to establish “headers carry metadata,” without a full catalogue of HTTP headers.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Anatomy of a Response
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"id": 42, "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@example.com"}

Status line: the protocol version and a status code (200 OK) — did the request succeed, and how?
Headers: here, Content-Type tells the client the body is JSON — this is literally how a client knows how to parse what follows.
Body: the actual data requested.


Timing: 4 min. Point out explicitly: Content-Type is how Checkpoint 2’s third question (“what format is the response in, and how do you know”) gets answered — it’s not a guess, it’s stated in the headers.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
HTTP Status Codes








Range
Meaning
Examples




2xx
Success
200 OK, 201 Created


3xx
Redirect
301 Moved Permanently


4xx
Client error — you asked for something wrong
400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found, 401 Unauthorized


5xx
Server error — something broke on their end
500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable









Think about it


Why does it matter whether an error is 4xx (your fault) versus 5xx (their fault)? What would you do differently, as the client, in each case?




Timing: 5 min. The callout’s intended answer: a 4xx means retrying the exact same request will fail again (you need to fix your request), while a 5xx might succeed on retry (the problem is transient, on the server side) — this is a genuinely useful distinction for real debugging, not just quiz trivia. Memorize 200, 201, 400, 401, 403, 404, 500 — the most commonly tested set.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: JSON: The Language of REST Responses
text:
JSON: The Language of REST Responses
{
  "book": {
    "title": "Designing Data-Intensive Applications",
    "author": "Martin Kleppmann",
    "year": 2017,
    "tags": ["distributed", "databases", "systems"],
    "available": true
  }
}

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a language-independent text format for structured data — despite the name, it’s used by virtually every programming language, not just JavaScript.
Building blocks: strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays [ ], and objects { } — objects and arrays can nest inside each other, as seen here.
This is the near-universal body format for REST API responses, which is exactly why Content-Type: application/json matters — it tells you this is the format to expect.


Timing: 4 min. Point out the nesting explicitly — tags is an array inside an object, which is itself the value of "book" — reading nested JSON correctly is exactly what Checkpoint 2 requires.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
section: Worked Example: Reading a Real Response
text:
Worked Example: Reading a Real Response
GET https://api.example.com/books?isbn=9780132350884

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "isbn": "9780132350884",
  "title": "Clean Code",
  "author": "Robert C. Martin",
  "pages": 464
}
As a class: what HTTP method was used? What does the 200 mean? What format is the body in, and how do we know? What is the title of the book returned?

Timing: 6 min. This is deliberately the same shape of question as Checkpoint 2, using a different book — walk through it as a group so students rehearse the exact reasoning they’ll need to do individually on the checkpoint, without literally seeing the checkpoint’s example in advance.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Why Industry Uses REST Everywhere

Universality: any client that speaks HTTP — a browser, a phone app, a Java program, another server — can talk to any REST API, with no special client software required.
Statelessness → scalability: since no server needs to remember you between requests, requests can be handled by any available machine, which is exactly what lets services scale by adding more machines (Session 1’s scaling motivation, realized).
Human-readable, debuggable: JSON and plain URLs mean you can inspect what’s happening with nothing more than a web browser or a simple command-line tool.







Think about it


What would calling an API look like without a standard like REST — if every company invented its own request/response format? What would that cost you as a developer?




Timing: 3 min. Let this connect back to Session 4’s “why does everyone need to agree” callout — same underlying idea (standardization enables interoperability), now applied specifically to REST’s dominance.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Lab 3 Preview
Lab 3 (this Friday, Oct 2): you’ll write a Java program that calls a real public API (the Open Library API), parses the JSON response using HttpClient and org.json, and handles a request that fails.
Everything you need — the request/response anatomy, status codes, JSON structure — is exactly what today covered.

Timing: 2 min. Keep this brief — Lab 3 itself teaches the Java syntax (HttpClient, JSONObject, optString) hands-on; this slide is a pointer, not a code walkthrough.

title: Module 2: Distributed Systems Concepts
text:
Checkpoint 2 Preview & Review
Checkpoint 2 runs now, in the last 15 minutes of this session: given a REST API response, identify the HTTP method used, what the status code means, the response format (and how you know), the actual data returned, and one thing that could realistically go wrong.
Quick review before you start: - HTTP methods: what each of GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE actually does (Session 4). - Status codes: the 2xx/4xx/5xx ranges, and what 200 specifically promises (this session). - Reading JSON: finding a specific field inside a nested object or array (this session’s worked example). - What can go wrong: connect back to Session 1 — a request can be lost, delayed, or the server can be down; a real API call has real failure modes to name.

Timing: 4 min for this review slide — the 15-min checkpoint itself follows separately and isn’t slide content. The “what can go wrong” review point is worth emphasizing — it’s the one Checkpoint 2 question that pulls all the way back to Session 1’s failure vocabulary rather than just this session’s REST content.

title: Review
text:
When Do You Need Concurrency?
Back in Session 2 you saw two plain-language reasons to use threads: “waiting on something” and “more hands, more work.” Those have formal names, worth knowing precisely:

I/O-bound tasks — the program spends most of its time waiting: for a network reply, a disk read, a database query. Threads let other work happen during that wait instead of the CPU sitting idle. (“Waiting on something,” Session 2.)
CPU-bound tasks — the program spends most of its time computing. Splitting the computation across multiple cores gives genuine speed-up. (“More hands, more work,” Session 2.)
Event handling — a web server fielding many simultaneous requests is a common real-world mix of both: mostly waiting on each individual request, but needing to handle many at once.







Warning


Concurrency is not free — it’s the entire subject of Sessions 3 and 4 that sharing state across threads introduces race conditions, deadlock, livelock, and starvation. Only reach for it when the performance benefit is clear and measurable, and only protect the shared state that actually needs it.




Timing: 4 min. This is the payoff of a deliberate choice made back in Session 2: the informal “waiting vs. more hands” framing was taught first, precisely so this slide could attach the formal vocabulary to an idea students already have, instead of introducing both at once.

title: Review
Review
text:
Practice 1: Solution
No — add() is not thread-safe. total = total + amount is a read-modify-write, exactly like counter++ in Session 3:

Read the current value of total.
Modify it — compute total + amount.
Write the new value back to total.

If Thread A and Thread B both read total before either writes back, one of their additions is lost — identical shape to the lost-update table from Session 3, just with += amount instead of ++.
The fix: mark add() (and, for consistency, getTotal()) synchronized, so the whole read-modify-write sequence completes on one thread before another can begin it.

Timing: 4 min. Worth noting getTotal() in the fix — students often synchronize only the method that writes and forget that an unsynchronized read can still observe a half-updated or stale value.

text:
Practice 3: Solution
No — this does not fix anything. Recall from Session 4: the lock is attached to a specific object, and only protects threads that are trying to acquire the lock on that same object.

new Object() creates a brand-new object every single time add() is called.
Thread A and Thread B each get their own new lock object — they’re never competing for the same lock, so synchronized here provides no mutual exclusion at all. The race condition is completely unaffected.
The real fix: lock on an object that’s shared and stable across all calls — e.g., this (method-level synchronized, Practice 1’s solution), or a single lock field created once, like private final Object lock = new Object();, referenced by every call.







Tip


Rule to carry into the exam: synchronized (X) only protects against other threads also trying to synchronize on that same X. If every thread gets a different X, you have the syntax of locking with none of the effect.




Timing: 4 min. This is worth calling out as checkpoint/exam-relevant — “synchronized but on the wrong object” is a realistic, subtle bug, distinct from “forgot to synchronize at all.”

title: Synchronization, Locks, and Their Failure Modes
section: Recap: The synchronized You’ve Already Used
text:
Recap: The synchronized You’ve Already Used

You’ve written synchronized twice now: Lab 1 Part 2 (the shared counter) and Lab 2 Task 3. Both times it worked — the count came out right on every run.
What you haven’t seen: why one keyword is enough, what it’s actually locking, and what it costs. That’s today.
By the end of this session you’ll be able to explain, precisely, why the keyword you already used solves the exact problem from Session 3 — and name three ways locking can go wrong.


Timing: 3 min. Ask a student to describe what synchronized did for them in Lab 1/2 in their own words before you give the formal mechanics — you’ll likely get an intuitive-but-imprecise answer (“it stops them from messing it up”), which is a good springboard into the precise version. Keep this short: they know it works, so don’t over-sell the motivation.

title: Synchronization, Locks, and Their Failure Modes
text:
The synchronized Keyword: The Lock
Every object in Java has an invisible lock attached to it (called a monitor lock, or intrinsic lock). synchronized is how you use it.
static synchronized void increment() {
    counter++;  // only one thread at a time can be inside here
}

Marking a method synchronized means: before any thread can run this method, it must first acquire the lock on the object the method belongs to (this, for an instance method).

Timing: 3 min. The “attached to every object” framing is worth stating explicitly and slowly — it’s not obvious to students that locking is a property of objects, not of methods or variables in the abstract. Stop here; acquire/release and the kitchen picture are the next slide.

title: Synchronization, Locks, and Their Failure Modes
text:
synchronized: Acquiring and Releasing

Only one thread can hold a given object’s lock at a time. Any other thread that calls a synchronized method on that same object must wait until the lock is released.
The lock is automatically released when the method returns — you never unlock it by hand.


Kitchen picture: the lock is a single claim ticket for the stove. A cook must hold the ticket to use the stove; every other cook who wants it simply waits in line until it’s returned.

Timing: 3 min. Emphasize “automatically released” — students coming from other languages sometimes expect an explicit unlock and worry about forgetting it. The kitchen picture (single claim ticket) is the one to carry forward; it’s reused on the Tradeoffs slide.

title: Synchronization, Locks, and Their Failure Modes
Synchronization, Locks, and Their Failure Modes
section: Worked Fix: Closing the Loop on Session 3
text:
Worked Fix: Closing the Loop on Session 3
Recall Session 3’s “wrong interleaving” — two threads both read 5, both write 6, one increment lost. With synchronized protecting the increment:










Time
Thread A
Thread B
counter




t1
acquires lock, read → 5
(calls increment(), blocks — waits for lock)
5


t2
write 6, releases lock
(still waiting)
6


t3

acquires lock, read → 6
6


t4

write 7, releases lock
7 ← correct, every time





Thread B cannot even begin its read until Thread A has finished its entire read-modify-write sequence and released the lock. The interleaving that produced the wrong answer in Session 3 is now impossible — not unlikely, impossible, by construction.

Timing: 6 min. This is the payoff slide of the whole session — literally reuse the Session 3 slide’s wrong-interleaving table as a mental side-by-side if you have it up on a second screen or printed. The word “impossible, not unlikely” is worth emphasizing — synchronized doesn’t reduce the odds of a race, it removes the possibility entirely.

title: Synchronization, Locks, and Their Failure Modes
text:
synchronized — Tradeoffs

✅ Correctness: eliminates this entire class of race condition.
❌ Performance: threads that would have run simultaneously now wait in line — the protected section runs one-at-a-time no matter how many CPU cores you have. This is called serializing execution.
Kitchen picture: one claim ticket for the stove means every cook who needs the stove queues up, even if only one of them is actually using it at any instant. If ten cooks all need the stove for one second each, the kitchen just spent ten seconds on stove work that could have taken one second with ten stoves.








Tip


Rule of thumb: lock the minimum amount of code needed for correctness. Every line inside a synchronized block is a line no other thread can run concurrently with it — block-level locking (previous slide) exists specifically so you can keep that minimum small.




Timing: 5 min. Tie directly back to the block-level slide — “this is why you’d choose block-level over method-level,” not just a syntax option.

title: Synchronization, Locks, and Their Failure Modes
Synchronization, Locks, and Their Failure Modes
section: Deadlock: The Picture and How to Prevent It
text:
Deadlock: The Picture and How to Prevent It

Kitchen picture: Cook A is holding the only knife and waiting for the only cutting board; Cook B is holding the only cutting board and waiting for the only knife. Neither will let go of what they’re holding. Nobody cooks again.
Prevention: always acquire multiple locks in the same order, everywhere in your code. If both threads had grabbed lockA before lockB, this deadlock could not happen.





Timing: 3 min. The closed-loop picture is the payoff — “circular wait” clicks as a shape, not as prose. State the same-order prevention rule as the one thing to memorize.

title: Synchronization, Locks, and Their Failure Modes
text:
Livelock
A subtler failure: both threads are actively doing something, repeatedly — they’re just never making actual progress.

Two threads each detect they might be about to conflict, and both politely back off and retry — but they back off in a way that causes them to collide again immediately, forever.
Kitchen picture: two cooks meet in a narrow doorway, both step to the same side to let the other pass, still blocked, both step to the other side, still blocked — repeating indefinitely. Both are constantly moving. Neither ever gets through.
Unlike deadlock (frozen, doing nothing), livelock burns CPU time on threads that are busy but unproductive — which can make it harder to notice, since the program doesn’t look stuck.



Timing: 4 min. Contrast directly with deadlock on this slide: “deadlock looks frozen, livelock looks busy but goes nowhere” — that contrast is the exam-relevant distinction.

title: Synchronization, Locks, and Their Failure Modes
text:
Starvation
A third failure mode: a thread is technically able to run, but never actually gets the chance.

If some threads are consistently prioritized over others (explicitly, via thread priorities, or implicitly, through unlucky scheduling), a lower-priority thread can wait indefinitely while higher-priority threads keep cutting in front of it.
Kitchen picture: a junior cook keeps stepping up to use the stove, but senior cooks keep arriving and taking their turn first, over and over. The junior cook is never explicitly blocked — they’re just never actually first.
Starvation is different from deadlock and livelock: the system is making progress overall, it’s just one specific thread that never gets its share.


Timing: 4 min. Keep this the shortest of the three failure-mode slides — starvation is the least likely to show up in checkpoint/quiz questions compared to deadlock, but it completes the set and is worth naming.

title: Synchronization, Locks, and Their Failure Modes
section: The Three Failure Modes, Side by Side
text:
The Three Failure Modes, Side by Side









Failure
What it looks like
Threads doing work?
Kitchen picture




Deadlock
Both threads frozen, forever
No — completely stuck
Two cooks each holding what the other needs, neither lets go


Livelock
Both threads active, but no progress
Yes — but wasted
Two cooks stepping aside for each other in a doorway, endlessly


Starvation
One thread never gets its turn
Yes — everyone else makes progress
A junior cook is always pre-empted by senior cooks at the stove




All three are consequences of introducing locks to fix race conditions — you traded “sometimes wrong” for “sometimes stuck,” and avoiding all three is a real design skill, not just a syntax rule.

Timing: 4 min. This table is worth putting up as the one thing students photograph for exam review — it’s the single highest-density slide in the session.

title: Synchronization, Locks, and Their Failure Modes
text:
Threads Cost Something to Create
Locking solves correctness. But there’s a cost we haven’t addressed: creating a thread itself is not free.

Every new Thread(...) creates a brand-new cook from scratch — real overhead, every time. Thousands of short tasks × one new-then-discarded thread each = wasteful.
The fix is a thread pool: a fixed set of reusable worker threads pulling tasks off a shared queue. Hire a fixed kitchen staff on payroll instead of a new cook per order.


Timing: 3 min. Set up the cost problem and name the fix (a pool). The concrete Lab 2 API and the “extra tasks wait” behavior are the next slide.

title: Synchronization, Locks, and Their Failure Modes
section: A First Look at Pools (from Lab 2)
text:
A First Look at Pools (from Lab 2)
You already used a thread pool in Lab 2. The three pieces you touched there:
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);  // fixed staff of 2
pool.submit(new PrintTask("A"));                          // hand a task to the queue
pool.shutdown();                                          // no new tasks; finish what's queued

With 3 tasks and a pool of 2, the third waits until a thread is free — the behavior you observed in Lab 2 Task 2.
Next session (Sep 16): how the queue actually works, getting results back with Future, Callable vs Runnable, and where industry uses pools — then Checkpoint 1.


Timing: 3 min. This is a real intro, not just a teaser, because Lab 2 (Sep 11) already had students use ExecutorService. Keep it to the three methods on the slide and the “extra tasks wait” behavior. Do not get into Future.get(), awaitTermination semantics, or pool-sizing strategy — those are Session 5. The goal is that Session 5 opens on something students have both done (Lab 2) and seen named (here), not something cold.

title: Race Conditions In Depth
section: Recap: What You Saw in Lab 1
text:
Recap: What You Saw in Lab 1

In Lab 1, two threads each incremented a shared counter 10,000 times. Expected total: 20,000.
Most of you got something less than 20,000 — and if you ran it again, you probably got a different wrong number, not the same one.
That’s not a bug in the sense of “code with a typo.” The code is doing exactly what it says. The problem is something subtler: what “one line of code” actually means to the computer underneath your program.
In Part 2 you also fixed it by adding synchronized — and it worked, every run. Today and Sep 14 are about the part Lab 1 skipped: why it happens, why the wrong number changes between runs, why that one keyword was enough, and where it bites back.


Timing: 6 min. Ask a few students what number they actually got in Lab 1 — different students will report different wrong numbers, which is itself the demonstration you want before you’ve even started teaching.

title: Race Conditions In Depth
text:
counter++ Isn’t One Step
counter++ reads like a single, indivisible action. It is not. It is three separate steps:

Read the current value of counter from memory.
Increment that value by one.
Write the new value back to counter in memory.


Any of those three steps can be interrupted by another thread doing the exact same three steps, on the exact same shared variable, at the exact same time.

Timing: 4 min. Keep this slide purely conceptual — the register-level version is next, don’t merge them or it gets dense too fast.

title: Race Conditions In Depth
text:
Down to the Registers
You already know from computer organization that a CPU can’t operate on a value sitting in RAM directly — it has to move it into a register first.

counter++ compiles to something like:
LOAD  counter → R1      // read step: copy counter into a register
ADD   R1, 1             // increment step: add 1, inside the CPU
STORE R1 → counter      // write step: copy the register back to memory

Two threads running this on the same shared counter are each using their own register (registers are per-core / per-thread, not shared) — but they’re both reading from and writing to the same memory location.
The danger window is exactly the gap between LOAD and STORE: if Thread B’s LOAD happens before Thread A’s STORE, Thread B reads the stale value, and one increment is silently lost.


Timing: 6 min. This is the payoff of Session 2’s “shared heap, private stack” slide — counter lives on the shared heap, but the register doing the arithmetic is private to each thread’s execution. Make that connection explicit out loud.

Both threads read 5 before either one writes. Both compute 6. Both write 6. One increment vanished — the counter should be 7, since two increments happened, but it only reflects one. This exact interleaving can happen millions of times per second on a real CPU.

Timing: 5 min. Walk the table top to bottom, pausing on t2: “Thread B just read a value that’s about to become outdated — it doesn’t know that.”

title: Race Conditions In Depth
section: The Same Code, the Right Interleaving
text:
The Same Code, the Right Interleaving
The critical, unsettling part: the exact same code, the exact same two threads, can also produce the correct answer — if the timing happens to work out differently.



Time
Thread A
Thread B
counter

7 ← correct!



Nothing in the code changed between these two tables. Only the timing of which thread reached which step first changed — and that timing is decided by something outside your program’s control (Session 2’s closing point).

This is why race conditions are called races: the outcome depends on who reaches the shared variable first, and that can go either way from one run to the next.

Timing: 5 min. This is the single most important slide in the session — sometimes-right is what makes race conditions dangerous in practice, because testing your code and having it “work” proves nothing. Let that land before moving on.

title: Race Conditions In Depth
text:
Why This Is a “Heisenbug”

A bug that changes behavior — or disappears entirely — depending on timing is nicknamed a Heisenbug, after the uncertainty principle: observing the system (running it under a debugger, adding a print statement) can itself change the timing enough to make the bug vanish.
This is why race conditions are notoriously hard to catch in testing: your test suite runs the code a handful of times, gets the lucky interleaving, and passes — while the unlucky interleaving is still sitting there, waiting for production traffic to trigger it.
The same variability you already know from computer organization — cache hits vs. misses, branch prediction guessing right or wrong — means even identical code run twice rarely takes the exact same number of CPU cycles. Multiply that natural per-run variability across multiple threads, and the interleaving order becomes essentially unpredictable without an explicit mechanism forcing it.


Timing: 6 min. If time allows, ask: “Why might adding a print statement while debugging make a race condition seem to disappear?” — the answer (it changes timing enough to shift which interleaving occurs) is a nice concrete payoff of the Heisenbug idea.

title: Race Conditions In Depth
text:
Real-World Stakes: The Bank Account
Picture a joint bank account with a $1,000 balance, and two people withdraw $700 each, at two different ATMs, at nearly the same instant.

Each ATM checks the balance (read step): both see $1,000, both see “sufficient funds,” both proceed.
Each ATM subtracts $700 and writes the new balance back — if this happens the same way as the counter example, the second write simply overwrites the first, and the balance ends up at $300, not the correct $-400 (i.e., overdrawn) — but the bank just let $1,400 leave a $1,000 account.
This is not hypothetical — it is precisely the class of bug real financial and e-commerce systems must guard against, using the same synchronization ideas you’ll see starting next session.


Timing: 5 min. Note this is structurally identical to the counter race — same read/modify/write shape, just dollars instead of an integer. Point that out explicitly: once students see the shape, they can recognize it anywhere.

title: Race Conditions In Depth
section: Real-World Stakes: The Last Item in Stock
text:
Real-World Stakes: The Last Item in Stock
Recall the Amazon example from Session 1: thousands of orders per second, all touching the same inventory data.

One unit of an item left in stock. Two customers click “Buy” within milliseconds of each other.
Both requests read “1 in stock” before either one writes the updated count. Both proceed to charge the customer and confirm the order. The store just sold one physical item to two different people.
Same shape, again: read, decide, write — with a gap in between where another thread can sneak in and act on the stale value you already read.


Timing: 5 min. By now students should be able to predict the “read-modify-write” shape themselves before you show it — ask “what three steps do you think happen here?” before revealing the bullet.

title: Race Conditions In Depth
section: Bridge: We Need “One Cook at a Time”
text:
Bridge: We Need “One Cook at a Time”
Every example today has the same shape: multiple threads read a shared value, decide something based on it, then write a new value back — and if another thread sneaks its own read-decide-write in the middle, the result is wrong.
What we need is a way to say: while one cook is in the middle of this read-decide-write sequence at the shared counter, no other cook may touch it until they’re done. That’s not something Java gives you for free — you have to ask for it explicitly.
You already know the name of the tool that does this: synchronized, the keyword you added in Lab 1 Part 2. Next session (Sep 14): exactly how it works, and what it costs you.

Timing: 5 min. Students have used synchronized once, mechanically — so the hook here is “you already know it works; do you know why, or what it breaks?” rather than a blind cliffhanger. Still don’t get into the monitor-lock mechanics today; that’s Session 4’s clean start.

title: Race Conditions In Depth

Lab 2 Preview

Lab 2 (this Friday, Sep 11): write your own Runnable, then submit tasks to an ExecutorService thread pool.
Tasks: a PrintTask run across 3 threads, a thread pool with varying sizes, and a shared counter you make safe with synchronized again (as in Lab 1).
Same pattern as synchronized in Lab 1: you get hands-on with thread pools first, then Session 5 (Sep 16) covers how they work in depth. Session 4 ends with a short intro so it’s not cold.


Timing: 3 min. This course front-loads the hands-on: Lab 1 used synchronized before Session 4 explains it, Lab 2 uses a thread pool before Session 5 explains it. Tell students that’s deliberate — the lab gives them a concrete thing the lecture then makes sense of, not the other way around.

title: Processes vs. Threads
text:
Recap: One Kitchen, Many Cooks
Last session: parallel = one kitchen, many cooks, sharing the same counters and stove.
Today we make that literal:

Process = a kitchen staff — its own space, its own equipment, its own ingredients
Thread = a cook working inside that kitchen
Core = the kitchen itself, or more precisely, the counters, where all the cooking happens

Everything for the next three weeks is about what happens when multiple cooks share one kitchen.

Timing: 3 min. Don’t re-derive the analogy from scratch — restate it and move straight to today’s vocabulary.

title: Processes vs. Threads
text:
Processes vs. Threads

A process = a running program with its own memory space — the kitchen staff.
A thread = a lightweight unit of execution within a process — a cook. A process can contain many threads, just like a kitchen can employ many cooks.
Threads in the same process share memory — this is both powerful (cooks can hand ingredients to each other instantly) and dangerous (two cooks can grab the same thing at once).


Timing: 2 min on this slide. Move to the comparison table next.

title: Processes vs. Threads
section: Processes vs. Threads — Side by Side
text:
Processes vs. Threads — Side by Side









Process
Thread




Memory
Own, private space
Shared with sibling threads


Creation cost
High — a whole new kitchen staff
Low — hire another cook and add to the existing kitchen staff


Communication
Complex (must send messages between kitchens)
Easy but risky (just reach for the shared counter)




Memory is the difference everything else follows from: separate spaces vs. one shared space.
Creation cost is why real programs prefer threads when they can — spinning up a process is expensive.
Communication: “complex” vs. “easy but risky” are the two phrases that matter. The risky half of that last cell is exactly what Session 3 is about.


Timing: 2 min on this slide. Read the last row aloud in full sentences, not just as column labels.

title: Processes vs. Threads
text:
Stack and Heap
A running program is loaded into RAM with its own code, heap, and stack.


Timing: 2 min. This diagram is the anchor for the next slide — point out the one shared heap and the separate per-thread stacks before moving on.

title: Processes vs. Threads
text:
Connecting to Computer Organization
You already know a running program has a code segment, a heap, and a stack. Threads change exactly one part of that picture.

A process is exactly that instance — one program, loaded once, with one code segment, one heap, one set of open resources.
A thread inside that process reuses the same heap — that’s the shared kitchen counter, the same memory every thread in the process can read and write.
But each thread gets its own stack — its own private scratch space for local variables and function-call frames. This is the same stack you already know from comp org; the only change is there’s now one stack per cook, not one per kitchen.


Timing: 3 min on this slide. The payoff sentence is on the next slide — don’t rush past it.

title: Processes vs. Threads
section: Local Variables Are Safe. Shared Variables Are Not.
text:
Local Variables Are Safe. Shared Variables Are Not.






Tip


This is why two threads can run the same method at the same time without their local variables colliding — each has its own stack frame for that call — while still being able to corrupt a variable declared outside any method (a shared/global variable, living on the heap).
Local variables are safe by default. Shared variables are not.
That one sentence is the entire reason race conditions exist, and you’ll see it proven directly in Session 3.





Timing: 2 min on this slide (part of the 5-min block). This is the single most useful idea in the session — it transfers directly from what students already know, and it demystifies the local-safe/shared-risky distinction before they’ve even seen a race condition. Don’t rush it to get to the code slides.

title: Processes vs. Threads
text:
Why Bother With Threads?
Two cooks in the kitchen: one chops vegetables while the other stirs the pot. Same wall-clock time, more gets done.
There are two distinct reasons real programs reach for threads:

Waiting on something. A cook standing at the oven doing nothing while a timer counts down is wasted time — they could be chopping vegetables instead. Likewise, a thread waiting on a network reply or a disk read can step aside and let another thread use the CPU instead of it sitting idle.
More hands, more work. Four cooks each grilling one dish finish four dishes in the time it takes one cook to finish one — genuine parallel speed-up. A CPU with multiple cores can run multiple threads at the literal same instant, not just take turns quickly.


Timing: ~3 min on this slide. Deliberately no “I/O-bound” / “CPU-bound” vocabulary yet — that formal pairing returns in Session 6 (Fri Sep 18, the practice/quiz session). Today it’s plain language only.

title: Processes vs. Threads
section: Why Bother With Threads? — In Real Software
text:
Why Bother With Threads? — In Real Software
Both reasons show up constantly:

A web server handling thousands of simultaneous requests is mostly “waiting on something” — each request waits on a database.
A program crunching a large computation across all your CPU’s cores is “more hands, more work.”


Timing: ~2 min on this slide. These two examples come back in Modules 3–6, so plant them now.

Timing: ~3 min. Point and narrate row by row rather than reading the whole table at once.

title: Processes vs. Threads
text:
Tracing It: The Key Takeaway
Notice step 2: start() doesn’t wait for the new thread to do anything — it hands off the work and returns control to main immediately.
The two threads are now running at the same time, until join() in step 3 forces main to pause and wait.

Timing: ~1 min. This is the sentence the run() vs start() slide builds on next.

title: Processes vs. Threads
text:
The run() vs. start() Bug






The most common bug in this whole module


t.run() does not create a new thread. It calls the method exactly like any normal function call — on the current thread, in program order, right where you called it. You’ll see printed output and it may even look correct, but no concurrency happened at all.




t.start() → a genuinely new cook enters the kitchen and starts working alongside everyone else.
t.run() → you did the cooking yourself, in your own normal sequence, then moved on. No new cook, no overlap, no concurrency.
Rule to memorize: you call start(), Java calls run() for you, on the new thread. You should almost never write .run() in your own code.


Timing: 4 min. Ask directly: “If line 3 in the previous trace table said t.run() instead of t.start(), what would the table look like?” Let students work out that every row would collapse into the Main-thread column, executed strictly in order — that contrast is what makes this stick.

title: Processes vs. Threads
section: The Thread Lifecycle — The Five States
text:
The Thread Lifecycle — The Five States
NEW → RUNNABLE → (RUNNING) → TERMINATED
                    ↕
                 BLOCKED/WAITING







State
Kitchen equivalent




New
Recipe written, cook hasn’t arrived yet


Runnable
Cook clocked in, ready to work, waiting for a free stove


Running
Cook actively cooking


Blocked/Waiting
Cook paused — waiting on the oven timer, a lock, or sleep()


Terminated
Dish plated, cook leaves




Timing: ~3 min. Read each state against its kitchen equivalent.

title: Processes vs. Threads
section: The Thread Lifecycle — How a Thread Moves Through It

title: Processes vs. Threads
section: Who Decides When a Thread Runs?
text:
Who Decides When a Thread Runs?






Warning


Who decides when a Runnable cook actually gets the stove and becomes Running? Not you, not your code — something outside your control. That single fact is the root cause of almost every bug in this module.




You can ask a thread to start. You cannot control exactly when it gets CPU time, or how its execution interleaves with other threads.
This means the same program can produce different results on different runs — not because the code is wrong, but because the timing of “whose turn it is” isn’t something your code decides.
Hold onto this. Session 3 is entirely about what goes wrong when two threads touch the same shared data and you have no control over whose turn comes first.


Timing: 3 min. Deliberately avoid the term “OS scheduler” — no OS course assumed, and the word invites a derailing “wait, what’s a scheduler” tangent. “Something outside your control decides whose turn it is” carries the idea without the vocabulary, and Session 3 opens by cashing in this exact sentence.

title: Processes vs. Threads
section: Lab 1 Preview: The Race Condition Game
text:
Lab 1 Preview: The Race Condition Game

Observe a race condition happen in real code.
Two threads both increment a shared counter 10,000 times each.
Expected result: 20,000. Actual result: often less — and it changes between runs.
You’ll observe it happen, then fix it, and be able to explain why the fix works.


Lab 1 is this Friday (Sep 4).

Timing: 3 min. Close on the open question — “why would the count come out wrong?” — without answering it. Session 3 answers it in the first five minutes.

title: COSC420 - Distributed/Parallel Computing
text:
Course Description
Official catalog description:

This course studies the methods for using several computers connected by a network to solve a single problem. Topics include networking services, middleware (CORBA, DCOM, SOAP, RMI and RPC), two- and three-tier client-server systems, algorithms for parallel computing, performance evaluation and hardware architectures (clusters, grids, surfaces).

Course focus, Fall 2026:
COSC420 is a hands-on introduction to the ideas and tools behind modern distributed and parallel computing. The course moves through six modules: (1) concurrency and thread safety in Java; (2) distributed systems concepts, including partial failure and the CAP theorem; (3) big data and the MapReduce model on Apache Hadoop/HDFS; (4) large-scale data analysis with Apache Spark and PySpark; (5) distributed storage and NoSQL databases with MongoDB; and (6) cloud computing service models and microservices, including building a REST API with Python Flask. The term culminates in a capstone in which pairs of students build an end-to-end data pipeline that moves a real dataset through HDFS, Spark, MongoDB, and a Flask dashboard. Work is done on the student’s own laptop against an instructor-hosted Hadoop/Spark cluster; no paid services are required.

title: COSC420 - Distributed/Parallel Computing
text:
Course Learning Outcomes
Official catalog outcomes:
Upon completion of the course, students will be able to:

Explain networking for distributed computing as demonstrated by short answers during examination.
Execute performance evaluation of a parallel and distributed system.
Explain middleware for distributed and parallel computing as demonstrated by short answers during examination.
Model hardware architectures for distributed and parallel computing as demonstrated by short answers during examination.
Implement common parallel and distributed computing algorithms as demonstrated by development of programs.
Construct parallel and or distributed computing solution as demonstrated by development of a significant project.

Course-Level Learning Outcomes, Fall 2026.
Upon completion of the course, students will be able to:

Write thread-safe Java programs using synchronization primitives and thread-pool mechanisms.
Analyze distributed system design decisions by applying the CAP theorem to evaluate consistency and availability trade-offs.
Explain the MapReduce execution model and use Apache Hadoop to run distributed data-processing jobs on HDFS.
Use PySpark to load, transform, and analyze large datasets with the DataFrame API.
Compare relational and NoSQL storage approaches and select an appropriate database design for a given scenario.
Describe cloud computing service models and the microservices architectural pattern, and build a simple REST API using Python Flask.
Design and implement an end-to-end distributed data pipeline integrating HDFS, Apache Spark, a NoSQL database, and a REST API.

text:
Methods of Evaluation
Your course grade is based on checkpoints, labs, quizzes, a midterm exam, a final exam, a capstone project, and engaged-learning activities. Most components emphasize hands-on work with real tools.

Checkpoints (8) - Short, timed, individual exercises in the last 15–20 min of a lecture session, testing understanding of what was just taught that day. Graded on output: correct = full credit, genuine attempt = partial credit, not attempted = 0.
Labs (10) - Full 50-minute hands-on Friday sessions in which you build and run something end-to-end using real tools (Java threading, REST APIs, Hadoop/HDFS, PySpark, MongoDB Atlas, Flask). Graded on completion and correct output.
Quizzes (8) - Blackboard multiple-choice and true/false, auto-graded, taken during the last 10–15 min of a Friday lab session. They cover the building-block concepts of each module.
Midterm Exam - In-class Blackboard exam (MC + short answer) covering Modules 1–3.
Final Exam - Blackboard exam (MC + short answer) during finals week. Comprehensive, but weighted toward Modules 4–6, which are not on the midterm.
Capstone - A pair project with a live demo: an end-to-end data pipeline (HDFS → PySpark → MongoDB → Flask dashboard). Graded against a checklist rubric.
Engaged Learning (6) - Completion-graded reflection and self-study activities done outside class (see the Engaged Learning section above).

Course Attendance Policy
Attendance is not mandatory, and thus absence from class is not penalized directly, but you will lose out in other ways. Class attendance is the #1 indicator of academic success. OS3 emphatically encourages all students to Go To Class! Class attendance is important for numerous reasons:

Students tend to remember info more when they attend class.
Your presence in class shows your instructor that you care about the course and it is important to you. If your grade is borderline at the end of the semester, the instructor may give you the benefit of the doubt because you regularly attended class.
You/your families are paying to be in class. In-state residents who miss a class are wasting over $56 per class. Out-of-state students who miss a class are throwing away $110 per class!
Your instructor will likely explain material differently/better than you can learn it yourself, and can answer questions more directly.
Going to class helps you build community and relationships with peers and your instructors.
By not going to class, you may miss a pop quiz, participation points, extra credit opportunities, important info, or in-class assignments that can impact your grade.

To the Point establishes the baseline attendance policy for SMCM courses. 
Please note: Per the SMCM policy, there is no distinction between “excused” or “unexcused” absences; an absence is an absence.

Late Work and Missed Assignment Policy
Assignments are due at 11:59 PM Eastern Time (UTC – 4) on the posted due date, with a one-hour grace period. Submissions received after that time will be subject to a late penalty of 10% of the maximum possible points per additional day past the deadline. The minimum grade on any assignment is zero; late penalties will not reduce a score below this.
Because the penalty accumulates continuously, assignments submitted several days late will earn little or no credit. Please plan accordingly and submit on time.

section: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Classroom
text:
Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Classroom 
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) (tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot) is a fast-developing tool that greatly impacts the learning process. As with many things, there are times when using these tools is appropriate and when it is not.  For this course, I encourage you to use the generative AI tools at your disposal for learning and practice, but not for checkpoints and quizzes. However it is your responsibility to properly evaluate the information created through generative AI. We will discuss how to do this in class, and you should contact me with any questions that you may have if you encounter a situation where it is unclear how to do use AI. Failure to disclose the use generative AI tools in assignments and quizzes may be considered plagiarism and will be handled via the SMCM Academic Misconduct policies.

title: Creative Coding 3 — Boolean Hit-Testing
section: The problem: is the mouse inside a box?
text:
The problem: is the mouse inside a box?
A single comparison can’t answer that — you need four, all true at once:

is the point right of the box’s left edge?
is it left of the box’s right edge?
is it below the box’s top edge?
is it above the box’s bottom edge?

Miss any one and the point isn’t actually inside.

title: Creative Coding 1 — Shapes & Coordinates
text:
What is Processing?
Processing is still Java — the same variables and arithmetic you’ve been writing already.
What’s new: instead of printing text with IO.println, you’re drawing shapes onto a small rectangular canvas.
Every sketch on this page runs live in your browser — no installation needed.

title: Creative Coding 1 — Shapes & Coordinates
section: Two blocks instead of one main

title: Creative Coding 1 — Shapes & Coordinates
text:
Reading setup() and draw()

setup() — “things I only need to do once.” Mainly, telling Processing how big the canvas should be.
draw() — “the current frame of a flipbook.” Processing calls it again and again, and whatever you draw inside becomes the picture for that instant.

You never call draw() yourself — Processing does that automatically, forever, once the sketch starts.

title: Creative Coding 1 — Shapes & Coordinates
section: Two things to file away for later
text:
Two things to file away for later

These named blocks are called methods — you’ll learn to write your own soon. For now, just copy the void setup() { ... } / void draw() { ... } shape exactly and put your code inside the braces.
You’ll see float below where you might expect double. float is just another type for decimal numbers, a little less precise than double. Processing uses it everywhere, so read float as “a number that can have a decimal point.”

title: Creative Coding 1 — Shapes & Coordinates
Creative Coding 1 — Shapes & Coordinates
text:
The coordinate system
Before drawing anything, you need to know how Processing measures position. It is not the x/y grid from math class.

(0, 0) is the top-left corner, not the center and not the bottom-left.
x increases as you move right — as you’d expect.
y increases as you move down — the opposite of a math-class graph. This trips almost everyone up at least once.

title: Creative Coding 1 — Shapes & Coordinates
text:
width and height
width and height are two variables Processing fills in for you automatically, based on whatever you passed to size(...).
So width / 2 always means “the horizontal middle of the canvas,” no matter what size you chose.

title: Putting It Together
text:
The Big Picture
You now have a full toolkit:



Tool
What it’s for




Variables & types
Storing and naming individual values


if / else
Making decisions


while / for
Repeating


Methods (decks 08–10)
Naming and reusing a block of work


Arrays (decks 15–17)
Storing many values of the same type


Classes & objects (decks 18–21)
Bundling related data and behavior


null (deck 22)
Representing “no object”



Today’s lecture: using all of them together.

Step back and let students see the whole map before the deep dive. Each tool solves a specific problem; combining them is what real programming looks like. The goal of this lecture is not to teach new syntax — it’s to teach design: given a problem, how do you decide which tools to reach for and in what order?

title: Putting It Together
text:
A Design Process
When given a problem, ask these questions in order:

What are the “things” in this problem? → Make a class for each
What data does each thing carry? → Those are the fields
What can each thing do? → Those are the instance methods
What work spans many things? → Arrays of objects, loops
What utility calculations don’t belong to any one thing? → Static methods
How does everything start? → main orchestrates it all


This is a design checklist, not a rigid recipe. Walk through it with students: “What are the things in a grade book? Students. What data does a student carry? Name, grade, maybe ID. What can a student do? Report their grade, say whether they’re passing, compute their letter grade. What spans many students? The roster — an array of Student objects with a loop. What utility? Maybe a static letter-grade converter. Main creates the roster, fills it, and calls a print method.” This makes OOP feel natural rather than arbitrary.
