title: Putting It Together
Putting It Together
text:
Choosing the Right Tool
When you see a problem description, map its language to tools:







Phrase in the problem
Tool




“store many ___ of the same type”
array


“for each ___”
for loop


“keep asking until ___”
while loop


“a ___ has properties: X, Y, Z”
class with fields


“a ___ can ___”
instance method


“a calculation that doesn’t belong to any one object”
static method


“the same value for all objects”
static field


“might not exist / not found”
null check




Putting this table up invites students to use it as a design vocabulary. “For each student in the roster” → for loop over an array. “A student has a name and grade” → class with fields. “Might not find the student” → return null, check null. This is the language-to-tool translation skill that separates programmers who can read problems from those who blank out.

title: Putting It Together
text:
Common Design Mistakes






Warning


Putting everything in main main should orchestrate, not compute. If main has 50 lines of calculation, refactor: extract methods and classes.









Warning


Making every field public and every method static If you never use new, you’re not doing OOP. Objects bundle state and behavior together.









Warning


Parallel arrays instead of an array of objects String[] names; int[] grades; that must stay in sync → replace with Student[] roster.









Warning


Writing all code before testing anything Write the class, test it. Write one method, test it. Don’t write 100 lines and then debug all at once.




The last point is software engineering practice, not just syntax. Encourage students to test incrementally: write the Student class and immediately write a main that creates one student and prints its name. Add letterGrade(), test it. Add isPassing(), test it. Only then build the roster and statistics.

title: Putting It Together
text:
Worksheet
Build the following program:
You are managing a library’s book collection.

Write a class Book with fields String title, String author, and boolean checkedOut (initially false). Add a constructor, and methods:

void checkOut() — marks the book as checked out
void returnBook() — marks it as available
boolean isAvailable() — returns !checkedOut
void printStatus() — prints title, author, and “Available” or “Checked Out”

In main, create an array of 4 Book objects.
Write a method int countAvailable(Book[] books) that counts available books.
Write a method Book findByTitle(Book[] books, String title) that returns the first matching book, or null if not found. Guard against null in main.
Check out two books, then print the full inventory using a loop and printStatus(). Print how many books are still available.

title: static vs Instance
text:
Learning Outcomes

Write a static method — declared with static, taking only parameters (no access to instance fields) — and call it with ClassName.method(args)
Write a static field — declared with static — and explain that all objects of the class share the same copy
Distinguish static members (belong to the class) from instance members (belong to each object) in a class definition
Decide whether a method or field should be static or instance for a given design problem
Write a class that combines static and instance members and call each correctly from main

title: static vs Instance
section: You Have Already Used Static Methods
text:
You Have Already Used Static Methods
You have been calling static methods since day one:
Integer.parseInt("42")     // static — called on Integer, not on an object
Math.abs(-5)               // static — called on Math
Math.max(3, 7)             // static — called on Math
Notice: no new Integer() or new Math() first. You call directly on the class name.
That is the signature of a static member — it belongs to the class itself, not to any specific object.

Callback to familiar code. Students have been calling Integer.parseInt() since they first read user input, and Math.abs() when they needed absolute value. They never wondered why there’s no “new Integer()” — now they find out. The class name before the dot, rather than an object variable, is the tell.

title: static vs Instance
text:
What Does static Mean?









Instance member
Static member




Belongs to
Each individual object
The class itself


How many copies
One per object
Exactly one, shared by all


How to call/access
object.method() or object.field
ClassName.method() or ClassName.field


Knows this?
Yes
No — there is no “this” object



One-line rule: if the method or field doesn’t need to know which object it’s working with, make it static.


The table is the core reference — come back to it. The “no this” rule is the practical guide: if you tried to write a static method that accessed name or grade (instance fields), the compiler would refuse with “non-static field cannot be referenced from a static context.” Static methods only know about their parameters and other static fields.

title: static vs Instance
static vs Instance
static vs Instance
static vs Instance
static vs Instance
text:
When to Use Each







Situation
Use




The method needs to read or change this object’s fields
instance method


The method is a pure utility — only needs its parameters
static method


Each object should track its own value
instance field


All objects should share one value (counter, constant)
static field



Quick test: Can the method be written without ever mentioning any object? → static. Does it need “this” object’s data? → instance.

Walk through the decision table with concrete examples: area() needs this rectangle’s width and height → instance. gradeToLetter(int g) only needs the integer → static. name, grade — each student has their own → instance. totalCreated — one number for all students → static. Drill this with a few more examples until the decision becomes automatic.

title: static vs Instance
static vs Instance
text:
Common Mistakes






Warning


Accessing an instance field from a static method
static void print() { IO.println(name); }  // ✗ — which object's name?
Static methods have no this. They can only use parameters and other static members.









Warning


Calling an instance method without an object
class Foo { void bar() { } }
Foo.bar();   // ✗ — bar() is an instance method, not static
Use new Foo().bar() or store an object first.









Warning


Making everything static “just to be safe” If every method is static, you’re not doing OOP — you’re just using a class as a namespace. Reserve static for methods that genuinely have no object state to read.




The first mistake produces the compiler error “non-static variable cannot be referenced from a static context” — one of the most common errors beginners see. Reading the error carefully: “non-static” = instance field, “static context” = inside a static method. The fix is always the same: either make the method instance (remove static), or pass the data as a parameter instead of reading a field.

title: static vs Instance
Writing a Class
text:
Learning Outcomes

Write a class definition with the correct syntax: fields declared in the class body, a constructor with the same name as the class
Write a constructor that initializes fields using this.field = parameter
Create an object by calling new ClassName(args) and passing arguments that match the constructor
Access and modify an object’s fields using dot notation after construction
Use a student-defined class inside a loop or alongside other objects to solve a problem

title: Writing a Class
Writing a Class
Writing a Class
text:
Fields — The Object’s State
Fields are variables declared inside the class, outside any method:
class Student {
    String name;    // each Student object gets its own name
    int grade;      // each Student object gets its own grade
    int year;
}

Every object built from Student gets its own copy of name, grade, and year
Fields are accessible from any method inside the class
Default values if not set: 0 for numbers, null for Strings



Distinguish fields from local variables (which only exist during one method call). A field lives for the entire lifetime of the object — created when the object is created, destroyed when the object is no longer used. Each object’s fields are completely independent, just like each student has their own grade on a test.

title: Writing a Class
Writing a Class
section: this — Which Object Are We Talking About?
text:
this — Which Object Are We Talking About?
Inside the constructor (or any instance method), this refers to the object currently being built or called on.
Student(String name, int grade) {
    this.name  = name;    // this.name  = the FIELD;  name  = the PARAMETER
    this.grade = grade;   // this.grade = the FIELD;  grade = the PARAMETER
}
Without this, the parameter would shadow the field — Java wouldn’t know which name you meant.






Tip


Rule of thumb: use this.fieldName on the left-hand side whenever the parameter has the same name as the field. It removes all ambiguity.




The this keyword is the biggest stumbling block in constructors. Draw it out: when we write new Student(“Alice”, 88), Java creates a fresh empty Student object, then calls the constructor with that object as “this”. this.name refers to the field inside that brand-new object; name (alone) refers to the parameter. Assigning this.name = name copies the parameter value into the field — that’s what “initializing” means.

title: Writing a Class
text:
Creating an Object with new
Student alice = new Student("Alice", 88);
Student bob   = new Student("Bob",   74);
What happens step by step:

Java creates a fresh Student object in memory
The constructor Student("Alice", 88) runs
this.name = "Alice" and this.grade = 88 are set
The finished object is handed to alice

Now alice.name is "Alice" and alice.grade is 88.


Walk through the four steps slowly. Step 2 is the key one students miss — the constructor isn’t called manually, it’s called by new automatically. Step 4 is the reference assignment: alice doesn’t hold the object itself, it holds a link to it (just like arrays). This is why alice.name accesses the field through the dot.

title: Writing a Class
text:
Accessing Fields After Construction
Once an object exists, use dot notation to read or change its fields:
Student alice = new Student("Alice", 88);

IO.println(alice.name);    // Alice
IO.println(alice.grade);   // 88

alice.grade = 95;          // update the field
IO.println(alice.grade);   // 95
Fields set by the constructor are just variables — you can read and change them the same way as in deck 18.

Nothing new syntactically here — reinforce that dot notation works exactly as shown in deck 18. The constructor set the initial values; nothing prevents the field from being changed afterward. (Later, the private keyword and getters/setters will control this — but that’s deck 20+.)

title: Writing a Class
section: Using a Class in a Loop

title: Writing a Class
Writing a Class
text:
Common Mistakes






Warning


Constructor name doesn’t match class name class Student { student(...) { } } — lowercase s gives a compile error. The constructor name must match exactly, capital letter included.









Warning


Adding a return type to the constructor void Student(...) — a void return type turns it into a regular method, not a constructor. The real constructor never runs.









Warning


Forgetting this. when field and parameter share a name name = name; — both sides refer to the parameter. The field is never set (stays null).









Warning


Forgetting new Student alice = Student("Alice", 88); — missing new is a compile error. You must use new to create an object.




The “void Student” mistake is subtle — Java sees it as a regular method named Student, not a constructor, and generates a default constructor instead. Students will then find their fields are null despite “calling the constructor.” The this.name = name vs name = name mistake silently leaves the field at its default value — a null name or 0 grade.

Passing Arrays to Methods
text:
Learning Outcomes

Declare and call a method that takes an int[] parameter and returns a computed value
Explain that arrays are passed by reference — changes inside the method persist in the caller’s array
Contrast array parameters (reference) with primitive parameters (copied) and predict the outcome of each
Write void methods that modify an array in place (fill, double elements, replace)
Compose array methods — call one from another and use the return value as an argument

title: Passing Arrays to Methods
Passing Arrays to Methods
text:
Two Ways to Pass Data
When you pass something to a method, Java has two strategies:


Photocopy
The method gets its own copy. Changes don’t affect the original.
Used for: int, double, boolean, char, String

Shared link
The method gets a link to the same thing. Changes affect the original.
Used for: arrays (and objects)



The photocopy/shared-link analogy works for almost every student. A photocopy: you can mark it up however you want; your friend’s original is untouched. A shared Google Doc link: your edit appears in their browser immediately. Arrays behave like the shared link. Primitives behave like the photocopy. Spend time here — this is one of the most surprising concepts in the course.

title: Passing Arrays to Methods
Passing Arrays to Methods
Passing Arrays to Methods
text:
Side-by-Side Comparison









Primitive
Array




What is passed
A copy of the value
A link to the array


Method modifies its parameter
Original unchanged
Original changes


Way to think about it
Photocopy
Shared link


Example type
int, double
int[], String[]



void test(int n, int[] arr) {
    n = 99;           // no effect on caller's variable
    arr[0] = 99;      // DOES affect caller's array
}

The table summarizes the rule. After showing the table, trace the test() example: n is a local copy (changing it does nothing outside), arr is a shared link (changing arr[0] changes the original). Ask students: “After calling test(x, scores), what is x? What is scores[0]?” x is unchanged; scores[0] is 99.

title: Passing Arrays to Methods

title: Passing Arrays to Methods

title: Passing Arrays to Methods
Passing Arrays to Methods
Passing Arrays to Methods
text:
Common Mistakes






Warning


Expecting a modified primitive to persist If a method changes int n, the caller’s variable is unaffected. Primitives are copied.









Warning


Accidentally modifying an array you meant to leave alone If your method reads the array but a bug writes to it, the caller’s data is silently corrupted. Double-check that read-only methods don’t do any arr[i] = ... assignments.









Warning


Forgetting .length when passing an array between methods The array carries its length — you don’t need to pass it separately. arr.length works inside any method that received arr.









Warning


Returning an array index when you should return the value (or vice versa) Linear search returns the index. Sum returns the value. Be clear about which your method promises to return.




The second mistake is especially insidious because there’s no error message — the bug is silent. Write tests that print the caller’s array before and after any method call until the pass-by-reference behavior becomes second nature.

title: Passing Arrays to Methods
Arrays: Basics
text:
Learning Outcomes

Explain what an array is and describe the problem it solves
Declare and initialize a one-dimensional array using new int[n] or initializer syntax {...}
Access and modify array elements using zero-based index notation, including arr[arr.length - 1] for the last element
Loop over an array using for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) to read or write every element
Apply array algorithms — sum, max, min, linear search, count — using accumulator and counter patterns
Identify the cause of an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and correct it

title: Arrays: Basics
Arrays: Basics
text:
The Mailbox Analogy
Imagine a row of numbered mailboxes in an apartment building:

Every mailbox holds one letter (one value)
All mailboxes hold the same type of mail (same type)
The building has a fixed number of mailboxes (fixed length)
Mailboxes are numbered starting at 0 (zero-based index)


An array is that row of mailboxes — a single named container holding many values of the same type.

The physical image matters. Zero is the first mailbox because it is 0 steps from the front of the row — the index is an OFFSET, not a count. This is why the last mailbox is always one less than the total: 5 boxes → last index is 4. Come back to this image whenever students get confused about indexing.

title: Arrays: Basics
text:
Declaring an Array
int[] scores = new int[5];



Part
Meaning




int[]
Type: an array of int values


scores
Name of the array variable


new int[5]
Create a new array with space for 5 integers



After this declaration, scores holds 5 integers, all initialized to 0.
String[] names = new String[3];    // 3 Strings, all null
double[] prices = new double[10];  // 10 doubles, all 0.0

new int[5] reserves a fixed block of 5 adjacent memory slots. The size is set once — you cannot expand an array after creation. This is a key limitation to mention early (lists/ArrayLists solve this, but that’s a later topic). Default values: numeric types get 0, booleans get false, object types (String, etc.) get null.

title: Arrays: Basics
Arrays: Basics
text:
Array Length
Every array knows how long it is:
int[] scores = new int[5];
IO.println(scores.length);   // prints 5






Note


arr.length is a property, not a method — no parentheses! Compare: str.length() for Strings uses (), but arr.length does not.







Syntax
Note




String length
str.length()
Method — use ()


Array length
arr.length
Property — no ()




Students who just learned String.length() will immediately write arr.length() — a very common mistake that produces a compile error. The distinction is that arr.length is a public field, not a method call. It’s worth saying out loud: “No parentheses on arrays.” They will thank you later.

title: Arrays: Basics
Arrays: Basics
text:
Looping Over an Array
The standard idiom for visiting every element:
int[] scores = {88, 74, 91, 65, 78};

for (int i = 0; i < scores.length; i++) {
    IO.println("Score " + i + ": " + scores[i]);
}
Output:
Score 0: 88
Score 1: 74
Score 2: 91
Score 3: 65
Score 4: 78

Start at i = 0 (first index)
Stop when i < arr.length (not <=!)
Access the element as arr[i]


The condition i < arr.length (not <=) is the most important line. Walk through why: if length is 5, valid indices are 0–4. When i reaches 5, i < 5 is false — loop exits safely. i <= 5 would try to access scores[5], which doesn’t exist (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException). Burn this pattern into muscle memory: 0 to < length.

title: Arrays: Basics
Arrays: Basics
Arrays: Basics
text:
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
Accessing an index that doesn’t exist crashes the program:
int[] arr = new int[5];   // valid indices: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

IO.println(arr[5]);       // ✗ crash! index 5 doesn't exist
IO.println(arr[-1]);      // ✗ crash! negative indices don't exist
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: 5
Common causes:

Using i <= arr.length instead of i < arr.length
Hardcoding an index equal to the length
Calculating an index incorrectly


When students see this exception, ask them to find the line number in the error message and look at the index that was used. Is it equal to the length? That’s the <= vs < mistake. Is it negative? They probably subtracted one too many. The stack trace line number is their friend.

title: Arrays: Basics
Arrays: Basics
text:
Common Mistakes






Warning


arr.length without parentheses arr.length() is a compile error — arrays use a property, not a method.









Warning


i <= arr.length in the loop condition This accesses one index past the end → ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Always use i < arr.length.









Warning


Starting at index 1 accidentally If you want every element, start at i = 0. Starting at 1 skips the first.









Warning


Confusing the index with the value scores[i] is the value; i is the position. IO.println(i) prints the index, not the grade.




Walk through each mistake with a short “what would happen?” exercise. Students often get length vs last-index confused even after the first example — it helps to ask them explicitly: “If the array has 5 elements, what is scores.length? What is the last valid index?”

title: Arrays: Basics
Loop Patterns
text:
Learning Outcomes

Implement the accumulator pattern to compute a running total, product, or maximum
Implement the counter pattern to count elements that satisfy a condition
Implement the sentinel pattern to loop until a special input value signals termination
Combine accumulator and counter patterns in a single loop to solve multi-goal problems
Identify which loop pattern applies to a given problem

title: Loop Patterns
text:
What Is a Pattern?
A loop pattern is a reusable template — the same loop shape works for many different problems.
Think of it like a cookie cutter: the cutter doesn’t care what flavor of dough you use. You just press and cut.



Pattern
What it does




Accumulator
Builds up a value iteration by iteration


Counter
Counts how many iterations satisfy a condition


Sentinel
Runs until a special “stop” value appears




Frame this deck as building a toolkit. Students already know the mechanics from decks 11–12; now they’re learning to NAME the shapes. Naming patterns matters: it lets you talk about code, recognize problems faster, and write solutions without starting from scratch each time.

title: Loop Patterns
text:
The Accumulator Pattern
Template:
type result = <identity>;    // initialize BEFORE the loop

for (...) {
    result = result <op> nextValue;    // update each iteration
}

// use result AFTER the loop
Three variations:



Goal
Identity
Operation




Sum
0
+


Product
1
*


Concatenation
""
+ (String)




The “identity” value is the one that leaves the result unchanged: 0 + anything = anything; 1 * anything = anything; “” + anything = anything. Starting with the wrong identity gives a wrong answer (e.g., starting a product at 0 always gives 0).

title: Loop Patterns
Loop Patterns
Loop Patterns
Loop Patterns
Loop Patterns
Loop Patterns
Loop Patterns
Loop Patterns
text:
Identifying the Pattern
When you see a loop problem, ask these questions:

Do I need to build up a value? → Accumulator (sum, product, max)
Do I need to count how many meet a condition? → Counter
Do I not know how many iterations there will be? → Sentinel (while)
Do I need both a total AND a count? → Both, same loop



Walk through the decision tree slowly. Many real problems combine two or more patterns — average is accumulator + counter, grade stats is accumulator + counter + max. Learning to spot each pattern independently is the first step to composing them correctly.

title: Loop Patterns
Loop Patterns
text:
Worksheet

Write a loop that reads 10 integers from the user and prints their product.
Write a loop that reads integers until the user enters 0. Count how many of the entered numbers were negative. Print the count.
Write a loop that reads integers until the user enters -1 (the sentinel). Compute and print the sum and the maximum. Guard against the case where no numbers were entered.
Identify the pattern. For each problem below, name the pattern(s) you would use:


Add up all even numbers from 1 to 100.


Find the smallest number entered by the user (stop at "done").


Count how many words in a list start with the letter 'A'.


Compute the average of grades entered until the user types -1.


Challenge: Write void gradeReport() that reads grades from the user until they enter -1. Print the average, the number of passing grades (≥ 60), and the highest grade. Use a single loop.

title: while Loops
text:
Learning Outcomes

Write a while loop with a correct initialization, condition, and update
Write accumulator loops that maintain a running sum, product, or count
Write sentinel loops that read input until a special value is seen
Identify and correct off-by-one errors in loop conditions
Trace a loop’s execution iteration by iteration using a variable table

title: while Loops
while Loops
section: The Real World Already Has Loops
text:
The Real World Already Has Loops

“Keep hitting snooze until you feel rested.”


“Keep stirring until the sauce thickens.”


“Keep reading messages until the inbox is empty.”

Computers need the same idea — repeat an action while a condition holds.

Draw on universal experiences. The snooze alarm lands especially well for college students. The key insight: the condition is checked before each repetition, not just once at the start. This is the mental model they need before seeing any syntax.

title: while Loops
while Loops
text:
Loop Anatomy
Every while loop has three essential parts:
int i = 1;           // 1. INITIALIZE  — set up the variable before the loop

while (i <= 5) {     // 2. CONDITION   — checked before every iteration
    IO.println(i);
    i = i + 1;       // 3. UPDATE      — move toward the condition becoming false
}


The three-part structure is the grammar of every while loop. If any one part is missing, the loop either never runs or runs forever. Drill this cycle aloud: Initialize — Check — Body — Update — Check — Body — Update — Check…

title: while Loops
section: Tracing a Loop — The Variable Table
text:
Tracing a Loop — The Variable Table
int i = 1;
while (i <= 3) {
    IO.println("Hello " + i);
    i = i + 1;
}



Iteration
i at start
i <= 3?
Output
i after update




1
1
true
Hello 1
2


2
2
true
Hello 2
3


3
3
true
Hello 3
4


—
4
false
(loop exits)
—




Walk through the table row by row, slowly. The variable table is THE debugging skill for loops — students should be able to fill one in for any while loop. Emphasize: the condition is checked with the NEW value of i AFTER the update, before the next body runs.

title: while Loops
while Loops
text:
The Accumulator Pattern
Goal: add up all numbers from 1 to 5.
int sum = 0;          // accumulator — starts at 0 (the identity for addition)
int i = 1;

while (i <= 5) {
    sum = sum + i;    // add current number to running total
    i = i + 1;
}

IO.println("Sum: " + sum);   // Sum: 15



i
sum before
sum after




1
0
1


2
1
3


3
3
6


4
6
10


5
10
15




The accumulator pattern: set up a “bucket” (sum = 0) before the loop; pour each value in during the loop; read the bucket after the loop. For products, start at 1 instead of 0. For counting, add 1 conditionally inside the loop. These are the three flavors mentioned in the learning outcomes.

title: while Loops
while Loops
while Loops
while Loops
while Loops
while Loops
text:
Common Mistakes






Warning


Forgetting the update The condition never becomes false → program freezes. Press Ctrl + C.









Warning


Off-by-one i < n stops one short. i <= n includes n. Trace the last iteration to be sure.









Warning


Wrong initialization Starting at 0 vs. 1 changes how many times the body runs. Count on your fingers if needed.









Warning


Forgetting the second read in a sentinel loop Read the value both before the loop and at the bottom of the body. Miss either one and things break.




These four mistakes cover the vast majority of while loop bugs students will write. Pair each with the variable-table tracing technique — it catches all of them mechanically.

Methods with Parameters
text:
Learning Outcomes

Explain what a parameter is and why methods need them
Define methods that accept one or more parameters of specified types
Distinguish between a parameter (in the definition) and an argument (in the call)
Explain that argument order matters and that parameters are local to the method
Trace a method call and show how argument values flow into parameters

title: Methods with Parameters
section: The Problem with Last Lecture’s Methods

title: Methods with Parameters
text:
The Spell Needs a Target

This is the key conceptual slide of the lecture. Start with the actual spells from last lecture — avadaKedavra() and protego() — and expose their vagueness. They didn’t take any targets. In a real duel, that would be absurd: you aim every spell. Then introduce Reparo as a new example that makes the targeting idea especially vivid: the same spell can fix glasses, a vase, a wand — the only thing that changes is what you point it at. The spell name tells Java what to do; the target tells it what to do it to. That target is what we are about to call a parameter. Let this slide land before any code or vocabulary appears — the intuition must come first.

Last lecture, our spells looked like this:
avadaKedavra();   // attacks... whom, exactly?
protego();         // defends... against what?
In a real duel, that would be absurd. Harry doesn’t just cast Expelliarmus into the air — he aims it. Every spell needs a target.
Consider a different spell: Reparo — it fixes broken things.
But which broken thing? That depends on what you point your wand at:

Point at Harry’s cracked glasses → the glasses are fixed
Point at a shattered vase → the vase is fixed
Point at a broken wand → the wand is fixed

The spell is the same every time. What changes is the target — the thing you aim it at.
The spell name tells Java what to do. The target tells Java what to do it to.
That target is what we are about to call a parameter.

title: Methods with Parameters
text:
The Coffee Machine

A third analogy that makes the parameter/argument distinction extremely concrete, and additionally explains type enforcement. The coffee machine has three containers — water, beans, milk. Each container is a parameter. What you pour into each container is the argument. You can vary the contents: soy milk, almond milk, oat milk all work in the milk container. Dark roast, medium roast, decaf all work in the beans container. But you cannot put beans in the water container — wrong type. The machine won’t run. This maps perfectly to Java: the method defines named slots (parameters) of specific types; what you provide at call time (arguments) must match those types; and within a type, you have freedom to vary the value. The “press the button” moment is calling the method. Take time on this slide — the tactile nature of containers and contents lands differently from the spell/recipe analogies, and the three together reinforce the same idea from three angles.

Imagine a single-serve coffee machine with three labeled containers:

A water container — holds water
A beans container — holds coffee beans
A milk container — holds milk

You fill each container, press the button, and the machine makes your coffee using whatever you put in.

The containers are the parameters — named slots that hold the inputs.
What you pour in is the argument — the actual value you provide each time.

title: Methods with Parameters
text:
What Is a Parameter?

Now the vocabulary arrives — AFTER two analogies have established the intuition. A parameter is the named slot (the container) in the method definition. An argument is what you pour into the slot at call time. The blank-form analogy is a third reinforcement: the parameter is the label on the blank (“Name:”); the argument is what you write in the blank (“Alice”). Students who connect with the magic analogy, the coffee machine, or the form — at least one of the three will stick. Present all three briefly and let students find their own anchor.

A parameter is a named placeholder in a method definition.
It represents a value that will be provided each time the method is called.
Think of it like a blank in a form:
Hello, _______!
         ↑
      parameter: "name"
      (blank to be filled in)
The form is written once. Each time someone fills it in, they provide a different name.
In Java, the parameter goes inside the parentheses of the method definition:
void greet(String name) {
    IO.println("Hello, " + name + "!");
}
The word name is the parameter. Inside the method body, name stands in for whatever value will be provided at call time.
One definition. Works for any name.






Note


A parameter has two parts: a type (String) and a name (name). The type tells Java what kind of value to expect. The name is how you refer to the value inside the method body.

title: Methods with Parameters
section: Defining a Method with a Parameter

title: Methods with Parameters
text:
What Is an Argument?

Now the second vocabulary word: argument. The distinction between parameter and argument is one of the most commonly confused pairs in intro CS. The mnemonic: parameter is in the (definition), argument is in the (call). The parentheses start with the same letter as definition and call — P for parameter/definition, A for argument/actual. Or just: parameter is what you name it in the definition; argument is what you put there when you call it. The blank-form analogy extends naturally: the parameter is the label on the blank (“Name:”); the argument is what you write in the blank (“Alice”).

When you call a method that has a parameter, you provide a value inside the parentheses. That value is called an argument.
greet("Alice");   // "Alice" is the argument
greet("Bob");     // "Bob" is the argument
Two new words — one for each side of the exchange:



Word
Where it appears
What it is




parameter
in the method definition
the placeholder


argument
in the method call
the actual value



Think of the blank-form analogy: - The blank labeled “Name:” is the parameter — it’s in the form definition - “Alice” written in the blank is the argument — it’s what you fill in
The form (method) is defined once with a blank. Each time you fill it in (call it), you provide a different argument.






Tip


An easy way to remember: Parameter is in the definition (think: Planning). Argument is in the call (think: Actual value).

title: Methods with Parameters
section: Calling a Method with an Argument

title: Methods with Parameters
text:
Tracing: How the Argument Flows

This is the most important mechanical slide of the lecture. Students need to see exactly what Java does when it hits a method call with an argument: it takes the argument value, copies it into the parameter, and then runs the method body with the parameter holding that value. Walk through the numbered steps explicitly. The “as if Java wrote” framing is useful: calling greet(“Alice”) is as if Java wrote String name = “Alice”; at the top of the method body, then ran the body. Show the trace for two different calls to make the substitution concrete.

When you call greet("Alice"), here is exactly what Java does:
void greet(String name) {         // 2. "Alice" is copied into name
    IO.println("Hello, " + name + "!");  // 3. name IS "Alice" here
}

void main() {
    greet("Alice");   // 1. call — argument "Alice" is provided
    greet("Bob");     // 4. call again — argument "Bob" is provided
}
Step by step:

greet("Alice") — Java sees a method call with argument "Alice"
Java copies "Alice" into the parameter name
The method body runs — everywhere name appears, it holds "Alice"
The method finishes. Then greet("Bob") starts the same process with "Bob"

It is as if Java wrote String name = "Alice"; at the very top of the method body, ran everything, then came back and did it again with String name = "Bob";.
Output:
Hello, Alice!
Hello, Bob!

Common Mistakes

Four mistakes, each tied to a specific concept in this lecture. Wrong argument count and wrong argument type are compile errors — caught early. Wrong argument order may compile (if types match or can be converted) but produces wrong output — the sneakiest kind of bug. Using a parameter outside its method is a compile error. Walk through each one and ask students to identify the problem before revealing it.

1. Wrong number of arguments
void greet(String name) { ... }

greet();             // ✗ — missing argument; won't compile
greet("Alice", "B"); // ✗ — too many; won't compile
greet("Alice");      // ✓

Learning Outcomes

Describe a String as a sequence of characters and use zero-based index positions to locate individual characters
Use .length(), .charAt(), .substring(), .toUpperCase(), and .toLowerCase() to work with String values
Explain what String immutability means and predict the result of String operations
Chain String operations to perform multi-step text transformations
Explain why .equals() must be used to compare Strings and apply it correctly

title: Strings
text:
What Is a String?

Students have been using Strings since week one — now they learn what is actually inside one. A String is a sequence of characters, stored in order, with each character at a numbered position starting from zero. The zero-based indexing is the key new idea here and it will come back in arrays. Use a concrete word — “Alice” — and show the index box diagram. Make sure students absorb: the LAST index is always length minus one, never length itself.

A String is a sequence of characters stored in order.
Each character sits at a numbered position, called its index.
Indexes start at zero — not one.
String name = "Alice";



Index
0
1
2
3
4




Character
A
l
i
c
e




First character: index 0
Last character: index 4 (which is length 5 minus 1)







Warning


The last valid index is always length - 1, never length itself. Asking for index 5 on "Alice" is an error.

title: Strings
section: Asking a String Things — The Dot
text:
Asking a String Things — The Dot

This is the key conceptual slide before any specific operations. Students have already seen .equals() on Strings — so they have encountered the dot before, but without explanation. Now explain it: when you put a dot after a String variable, you can ask that String to tell you something about itself or give you a transformed version. Each operation is written as variable.operationName(…). The parentheses are required even if there is nothing inside them. This framing — “asking the String something” — avoids the word method and is genuinely intuitive.

You already know how to do things with numbers: score + 10, total / count.
Strings work differently. To do something with a String, you write:
variableName.whatYouWantToDo(...)
The dot connects the String to the operation you want to perform.
String name = "Alice";

name.length()          // ask: how many characters are you?
name.charAt(0)         // ask: what is your character at index 0?
name.toUpperCase()     // ask: can you give me an uppercase version?
name.substring(1, 3)   // ask: can you give me characters 1 through 2?
Think of it as asking a question directly to the String value.
The String produces an answer — a new value you can store, print, or use.






Note


The parentheses () are always required, even when you are not putting anything inside them. You will see why this matters more when we cover methods later in the course.

title: Strings
Strings
text:
.charAt()

.charAt(i) produces the character at index i. This introduces char — a new type students haven’t seen. Keep it brief: a char holds exactly one character, written in single quotes. The main use of charAt for beginners: get the first character (charAt(0)), get the last character (charAt(length - 1)), check what a String starts with. Make sure students practice the zero-based index by asking them to predict charAt(0), charAt(1), etc. for a given String before showing the answers.

.charAt(i) asks the String for its character at index i.
String word = "Hello";

IO.println(word.charAt(0));   // H
IO.println(word.charAt(1));   // e
IO.println(word.charAt(4));   // o  (last character)
The result is a single character. In Java, a single character has its own type: char.
char first = word.charAt(0);   // first holds 'H'
IO.println(first);             // H
Note: char values are written in single quotes ' ' — not double quotes " ".

title: Strings
text:
.substring()

.substring() extracts a portion of a String. It has two forms: one argument (from start to end) and two arguments (from start, up to but not including end). The “end is exclusive” rule is the hardest part — stress it with examples. The diagram showing the slice with start included and end excluded is essential. Analogy: substring(1, 4) means “start at 1, stop just before 4” — like a half-open interval in math.

.substring() asks the String for a piece of itself.
One argument — from that index to the end:
String word = "Hello";
IO.println(word.substring(2));    // "llo"  (from index 2 to the end)
IO.println(word.substring(0));    // "Hello" (the whole thing)
Two arguments — from start up to (but not including) end:
String word = "Hello";
IO.println(word.substring(1, 4));   // "ell"  (indexes 1, 2, 3 — not 4)
IO.println(word.substring(0, 3));   // "Hel"  (indexes 0, 1, 2 — not 3)






Warning


The second argument is exclusive — the character at that index is not included.
substring(1, 4) gives you indexes 1, 2, 3 — not 4.

title: Strings
text:
.toUpperCase() and .toLowerCase()

These produce a new String with all characters converted. They do not affect the original. This is a preview of immutability (covered next slide). Show both directions, show that the original is unchanged, show that you must store the result to use it. Good practical use: normalizing user input for comparison — convert to lowercase before using .equals() so the comparison is case-insensitive.

.toUpperCase() produces an all-uppercase version of the String. .toLowerCase() produces an all-lowercase version.
String name = "Alice";

IO.println(name.toUpperCase());   // ALICE
IO.println(name.toLowerCase());   // alice
IO.println(name);                 // Alice  ← unchanged!
The original String is not affected — you get a new value back.
To use the result, store it:
String name  = "Alice";
String upper = name.toUpperCase();   // store the result

IO.println(upper);   // ALICE
IO.println(name);    // Alice — still the original

title: Strings
text:
Strings Are Immutable

Immutable means cannot be changed. Once a String is created, its characters are fixed — no operation changes it. Every String operation produces a NEW String. This is the most common source of bugs in this unit: students write name.toUpperCase() and then wonder why name is still lowercase. Because they did not store the result. The photocopy analogy works well: toUpperCase() makes a photocopy in uppercase — it does not alter the original.

Immutable means: once created, a String cannot be changed.
Every operation on a String produces a new String — it never alters the original.
String name = "alice";
name.toUpperCase();        // produces "ALICE" — but where did it go?

IO.println(name);          // alice — name is still lowercase
name.toUpperCase() produced a value. But we did not store it anywhere, so it was immediately discarded.
The fix — store the result:
String name  = "alice";
String upper = name.toUpperCase();   // store the new String

IO.println(name);    // alice  — original unchanged
IO.println(upper);   // ALICE  — the new one






Warning


String operations do not change the original. If you want to keep the result, you must store it in a variable.

title: Strings
text:
Chaining String Operations

Chaining means applying one operation to the result of another, in a single expression. The key insight: since each operation produces a new String, you can immediately apply another operation to that new String. Walk through the evaluation left to right. The most common use: lowercase before comparing (case-insensitive check). Or get the first character uppercased. Keep examples to two operations chained — more than two becomes hard to read.

Since each String operation produces a new String, you can immediately ask that new String another question.
String name = "alice smith";

// One at a time:
String upper = name.toUpperCase();      // "ALICE SMITH"
char first   = upper.charAt(0);        // 'A'

// Chained into one expression:
char first = name.toUpperCase().charAt(0);   // 'A'
The evaluation goes left to right:
name.toUpperCase().charAt(0)
      ↓
"ALICE SMITH".charAt(0)
      ↓
'A'

title: Strings
Strings
Strings
text:
Common Mistakes

Four mistakes that will appear constantly this week. The first two — not storing the result, and using == — are the most damaging because they produce no compile error, just wrong behavior. Off-by-one in substring is a close third.

1. Forgetting to store the result of a String operation
String name = "alice";
name.toUpperCase();         // result is produced and immediately discarded
IO.println(name);           // still "alice" — nothing changed

String upper = name.toUpperCase();   // ✓ — store it
IO.println(upper);          // ALICE
2. Using == instead of .equals()
String color = IO.readln("Favorite color: ");
if (color == "blue") { ... }          // ✗ — unreliable
if (color.equals("blue")) { ... }     // ✓
3. Off-by-one in .substring()
String word = "Hello";
IO.println(word.substring(1, 4));   // "ell" — indexes 1, 2, 3
IO.println(word.substring(1, 5));   // "ello" — indexes 1, 2, 3, 4
// The second argument is the first index NOT included
4. Using .length() as an index
String name = "Alice";           // length is 5
char last = name.charAt(5);      // ERROR — index 5 does not exist
char last = name.charAt(name.length() - 1);   // ✓ — index 4

text:
Learning Outcomes

Explain why programs need conditionals and how they change the flow of execution
Write if and if/else statements to control which code runs based on a condition
Construct conditions using relational operators (<, >, <=, >=, ==, !=)
Trace the execution path of a conditional given a specific input value
Compare Strings with .equals() and explain why == does not work for Strings

title: Conditionals: if and else
text:
Programs Don’t Always Go Straight

Every program written so far runs the same way every time: top to bottom, one line after another, no detours. That is a straight line. But real useful programs need to make decisions — do this in one situation, do something else in another. That is a branch. The visual of a straight line versus a Y-shaped split is the central image of this lecture. The humor slide is the hook: students already know “If you are happy and you know it, clap your hands.” Java says the same thing. Show the Java version first for laughs, then use it to introduce the real syntax.

Every program we have written so far does the same thing every run — top to bottom, no detours.

But most programs need to make decisions.

title: Conditionals: if and else
text:
Conditionals in Everyday English

Before showing any more Java syntax, ground the idea in language students already use. Conditionals are not a computer science invention — they are a feature of every human language. We navigate our entire lives using if/else logic. Java just requires us to be more precise about it: the condition must be something that is either true or false, and the body must be inside braces. Show the English-to-Java translation side by side. This makes the syntax feel like a formality rather than something alien.

We use conditionals constantly — in language, in decisions, in instructions.


In English:

If it is raining, take an umbrella.
If the light is red, stop.
If you are hungry, eat something.
If the tank is empty, get gas.


The structure is always the same:
if [some condition is true]
    then do [something]

title: Conditionals: if and else
text:
Relational Operators

Relational operators produce a boolean — true or false. Students have seen these symbols in math class; the only ones that look different are == (equality, not assignment) and != (not equal). Spend a moment on == vs = — this is the most common mistake in this entire unit. In math, = means equality. In Java, = means assignment and == means equality. They are completely different. Mention this now, and it will appear again in common mistakes.

A condition is built from a relational operator — a comparison that produces true or false.



Operator
Meaning
Example
Result




<
less than
3 < 5
true


>
greater than
3 > 5
false


<=
less than or equal to
5 <= 5
true


>=
greater than or equal to
6 >= 10
false


==
equal to
4 == 4
true


!=
not equal to
4 != 5
true

title: Arithmetic Expressions
text:
Learning Outcomes

Write arithmetic expressions using +, -, *, /, and %
Explain how integer division differs from regular division and predict its result
Predict the order of evaluation in an expression by applying operator precedence rules
Use parentheses to control evaluation order
Convert string input to an integer with Integer.parseInt and use it in a computation

title: Arithmetic Expressions
text:
Arithmetic

This is the motivational opener — spend real time here. The goal is to make students feel the significance of what they are about to learn. Every useful computation that a computer performs, from a video game physics engine to GPS navigation to the systems that guide spacecraft, reduces to arithmetic. Not magic — arithmetic. And the computer does it at a scale and speed that is hard to grasp. The course arc: we learn the operators today, then we combine them in expressions, then we repeat them billions of times using loops, then we apply them to collections of data. Today is the foundation of all of that.

title: Arithmetic Expressions
text:
Arithmetic
Every program that has ever run on a computer — games, GPS, streaming video, weather forecasts, the systems that control spacecraft — is built on arithmetic.
A modern computer can perform hundreds of millions to billions of arithmetic operations every second.

title: Arithmetic Expressions
text:
Arithmetic
What makes programs powerful is not any one operation — it’s combining simple operations and repeating them at enormous speed.
Here is the course in one sentence:

Learn the operators → combine them into expressions → repeat them with loops → apply them to collections of data.

Today: the operators.

title: Arithmetic Expressions
text:
What Is an Expression?

Name the concept before diving into operators. An expression is any piece of code that the computer can evaluate to produce a single value. 3 + 4 is an expression. score * 2 is an expression. Even a lone literal like 42 is an expression. Expressions appear everywhere in programs — on the right side of an assignment, as arguments to IO.println, and later as conditions in if statements and loops. Once students see that distinction, every piece of syntax they encounter will feel more organized.

An expression is any combination of values, variables, and operators that the computer can evaluate to produce a single value.



Expression
Evaluates to




3 + 4
7


10 - 3
7


score * 2
twice whatever score holds


100
100

title: Arithmetic Expressions
text:
Arithmetic Operators

Walk through each operator one at a time. Addition, subtraction, and multiplication are unsurprising — just flag that multiplication uses * not ×. Division is where things get interesting; hold the full explanation for the next slide. Modulo is the one students have never seen before — introduce the symbol and give the one-line definition, then hold examples for its own slide. The table is a reference; students should not try to memorize it on first pass.

Java has five arithmetic operators:



Operator
Name
Example
Result




+
Addition
3 + 4
7


-
Subtraction
10 - 3
7


*
Multiplication
6 * 7
42


/
Division
10 / 4
2 ← watch out


%
Modulo (remainder)
10 % 3
1

title: Arithmetic Expressions
text:
Operator Precedence

PEMDAS from math class still applies in Java. Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction. Within the same level, evaluation goes left to right. Parentheses override everything. Show a worked example where the answer changes depending on whether parentheses are present. The practical advice — when in doubt, add parentheses — is worth repeating. A program with extra parentheses is easier to read and less likely to have a subtle bug.

Java follows the same precedence rules as mathematics.
PEMDAS still applies:

Parentheses first
Multiplication and division (left to right)
Addition and subtraction (left to right)

title: Arithmetic Expressions
text:
Integer Division

This is one of the most common surprises for beginners and it will bite them for weeks if they do not understand it clearly. When both operands are ints, Java performs integer division: the result is always a whole number and the decimal part is simply dropped — not rounded, just gone. 7 / 2 is 3, not 3.5, not 4. Show this with several examples. Then show how to get a decimal result: if either operand is a double, the division is decimal division. Make the connection back to types: it is the type of the operands that determines what kind of division happens.

Here is the most common surprise in this entire lecture:
int result = 7 / 2;
IO.println(result);    // prints 3, not 3.5

When both values are whole numbers, Java does integer division — the decimal part is dropped.

title: Arithmetic Expressions
text:
The Modulo Operator %

Modulo is the one operator most students haven’t seen before. The concept is simple — it is the remainder after division — but it takes a moment to click. Walk through the division-with-remainder picture: 7 divided by 2 goes 3 times with 1 left over. That leftover is what % gives you. Then show the practical uses, which are genuinely useful and will appear repeatedly throughout the course: checking even/odd, extracting the last digit of a number, wrapping around a fixed range.

% gives the remainder after integer division.

Think of it as division with leftovers:
7 ÷ 2 → goes 3 times, with 1 left over
7 % 2  →  1

title: Arithmetic Expressions
text:
Introducing Flowcharts

Introduce flowcharts as a planning tool before writing code. Professional programmers sketch the logic of a program before writing a single line — flowcharts are one way to do that. Three symbols are enough for now: the oval marks where a program starts and ends; the rectangle describes a step or action; the arrow shows what happens next. Diamonds (for decisions) come in the next lecture when we cover conditionals. Show a completely non-programming example first — making toast — so students absorb the symbols without the distraction of syntax. Then show a programming example.

Before writing code, it helps to plan what the program should do.

A flowchart is a diagram that shows the steps of a program and how they connect.


Three symbols are enough for now:



Symbol
Shape
Meaning




Start / End
Oval
Where the program begins and ends


Step
Rectangle
A single action (compute, read, print)


Flow
Arrow
What happens next

title: Arithmetic Expressions
text:
Integer.parseInt — Numbers from the User

IO.readln always produces a String — even if the user types 42, the program receives the text “42”, not the number 42. That distinction matters because you cannot do arithmetic on text. To convert “42” to the number 42, use Integer.parseInt. The syntax is straightforward: wrap the String in Integer.parseInt(…). Mention that if the user types something that is not a valid number — like “hello” — the program will crash. Handling that gracefully is a topic for later in the course.

IO.readln always produces a String — even if the user types a number.
String input = IO.readln("How many minutes? ");
// input holds "137" — the TEXT, not the number

You cannot do arithmetic on a String:
input / 60    // ERROR — can't divide text

title: Arithmetic Expressions
text:
Putting It Together

Walk through the flowchart first, then the code. Trace through a concrete example — 137 minutes — step by step with the class before running the program. 137 / 60 = 2 (integer division, decimal dropped). 137 % 60 = 17 (remainder). Output: “2 hours and 17 minutes.” Make sure students verify the math by hand before the program confirms it. This builds the habit of reasoning about code before running it.

Problem: Ask the user how many minutes they have been studying. Print the equivalent hours and minutes.

title: Arithmetic Expressions
text:
String Concatenation

This is the formal introduction of string concatenation, deferred from the variables deck. The + operator does two different things depending on the types involved. int + int is arithmetic. String + anything is concatenation — the values are joined into a single String. The anything part is important: Java automatically converts a number to its text form before joining. Show the clean cases first, then the surprising mixed case. The left-to-right evaluation rule is the key to understanding “5” + 3 + 4 = “534” vs 5 + 3 + “4” = “84”. Connect back to deck 02: we printed labels and values on separate lines because we did not have concatenation yet — now we can put them on the same line.

The + operator does different things depending on the types involved.

With two numbers — addition:
int a = 5;
int b = 3;
IO.println(a + b);     // prints: 8

title: Arithmetic Expressions
text:
Common Mistakes

Four mistakes that will appear in student code in the first few weeks. Integer division truncation is the most common — stress it again. The concatenation surprise (mixing + with Strings and numbers in unexpected ways) is the most confusing. Make sure students leave knowing these pitfalls by name so they can recognize them when they appear.

1. Expecting a decimal from integer division
int result = 7 / 2;
IO.println(result);    // prints 3 — not 3.5

Fix: make one operand a decimal — 7.0 / 2.

title: Arithmetic Expressions
text:
Practice problems

Reserve the last 20-30 minutes. Problems 1-3 are prediction/tracing — students work on paper first, then verify in the IDE. Problems 4-5 require writing code. Problem 6 is the synthesis problem that combines everything from today with IO.readln. Common things to watch for: integer division surprises, concatenation vs addition confusion, forgetting Integer.parseInt.

text: Hello World

title: What Is a Program?
text:
Learning Outcomes


Concepts

Using vs. programming a computer
Precision, ambiguity, and programming languages
Hardware basics (CPU, RAM, Storage)
Sequential top-to-bottom execution


Skills

Write a Java program using void main()
Print exact console output via IO.println
Trace and predict program output
Document code with single-line comments (//)

title: What Is a Program?
text:
What Is a Computer?

Brief and grounded — just enough to set up the “everything is a computer” point later. Hit the three parts: CPU executes instructions, RAM is fast scratch-pad memory that vanishes when power goes off, storage is where things persist. The goal is not a hardware lecture — it’s to plant the idea that a computer is a machine that executes instructions, and that a phone is also a machine that executes instructions.

A computer is a machine built around three things:












Part
What it does




CPU
The brain — fetches and executes instructions, billions per second


Memory (RAM)
The scratch pad — fast, but gone when the power goes off


Storage
The filing cabinet — slow, but permanent




Everything else — keyboard, screen, WiFi — is just input and output.

title: What Is a Program?
section: Your Phone Is Also a Computer
text:
Your Phone Is Also a Computer

Students relate to phones far more than to desktop PCs. The key insight: a phone has a CPU, RAM, and storage — it IS a computer. The difference is that phone manufacturers have wrapped everything in a layer of apps and made it very hard to program the device directly. But every single app was written by a programmer. This sets up the “using vs. programming” distinction on the next slide.

Under the hood, your phone has a CPU, RAM, and storage.
It is a computer — manufacturers just hide the machinery behind apps.

Think about every app on your phone:

The alarm app
The maps app
The game you play on the bus
The on-screen keyboard

title: What Is a Program?
section: Your Phone Is Also a Computer
text:
Your Phone Is Also a Computer
Every one of these was written by a programmer who sat down and wrote instructions, one line at a time.
That is what you are learning to do.

title: What Is a Program?
section: Two Ways to Use a Computer
text:
Two Ways to Use a Computer

This is the conceptual heart of the first lecture. Spend time here. When you “use” a computer you’re running someone else’s program. When you “program” a computer you are the one writing the instructions the machine will follow. The second path is harder but it’s also what gives you real power over the machine.

title: What Is a Program?
section: Two Ways to Use a Computer
text:
Two Ways to Use a Computer


Using a Computer

Open an app → it runs
Click a button → something happens
Someone else wrote those instructions
You follow the rules someone else set


Programming a Computer

You write the instructions
The computer does exactly what you say
You set the rules
(Whether or not that’s what you meant is another story)




Most people use computers. This course teaches you to program them.

title: What Is a Program?
text:
What Is a Program?

Introduce the recipe analogy here — it’s intuitive and you’ll return to it. A recipe is a list of precise, ordered steps that a cook follows. A program is exactly that, but for a CPU instead of a cook. Key word: PRECISE. “Add salt to taste” would be a bug.

A program is a precise, ordered sequence of instructions for a computer.
The best analogy: a recipe.



Recipe
Program




Ingredients
Data — numbers, text, …


Steps
Instructions


Cook
CPU


Finished dish
Output



A recipe tells a cook exactly what to do. A program tells a CPU exactly what to do.

title: What Is a Program?
text: What Is a Program?

title: What Is a Program?
section: Programming Is Like Mailing a Recipe
text:
Programming Is Like Mailing a Recipe

This is the key insight about completeness and unambiguity. When you cook yourself you can improvise. When you mail the recipe to a stranger, every step must be spelled out — they can’t call you mid-bake. A program is a mailed recipe: the computer follows it exactly with no improvisation and no common sense. If a step is missing or ambiguous, it either fails or does something wrong.

Imagine you’re cooking something following a recipe:

Something unclear? Improvise. Ask a friend. Use judgment.


Now imagine giving that recipe to a friend who is going camping for a few days and has no internet or phone:

They follow only what is written
They cannot call you mid-cook
“Add salt to taste” → useless. How much?
Every step must be complete and unambiguous

title: What Is a Program?
text:
Programs as recipes
A program is a recipe - the computer opens the envelope and follows the instructions exactly.
No improvising, no common sense, no filling in gaps.
 {fig-alt=“robot/computer holding an open envelope with a recipe inside that says”add a pinch of salt” — robot has a large “?” above its head and cannot proceed.”}

title: What Is a Program?
section: Why Can’t Computers Just Understand English?
text:
Why Can’t Computers Just Understand English?

Natural language is wonderfully ambiguous — that’s a feature for poetry and conversation, and a serious bug for programming. We invented programming languages precisely to eliminate ambiguity. This is why programs look the way they do: strange syntax, strict rules, no shortcuts. Every quirk of a programming language exists to make sure there is exactly one valid reading of every statement.

English is beautifully ambiguous:

“I saw a man on a hill with a telescope.”

title: What Is a Program?
section: Why Can’t Computers Just Understand English?
text:
Why Can’t Computers Just Understand English?
Humans resolve ambiguity with context, tone, and common sense.
Computers have none of these.
Programming languages are designed so every statement has exactly one meaning.
That is why they look the way they do — no shortcuts, no “you know what I mean.”

title: What Is a Program?
text:
Learning a New Language

Programming IS like learning a new language — make this connection explicit. The vocabulary is small compared to French or Spanish, but the grammar is absolute: no partial credit, no “close enough”, no context to save you from a typo. The good news is the vocabulary is tiny. The bad news is every rule is enforced by a machine that has no sympathy. Emphasize that this takes practice, not just reading.

Programming is genuinely like learning a new language:

Vocabulary: small — a few dozen keywords in Java
Grammar: absolute — one wrong character breaks everything
Accent: none allowed — spelling, capitalization, and punctuation are all exact

But like any language, you don’t learn it by reading about it.
You learn it by using it — making mistakes, getting confused, and practicing until it clicks.






Important


The in-class worksheets and homework are not optional extras. They are the practice reps. You cannot get fluent by watching someone else do it.

title: What Is a Program?
text:
What About AI?

Students are thinking about this already — address it directly and honestly. AI tools like ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot can write Java code, often impressively well. Don’t dismiss this. Be honest. Then give the real reason it’s not allowed: you’re here to build understanding and skill. If AI does the reps for you, you don’t build anything — and in an exam, on a job, when something breaks at 2am, you’re on your own. The calculator analogy is strong: you learned arithmetic before you were allowed to use a calculator, not because arithmetic is more important than calculators, but because you needed to understand what the calculator was doing.

Yes — AI tools can write code. Sometimes very well.
So why aren’t you allowed to use them in this course?
The same reason you learned long division before using a calculator:

Understanding why the code works is what makes you a programmer.

AI can hand you a correct answer without you understanding a thing. That works great — until:

You need to modify the code
Something breaks and you have to debug it
You sit down for an exam







Warning


AI use on assignments and tests is not allowed. This is not because AI is bad — it is a powerful tool you will likely use in your career. But right now, you need to build the skills. The reps matter.

title: What Is a Program?
text:
Your First Java Program

Use the modern Java 25 flexible-main syntax: void main() with no public static. IO.println is the course’s simplified output wrapper — no System.out.println boilerplate. Walk through each piece of the program carefully: void main() means “start here”, curly braces wrap a block of code, IO.println prints a line, the string is in double quotes, and the semicolon ends the statement like a period ends a sentence. Do NOT spend time on the compile/run cycle — students use an online IDE where that is invisible.

void main() {
    IO.println("Hello, World!");
}
Every piece has a job:



Piece
What it means




void main()
“Start here when the program runs”


{ }
Curly braces wrap a block of code


IO.println(...)
Print a line to the screen


"Hello, World!"
The text to print — always in double quotes


;
End of statement (like a period at the end of a sentence)

title: What Is a Program?
text:
What the Computer “Hears”

Lighten the mood — this is intentionally humorous. The underlying point is serious: the computer is completely literal. It has no intuition about what you “meant.” This slide sets up the importance of exact syntax, matched braces, and semicolons. Use it to open a conversation: what happens if the semicolon is missing? What if you write Println instead of println?

// What you type:                   // What the computer hears:
void main() {                       // "Dear Computer,"
    IO.println("Hello");            // "Please print 'Hello' on the screen."
}                                   // "Thanks and regards, Programmer"
The computer is completely literal. It does precisely what you wrote.
Miss a semicolon — error. Write Println instead of println — error. Forget a closing brace — error.

Programming feels hard at first because you are learning to think like someone with no common sense whatsoever.

That gets easier with practice. Promise.

title: COSC120 - Introduction to Computer Science I
text:
Course Description
This course surveys computer science and introduces object-oriented programming. A survey of the pivotal fields of computer science, including software engineering, computer networks, programming languages, algorithms, computer architecture, models of computation and operating systems. Students begin to solve simple problems using object-oriented programming. The emphasis is on implementing object-oriented designs. This course is suitable for non-majors who want an overview of computer science and to learn to solve problems with programs. COSC 120 satisfies the Core Curriculum requirement in Mathematics.
More specifically, in this course, we would

Learn to think algorithmically — breaking problems into precise, ordered steps that a computer can execute
Read, write, and reason about programs in Java
Understand how core programming concepts — variables, conditionals, loops, methods, and objects — work and interact
Build a foundation for further study in computer science

title: COSC120 - Introduction to Computer Science I

Course Learning Outcomes
Upon completion of the course, students will be able to:

Interpret class and activity diagrams as demonstrated by creating Java classes based on the diagrams.
Identify areas of concentration in computer science as demonstrated by answering related questions on examinations through the semester.
Use decision making control structures as demonstrated by writing a Java program which utilizes if else or switch statements.
Use looping control structures as demonstrated by writing a Java program which utilizes loops.
Replicate object-oriented programs as demonstrated by developing programs from given class diagrams.
Implement variables of assorted types as demonstrated by developing programs using simple and complex variables.
Explain a basic description of computer science and who a computer scientist is as demonstrated by writing a short paper.

title: Variables and Data Types
text:
Variables — What Are They?

This slide is the conceptual foundation — no syntax, no types, no code yet. The only goal is to give students an intuitive mental model before anything else. Programs need to remember things: a score, a name, a temperature. A variable is just a named place to hold one piece of information. The scoreboard and sticky-note examples are deliberately mundane — the point is that this idea already exists in everyday life. Students already understand “Score: 47” as a label paired with a value. That’s all a variable is.

Before a program can do anything useful, it needs to remember things.
Think about situations where you already use named values without thinking about it:

A scoreboard: Score: 47 — the word “Score” is the label; 47 is what’s stored there right now
A thermostat: Temperature: 68°F — same idea
A name badge: Name: Alice — a label that identifies what the value means

A variable is the same thing inside a program:

A variable is a named container that holds one piece of information.

Your program can:

Store a value in it
Look at what’s currently inside
Change it whenever needed

That’s it. Everything else — types, syntax, declarations — is just the details of how Java makes you write this down.

title: Variables and Data Types
text:
Why Do Programs Need Variables?

The recipe analogy works well here — and keep it as plain text, no code. A recipe hardcoded for 2 people has to be rewritten by hand every time you want to change the serving size. With a variable, you change one number and every quantity updates. The point is conceptual: variables let one set of instructions work for many different inputs. The code version of this will make sense once students have seen declarations, printing, and arithmetic.

Imagine a recipe written for exactly 2 people:
- 2 cups of flour
- 1 cup of sugar
- 3 eggs
Want to make it for 4? You cross everything out and rewrite it.
Now imagine a version with a note at the top:
Servings: 2

- [servings] cups of flour
- [servings / 2] cups of sugar
- [servings * 2 - 1] eggs
Change the one number at the top → every quantity updates automatically.
That note at the top is a variable. One change, everywhere.

title: Variables and Data Types
text:
Variables in Algebra vs. Programming

Students have seen variables in algebra — start there. The similarities are real and worth naming: a variable is a named placeholder for a value. Then get into the differences. In algebra, the variable is unknown and you solve for it. In programming, you are the one who sets the value — the computer doesn’t “solve” for anything. Also: algebra variables are almost always single letters; programming variables have full descriptive names. And the biggest one: in programming, a variable’s value can change.

You have seen variables before — in algebra.









Algebra
Programming




What it is
Named placeholder for a value
Named placeholder for a value


Who sets the value
You solve for it
You tell the computer


Names
x, y, z
score, temperature, userName


Can it change?
No — x is fixed once solved
Yes — can be updated anytime


Has a type?
No
Yes — must declare one



The core idea is the same. The rules are different.

title: Variables and Data Types
section: Think of Variables as Labeled Cups
text:
Think of Variables as Labeled Cups

The Starbucks analogy is intuitive and memorable. At a Starbucks counter, your cup has your name written on it (so the barista knows whose order it is), a size (tall, grande, venti — that’s the type), and whatever drink is actually inside (the value). A variable works exactly the same way. The name identifies it. The type says what kind of thing it can hold. The value is what’s actually in there right now. And just like a cup can be emptied and refilled, a variable’s value can change.

When you order at Starbucks, your cup has three things:

Your name written on it — so the barista knows whose it is
A size — tall, grande, venti — that determines what it can hold
The actual drink inside

A variable works the same way:



Cup
Variable




Name on cup
Variable name (score, userName)


Cup size / type
Data type (int, double, String)


Drink inside
The value stored (42, 3.14, "Alice")



And just like a cup can be emptied and refilled — a variable’s value can change.

title: Variables and Data Types
text:
Why Do Variables Have Types?

The food container analogy gets at the intuition. Different foods need different containers — you wouldn’t put soup in a paper bag. The container type isn’t arbitrary: it’s determined by what you’re storing. Same with data. Types tell the computer what kind of data the variable holds, which determines what operations make sense on it.

Different foods need different containers:



Coffee → cup
Burger → box or wrapper
Fries → paper bag
Ice cream → cone or cup


You wouldn’t put soup in a paper bag. The container depends on what you’re storing.

Data is the same way:



Data
Java type




Whole numbers
int


Decimal numbers
double


True / false
boolean


Text
String
