"Hello", "Alice", "42"



A few things worth noting:

String is capitalized — it’s special. More on this soon.
true and false are lowercase, no quotes.
"42" (String) and 42 (int) are not the same. You cannot do arithmetic on "42".

title: Variables and Data Types
Variables and Data Types
section: Printing the Value of a Variable

title: Variables and Data Types
section: The Assignment Operator — Not What You Think
text:
The Assignment Operator — Not What You Think

This is a genuine conceptual stumbling block. In mathematics, = means “these two things are equal.” In Java, = means “take the value on the right and store it in the variable on the left.” They look the same but behave completely differently. The clearest demonstration is a = a + 1: mathematically nonsense (subtract a from both sides: 0 = 1), but in programming it’s completely normal and means “add 1 to whatever is currently in a”. Do this on the board slowly: if a was 5, evaluate the right side (5+1=6), then store 6 into a. Now a is 6.

In algebra, = means “these are equal” — a statement of fact.
In Java, = means “store this value” — a command.
These are completely different things.


Algebra:
a = a + 1
Subtract a from both sides:
0 = 1   ← impossible

Java:
a = a + 1;
“Take the current value of a, add 1 to it, store the result back in a.”


int a = 5;
a = a + 1;           // a is now 6
a = a + 1;           // a is now 7
IO.println(a);       // prints 7

title: Variables and Data Types
text:
Reassigning Variables

Show that a variable holds the MOST RECENT value assigned to it. Trace through the program step by step — this is a good opportunity to introduce the idea of tracing, which will be a recurring skill throughout the course. Emphasize: println shows what’s in the variable at that moment in time, not some average or history.

Once declared, a variable’s value can be changed:
int score = 0;
IO.println(score);       // prints 0

score = 10;
IO.println(score);       // prints 10

score = score + 5;
IO.println(score);       // prints 15
The variable always holds the most recently assigned value.
Let’s trace it step by step:



Line
What happens
score




int score = 0;
Declared and set to 0
0


score = 10;
Overwritten with 10
10


score = score + 5;
10 + 5 = 15, stored back
15

title: Variables and Data Types
Variables and Data Types
section: Programs That Always Do the Same Thing

title: Variables and Data Types
text:
What Is Input?

Pure concept — no code yet. Students already know about output (IO.println sends information from the program to the screen). Input is the other direction: information flows from the user to the program. The two-arrow figure makes this concrete. Spend time here — the mental model of “two directions of information flow” is foundational for everything interactive they will ever write.

So far, information has only flowed one direction:

Program → Screen — using IO.println

Input is the other direction:

User → Program — the user types something; the program receives it



Output (IO.println)
The program sends information out. The screen shows it.

Input (IO.readln)
The user types information in. The program receives it.

Together, these two directions let you write programs that have a conversation with the user.

title: Variables and Data Types
text:
IO.readln — The Simplest Form

Introduce the mechanics first, without a prompt string — so students can focus entirely on what readln DOES. When Java hits IO.readln(), execution stops. A cursor blinks. The program waits. The user types something and presses Enter. Whatever they typed is produced as a String. That’s it. Walk through the sample run line by line. Emphasize: the program is paused — it is not broken, it is not slow, it is waiting for the user.

IO.readln() pauses the program and waits for the user to type a line of text.
void main() {
    String name = IO.readln();
    IO.println(name);
}
When Java reaches IO.readln():

The program stops
A cursor appears — the program is waiting
The user types something and presses Enter
IO.readln produces the typed text as a String
That String is stored in name
The program continues

Sample run:
Alice
Alice






Warning


If you do not store the result in a variable, it is gone the instant the line finishes — the program read the input and immediately forgot it.

title: Variables and Data Types
Variables and Data Types
text:
Adding a Prompt

The no-prompt form works but is confusing in practice — users see a blank screen and have no idea what to type. The prompt string solves this. It is printed before the program pauses, giving the user a cue. Key point: the prompt does not change what gets produced — it is purely for the human’s benefit. Show a side-by-side comparison of sample runs so the difference is vivid. This is the form students will use in all their programs.

Without a prompt, the user just sees a blinking cursor — and has no idea what to type.
IO.readln accepts an optional prompt: a message to display before waiting.
void main() {
    String name = IO.readln("What is your name? ");
    IO.println(name);
}
Sample run:
What is your name? Alice
Alice
The prompt is printed first — then the program pauses for input.


Without prompt:
▌
(User sees a blank cursor — confused)

With prompt:
What is your name? ▌
(User knows exactly what to type)







Note


The prompt does not affect what the program receives. It is a message for the user, not part of the input.









Note


IO.readln always produces a String — even if the user types 42, the program receives the text "42", not the number. Converting it to a number is coming in the next lecture.

title: Variables and Data Types
Variables and Data Types
Variables and Data Types
Variables and Data Types
text:
Why Does the Type Matter?

Now that students have written declarations and feel some comfort with the syntax, this slide gives the intuition for why types exist — without any technical jargon. The key point: the type changes what operations make sense. You can add two ints. You can’t add two names. The computer uses the type to figure out what “+” even means.

2 + 3 and 2.0 + 3.0 look the same to us. The computer handles them differently.

2 + 3 — whole-number addition. The result is always exact.
2.0 + 3.0 — decimal addition. Works differently, and can occasionally produce small surprises.

IO.println(0.1 + 0.2);   // you might expect 0.3 ...
                          // the computer prints 0.30000000000000004
This is not a bug — it’s just how decimal math works on a computer.
The type also tells the computer which operations make sense:

You can multiply two int values.
You cannot multiply two String values — what would "Alice" * "Bob" even mean?


The type is not just a label for you. It tells the computer what kind of thing the variable holds.

title: Variables and Data Types
section: Should You Always Use double for Numbers?
text:
Should You Always Use double for Numbers?

Students sometimes wonder: if double can hold whole numbers too (5.0 is a valid double), why ever use int? The key reasons are semantic clarity and the decimal surprise shown above. Don’t mention memory or performance — that’s too deep for this stage. Focus on meaning: an int says “this is always a whole number.” That’s both clearer and safer.

double can store whole numbers too — 5.0 is perfectly valid.
So why use int at all?
Whole numbers stay exact. Decimal math can have small surprises (see previous slide). If a value is always a whole number, int guarantees it stays clean.
The type says what you mean.
double numberOfStudents = 2.7;  // What does this even mean?
int numberOfStudents = 27;      // Clear and correct
You cannot have 2.7 students. Using int communicates that — and if you accidentally compute a decimal result, Java will warn you.






Tip


Rule of thumb: Use int for things you count. Use double for things you measure.

Count: students, quiz scores, laps → int
Measure: temperature, GPA, price → double

title: Variables and Data Types
text:
Common Mistakes

These are the mistakes you will see most frequently in the first few weeks. Go through each one briefly and show what error it produces or what wrong output it causes. The goal is to make students recognize these errors when they see them, not to memorize a list.

1. Using a variable before giving it a value
int score;
IO.println(score);   // ERROR — score has no value yet
2. Wrong type for the value
int name = "Alice";   // ERROR — can't store text in an int
3. Forgetting to store IO.readln’s result
IO.readln("Enter your name: ");   // the returned value is lost
IO.println(name);                 // ERROR — name was never declared
4. Confusing = (assignment) with equality
score = 10;    // stores 10 in score ✓
score == 10;   // checks if score equals 10 — but does nothing here (coming later)
5. Case errors
int playerScore = 0;
IO.println(PlayerScore);   // ERROR — Java is case-sensitive

title: Variables and Data Types
text:
Worksheet

Reserve the last 20-30 minutes. Students work in the online IDE. Common things to check on: are they remembering the type keyword? Are they using = correctly? Are they storing the result of IO.readln? Are they printing the variable name without quotes?

title: Type Conversion and Casting
text:
Learning Outcomes

Explain why type conversion is sometimes necessary, even when types were chosen carefully
Distinguish between widening (automatic) and narrowing (explicit) conversion
Predict the result of a mixed-type arithmetic expression
Cast between int and double using (int) and (double)
Explain why (double) a / b and (double)(a / b) produce different results
Explain that (int) truncates a decimal value rather than rounding it

title: Type Conversion and Casting
section: Why Can’t We Just Choose the Right Type Once?
text:
Why Can’t We Just Choose the Right Type Once?

Start with the student’s natural objection: if we pick the right type upfront, why would we ever need to convert? The answer is that we often do not control what type a value comes in as. IO.readln always produces a String — even if the user types a number. Two int values divided can produce a fraction — but int cannot hold a fraction, so something has to give. And sometimes a piece of code we did not write gives us a value in a type we did not expect. Types in real programs collide constantly, and knowing how to handle those collisions is a core skill.

You might be thinking: “If I pick the right type from the start, why would I ever need to change it?”

That is a fair question. Here is why it comes up anyway:

title: Type Conversion and Casting
text:
The Starbucks Cup Analogy

The Starbucks analogy from the variables deck extends naturally here. A tall cup is small — like int. A venti cup is large — like double. Pouring a tall into a venti is easy: all the coffee fits, the cup just is not full. Nothing is lost. That is widening. Pouring a venti into a tall is the problem: the tall cup cannot hold everything. Coffee spills. You lose some. That is narrowing — and it is why Java makes you do it explicitly. The analogy also sets up truncation nicely: the coffee that spills (the decimal part) is simply gone — it does not round up.

Remember our Starbucks cup analogy from the variables lecture?
A tall cup (small) ↔︎ int A venti cup (large) ↔︎ double

title: Type Conversion and Casting
text:
Widening — int to double

Widening is the safe direction: going from a smaller type to a larger one. An int can always fit inside a double — a whole number is just a decimal number with nothing after the decimal point. Java does this automatically whenever it is needed: assigning an int to a double variable, using an int where a double is expected. Show several examples. Emphasize that nothing is lost and nothing has to be written — Java handles it silently.

Going from int to double is always safe — a whole number fits perfectly inside a decimal type.

Java does this automatically, without any special syntax.

title: Type Conversion and Casting
text:
Narrowing — double to int

Narrowing is the risky direction. A double might have a decimal part that simply cannot exist in an int. Java will not do this automatically — it refuses at compile time if you try. You have to write an explicit cast to say: “I know something might be lost, and I am okay with that.” The syntax is (int) in front of the value. The critical point: (int) truncates — it drops the decimal part regardless of its size. 3.1 and 3.9 both become 3. This surprises students who expect rounding.

Going from double to int may lose the decimal part.

Java refuses to do this automatically — you must ask explicitly.
double price = 9.99;
int dollars = price;          // ERROR — Java will not compile this
int dollars = (int) price;    // OK — you asked explicitly; dollars is 9


The (int) before a value is called a cast. It means: “convert this to an int.”

title: Type Conversion and Casting
text:
Mixed-Type Expressions

When an arithmetic expression involves both int and double values, Java widens the int to a double before computing. The rule is: if either operand is a double, the result is a double. This is the key to getting decimal division: put a .0 on one of the numbers, or use a cast. Show a series of examples where the only change is one type, and walk through how the result changes. Connect explicitly to the integer division surprise from last lecture — this is the explanation for why 7/2 is 3.

When int and double values appear together in an expression, Java widens the int to double before computing.

The rule: if either operand is a double, the result is a double.
IO.println(7 / 2);       // 3   — both int → integer division
IO.println(7 / 2.0);     // 3.5 — one is double → decimal division
IO.println(7.0 / 2);     // 3.5 — one is double → decimal division
IO.println(7.0 / 2.0);   // 3.5 — both double → decimal division


The only case that gives 3 is when both sides are int.

title: Type Conversion and Casting
Type Conversion and Casting
text:
Code Example — Grade Percentage

A complete program that brings together everything from today: int variables, a cast to force decimal division, and a mixed-type expression. The scenario is immediately relatable — every student cares about their grade percentage. Walk through the flowchart, then the code. Trace through with concrete values: earned = 43, possible = 50. Without the cast: 43 / 50 = 0 (integer division) → 0 * 100 = 0. With the cast: 43.0 / 50 = 0.86 → 0.86 * 100 = 86.0. The cast is not optional.

Problem: Ask the user how many points they earned and how many were possible. Calculate and print their percentage.

title: Type Conversion and Casting
text:
Common Mistakes

Four mistakes that follow directly from this lecture. The first two are both about casting too late or not at all — the most common. The third is the truncation surprise. The fourth is trying to let Java narrow automatically, which it refuses to do.

1. Forgetting to cast before integer division
int a = 3;
int b = 4;
double result = a / b;           // 0.0 — integer division happened first
double result = (double) a / b;  // 0.75 ✓

title: Type Conversion and Casting
text:
Worksheet

Reserve the last 20-30 minutes. Problems 1-2 are prediction problems — students work on paper first. Problems 3-4 require writing expressions. Problem 5 is the synthesis program. Watch for: students who forget the cast; students who cast too late; students who expect truncation to round.

title: Worksheet: Input → Processing → Output
text:
Learning Outcomes

Identify the input, processing, and output stages in a program’s description before writing any code
Read one or more values with IO.readln, convert numeric input with Integer.parseInt
Compute a result using arithmetic operators (+, -, *, /, %)
Print a labeled result using IO.println and String concatenation
Explain, for a program that fails, which of the three stages is broken
Explain why a silent IO.readln() is confusing to a user, and fix it with a printed prompt — either as a separate IO.println/IO.print or built into IO.readln("...")

title: Worksheet: Input → Processing → Output
section: Why New Programmers Hit a Wall Here
text:
Why New Programmers Hit a Wall Here

This deck is a remediation/consolidation session, not new content — everything here uses only what lecture 2 (variables, IO.readln, IO.println) and lecture 3 (arithmetic, Integer.parseInt) already covered. The wall students hit is usually not syntax, it’s not having a plan before they start typing. They stare at a word problem and don’t know where to begin because they’re trying to write the whole program in one motion. The fix is a habit: before touching the keyboard, name the three stages out loud (or in a comment). Use this slide to diagnose that out loud with the class — ask “when a program you wrote doesn’t work, do you know if the input is wrong, the math is wrong, or the print statement is wrong?” Most say no. That’s the gap this worksheet closes.

You already know IO.readln, IO.println, variables, and arithmetic.
You must have a plan before you start typing.
Every program you’ve written so far, no matter how small, does the same three things:

Get some data in
Do something with it
Show a result

title: Worksheet: Input → Processing → Output
text:
The Pattern: Input → Processing → Output

Name the pattern explicitly and give it an acronym (IPO) so students have a label to reach for. Map each stage directly onto the Java constructs they already know — this is not new material, it’s a lens for organizing material they have. Emphasize that not every program has all three (a program can print a fixed message with zero input or processing), but almost every interesting program does.









Stage
Question to ask
Java tools you already know




Input
What data does the program need, and where does it come from?
IO.readln(), IO.readln("prompt: ")


Processing
What computation turns that data into the answer?
+ - * / %, Integer.parseInt(...)


Output
What exactly should be printed, and in what format?
IO.println(...), + for concatenation









Note


Not every program needs all three. A program that just prints a message has output only — zero input, zero processing. But most real programs use all three, in that order.

title: Worksheet: Input → Processing → Output
Worksheet: Input → Processing → Output
text:
Prompts: Three Ways to Ask

This is the second confusion point layered on top of IPO, and it deserves its own slide before students hit the worksheet. A silent IO.readln() is technically correct Java but a terrible user experience — the cursor just blinks and the student (or grader) doesn’t know the program is waiting for anything. Walk through all three versions live: run the silent one first and let the awkward silence land, then show the two fixes. The IO.println + IO.readln() version matters because it’s the one students reach for instinctively once they realize they need to say something before reading — but it puts the prompt on its own line, and the input the user types appears on the next line, which looks different from the inline-prompt version. Point that out explicitly: same information reaches the program either way, but the on-screen layout differs. IO.readln("prompt: ") is the idiomatic one-line version and should become the default once it’s introduced.

IO.readln doesn’t require a prompt — but leaving one out makes the program confusing to use.


No prompt
String name = IO.readln();
The program just waits. The user has no idea what to type. 


Separate print, then read
IO.println("Enter your name:");
String name = IO.readln();
The prompt appears on its own line; the user’s answer appears on the next line. 


Prompt built into readln
String name =
    IO.readln("Enter your name: ");
Prompt and answer share one line — the style you should default to from here on.

title: Worksheet: Input → Processing → Output
text:
Worksheet

Reserve the last 20-30 minutes, or use as a standalone remediation session. Require the // INPUT / // PROCESSING / // OUTPUT comment scaffold on every problem, even the trivial ones — the habit is the point, not the code. Problem 1 is intentionally degenerate (missing a stage) so students see that the pattern is a lens, not a rigid template. On top of the IPO progression, prompts are layered in gradually: Problems 2-4 read with no prompt at all (let them feel the confusion), Problems 5-7 print a prompt separately with IO.println/IO.print before calling IO.readln(), and Problems 8-10 fold the prompt into IO.readln("..."), which should become the default from here on. Problems 7-9 also require two or more processing steps in sequence, and Problem 10 is the synthesis problem. Common failure: students try to read all inputs, then do all processing, then print — which is actually correct and is exactly the pattern; the more common bug is interleaving a println into the middle of processing and getting confused about what’s been computed yet. Watch for forgotten Integer.parseInt, and for / vs % confusion.

For every problem below, start by writing // INPUT, // PROCESSING, and // OUTPUT as comments in your file, in that order. Then fill in the code under each one. If a problem has no input or no processing, leave that comment in place with nothing under it — that’s fine, and worth noticing.






Important


Watch the prompt style change as you go: Problems 2-4 use no prompt at all (read silently), Problems 5-7 print a prompt with IO.println/IO.print before reading, and Problems 8-10 build the prompt into IO.readln("...").

title: Boolean Logic and else if
text:
Learning Outcomes

Combine conditions using &&, ||, and ! to form compound boolean expressions
Translate English conditions with “and,” “or,” and “not” into Java
Evaluate compound boolean expressions by working through them step by step
Write else if chains to handle multiple mutually exclusive cases
Order conditions in an else if chain correctly so no branch is unreachable
Choose between else if and nested if based on the structure of the problem
Trace execution through compound and chained conditionals for a given input

title: Boolean Logic and else if
text:
Boolean Expressions — A Quick Recap

Recap from last lecture: a boolean expression is anything that evaluates to true or false. Relational operators (< > <= >= == !=) produce boolean results. This lecture extends that: what if we need a condition that combines two checks? We already say things like “if you are 16 and have a license, you can drive” — today we learn to write that in Java. Set up the need before introducing the operators.

Last lecture: a condition is an expression that produces true or false.
score >= 60       // true or false
name.equals("Alice")  // true or false
temperature < 32  // true or false
Sometimes one condition is not enough.
We say things like:

“You can drive if you are 16 and have a license.”
“You get a discount if you are a student or a senior.”
“The alarm triggers if it is not disarmed.”

Java has three operators for exactly this: &&, ||, and !.

title: Boolean Logic and else if
text:
The && Operator — AND

Both conditions must be true. Walk through the English examples first — students already reason this way. Then show the Java translation. The Venn diagram with the intersection highlighted is the most intuitive visual. The mini truth table shows all four combinations. Mention short-circuit evaluation only briefly: if the first condition is false, Java does not even check the second. This is a “fun fact” at this stage, not something students need to memorize.

&& means AND — both conditions must be true for the whole expression to be true.
English → Java:







English
Java




“16 or older and has a license”
age >= 16 && hasLicense


“Score above 60 and homework submitted”
score > 60 && homeworkDone


“Temperature below 32 and it is snowing”
temp < 32 && isSnowing


“Price over $50 and you have a coupon”
price > 50 && hasCoupon



Truth table for &&:



A
B
A && B




true
true
true


true
false
false


false
true
false


false
false
false



&& is only true when both sides are true.
int age = 20;
boolean hasLicense = true;

if (age >= 16 && hasLicense) {
    IO.println("You may drive.");
}

title: Boolean Logic and else if
text:
The || Operator — OR

At least one condition must be true. The English examples help ground it: a discount for students OR seniors — either one qualifies. The Venn diagram for OR is the union of both circles. The key distinction from AND: with OR, both sides being true is still fine — only “both false” produces false. Walk through the truth table. A common mistake: students think OR means “one or the other but not both” — like in everyday English. In Java (and logic), OR means “at least one.”

|| means OR — at least one condition must be true.
English → Java:







English
Java




“Student or senior”
isStudent \|\| isSenior


“Rainy or below 40°F”
isRaining \|\| temp < 40


“Score is 0 or answer is blank”
score == 0 \|\| answer.equals("")


“Monday or Wednesday or Friday”
day.equals("Mon") \|\| day.equals("Wed") \|\| day.equals("Fri")



Truth table for ||:



A
B
A \|\| B




true
true
true


true
false
true


false
true
true


false
false
false



|| is only false when both sides are false.
boolean isStudent = false;
boolean isSenior  = true;

if (isStudent || isSenior) {
    IO.println("Discount applied.");   // runs — isSenior is true
}






Note


In everyday English, “or” sometimes means “one or the other, but not both.” In Java, || means “at least one” — both being true is also fine.

title: Boolean Logic and else if
text:
The ! Operator — NOT

NOT flips the value: true becomes false, false becomes true. The English translations are straightforward — “not logged in,” “not raining,” “not game over.” Show the truth table (just two rows). Common use: checking for the absence of something. Also: !condition is cleaner than condition == false, which students sometimes write instead.

! means NOT — it flips true to false and false to true.
English → Java:



English
Java




“Not logged in”
!isLoggedIn


“Not raining”
!isRaining


“Game is not over”
!isGameOver


“Name does not equal Alice”
!name.equals("Alice")



Truth table for !:



A
!A




true
false


false
true



boolean isRaining = false;

if (!isRaining) {
    IO.println("Good day for a walk!");   // runs — !false is true
}

boolean isLoggedIn = false;

if (!isLoggedIn) {
    IO.println("Please log in first.");   // runs
}






Tip


!condition is cleaner than writing condition == false. Use ! instead.

title: Boolean Logic and else if
text:
Combining Operators

Now that students know each operator individually, show how to combine them. Walk through several examples — one condition at a time. Precedence: ! is evaluated first, then &&, then ||. Parentheses override everything and are always clearer. Stress the parentheses habit: when in doubt, add parentheses. Compound conditions can get confusing fast; explicit parentheses make the intent clear and the bug easier to find.

You can combine &&, ||, and ! to express complex conditions.
Examples:
// Must be 18+ AND (student OR senior)
age >= 18 && (isStudent || isSenior)

// Temperature is extreme (very cold OR very hot)
temp < 10 || temp > 100

// Eligible if NOT banned AND has enough credits
!isBanned && credits >= 3

// Pass if exam score is 60+ AND (homework done OR extra credit earned)
examScore >= 60 && (homeworkDone || extraCredit)
Precedence — order of evaluation:

! first (like a minus sign in front of a number)
&& next
|| last

// Without parentheses:
a || b && c     // means: a || (b && c)

// Much clearer with parentheses:
a || (b && c)   // same result, but obvious
(a || b) && c   // different result!






Tip


When combining && and || — always use parentheses. The precedence rules are subtle. Parentheses make your intent clear and prevent bugs.

Methods: void Methods
text:
Learning Outcomes

Explain what a method is and describe how methods reduce repetition and improve readability
Define a void method with no parameters
Call a method from main, including calling the same method multiple times
Write a method that calls other methods to build a structured program
Trace the flow of execution through a method call and back to the call site

title: Methods: void Methods
text:
What Is a Method?

Before doing anything else, plant two vocabulary words the students will hear for the rest of the course: “method” and “call.” Don’t define them formally — just give them enough meaning to follow what comes next. The table is intentionally minimal. Two words. That’s the whole slide. Students should leave this slide knowing what to listen for, not feeling like they learned something hard. The aha moments and the examples come on the slides that follow.

You have written dozens of programs. Every instruction lived inside main.
But what if a group of instructions belongs together and you want to use it in multiple places?
Java lets you package a group of instructions, give that package a name, and run it anywhere — just by writing the name.



Word
Meaning




method
a named group of instructions


call
to make a method run by writing its name



These two words are the most important new ideas in this lecture. By the end, both will feel completely natural.

title: Methods: void Methods
section: You Have Already Been Calling Methods
text:
You Have Already Been Calling Methods

This is the big callback moment. Now that “method” and “call” have been introduced as vocabulary, show students that the words describe something they have been doing all semester. The list is intentionally long to make the point land — every single item has the same pattern: a name followed by parentheses. Pause and let that sink in. Then: “Today, you learn how to write your own.” This reframes a scary-sounding topic as a natural next step.

Here are some lines of code from the last seven lectures:
IO.println("Hello, world!")         // Lecture 1
IO.readln("Enter your name: ")      // Lecture 2
name.toUpperCase()                   // Lecture 7
name.length()                        // Lecture 7
word.charAt(0)                       // Lecture 7
word.substring(1, 4)                 // Lecture 7
answer.equals("yes")                 // Lecture 5
Integer.parseInt(IO.readln("n: "))  // Lecture 3
Every single one of these is a method call — you wrote a name followed by (), and a group of instructions ran.
Notice the pattern: a name, followed by parentheses.
You have been calling methods since Day 1. Today, you learn how to write your own.

title: Methods: void Methods
text:
The Duel

This is the central analogy for the whole lecture. The goal is maximum drama before any code appears. Harry and Voldemort are mid-duel — spells flying, stakes high. Neither wizard stops to describe what the spell does. They just shout the name. The audience doesn’t need to know the magical mechanics of Avada Kedavra — they just see the result. The key idea to land: a name that, when said, triggers a complete sequence of actions. Students who don’t know Harry Potter can substitute any battle magic from any fiction — the structure is universal. Let this slide breathe. No code. Just the analogy.

Picture the final duel. Harry faces Voldemort.
Spells are flying back and forth.
Harry does not shout:

“I am gathering magical energy in a protective dome shape around myself, calibrating the resonant frequency to deflect incoming dark magic, initializing the shield at full power…”

He shouts:

“Protego!”

Voldemort does not announce:

“I am directing a focused stream of lethal dark energy toward you at approximately 45 degrees, initiating the killing curse sequence…”

He shouts:

“Avada Kedavra!”

Each spell is a name for a complex sequence of actions. In the heat of battle, nobody cares about the steps — they call the spell, and the spell knows what to do.

title: Methods: void Methods
Methods: void Methods
text:
Methods Are Mini-Recipes

The recipe analogy complements the spell analogy: where the spell emphasizes simplicity of invocation, the recipe emphasizes how a large task is decomposed into smaller named tasks. A Thanksgiving dinner recipe does not copy the gravy recipe inline — it says “make the gravy” and points elsewhere. This is exactly how a well-structured program works: main reads like a table of contents, and each method is a self-contained sub-recipe. The visual hierarchy (big card at top, smaller cards below) should make the structure feel natural and obvious.

Imagine writing a recipe for a full Thanksgiving dinner.
At one point it says: “Step 4: Make the gravy.”
It does not paste the entire gravy recipe into the middle of the Thanksgiving recipe. It just says the name. The gravy recipe exists separately, and you look it up when you need it.
Your program works the same way:
void main()         ←  "Cook Thanksgiving Dinner"
    roastTurkey()   ←  Step 1 — see turkey recipe
    makeSides()     ←  Step 2 — see sides recipe
    makeGravy()     ←  Step 3 — see gravy recipe
    serveDinner()   ←  Step 4 — see service recipe
main is the head chef — it coordinates everything but delegates the actual work. Each method is a focused, self-contained task. The head chef doesn’t need to know how to make gravy — they just need to know when to call for it.

title: Methods: void Methods
section: void main() — You Already Wrote a Method

title: Methods: void Methods
Methods: void Methods
text:
Why Write Your Own Methods?

Three reasons, stated plainly before any code. Keep this slide short — the code examples on the next two slides will make the argument concrete. Students often get the “avoid repetition” point immediately; the “change in one place” and “better names” points need the code examples to land properly. Plant the ideas here, let the code make them real.

There are three reasons to write your own methods:
1. Avoid repetition. Write a group of instructions once. Call it as many times as you need. Never copy-paste the same lines again.
2. Give things names. printHeader() tells the reader exactly what is about to happen. Three raw IO.println lines tell them nothing until they’ve read all three.
3. Change in one place. Need to update the steps? Update the method body — not every place you used it.
These three benefits compound as programs get longer. Let’s see them in action.

title: Methods: void Methods
Methods: void Methods
Methods: void Methods
text:
Defining a void Method

Walk through the anatomy one piece at a time. Students have seen every one of these elements before: “void” is in main; the name follows the same naming rules as variables; the parentheses have been in every method call they have ever written; and the braces are the same as in if-statements. Nothing here is truly new — this is just putting a name to something they already know. The anatomy figure with labeled arrows is the most important visual on this slide.

A void method has this structure:
void methodName() {
    // the body — steps that happen when this method is called
}
Every part has a job:

void — this method does not produce a value
methodName — the name you choose (write it like a short command)
() — parentheses, always required
{ } — the body: the steps that run when the method is called

Nothing here is new. You have seen every one of these pieces before — in main, in if statements, in every method you have already been calling.

title: Methods: void Methods
Methods: void Methods
Methods: void Methods
text:
Calling a Method

The mechanics are simple: name followed by parentheses and a semicolon. Two points to stress: (1) defining a method does not run it — you must call it; and (2) you can call it as many times as you want, and the method body runs fresh each time. The note about definition order is useful: in Java, unlike some other languages, the order of method definitions doesn’t matter. Java reads all definitions before running anything. Students who have internalized “Java reads top to bottom” will be surprised, so flag it explicitly.

Once a method is defined, you call it — write its name, parentheses, semicolon:
void main() {
    printWelcome();       // the lines inside printWelcome run now
    printSeparator();     // then the lines inside printSeparator
    printGoodbye();       // then the lines inside printGoodbye
}
That is the whole spell. One line. The details are inside the method.

title: Methods: void Methods
text:
The Flow of Execution

The most important mechanical concept of the lecture. Students need a clear mental model: the computer is executing line by line in main, hits a method call, leaves main, jumps to the method body, executes every line top to bottom, reaches the closing brace, and returns to main at exactly the next line. “Exactly where it left off” is the key phrase. Walk through the numbered comments one by one, waiting after each step. Then show the output. The figure — two vertical timelines connected by forward and return arrows — is what makes this concrete. Call stack mechanics are intentionally omitted.

When your program hits a method call, here is exactly what happens:
void main() {                       // 1. Java starts here
    IO.println("Before");           // 2. prints "Before"
    printBanner();                  // 3. JUMP to printBanner
    IO.println("After");            // 6. back here — continues
}

void printBanner() {                // 4. runs from top to bottom
    IO.println("=========");        //    prints "========="
    IO.println("  Hello!  ");       //    prints "  Hello!  "
    IO.println("=========");        //    prints "========="
}                                   // 5. closing brace — COME BACK
Output:
Before
=========
  Hello!
=========
After
The program jumps into the method, runs it completely, then comes back to the next line in main. “After” prints after the banner, not before it.

text:
Learning Outcomes

Define methods that compute and return a value using the return statement
Store and use a method’s return value in a variable, expression, or condition
Write methods with multiple return statements in different branches
Explain what scope means and identify the scope of a local variable
Trace a method call with a return value and show what the caller receives

title: Return Values and Scope
Return Values and Scope
text:
Functions in Mathematics

Students have been writing functions since middle school. This slide is the central hook for the lecture — the direct bridge between math and programming. Go slowly and make the parallel explicit. f(x) = x² is a function: it takes a number, squares it, and produces a result. g(x, y) = x + y takes two numbers, adds them, and produces a result. The “produces a result” part is the key — the function doesn’t just DO something, it GIVES YOU BACK A VALUE. Draw the parallel: the method name corresponds to f, the parameters correspond to x and y, and the “produces a result” part is what the return statement does.

You have been working with functions in math for years:
\[f(x) = x^2\] \[g(x, y) = x + y\] \[h(x) = 2x + 1\]
Each function: - Takes input (the values in the parentheses) - Computes something - Produces a result — a value you can use anywhere
When you write \(f(3)\), you get back \(9\). You can use that \(9\) directly:
\[f(3) + 1 = 10 \qquad \text{or} \qquad y = f(3) \qquad \text{or} \qquad \text{if } f(3) > 5 \ldots\]
The function’s result is a value you can store, combine, or compare — not something that just disappears.
Java methods work exactly the same way. The only difference is that you also have to tell Java what type of value the method will produce.

section: void vs. Return: Which to Use?
text:
void vs. Return: Which to Use?

A simple decision rule that maps to the do/compute distinction. Methods that perform an action (print, modify, draw) are usually void. Methods that compute a value the caller needs to use have a return type. The math analogy is useful: in math you distinguish between “procedures” (algorithms that do a sequence of steps) and “functions” (mappings that produce a value). In Java, void = procedure, return type = function. The rule of thumb: if the caller needs to DO SOMETHING WITH the result, use a return type. If the caller just needs the method to ACT, use void.

Two kinds of methods. Two different jobs:




void
With return type




Does what?
Performs an action
Computes a value


Gives back
Nothing
A value the caller can use


Math analogy
Procedure
Function


Example
printBanner()
square(int x)



Use void when the method’s job is to do something: - Print output - Draw something - Save something
Use a return type when the method’s job is to compute and hand back a value: - Calculate a result - Check a condition and answer yes/no - Transform a value (uppercase, round, format)






Tip


Ask yourself: “Does the caller need to use this result somewhere?” If yes → return type. If the method just acts and the caller moves on → void.

for Loops
text:
Learning Outcomes

Write a for loop and identify its three components: initializer, condition, and update
Write accumulator loops that compute a sum, product, or count using for
Combine a for loop with if/else inside the body to filter or classify values
Convert between while and for loops for the same problem
Choose between while and for for a given problem and justify the choice

title: for Loops
text:
A Familiar Problem
Last lecture we wrote this countdown:
int count = 5;          // initialize
while (count >= 1) {    // condition
    IO.println(count);
    count = count - 1;  // update
}
The three parts — initialize, condition, update — are spread across three different places.
Java has a second kind of loop that keeps all three in one line.

Callback to deck 11. Students already know while loops. The for loop is not a new idea — it’s a more compact way to write the same thing when you know how many iterations you need. Frame it as syntactic convenience first, not a new concept.

title: for Loops
for Loops
text:
How for Executes — The Order
for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i = i + 1) {
    IO.println(i);
}
Java follows this exact sequence:

Initialize once: int i = 1
Check condition: i <= 3 → true, so run body
Run body: IO.println(i)
Update: i = i + 1
Check condition again: repeat from step 2

The update happens after the body, before the next condition check.

Walk through this sequence verbally while pointing to each part of the for header. Students get confused about when the update fires. It is NOT the first thing that happens — it fires AFTER the body runs, then control goes back to the condition check. Initialize fires ONLY once, at the very start.

title: for Loops
text:
Tracing a for Loop
for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i = i + 1) {
    IO.println("Step " + i);
}



i (start of check)
i <= 4?
Output
After update

true

2
true

4
true

5


5
false
(exits)
—




Same variable table technique from deck 11 — identical skill, different loop syntax. Emphasize: the table doesn’t care whether it’s a while or a for; the loop mechanics are the same.

title: for Loops
text:
Shorthand: i++
i = i + 1 is so common that Java has a shorthand:



Long form
Shorthand




i = i + 1
i++


i = i - 1
i--



So the countdown can be written:
for (int i = 5; i >= 1; i--) {
    IO.println(i);
}






Note


i++ and i-- work inside for updates only. Do not use them mid-expression until you understand precedence — keep it in the update slot for now.




Introduce i++ now so students can read real code. Many textbooks and examples use it. But caution against using it in complex expressions — just the update slot is safe and readable for beginners.

title: for Loops
for Loops
for Loops
section: while vs for — Side by Side

title: for Loops
text:
When to Use Each







Situation
Prefer




You know exactly how many iterations you need
for


You’re counting from A to B
for


You’re stepping through a range of numbers
for


You’re waiting for user input or an event
while


The stop condition depends on what happens inside the loop
while


Sentinel loops (“repeat until the user types ‘quit’”)
while



Rule of thumb: if you can write the three parts (init, condition, update) before you know what the body does, use for. If the body needs to run first to know whether to stop, use while.

This decision rule is the practical payoff of teaching both loops. Drill it: “for = count-controlled; while = event-controlled.” Sentinel loops are the canonical while use case — the stop condition depends on what the user types, which you can’t know in advance.

title: for Loops
for Loops
text:
Common Mistakes






Warning


Semicolons, not commas for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) — the three parts are separated by ; not ,.









Warning


Off-by-one (again) i < 5 runs 5 times (0–4). i <= 5 runs 6 times (0–5). Trace the last iteration.









Warning


Modifying the loop variable inside the body Changing i inside the body in addition to the update makes the loop very hard to reason about. Put all updates in the update slot.









Warning


Using i after the loop int i declared in the for header only exists inside the loop. It disappears after the closing }.




The scoping mistake (last one) previews deck 10’s scope concept in a new context. i declared in the for header is local to the loop — another bubble. Students will hit this when they try to use i after the loop and get a “cannot find symbol” error.

title: for Loops
Nested Loops
text:
Learning Outcomes

Write a nested loop with distinct inner and outer variables to produce two-dimensional output
Use IO.print inside the inner loop and IO.println at the end of each outer iteration to build 2D patterns
Reset and recompute an accumulator inside the outer loop using an inner loop (e.g., row sums, row max)
Trace a nested loop and determine the values of both loop variables and any accumulators at each step
Calculate the total number of inner-loop iterations and identify problems that require nested loops

title: Nested Loops
text:
The Clock Analogy
Think about how a clock works:

The hour hand (outer loop) moves once every 12 ticks of the minute hand
The minute hand (inner loop) completes one full revolution for every single tick of the hour hand

Nested loops work the same way: the inner loop runs completely for every single iteration of the outer loop.


The clock is a perfect physical analogy because every student has seen one. Spend time on this before showing any code — if they understand the clock, they understand nested loops. The key word is “completely”: the minute hand doesn’t pause at 30 waiting for the hour hand; it finishes 60 minutes before the hour advances.

title: Nested Loops
Nested Loops
text:
IO.print vs IO.println



Method
Effect




IO.println(value)
Prints value then moves to a new line


IO.print(value)
Prints value but stays on the same line



Building a row one piece at a time:
IO.print("A");   // A
IO.print("B");   // AB
IO.print("C");   // ABC
IO.println();    // ABC  ← then newline
This is the pattern for nested-loop output: IO.print inside the inner loop, IO.println() in the outer loop body.

This is many students’ first encounter with IO.print. Make sure they understand that IO.print and IO.println are the same idea — IO.print just doesn’t advance to the next line. The empty IO.println() at the end of the outer body is the “carriage return” that starts the next row.

title: Nested Loops
text:
Tracing a Nested Loop
for (int row = 1; row <= 2; row++) {
    for (int col = 1; col <= 3; col++) {
        IO.print("* ");
    }
    IO.println();
}

Output: * * * / * * *

Walk through the trace table row by row aloud. When col reaches 3 and increments to 4, the inner loop condition (col <= 3) becomes false, the inner loop exits, and println fires. Then row increments and the inner loop starts FRESH from col = 1. Students are often surprised that col resets — it’s because col is declared inside the outer loop, so it’s re-initialized every outer iteration.

title: Nested Loops
text:
Counting Total Iterations
Rule: total inner-loop iterations = outer iterations × inner iterations per outer
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {        // 5 outer iterations
    for (int j = 1; j <= 10; j++) {   // 10 inner iterations EACH
        // this body runs 5 × 10 = 50 times
    }
}



Outer range
Inner range
Total body executions




1 to 5
1 to 10
50

1 to 3
9


1 to n
1 to n
n²









Note


Nested loops can get expensive fast. A 1000 × 1000 nested loop runs 1 000 000 times.




The n² observation is a preview of algorithmic complexity — don’t dwell on it, but worth naming. The practical warning: students sometimes accidentally write nested loops with huge ranges and wonder why their program seems frozen.

title: Nested Loops
Nested Loops
Nested Loops
text:
When Do You Need Nesting?
Nested loops appear whenever the problem is two-dimensional:



Problem
Outer loop
Inner loop




Multiplication table
Each row
Each column


Seating chart
Each row of seats
Each seat in the row


Grid of pixels
Each row of pixels
Each pixel in the row


All pairs from two lists
Each item in list A
Each item in list B


Pattern of stars
Each line
Each character on the line



Ask yourself: “For each ___, do I need to repeat something across ___?”


The “for each … for each …” phrasing is a reliable signal that nested loops are needed. If students can articulate “for each row, for each column in that row, do X,” the code almost writes itself.

title: Nested Loops
Nested Loops
text:
Common Mistakes






Warning


Reusing the same variable name for inner and outer for (int i ...) { for (int i ...) } — the inner i shadows the outer i. Use distinct names: row/col, i/j, outer/inner.









Warning


Forgetting IO.println() after the inner loop Without it, all rows print on one long line.









Warning


Declaring the accumulator outside the outer loop If rowSum = 0 is outside both loops, it never resets between rows. Declare it at the top of the outer loop body.









Warning


Off-by-one on the inner range When the inner limit depends on the outer variable (like the triangle), trace a couple of rows to confirm the count is right.




The first mistake (reusing i) sometimes doesn’t cause a compile error in all Java versions but always causes confusion. Using meaningful names like row/col sidesteps it entirely and makes code readable. The accumulator placement mistake is a direct consequence of scope, connecting back to deck 10.

Learning Outcomes

Compute the sum, average, and range of an array’s elements using the accumulator pattern
Find the minimum and maximum by initializing to arr[0] and looping from index 1
Implement linear search that returns the index of a match, or -1 if not found

Manipulate an array in place: reverse elements using a temporary variable

title: Array Algorithms
Array Algorithms
Array Algorithms
Array Algorithms
text:
Why NOT Initialize to Zero?
Wrong approach:
int max = 0;    // ✗ what if all scores are negative?



Array
Correct max
Wrong max (starts at 0)




{88, 74, 91}
91
91 (accidentally correct)


{-5, -12, -3}
-3
0 ← wrong!


{0, 0, 0}
0
0 (accidentally correct)



Rule: always initialize min and max to arr[0], not to 0 or any arbitrary value.

Show this table — the second row is the killer counterexample. Students often say “but my test cases work!” — yes, because they used positive numbers. The real-world lesson: test with negative values and edge cases. The fix is always the same: start at the actual first element.

title: Array Algorithms
Array Algorithms
Array Algorithms
text:
Swapping Two Elements
To reverse or rearrange an array, you need to swap two elements. The wrong way:
arr[0] = arr[4];   // arr[0] is lost before we save it!
arr[4] = arr[0];   // now both are the same value
The right way — use a temporary variable:
int temp = arr[0];   // save arr[0] before overwriting
arr[0] = arr[4];     // overwrite arr[0]
arr[4] = temp;       // put the saved value into arr[4]


The cup/glass pouring analogy is universal and concrete. You can’t pour juice from glass A into glass B without spilling A’s juice unless you use a third empty glass first. Temp is that third glass. Walk through the three assignments line by line, tracking what each variable holds after each step.

title: Array Algorithms
Array Algorithms
Array Algorithms
text:
Common Mistakes






Warning


Initializing min/max to 0 Works for positive arrays by accident. Fails for arrays containing negatives. Always use arr[0].









Warning


Starting the min/max loop at i = 0 after initializing to arr[0] Compares arr[0] against itself in the first iteration — harmless but redundant. Start at i = 1.









Warning


Swapping without a temp variable One value is overwritten and lost. Always use a temp.









Warning


Dividing before the loop is done sum / arr.length inside the loop gives the average so far, not the final average. Divide after the loop.




These four mistakes are very predictable on exams and homeworks. Have students trace through each “wrong” version to see what incorrect output it produces — error-spotting is a skill that only develops with practice.

title: Array Algorithms
text:
Worksheet

Write int sum(int[] arr) and double average(int[] arr). Call both from main on {3, 8, 1, 6, 4}.
Write int min(int[] arr). What happens if you initialize min = 0 and the array is {-5, -2, -8}? Show the (wrong) output, then fix it.
Write int linearSearch(int[] arr, int target) that returns the first index where target appears, or -1 if not found. Test with array {10, 30, 10, 20} and target 10 — it should return 0.
Given array {5, 3, 9, 9, 2, 9}:

Find the maximum value.
Count how many times that maximum appears. (Two-pass algorithm.)

Challenge: Write void reverse(int[] arr) that reverses the array in place (no second array). Verify by printing the array before and after calling reverse on {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}.

title: What Is an Object?
text:
Learning Outcomes

Distinguish a class (blueprint) from an object (instance) and use new ClassName() to create an object
Access and modify an object’s state using dot notation (obj.field = value)
Invoke an object’s behavior by calling its methods (obj.method()) and observe how method calls change state
Create multiple independent objects from the same class and predict each object’s state after a sequence of operations
Explain why grouping related fields and methods into a class leads to clearer, more organized code

title: What Is an Object?
What Is an Object?
section: Everything Around You Is an Object
text:
Everything Around You Is an Object
Look around the room. Every physical thing has:

Properties — things that describe it (color, size, model, charge)
Behaviors — things it can do (play, charge, ring, open)




Thing
Properties
Behaviors




Phone
brand, battery%, color
call(), text(), takePicture()


Dog
name, breed, age
bark(), eat(), fetch()


Bank account
owner, balance
deposit(), withdraw()



Programming objects work the same way. A class defines the properties and behaviors. An object is one specific instance of that class.

This is the core OOP intuition. Students should nod — they already think about the world in terms of things with properties and behaviors. The job of OOP is to let them bring that mental model directly into code. Don’t rush past this slide; it’s the entire foundation.

title: What Is an Object?
text:
Class vs Object


Class = Blueprint
The template that defines what all dogs look like and can do.
One blueprint exists.
Dog
------
name
breed
age
------
bark()
birthday()

Object = Instance
A specific dog built from that blueprint.
Many objects can exist.
rex
------
name = "Rex"
breed = "Lab"
age = 3
luna
------
name = "Luna"
breed = "Poodle"
age = 1



The blueprint/house or cookie-cutter/cookie analogies both work here. The class is defined once. Objects (instances) are created from it as many times as needed — each one gets its own independent copy of the fields. Changing rex’s name has zero effect on luna’s name.

title: What Is an Object?
text:
Cookie Cutter and Cookies

The cookie cutter (class) is made once.
Each cookie (object) is stamped out from it — same shape, but you can decorate each one differently.
Changing the decoration on one cookie does not affect the others.

Let students sit with this image. Some will say “but I could change all the cookies by changing the cutter!” — yes, that’s what changing the class definition does. But after they’re stamped out, the cookies are independent. Runtime state changes on one object don’t bleed into others.

title: What Is an Object?
What Is an Object?
text:
Creating an Object
Dog rex = new Dog();



Part
Meaning




Dog
The type — this variable holds a Dog


rex
The variable name


new Dog()
Create a brand-new Dog object in memory



After this line, rex exists but has no name, breed, or age yet — those fields hold default values (null, null, 0).






Note


new is the keyword that creates an object. Every time you write new ClassName(), Java builds a fresh independent object.




Compare new Dog() to new int[5] — students have already seen new, just not with classes. The parallel is helpful: new creates something fresh in memory. The variable (rex) holds a reference (link) to that new object — just like arrays. This is why arrays behave like objects: they ARE objects.

title: What Is an Object?
What Is an Object?
text:
Calling an Object’s Methods
Use dot notation to invoke behavior:
rex.bark();       // Rex says: Woof!
rex.birthday();   // Rex is now 4!
IO.println(rex.age);   // 4 — the field actually changed!
Methods can read and change the object’s own fields — that’s what makes them powerful.
birthday() didn’t need age passed as a parameter. It found age inside the same object.


This is the “behavior changes state” idea. birthday() modifies age — not a local copy, the actual field inside rex. That’s different from what primitive parameters do (deck 09). An object’s method has direct access to the object’s own state. This is what it means to bundle data and behavior together.

title: What Is an Object?
What Is an Object?
What Is an Object?
Instance Methods
text:
Learning Outcomes

Write an instance method inside a class body that reads fields and returns a computed value
Write a void instance method that modifies one or more fields (with or without a parameter)
Write a boolean method that computes a predicate from an object’s fields (e.g., isPassing(), isSquare())
Call an instance method on an object using dot notation — obj.method() or obj.method(arg)
Compose two or more instance methods in a single class to solve a multi-step problem

title: Instance Methods
Instance Methods
Instance Methods
section: The Method Sees Its Object’s Fields
text:
The Method Sees Its Object’s Fields
When an instance method runs, it automatically sees the fields of the object it was called on:
Student alice = new Student("Alice", 88);
Student bob   = new Student("Bob",   74);

alice.greet();   // Hi, I'm Alice!
bob.greet();     // Hi, I'm Bob!
Same method body — different output — because name resolves to a different field each time.


This is the magic of instance methods — one definition, personalized execution. The method code is shared, but the data each invocation reads is unique to the object it was called on. Ask: “If we add a third student carol and call carol.greet(), what prints?” They should be able to answer immediately.

title: Instance Methods
Instance Methods
Instance Methods
Instance Methods
Instance Methods
text:
Calling Instance Methods
Always call instance methods on an object using dot notation:
Student alice = new Student("Alice", 88);

alice.printReport();     // ✓
alice.isPassing();       // ✓ (result discarded — use in if or assignment)

boolean passing = alice.isPassing();  // ✓ store result
if (alice.hasHonors()) { ... }        // ✓ use in condition

printReport();           // ✗ compile error — which student?
The object before the dot is the receiver — the object whose fields the method sees.

“Which student?” is the right question when students forget the dot. The method needs to know whose fields to read — you must tell it by specifying the object. This contrasts with standalone methods (decks 08–10) where you just write the method name. Instance methods need a receiver.

title: Instance Methods
Instance Methods
text:
Common Mistakes






Warning


Calling an instance method without an object isPassing() alone is a compile error outside the class. Inside the class (from another instance method), it works — Java assumes this.isPassing(). Outside, you must specify which object: alice.isPassing().









Warning


Passing fields as parameters to an instance method int area(int width, int height) — the fields are already available; you don’t need to pass them. int area() is correct.









Warning


Calling an instance method on the class name, not an object Student.isPassing() — compile error. The class is the blueprint; you need an instance: alice.isPassing().









Warning


Forgetting to assign the return value alice.area() does nothing useful if you don’t store or print the result. Use: IO.println(alice.area()) or int a = alice.area().

title: Instance Methods
text:
Worksheet

Add methods area() and perimeter() to a Triangle class with fields double base and double height. (area = 0.5 * base * height; for perimeter, add a third field double hypotenuse.)
Write a class Temperature with a double celsius field. Add:

double toFahrenheit() — returns celsius * 9/5 + 32
boolean isFreezing() — returns true if celsius ≤ 0
void warmUp(double degrees) — adds degrees to celsius

Write void describe() for Temperature that prints something like: 15.0°C (59.0°F) — not freezing. Call warmUp first, then describe.
Extend the Student class with a method void applyBonus(int points) that adds points to grade but caps it at 100. Then write void printReport() that prints name, grade, and letter grade on one line.
Challenge: Write a class Counter that tracks int count. Add void increment(), void reset(), boolean isEven(), and String describe() (e.g. "Count is 4 (even)"). Demonstrate all four methods in main.

title: null and Object References
text:
Learning Outcomes

Explain what null means for an object reference variable
Recognize a NullPointerException and identify the line that caused it
Guard against null using an if (obj != null) check before calling a method
Distinguish an uninitialized reference (null) from an initialized object
Explain that null is not the same as 0, false, or "" — it means “no object at all”

title: null and Object References
text:
What Is null?
When you declare an object variable without assigning it:
String name;        // uninitialized — holds null
Dog rex;            // uninitialized — holds null
Student alice;      // uninitialized — holds null
The variable holds null — a special value meaning “this variable currently points to nothing.”
null is not a string, not a number, not an empty object. It means no object exists here.


The pointer/arrow mental model is essential here. An object variable is an arrow (reference) pointing to an object. null means the arrow leads nowhere. Dereferencing null (following an arrow that leads nowhere) causes a NullPointerException — the program crashes because there’s nothing there to access. This is one of the most common runtime errors in Java.

title: null and Object References
text:
Default Values for Object Fields
When an object is created and its fields aren’t set in the constructor, they get default values:



Field type
Default value




int, double, etc.
0 / 0.0


boolean
false


String
null


Any object type
null



class Person {
    String name;    // defaults to null
    int age;        // defaults to 0
}

Person p = new Person();
IO.println(p.name);    // null
IO.println(p.age);     // 0

Students are often surprised that p.name prints the word “null” — Java converts null to the string “null” for IO.println. But calling a method on p.name (like p.name.length()) would crash with a NullPointerException because p.name has no object behind it. The printing behavior can mask the bug. Always check whether a String field was properly set before using it.

title: null and Object References
text:
NullPointerException
Calling a method on a null reference crashes the program:
Dog rex = null;
rex.bark();       // NullPointerException!
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException
This is one of the most common errors in Java. The message says: you tried to follow an arrow that leads nowhere.
When does it happen? - Calling a method on a variable that was never assigned - Calling a method on a field that was never set in the constructor - A method returned null and you called a method on the result

NullPointerException (NPE) is so common it’s almost a rite of passage in Java. The error tells you a line number — that’s the line where you dereferenced null. Find that line, find the variable, trace back to where it was supposed to be assigned. Was it assigned? If not, that’s the bug. A newer Java will also tell you which variable was null in the message.

title: null and Object References
null and Object References
null and Object References
section: null Is Not the Same As…
text:
null Is Not the Same As…



Value
Meaning




null
No object at all — the reference points nowhere


0
The integer zero — a valid int value


false
The boolean false — a valid boolean value


""
An empty String — a real String object with length 0



String a = null;   // no String object exists
String b = "";     // a String object exists, but it has no characters

IO.println(a.length());   // NullPointerException!
IO.println(b.length());   // 0  — perfectly fine

This is a common confusion. An empty string (““) IS an object — you can call .length() on it and get 0. null is NOT an object — you can’t call any method on it. The distinction matters in every conditional check: if (name == null) and if (name.equals(”“)) are two different questions.

title: null and Object References
text:
Common Mistakes






Warning


Calling a method without checking for null If a variable might be null, always guard with if (obj != null) before the dot.









Warning


Using == to compare String content name == "Alice" compares references (are they the same object?), not content. Use name.equals("Alice") — but check name != null first!









Warning


Forgetting that unset fields default to null A field of type String that isn’t set in the constructor holds null — calling .length() on it will crash.









Warning


Printing null and thinking it’s fine IO.println(name) will print the word null if name is null — no crash. But IO.println(name.toUpperCase()) will crash. Printing without crashing doesn’t mean the variable is safe to use.




The fourth mistake is the sneakiest: IO.println(null) works because Java converts null to the string “null” for display. Students think “it printed something, so name must be set.” Wrong — name is still null, and any method call on it will crash. Always verify that a field was actually assigned, not just that println survived.

Key Vocabulary Checklist
Before the final exam, make sure you can define and use each of these:
Fundamentals: type, variable, literal, expression, operator, assignment, scope
Control flow: condition, branch, loop, iteration, sentinel, accumulator, counter
Methods: parameter, argument, return value, void, method call, call site

This is the vocabulary of the course, distilled. Students who can fluently use all these terms in conversation about code are ready for COSC121 or any intro CS course. Suggest flashcard review — writing the definition of “argument” vs “parameter” or “class” vs “object” in their own words solidifies the knowledge.

title: Review and What’s Next
text:
Common Exam Patterns
The most frequently tested skills in intro CS finals:
Trace a program — given code, write the output line by line. Variable tables help.
Find the bug — given broken code, identify the error and fix it.
Write a method — given a description and method signature, fill in the body.
Write a class — given a description, write the fields, constructor, and one or two methods.
Predict and explain — given null, reference semantics, or scope, predict behavior and justify why.

Walk through each pattern explicitly. Students often study by reading notes — that’s passive. Exam performance comes from active recall: writing code from scratch, tracing unfamiliar code, explaining behavior in words. Encourage practice on past worksheets without looking at answers first.

You have learned if/else to branch based on a condition — so far, checked once. In draw(), any if/else you write gets re-evaluated every single frame. If the condition depends on something that changes — like the mouse position — the branch it takes can flip from one frame to the next, live.

text:
New idea: sorting a value into “levels”
You have learned that dividing two ints with / truncates instead of rounding — 7 / 2 is 3, not 3.5. That’s genuinely useful here: it turns a continuous, constantly-changing number like mouseX (0 through 399) into a small number of discrete “buckets.”
int level = mouseX / 100;
For mouseX from 0–99, level is 0. For 100–199, level is 1. And so on.

title: Introduction
text:
Before We Start

COSC420: Distributed/Parallel Computing — Mon/Wed/Fri, 50 min each. Monday = Lecture A, Wednesday = Lecture B, Friday = Lab.
Grading has seven components: Checkpoints, Labs, Quizzes, Midterm, Final, Capstone, Engaged Learning — see the syllabus for exact weights.
What this course assumes you know: computer organization — memory, registers, the CPU. What it does not assume: any operating systems or networking course. Every explanation this semester is built from computer-organization concepts up, never from OS/networking vocabulary down.
The promise: by the last week of the semester, you and a partner will build and demo a real distributed data pipeline — files stored across machines, code that runs on a cluster, a live dashboard backed by a database. Today, every one of those phrases should sound unfamiliar. That’s the correct starting point.


Timing: 4 min. Don’t read the syllabus line by line — point at it, move on fast. The one sentence worth pausing on is “what this course does not assume” — say it out loud, it visibly lowers anxiety in the room before the cold open.

title: Introduction
text:
Your First Week at StreamBase



Imagine you just started a data engineering internship at StreamBase, a fast-growing streaming startup.




Your manager pulls you aside Monday morning:



“StreamBase has 200 million subscribers. Every stream, pause, skip, and rating gets logged — we’re sitting on 80 billion events in our data lake. The content licensing team meets in December and they need to know: which genres and films should we prioritize next quarter? That question requires distributed processing — one machine can’t touch 80 billion rows. We use HDFS and Spark for exactly this. Your job: build and validate the pipeline on a 100K-row sample first. If the aggregations are right and the dashboard answers the question, we scale it up. The code doesn’t change. Only the data does. Demo is December 11.”



You’d probably say: “Sure — what’s HDFS? What’s Spark?”

Timing: 4 min. Pause after the quote. Let it land. Ask: “How many of you know what HDFS is? Spark? MongoDB? A REST API?” Nobody should raise their hand.

title: Introduction
section: Why This Should Sound Like Gibberish
text:
Why This Should Sound Like Gibberish
That’s the correct reaction — and the whole point of this course.

HDFS, Spark, and MongoDB are all tools for working with data that doesn’t fit on one machine. You’ll meet each one by name later this semester: HDFS in Module 3, Spark in Module 4, MongoDB in Module 5.
The manager’s ask sounds intimidating because of the number — 80 billion events. But notice the actual instruction: build and validate on a 100K-row sample first.
The key idea for the entire course: the code you write for 100,000 rows is the same code that runs on 80 billion rows. Distributed tools are built so the program doesn’t change size with the data — only the number of machines running it does.
You are not learning toy versions of these tools. You are learning the real tools, on data small enough to fit in your head.


Timing: 4 min. This slide used to live only in speaker notes — it’s promoted to a real slide because “the code doesn’t change, only the scale does” is the single idea that makes the rest of the semester make sense, and students need it to study from, not just hear once.

title: Introduction
section: Why Can’t We Just Use Excel?
text:
Why Can’t We Just Use Excel?
80 billion rows. One machine. One core. Let’s do the arithmetic.


A laptop with 16 GB of RAM can hold roughly 200 million integers in memory at once.
80 billion rows is 400× that — you would need on the order of 400 machines just to store the data, before any processing starts.
Even if it fit, processing 80 billion rows sequentially at a generous 1 million rows/second would take over 22 hours — for one pass over the data, one time.



Distributed computing is the answer: split the data across many machines, process each machine’s chunk in parallel, then combine the results. That’s literally what HDFS (storage) and Spark (processing) exist to do — and it’s why this course spends three modules on them.

Timing: 4 min. Keep this to the arithmetic — it’s meant to be a quick, visceral “oh, that’s why” moment. The deeper “why parallel hardware exists at all” question is the next slide.

title: Introduction
section: Why Now? Clock Speeds & the Multicore Turn
text:
Why Now? Clock Speeds & the Multicore Turn
This isn’t a new problem tools just recently got good at solving — it’s a hardware story you can trace from what you already know.

From the 1970s to roughly 2005, CPUs got faster mainly by raising clock speed — more cycles per second, every year, like clockwork (literally).
Around 2005 that stopped. Faster clock speeds mean more heat, and chips had hit a thermal wall: you cannot dissipate the heat a much-faster single core would generate at a size that fits in a laptop.
The industry’s answer wasn’t “wait for a breakthrough” — it was stop making one core faster, and put more cores on the chip instead. Your laptop’s 8 or 16 cores are a direct consequence of that 2005 pivot.
Consequence for you as a programmer: the hardware is already parallel. A program that only ever uses one core is leaving most of the machine idle. Learning to write code that uses multiple cores isn’t optional specialization anymore — it’s how you use the hardware you already own.


Timing: 5 min. Ask first, before giving the answer: “Does anyone know why your laptop has multiple cores instead of one really fast core?” Let a guess or two land, then confirm with the thermal-wall explanation. This is the one moment all semester that connects directly to computer organization — transistors, clock cycles, heat — spend the full 5 minutes, don’t compress it.

title: Introduction
text:
Netflix: One Answer, 200 Million Times

Every subscriber’s homepage is personalized — Netflix computes a different ranked list of titles for each of its 200 million subscribers, and recomputes it continuously as viewing behavior changes.
Those rankings are trained on billions of individual signals: ratings, watches, pauses, skips, even how long you hovered over a title before clicking.
Put those together: 200 million personalized answers, each depending on a model trained on billions of events, updated continuously. No single machine reads billions of events and produces 200 million distinct outputs fast enough to matter — this is an aggregation-and-machine-learning problem that requires many machines working at once.


Timing: 4 min. The number that matters is 200 million distinct answers, not one shared answer computed once. Don’t get pulled into explaining how recommendation algorithms work — the point is scale, not ML technique.

title: Introduction
section: Google: The Problem That Started It All
text:
Google: The Problem That Started It All

In 2004, Google faced a concrete problem: index and rank the entire web — billions of pages, far more text than any one machine could even read through, let alone process into a searchable index.
Their solution was to split the job across thousands of ordinary machines, each handling a slice of the web, with a common pattern for combining partial results into one answer. They published this pattern as a paper: “MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters.”
That single paper is the reason Module 3 of this course exists. In a few weeks you will write a MapReduce job yourself, using the exact pattern Google described in 2004 — it’s not a historical curiosity, it’s the design underneath Hadoop and, indirectly, Spark.


Timing: 4 min. Say “Module 3” out loud — a direct forward-reference, not a vague “later in the course.” Worth noting explicitly that this is 20-year-old, still-load-bearing computer science, not a dated example.

title: Introduction
text:
Amazon: Black Friday

On Black Friday, Amazon processes thousands of orders per second — and many of those orders are competing to read and write the same piece of data: how many units of a given item are left in stock.
A single database server handling that load has two bad options: fall behind and get too slow to be usable, or let two operations touch the same data at once and corrupt it — for example, two customers both “successfully” buying the last unit of an item that only had one left.
The fix is to spread both the data and the load across many machines — techniques called replication and sharding, which you’ll see in detail in Module 5. For now, just notice the shape of the problem: multiple things touching the same data at the same instant, with no one in charge of ordering them. Hold onto that shape — it is exactly the problem this entire module is about, just at the scale of two threads instead of two machines.


Timing: 5 min, the longest of the three vignettes. The last sentence is a deliberate, explicit plant for Session 3’s race conditions — say it clearly rather than leaving it implicit, since this slide is what students will re-read when race conditions are introduced and should recognize the connection themselves.

title: Introduction
text:
The Pipeline
ratings.csv + movies.csv   ← 100K sample of an 80-billion-event data lake
        ↓  hdfs dfs -put
      HDFS                  ← distributed file system: stores the data across many machines
        ↓  %%spark (sparkmagic)
    Apache Spark            ← distributed processing: computes aggregations across many machines
        ↓
     MongoDB                ← distributed database: stores the computed results
        ↓
    Flask API               ← REST API: serves the results over the network
        ↓
  Plotly Dashboard          ← the live answer to the licensing team's question
Every concept taught in this course is one piece of this pipeline. Nothing you learn this semester is disconnected from it — that’s deliberate.

Timing: 5 min. Bookmark this slide mentally — come back to it at the start of every module. Read each arrow’s right-hand label out loud; by Module 6 students will understand every word on this diagram, and that recognition is the payoff worth setting up now.
