title: Module 3: Big Data & MapReduce
text:
Meet Map, Shuffle, Reduce
MapReduce is a programming pattern for processing a big dataset by splitting it into pieces, processing each piece independently, then combining the results — exactly what your cluster did Monday, generalized to any number of “machines” and any counting problem, not just suits or menu items.
Input data (split across N machines/files)
         ↓
    Map    — each machine processes only its own piece, in parallel
         ↓
  Shuffle/Sort — the framework groups everyone's output by key
         ↓
   Reduce — one machine per key combines that key's values into a final answer
         ↓
      Output






Diagram to add later (Excalidraw / pyxcd / draw.io)


Reuse Monday’s kitchen-branch icon language. Three small “branch” icons on the left, each with its own input pile, feeding downward arrows into a “Map” band where each branch is shown tallying its own pile independently (no arrows between branches at this stage). Below that, a “Shuffle” band where arrows converge from all three branches toward per-key collection points (e.g., one arrow bundle labeled “♠” converging on one point, another labeled “♥” converging elsewhere) — these are the only diagonal/crossing arrows in the whole diagram, visually marking this as the one phase that costs movement. Below that, a “Reduce” band where each collection point emits one final summed value. Caption: “Same shape as Monday — just relabeled.”




Timing: 4 min. Point at each band and ask “what did this look like in your cluster on Monday?” before naming it formally — let the room answer before you do.

title: Module 3: Big Data & MapReduce
section: The Map Phase: One Record In, Zero or More Pairs Out
text:
The Map Phase: One Record In, Zero or More Pairs Out
A map function takes one input record and emits (key, value) pairs — nothing more.
map(record):
    ... extract whatever matters from this one record ...
    emit(key, value)
Two examples of the same pattern, different data:







Problem
What map() emits




Count words in a line of text
emit(word, 1) for every word in the line


Total sales per region, given region, productID, saleAmount records
emit(region, saleAmount)



Notice what’s the same in both: one input record in, one small (key, value) pair out — the mapper never looks at any other record, and never talks to any other machine. Exactly like your cluster tallying your own pile alone, Monday.






Think about it


A log file has one line per web request: timestamp, userID, status_code. You want to count how many requests resulted in each status code (200, 404, 500, …). What should map() emit?




Timing: 5 min. Callout answer: emit(status_code, 1) — structurally identical to word count and the sales example, just a different field extracted. The point of showing three problems with the same shape is pattern transfer, since Lab 4 and CP3 both hand students a new extraction problem (email domains) they need to recognize as this same pattern.

title: Module 3: Big Data & MapReduce
section: The Shuffle/Sort Phase: The Framework’s Job
text:
The Shuffle/Sort Phase: The Framework’s Job
After every machine finishes its map phase, all the emitted (key, value) pairs need to end up grouped by key — every value for "gmail.com" in one place, every value for "yahoo.com" in another — regardless of which machine originally emitted them.

This is exactly Monday’s “carry your tally to whoever owns that key” step — except now it’s the framework doing the carrying, across a real network, not a student walking across a room.
You never write this step yourself. Hadoop and Spark both do shuffle/sort automatically — it’s the one phase of MapReduce with no function you implement.
It’s also the one phase that costs real network transfer — same as Monday, where trips were the only real cost. Map and Reduce, like your cluster’s own tallying and summing, happen locally.


Timing: 4 min. Emphasize “you never write this step” explicitly — CP3 only asks students to write map-phase output precisely because shuffle and reduce’s mechanics are the framework’s job, not something to hand-code.

title: Module 3: Big Data & MapReduce
section: The Reduce Phase: Combine Each Group Into One Answer
text:
The Reduce Phase: Combine Each Group Into One Answer
A reduce function receives one key and the full list of values shuffled to it, and produces one final result for that key.
reduce(key, values):
    total = sum(values)
    emit(key, total)

This runs once per key, on whichever machine the shuffle phase sent that key’s values to — the same role as the one teammate on Monday who “owned” a suit or menu item and summed everything handed to them.
Reduce doesn’t have to mean “sum” — it could compute a maximum, an average, a count of distinct values, anything that combines a list into one answer. Summing is just today’s example.


Timing: 3 min. Keep this brief — it’s the shortest of the three phase slides because it’s the most intuitive once Map and Shuffle are solid.

title: Module 3: Big Data & MapReduce
text:
Word Count Walkthrough
The classic “Hello World” of MapReduce — structurally identical to Monday’s activity, just counting words instead of suits or menu items.
Input:
the quick brown fox
the fox jumped over the lazy dog
Map phase (one mapper per line):
(the,1) (quick,1) (brown,1) (fox,1)
(the,1) (fox,1) (jumped,1) (over,1) (the,1) (lazy,1) (dog,1)
Shuffle/Sort (grouped by key — the framework’s work, not yours):
(brown,[1])  (dog,[1])  (fox,[1,1])  (jumped,[1])
(lazy,[1])   (over,[1]) (quick,[1])  (the,[1,1,1])
Reduce phase (sum each list):
(brown,1) (dog,1) (fox,2) (jumped,1) (lazy,1) (over,1) (quick,1) (the,3)

Timing: 5 min. Walk this top to bottom, pointing explicitly at which line is Map, which is Shuffle, which is Reduce — this is the exact shape CP3 and Lab 4’s email-domain problem reuse.

title: Module 3: Big Data & MapReduce
text:
Why This Scales
Module 2 put it this way: “a distributed system grows by adding more machines, not by buying an impossibly bigger one.” That’s called scaling out (add more machines) as opposed to scaling up (buy one bigger machine) — MapReduce is the mechanism that makes scaling out actually work for processing, not just storage.

Map tasks run in parallel, one per input chunk — on a real cluster, ideally on the same machine that already holds that chunk of data. This is called data locality: compute goes to the data, not data to the compute. Kitchen picture: send the recipe to the branch that already has the ingredients, don’t ship the ingredients to one central kitchen.
Reduce tasks also run in parallel, one per key (or range of keys).
Only shuffle moves data across the network — exactly the one phase that cost a trip on Monday. Everything else happens locally, at the same time, on every machine.
Adding a 21st machine to a MapReduce cluster doesn’t require rewriting map() or reduce() — it just means one more machine’s worth of chunks processed in parallel. That’s what “scaling out” buys you: capacity grows by adding machines, with the same code.







Important


This is the same instinct your best cluster found in Round 2: move the small thing (a tally), not the big thing (the raw pile). Data locality is that same idea, one level up — don’t move the raw data to the computation, move the (tiny, by comparison) computation to the data.




Timing: 4 min. The callout is the payoff of the whole activity — say explicitly that “data locality” is the formal name for the exact efficiency idea their best Round 2 strategy already discovered. The scale-up/scale-out distinction isn’t tested by any checkpoint, quiz, or exam — it’s here only so the slide’s own title (“scales”) is earned by a definition rather than assumed. Don’t spend more than a sentence on it.

title: Module 3: Big Data & MapReduce
section: What the Framework Handles For You
text:
What the Framework Handles For You
Beyond running Map, Shuffle, and Reduce, Hadoop and Spark both handle a list of things you never have to code yourself:

Task scheduling — deciding which machine runs which chunk
Fault tolerance — if a machine dies mid-job, its work gets reassigned and re-run elsewhere
Retries — a failed task is retried automatically, not left broken
Progress tracking — reporting how much of the job is done

You write map() and reduce(). The framework does everything else — a big part of why MapReduce was such a breakthrough in 2004.

Timing: 2 min. Keep brief — this is context for why the abstraction is valuable, not testable detail.

title: Module 3: Big Data & MapReduce
text:
Recap: From “How” to “Where”
Monday and Wednesday gave you MapReduce — the program that processes big data, split into Map, Shuffle, and Reduce. But every one of those tasks has to run somewhere, reading a file that has to live somewhere. Today: the file system that stores it (HDFS), and the software that decides which machine runs which task (YARN) — the two real pieces underneath what Lab 4 only simulated in local mode, and what Lab 5 runs for real this Friday.

Timing: 3 min. Say explicitly: “Lab 4 ran without HDFS or YARN at all — that was deliberate, so you could focus on the Mapper/Reducer code first. Today fills in the two pieces Lab 4 skipped.”

title: Module 3: Big Data & MapReduce
section: Why Not Just a Regular File System?
text:
Why Not Just a Regular File System?
A regular file system — the one on your laptop — lives on one machine’s one disk.

Its size is capped by that one disk, no matter how the rest of the data grows.
If that one disk fails, everything on it is gone — no backup, nothing to fall back on.
Only one machine can read it at a time — no way to spread the reading work across many machines.

HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System) splits a file into pieces and spreads those pieces — plus duplicate copies — across many machines’ disks. The file can now be bigger than any single disk, survives a disk failure, and can be read by many machines at once, in parallel. This is the same scaling out idea from Wednesday — now applied to storage, not computation.

Timing: 4 min. One-sentence callback to Wednesday’s scale-up/scale-out beat is enough — don’t re-derive it, just point at it: “same idea, different resource.”

title: Module 3: Big Data & MapReduce
text:
HDFS Blocks + Replication

HDFS splits a file into fixed-size blocks (default 128 MB) — a large file becomes many blocks, scattered across many machines.
Each block is stored on 3 machines, not one (replication factor = 3).
Kitchen picture: like stocking the same popular ingredient at 3 different branches, so one branch’s fridge breaking down doesn’t mean the whole company runs out of it.
This is a first, simpler taste of the replication idea — Module 5 covers the full version, including why 3 copies, consistency between them, and what happens when one goes stale. For now: 3 copies, automatic, so no single block is a single point of failure.

ratings.csv (say, 500 MB) → split into 4 blocks of ~128 MB each
  Block 1 → stored on Machine A, Machine C, Machine E
  Block 2 → stored on Machine B, Machine D, Machine A
  Block 3 → stored on Machine C, Machine E, Machine B
  Block 4 → stored on Machine D, Machine A, Machine C

Timing: 4 min. The block-placement example is illustrative, not something to test — the point is “different blocks can land on different machines, and each one is triplicated,” not the exact placement algorithm.

title: Module 3: Big Data & MapReduce
section: HDFS Architecture: The Address Book, Again
text:
HDFS Architecture: The Address Book, Again
Module 2 gave you DNS: the internet’s address book, translating a human-readable name into a numeric address before your browser could even connect. HDFS has the exact same shape of problem — given a filename, which machines actually hold its blocks?

The NameNode is HDFS’s version of that address book — it tracks which blocks belong to which file, and which machines hold each block. It does not store any of the actual file data itself.
DataNodes are the machines that store the real block data.
To read a file: the client asks the NameNode “where are this file’s blocks?”, the NameNode replies with a list of DataNode locations, and the client then reads the blocks directly from those DataNodes — the NameNode itself never touches the actual data.







Diagram to add later (Excalidraw / pyxcd / draw.io)


A client icon on the left. An arrow labeled “1. Where are ratings.csv’s blocks?” pointing to a central “NameNode” icon (drawn like an address-book/directory icon, visually matching Module 2’s DNS diagram style). A return arrow labeled “2. Blocks 1–4 are on Machines A, B, C…” pointing back to the client. Then separate direct arrows labeled “3. Read block data” from the client straight to 3–4 “DataNode” icons (plain server/disk icons) — these arrows should visually bypass the NameNode entirely, making clear the NameNode only answers the lookup, it doesn’t relay any data itself. Caption: “Same shape as DNS: ask the address book, then go straight to the real thing.”




Timing: 4 min. The “NameNode never touches the actual data” point is the one most worth stating explicitly and slowly — it’s the detail students most often get backwards, assuming the NameNode is a relay rather than a lookup service.

title: Module 3: Big Data & MapReduce
text:
HDFS Commands Demo
hdfs dfs -put ratings.csv /user/alice/    # upload: local file → HDFS
hdfs dfs -ls /user/alice/                 # list files in an HDFS directory
hdfs dfs -cat /user/alice/ratings.csv     # read a file's contents
hdfs dfs -get /user/alice/ratings.csv .   # download: HDFS → local file

-put and -get are opposites: local-to-HDFS, and HDFS-to-local.
-ls and -cat mirror the everyday Unix commands you already know, just pointed at HDFS instead of your local disk.
This -put command is not a hypothetical — it’s the literal first step of Week 1’s Pipeline diagram, and the exact command Lab 10 has you run on ratings.csv and movies.csv for the capstone.


Timing: 5 min. Actually run these four commands live against the classroom cluster if possible, on a small throwaway file — seeing real output (a real file listing, real file contents) lands better than reading the commands off a slide.

title: Module 3: Big Data & MapReduce
text:
HDFS Design Principles

Write once, read many — files aren’t modified after writing; you write a file once, then only ever read it (or replace it entirely) afterward.
Data locality — the same idea from Wednesday: MapReduce runs map tasks on the same machine that already holds the data block being processed.
Fault tolerance — if a DataNode fails, its blocks are automatically re-replicated elsewhere from the remaining copies, restoring the replication factor of 3.
Not good for: small files (overhead per file is high), low-latency access (built for throughput, not speed-of-single-lookup), or random writes (write-once-read-many, remember).


Timing: 3 min. HDFS was designed for exactly the workload MapReduce produces — large, sequential reads of immutable files. It’s a poor choice for transactional workloads (that’s what Module 5’s databases are for) — worth saying explicitly, since students may otherwise wonder why the capstone uses both HDFS and MongoDB instead of just one.

title: Module 3: Big Data & MapReduce
section: YARN: Who Actually Runs the Job?
text:
YARN: Who Actually Runs the Job?
HDFS answers “where does the data live.” YARN (Yet Another Resource Negotiator) answers “which machine actually runs each Map or Reduce task, and who’s keeping track?”

ResourceManager — the whole branch network’s dispatcher: one per cluster, deciding which worker machine handles a newly submitted job.
NodeManager — each branch’s own on-site manager: one per worker machine, actually running whatever tasks get assigned to that machine.
ApplicationMaster — a coordinator dispatched specifically for one job: tracks that job’s progress across whichever workers are running its tasks. One ApplicationMaster per job, not one for the whole cluster.







Diagram to add later (Excalidraw / pyxcd / draw.io)


A client icon submitting a job (arrow labeled “hadoop jar … job”) to a single “ResourceManager” icon at the top. The ResourceManager fans out to 3 “NodeManager” icons, one per worker machine, each drawn next to a small server/disk icon labeled “runs Map/Reduce tasks here.” Keep this diagram visually separate from the HDFS NameNode/DataNode diagram two slides back — same three worker machines can appear in both, but the arrows and roles are different, and drawing them as one combined diagram is exactly the confusion this split is meant to avoid.




Timing: 4 min. Keep this the lightest new-content slide of the session — YARN internals aren’t competency-tested, this exists so “run a MapReduce job on a Hadoop cluster” (C3.3) has a name attached to what’s actually happening, not to be memorized role-by-role.

title: Module 3: Big Data & MapReduce
text:
A MapReduce Job in Practice
The output directory of a completed Hadoop MapReduce job:
/output/
  _SUCCESS          ← empty file, signals the job completed successfully
  part-r-00000      ← actual output (one file per reducer)
  part-r-00001      ← (if 2 reducers were used)

Never overwrite an existing output directory — Hadoop refuses, specifically to prevent accidental data loss. You’ll see this exact error in Lab 5 if you forget to clean up first.
Delete it yourself before re-running: hdfs dfs -rm -r /output


Timing: 3 min. This is a direct preview of Lab 5’s Task 3, Question 3 — say plainly that they’ll hit this refusal-to-overwrite behavior themselves on Friday, so it isn’t a surprise.

title: Module 3: Big Data & MapReduce
text:
From MapReduce to Spark
MapReduce already gets you scaling out for processing — but it has real limitations:

Every job writes its intermediate results to disk, even between steps of the same pipeline — slow for anything iterative.
The Mapper/Reducer API is low-level and verbose — hard to express a multi-step pipeline cleanly.
No support for interactive, ask-a-question-and-wait-seconds-for-an-answer queries.

Spark (2009, Berkeley AMPLab) keeps intermediate data in memory instead of writing it to disk between steps — 10–100× faster for iterative workloads. Same scaling-out idea as MapReduce; Module 4 is about doing it faster.

Timing: 3 min. Keep the framing “same idea, faster mechanism” rather than “MapReduce is obsolete” — Hadoop/HDFS is still the storage layer under Spark in this course’s own pipeline.

text:
Recap: From Compute to Storage
Module 4 answered “how do you compute something at scale?” — load data into Spark, transform it, aggregate it, write out a result.
Module 5 answers the next question: where does that result actually live, once it’s computed, so that thousands of users can read it reliably at the same time? title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
section: The Problem: One Machine, Too Much Load
text:
The Problem: One Machine, Too Much Load
A single database server can fail in two different ways as demand grows, and they call for two different fixes:

Too much traffic, data fits fine: the machine simply can’t answer requests fast enough — every read and write funnels through one CPU, one network connection.
Too much data, traffic is fine: the dataset itself no longer fits on one machine’s disk (or even in a reasonable multiple of it), regardless of how much traffic there is.
Single point of failure, either way: if that one machine goes down, the data is completely unreachable until it comes back — recall Module 2’s “partial failures” idea, except now there’s nothing partial about it. One machine down means everything is down.


Timing: 4 min. Setting up the two-problems framing explicitly here pays off on the very next two slides — replication answers the first bullet, sharding answers the second.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
section: Replication: Many Copies of the Same Data
text:
Replication: Many Copies of the Same Data
Replication means keeping multiple full copies of the same data on different machines.

Every replica holds the entire dataset — not a piece of it.
Reads can be served by any replica, spreading read traffic across multiple machines instead of funneling it through one.
If one replica goes down, the others still have every record — the single-point-of-failure problem from the last slide goes away for reads.
Writes are more subtle: usually one replica (the primary) accepts writes, and the change is then copied out to the others.







Important


You’ve actually seen a first, simpler version of this already: Module 3’s HDFS stored each block on 3 machines — like stocking the same ingredient at 3 kitchen branches, so one branch’s fridge breaking down doesn’t lose it. That was replication for file blocks, specifically for MapReduce jobs to read. Today’s version is the general idea, for any database, read and written directly by users — not just batch jobs.









Diagram to add later (Excalidraw / pyxcd / draw.io)


One database-cylinder icon labeled “Primary” at the top, with two arrows fanning down to two more cylinder icons labeled “Replica 1” and “Replica 2,” each holding an identical small stack of document icons (same three icons repeated in all three cylinders, to show it’s a full copy each time). A read arrow pointing into any of the three; a write arrow pointing only into the Primary. Caption: “Same data, three times over. Reads go anywhere. Writes go through the primary.”




Timing: 4 min. Keep the “primary accepts writes” detail brief here — Session 2 goes deep on exactly how that copying happens (sync vs. async) and why it matters for consistency.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
Sharding: Splitting the Data Itself
Sharding means splitting the dataset itself across multiple machines — each machine holds a different slice of the data, not a full copy.
Shard key: user_id

Shard 1: user_id 0 – 9,999,999
Shard 2: user_id 10,000,000 – 19,999,999
Shard 3: user_id 20,000,000+

Each shard holds only its own fraction of the total data — together, all shards make up the whole dataset.
Both storage and write traffic get spread across machines, since different records live (and are written) on different shards.
The field used to decide which shard a record belongs to is called the shard key.
A query for one specific record only needs to go to the one shard that holds it — but a query that spans many records may need to check every shard.


Timing: 4 min. Contrast explicitly with the previous slide’s diagram: replication = same data N times; sharding = 1/N of the data, N times. That contrast is the single most important idea in today’s session.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
section: Replication vs. Sharding — Choosing Between Them
text:
Replication vs. Sharding — Choosing Between Them









Replication
Sharding




Solves
Read throughput, availability
Data volume, write throughput


Each node holds
A full copy of all the data
A fraction of the data


Use when
The dataset fits on one machine, but there’s too much read traffic
The dataset itself is too large for one machine


Single point of failure?
Fixed — any replica can serve reads if another fails
Not fixed by sharding alone — losing one shard still loses its slice of data









Think about it


A photo-sharing app’s user-profile database is only 2 GB (tiny), but gets 200,000 profile-page views per second during a viral event. A separate table logging every photo upload has grown to 40 TB and keeps growing. Which table needs replication, which needs sharding, and could a table ever need both?




Timing: 5 min. The callout’s last question is the important one to land: yes, a table can need both at once (e.g., MongoDB’s sharded clusters replicate within each shard) — that’s exactly what Session 5’s “Replication and Sharding in MongoDB” slides come back to.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
The Cost of Replication
Replication isn’t free — it trades storage and consistency for read throughput and availability.

Storage cost multiplies: 3 replicas means 3× the storage for the same data.
Replicas can briefly disagree: if a write hasn’t finished copying to every replica yet, a read from a lagging replica can return stale (out-of-date) data.
This lag is usually milliseconds, but it is never exactly zero — “how much staleness is acceptable” is a real design decision, not a solved problem. Session 2 goes deep on this.


Timing: 3 min. Plant this seed deliberately — “replicas can briefly disagree” is precisely what Wednesday’s session expands into strong vs. eventual consistency.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
The Cost of Sharding
Sharding isn’t free either — it trades query simplicity for scale.

Cross-shard queries are expensive: “find everyone named Alice” now has to ask every shard and merge the results, instead of asking one machine.
A bad shard key creates hot spots: if your shard key clusters too much traffic onto one shard (e.g., sharding by signup date when everyone signs up “today”), that one shard becomes the new single overloaded machine — sharding stops helping.
Resharding is hard: once data is split across shards, changing the shard key later means physically moving large amounts of data between machines.


Timing: 3 min. The hot-spot point is the one worth emphasizing if time is short — it’s the most common real mistake, and it directly explains why choosing a good shard key matters, not just that one is required.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
Single Points of Failure, Revisited
Tie this back to Module 2: a single point of failure (SPOF) is any one component whose failure takes down the whole system. An un-replicated database is a textbook SPOF.

Replication removes the SPOF for reads — any surviving replica can still answer queries.
It does not, by itself, remove the SPOF for writes if there’s still exactly one primary accepting them — if the primary goes down, something has to take over, which is a real, nontrivial problem (this is exactly the mechanism behind the GitHub split-brain case study from Module 2, Session 3 — a failover mechanism promoting a new primary is precisely what created that incident).
Sharding, on its own, does not remove any SPOF — it just changes what is lost when one machine fails: instead of losing everything, you lose that shard’s slice of the data.


Timing: 3 min. Explicitly naming the GitHub case study connection here rewards students who retained Module 2 — say it out loud rather than assuming they’ll make the connection themselves.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
Checkpoint 6
CP6 (today, last 15 minutes of class): given a scenario, decide whether replication or sharding better solves the described problem, and explain why in 2–3 sentences.
Review before you start: ask yourself which of the two problems from the start of today’s session the scenario describes — too much traffic on data that fits fine (→ replication), or too much data / write load that no longer fits on one machine (→ sharding).

Timing: 15 min for the checkpoint itself. See checkpoints/checkpoint_06.md for the exact graded scenarios — don’t preview its specific news-site/ride-sharing examples before students start; today’s slides deliberately used a different example (the photo-sharing app).

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
Recap: Replication’s Loose Thread
Monday ended on an unresolved tension: replicas are supposed to hold “the same data,” but a write takes time to copy from the primary to every replica. For that window of time, they don’t quite agree.
Today’s question: what should a read do when it lands in that window?

Timing: 3 min. This is the whole session in one sentence — keep this slide tight so it lands as a genuine open question, not a rhetorical one.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
Recap: The CAP Theorem (from Module 2)
Module 2, Session 2 covered this in full — a fast re-anchor:







Consistency
Every read gets the latest write, or an error


Availability
Every request gets a response


Partition tolerance
The system keeps working despite a network split



The theorem: during a network partition, a distributed system must choose between Consistency and Availability — it cannot fully guarantee both at once.

Timing: 3 min. Genuinely just a recap slide — if a student is shaky on this, point them back to Module 2’s slides rather than re-teaching the proof sketch here.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
section: Applying CAP to a Replicated Database
text:
Applying CAP to a Replicated Database
A replica set (Monday’s picture: one primary, several replicas) is itself a small distributed system — so CAP applies to it directly.

If a network partition separates a replica from the primary, that replica has a choice:

Refuse to answer reads until it can confirm it’s caught up (favors Consistency)
Answer with whatever data it currently has, possibly stale (favors Availability)

This is exactly Module 2’s CAP trade-off, just applied to “should this specific replica answer this specific read” instead of “should the whole system answer this specific request.”







Important


Even without a network partition, replication introduces a smaller version of this same choice: does the primary wait for replicas to confirm a write before telling the client “done” — trading speed for certainty — or does it say “done” immediately and let the copying happen in the background? That’s the next four slides.




Timing: 5 min. The callout is the pivot from “CAP during rare partitions” to “consistency trade-offs during totally normal operation” — make sure that shift is explicit, since it’s easy to think CAP only matters when something is broken.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
Strong Consistency
Strong consistency: every read reflects the most recent write, no matter which replica answers it.

To guarantee this, a write typically can’t be considered “done” until it has been confirmed by enough replicas that no read could possibly see stale data.
Cost: writes are slower — the primary has to wait for confirmation before responding to the client.
Benefit: no surprises. Once a write succeeds, every subsequent read, from any replica, sees it.


Timing: 4 min. Keep this and the next slide symmetric in structure (definition → cost → benefit) so the contrast is easy to hold in mind together.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
Eventual Consistency
Eventual consistency: replicas are allowed to be temporarily out of sync — but if no new writes happen, they will all eventually converge to the same value.

The primary can respond “done” to the client as soon as it has the write, without waiting for replicas to catch up.
Cost: a read immediately after a write might hit a replica that hasn’t caught up yet, and see the old value.
Benefit: writes are fast, and the system keeps working even if a replica is temporarily slow or unreachable.







Think about it


Quiz 7 will ask about this directly: asynchronous replication can lead to replicas temporarily having different versions of the data. Why “asynchronous,” specifically — what would synchronous replication have to do differently to prevent that?




Timing: 4 min. The callout’s answer is the bridge into the next slide: synchronous replication would have to wait for replicas to confirm before acknowledging the write — which is strong consistency’s mechanism, described from the replication-mechanics angle instead of the CAP angle.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
Synchronous vs. Asynchronous Replication
This is the actual mechanism behind the strong/eventual distinction:









Synchronous replication
Asynchronous replication




Primary waits for replicas before confirming write?
Yes
No


Write speed
Slower
Faster


Consistency
Strong
Eventual


Risk if primary crashes right after a write
None — replicas already have it
Replicas may be missing the most recent write(s)




Synchronous = strong consistency’s mechanism: the primary refuses to say “done” until replicas confirm.
Asynchronous = eventual consistency’s mechanism: the primary says “done” immediately and copies the change out afterward.


Timing: 5 min. This table is the payoff of the whole strong-vs-eventual discussion — make sure students leave able to map “strong consistency” → “synchronous replication” and “eventual consistency” → “asynchronous replication” without hesitation.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
section: A Worked Scenario: Checking Your Bank Balance
text:
A Worked Scenario: Checking Your Bank Balance
You just transferred $500 out of your checking account. One second later, you refresh the app and check your balance.

If the bank uses strong consistency: your new balance is guaranteed correct, every time — worth the extra write latency for money, where “slightly out of date” is unacceptable.
If the bank instead used eventual consistency and you got unlucky: you might briefly see your old balance, as if the transfer hadn’t happened — even though it genuinely went through.
Compare this to a social media “like” count: if that count is briefly off by one because of replication lag, essentially nobody notices or cares.







Think about it


Name one more real system where you’d insist on strong consistency, and one more where eventual consistency would be perfectly fine. What’s the actual property that decides which one you pick?




Timing: 5 min. The intended takeaway for the callout: the deciding property is roughly “cost of showing stale data” versus “cost of slower writes” — not some fixed rule about what kind of app it is.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
section: Read Preference: Choosing Where to Read From
text:
Read Preference: Choosing Where to Read From
Many real databases let you choose, per query, how strict to be — rather than picking strong or eventual consistency for the whole system once and for all.

Read from the primary: always current, but funnels all reads through one machine — no read-scaling benefit from having replicas at all.
Read from any replica (“secondary” reads): spreads read load across machines, at the cost of possibly-stale results.
This setting is usually called read preference, and it’s a real, named option you’ll see again in MongoDB specifically, in Session 5.


Timing: 4 min. Flag explicitly that this is forward-referencing real MongoDB terminology — students will see “read preference” again in two sessions and should recognize it as the same idea introduced here, not a new concept.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
section: Consistency Is a Spectrum, Not a Switch
text:
Consistency Is a Spectrum, Not a Switch
Strong and eventual consistency are the two ends of a range, not the only two options:

Some systems let you require confirmation from just some replicas (not all, not just one) — a middle ground between the two extremes.
Some systems guarantee causal consistency: if event B happened because of event A, every node sees A before B — even if unrelated events can still arrive in different orders on different nodes.
The exact terminology varies by database. What matters for this course: consistency is a design choice with a dial, not a single fixed property a database either has or doesn’t.


Timing: 4 min. Keep this conceptual and brief — the goal is “there’s more nuance here than strong-vs-eventual if you go looking,” not to teach every consistency model by name.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
Framing: No New Concepts Today
Everything you need is already covered: replication, sharding, single points of failure (Monday); strong vs. eventual consistency, synchronous vs. asynchronous replication (Wednesday).
Today’s job: combine those tools into an actual design decision, for three different scenarios, and defend your reasoning to the class.

Timing: 2 min. Set expectations: this is discussion and small-group work, not a lecture.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
Scenario 1: A Note-Taking App
A note-taking app has 3 million users. Each user’s notes are small (a few KB total) and are read and written almost exclusively by that one user — nobody else ever sees your notes.
In your group, decide: replicate, shard, both, or neither? If replicating, strong or eventual consistency? What’s the worst thing that happens if you get this wrong?

Timing: 10 min including group work. Push toward: total data volume is enormous (3M users × notes) but each individual user’s working set is tiny and only touched by one person — this maps cleanly to sharding by user ID, with mild replication for availability; strong consistency isn’t very important since each user only ever reads their own writes.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
Scenario 2: A Flight-Search Engine
A flight-search engine stores current seat availability for every flight, globally. Millions of users search and book simultaneously. Double-booking the same seat is a serious, costly problem.
In your group, decide: replicate, shard, both, or neither? If replicating, strong or eventual consistency? What’s the worst thing that happens if you get this wrong?

Timing: 10 min including group work. Push toward: this is the strong-consistency case — two people should never be told the same seat is available after one of them already booked it. Sharding by flight/route is reasonable for scale, but each shard’s availability data needs strong consistency, not eventual.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
Scenario 3: A Multiplayer Game’s Leaderboard
A multiplayer game shows a global “Top 100 players this week” leaderboard, updated as players finish matches. Millions of matches finish per hour, worldwide.
In your group, decide: replicate, shard, both, or neither? If replicating, strong or eventual consistency? What’s the worst thing that happens if you get this wrong?

Timing: 10 min including group work. Push toward: extremely high write volume (matches finishing constantly) argues for sharding; the leaderboard itself tolerates real staleness — if your new high score takes a few seconds to appear, nobody is harmed — so eventual consistency is an easy, correct call here, in sharp contrast to Scenario 2.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
Class Discussion: Comparing Answers






Think about it — full class, 10–12 min


Compare your group’s Scenario 2 (flight seats) and Scenario 3 (leaderboard) answers side by side. Both have huge write volume. Why did one need strong consistency and the other didn’t? What’s the actual question you should ask yourself to decide, for any new system?




Timing: 12 min. Push toward: the deciding question isn’t “how much traffic” — it’s “what’s the cost of a user briefly seeing wrong/stale data, versus the cost of slower writes.” Scale determines whether you need to shard; the cost of staleness determines how consistent you need to be. These are two separate axes, and today’s scenarios were picked to make that separation visible.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
Wrap-Up
Every real storage decision in this course — and in industry — comes down to combining the same handful of tools you now have: replicate for availability and read scale, shard for volume and write scale, and dial consistency to match how much staleness a given piece of data can tolerate.
Monday: what kind of database actually implements these tools — the landscape of NoSQL database types.

Timing: 6 min (including whatever discussion time is left over from the previous slide). Close on the forward-reference to keep momentum into Monday.

The last three sessions covered concepts that apply to any storage system — replication, sharding, consistency. Today: the actual kinds of database software that implement these concepts, and which kind fits which job.

Timing: 3 min. Fast bridge — the shift is from “storage design theory” to “here are the products.”

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
section: Why Not Just a Relational Database?
text:
Why Not Just a Relational Database?
Relational databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL) are excellent for structured, transactional data — and remain the right choice for a huge share of real applications. They start to struggle when you need to:

Store data whose structure varies from record to record (not every record has the same fields)
Scale out, in Module 3’s terms — spread both data and load across many machines — rather than scale up (buying one increasingly expensive bigger machine)
Serve extremely high read or write volume with a simpler, less rigid query model

NoSQL (“Not only SQL”) databases are a family of alternatives designed around these needs.

Timing: 4 min. Resist framing this as “NoSQL is better” — it’s a trade-off, and the slide right before the module summary makes that explicit again.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
Key-Value Stores
The simplest possible model: every value is stored under a unique key, and that’s it.
SET session:abc123 "user_id=42,expires=..."
GET session:abc123

The database treats the value as an opaque blob — it doesn’t know or care what’s inside.
Extremely fast, often in-memory (Redis) — ideal when you always look things up by one exact key and don’t need to query by the value’s contents.
Common uses: caching, session storage, rate limiting, real-time leaderboards.


Timing: 4 min. Tie “real-time leaderboards” back to Session 3’s Scenario 3 — same use case, now with a concrete technology attached to it.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
Column-Family Stores
Designed for massive write throughput distributed across many machines — think logging billions of events per day.

Rows have a partition key; the set of columns can vary per row within a partition (similar flexibility idea to document stores, different underlying structure).
No joins, and query patterns are deliberately limited — you design your tables around the specific queries you’ll run, not the other way around.
Used by companies with enormous, constant write volume: Netflix, Apple, Instagram all use Cassandra for parts of their infrastructure.


Timing: 4 min. Keep this brief relative to document/key-value — it’s the least directly relevant type to this course’s labs and capstone, included for landscape completeness and because Quiz 7 references NoSQL types generally.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
Graph Databases
Built around relationships as first-class data, not an afterthought.

Nodes (entities) and edges (relationships between them), both of which can have their own properties.
Query language example (Neo4j’s Cypher): MATCH (a:Person)-[:FRIEND]->(b:Person) RETURN b
Ideal when the interesting questions are about connections: “friends of friends,” “people who bought A also bought B,” fraud rings, recommendation engines.


Timing: 4 min. Quiz 7 Q5’s recommendation-engine question maps directly here — say the “people who bought A also bought B” phrase out loud, since it’s close to the quiz’s own wording.

Flexible, general-purpose records — user profiles, catalogs

Exact-key lookups, need extreme speed

Think about it


A ride-sharing app needs: (1) driver profile records that vary a bit driver-to-driver, (2) a constant firehose of GPS location pings from every active driver, and (3) “which drivers are friends/referred each other” for a referral bonus program. Which NoSQL type fits each piece?




Timing: 5 min. Intended mapping: (1) document store for profiles, (2) column-family for the GPS firehose, (3) graph for the referral relationships — the point is that one real system often uses multiple NoSQL types for different parts of itself, not just one.

text:
CRUD — Create
# Insert one document
result = col.insert_one({
    "name": "Alice",
    "dept": "Engineering",
    "salary": 95000
})
print(result.inserted_id)  # the auto-generated _id

# Insert many documents at once
col.insert_many([
    {"name": "Bob",  "salary": 62000},
    {"name": "Carol","salary": 78000},
])

_id is created automatically for every document — a unique identifier, unless you supply your own.
insert_one returns one new _id; insert_many returns a list of them.


Timing: 4 min. Quiz 7 Q8 tests insertOne syntax directly (shell form: db.students.insertOne(...)) — note that the Python driver spells it insert_one (snake_case) while the MongoDB shell spells it insertOne (camelCase); both are correct in their own context, and worth pointing out explicitly since Lab 9 uses the Python form and Checkpoint 7 uses shell syntax.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
CRUD — Read, and Query Operators
# Find all documents
for doc in col.find():
    print(doc)

# Find with an exact-match filter
engineers = col.find({"dept": "Engineering"})

# Filter with a comparison operator
high_earners = col.find({"salary": {"$gt": 80000}})

# Sort and limit
col.find().sort("salary", -1).limit(5)   # top 5 by salary



Operator
Meaning




$gt / $lt
Greater than / less than


$gte / $lte
≥ / ≤


$ne
Not equal


$in
Value is in a given list


$exists
Field exists on the document




Timing: 5 min. Quiz 7 Q9 and Q10 both test this directly — find({}) returns everything (Q10), and $lt versus $gt (Q9). Say both of those out loud explicitly, they’re easy to mix up under quiz pressure.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
CRUD — Update and Delete
# Update ONE matching document
col.update_one(
    {"name": "Alice"},
    {"$set": {"salary": 100000}}
)

# Update ALL matching documents
col.update_many(
    {"dept": "Engineering"},
    {"$mul": {"salary": 1.10}}   # 10% raise for everyone matched
)

# Delete
col.delete_one({"name": "Bob"})
col.delete_many({"active": False})

$set replaces a field’s value outright; $mul multiplies a numeric field by a factor.
update_one/delete_one affect only the first match; update_many/delete_many affect every match.


Timing: 4 min. This maps almost exactly onto Checkpoint 7’s Task 3 (updateOne + $set) and Task 4 (deleteMany) — don’t use the checkpoint’s own active/department fields as the live example here if you want to avoid spoiling it outright, though the operators themselves obviously must be taught plainly.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
Replication in MongoDB
Session 1’s general replication concept, applied concretely: MongoDB uses replica sets — typically 3 nodes, 1 primary + 2 secondaries.
Write → Primary → Secondary 1
                → Secondary 2
Read ← Primary (default) or a Secondary (if read preference allows it)

All writes go to the primary; changes replicate out to secondaries — asynchronously by default, which is Session 2’s “eventual consistency” in a real product.
If the primary fails, the remaining secondaries automatically elect a new primary.
Read preference (Session 2’s concept, by its real name here): primary (always current) or secondaryPreferred (may be slightly stale, spreads out read load).


Timing: 4 min. This is the payoff moment for Session 1 and Session 2 — say explicitly “this is the exact same replication and consistency material from last week, now with MongoDB’s own names on it.”

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
Sharding in MongoDB
Session 1’s general sharding concept, applied concretely: when a collection outgrows one machine, split it across shards using a shard key.
Shard key: user_id

Shard 1: user_id 0 – 9,999,999
Shard 2: user_id 10,000,000 – 19,999,999
Shard 3: user_id 20,000,000+

A router process (mongos) directs each query to the right shard(s), transparently to your application code — you don’t write different queries for a sharded vs. unsharded collection.
A poorly chosen shard key creates the hot spots Session 1 warned about — e.g., sharding by signup date sends all of today’s traffic to one shard.
In practice, each shard is also a replica set — sharding and replication are combined, not either/or, answering Session 1’s “can a table need both?” callout question directly: yes.


Timing: 4 min. Land the “combined, not either/or” point explicitly — it’s the resolution to the open question from Session 1’s photo-sharing-app callout.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
section: Beyond CRUD: Counting for the Capstone
text:
Beyond CRUD: Counting for the Capstone
One operation beyond plain CRUD is worth knowing now, because the capstone’s flask_app.py needs it for its dashboard’s stat cards:
# Count documents matching a filter
col.count_documents({"dept": "Engineering"})

# A simple aggregation: average salary
from pymongo import MongoClient
col.aggregate([
    {"$group": {"_id": None, "avg_salary": {"$avg": "$salary"}}}
])

count_documents(filter) — how many documents match, without fetching them.
MongoDB’s full aggregation pipeline (multi-stage $match/$group/$sort chains) is more than this course goes deep on — the capstone only needs simple counts and averages like the example above, not the full pipeline syntax.


Timing: 3 min. Keep this genuinely light — it exists so students aren’t caught off guard by flask_app.py’s stat-card queries, not to teach the aggregation pipeline as a topic in its own right.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
MongoDB Atlas — Cloud-Managed MongoDB

No server to set up yourself — MongoDB Atlas hosts and manages it for you.
Free tier (M0): enough storage for this course’s work, no credit card required.
Handles replication, backups, and monitoring automatically — the replica-set mechanics from two slides ago happen behind the scenes.
Connection string format: mongodb+srv://user:password@cluster.mongodb.net/







Tip


Atlas is what you’ll use in Lab 9, the capstone, and — realistically — in most entry-level industry jobs. The managed service is exactly what lets you use everything from today without running a database server yourself.




Timing: 3 min. This is largely logistics for Friday’s lab — keep it brief.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
Checkpoint 7
CP7 (today, last 15 minutes of class): given a MongoDB collection’s documents, write the query for four tasks: two find() queries (an exact match, and a comparison operator), one updateOne with $set, and one deleteMany with a filter.
Review before you start: - db.collection.find({field: value}) - db.collection.find({field: {$gt: value}}) - db.collection.updateOne({filter}, {$set: {field: value}}) - db.collection.deleteMany({filter})

Timing: 15 min for the checkpoint itself. See checkpoints/checkpoint_07.md for the exact graded prompt (an employees collection) — don’t preview its specific documents before students start.

title: Module 5: Distributed Storage & NoSQL
text:
Module 5 Summary







Concept
Key idea




Replication
Full copies of the data on multiple nodes — solves read throughput and availability


Sharding
Splitting the data itself across nodes — solves data volume and write throughput


Strong consistency
Every read reflects the latest write — costs write latency


Eventual consistency
Replicas converge over time — reads can briefly be stale


Document store
JSON-like documents, flexible schema — MongoDB


MongoDB CRUD
insert_one/many, find, update_one/many, delete_one/many


Replica set / sharded cluster
MongoDB’s names for replication and sharding, combined in practice



Connects to: Checkpoints 6 & 7, Quiz 7, Lab 9, Final Q31–Q45, Capstone (spark_job.py’s direct-to-MongoDB writes, flask_app.py’s queries)

Timing: 2 min. Bridge to Friday’s Lab 9 (MongoDB Atlas CRUD, hands-on) and Quiz 7, both on Nov 20 — then to Module 6: “everything computed and stored so far still needs a way for a user to actually see it — that’s Flask and the REST API, next.”

title: Introduction
text:
Today’s Plan

What GPU acceleration actually means, and why it’s suddenly everywhere
The question this whole course is built to answer
A live tour of Google Colab — where every line of code you write this semester will run


~1 min. Pure housekeeping/agenda slide — say it, don’t dwell on it.

title: Introduction
text:
Why This Course, Why Now

Every app you used this morning likely touched a GPU somewhere: the phone camera’s portrait mode, a voice assistant, a recommendation feed, a video call’s background blur
Large AI models (the kind behind ChatGPT, image generators, etc.) are trained and run almost entirely on GPUs — not CPUs
Five years ago, “GPU programming” was a niche graphics/gaming skill. Today it’s one of the most in-demand skills in computing, from finance to genomics to robotics
This course teaches you to think and program in the style that makes GPUs fast — not just to call a library


~3 min. Ask the room: “What app did you use this morning that was probably running on a GPU somewhere?” Let a few answers land before revealing the list above. The goal is to make “GPU” feel less like obscure hardware and more like the engine behind things they already use daily.

title: Introduction
text:
The Question This Course Answers

You are given a problem and a chip with thousands of tiny processors. How do you split the problem into thousands of pieces that can all run at the same time, and keep those processors from sitting idle?



Every module this semester answers one piece of this question
By the end, you’ll write code that runs on real GPU hardware — not simulate it, not read about it, actually run it


~2 min. This is the organizing question of the whole course — plant it early, return to it at the start of every module going forward (module01 already references “the question for this course”).

title: Introduction
section: The Capstone Teaser: Songs as Numbers
text:
The Capstone Teaser: Songs as Numbers

Imagine a music app with 100,000 songs. Each song is described by 64 numbers (a “fingerprint” capturing its tempo, mood, instrumentation, etc.)
To find songs similar to one you like, the app multiplies your song’s 64 numbers against every other song’s 64 numbers, and adds up the results — a dot product
Do that 100,000 times, for every user, in real time: that’s 100,000 × 64 multiply-and-add operations, repeated continuously — a textbook GPU workload
This exact computation is your semester-long capstone project


~3 min. Don’t explain the math of dot products yet — that’s Session 3 and EL-01 (3Blue1Brown). Here the point is purely motivational: a concrete, relatable, real system that needs exactly the kind of massive repeated arithmetic a GPU is built for.

title: Introduction
text:
One Cashier vs. Twenty Lanes



The single expert cashier is faster per customer — but the line is long
Twenty ordinary cashiers are each slower per customer — but together they clear the crowd faster
This is the entire CPU-vs-GPU design philosophy in one picture — Module 1 gives you the real numbers behind it


~4 min. This analogy will get reused (and made precise) in Module 1 — plant it now so it’s familiar vocabulary later. Deliberately avoid the word “throughput” here if it hasn’t landed yet; let the picture carry it, then attach the vocabulary word at the end.

title: Introduction
section: From Graphics Card to Compute Engine
text:
From Graphics Card to Compute Engine

GPUs were originally built for one job: color millions of screen pixels, many times per second, for video games
Coloring a pixel is simple arithmetic, and every pixel’s color is independent of its neighbors — the same simple job, repeated millions of times, with no coordination needed
Around 2007, NVIDIA released tools (CUDA) letting programmers repurpose that pixel-coloring hardware for any problem shaped like “the same simple job, repeated millions of times” — not just pixels
Scientific simulation, finance, and eventually AI all turned out to be full of exactly that shape of problem


~3 min. Keep this brief — it’s context, not testable content. The full CUDA programming model (kernels, threads, grids) is Module 2’s job; here we only need the historical “why does a graphics chip do AI” hook.

title: Introduction
text:
Meet Google Colab

Colab is a free, browser-based notebook environment — no install, no setup on your own laptop
Every notebook runs on a machine in Google’s data center, and that machine can include a real GPU
You write code in cells; Colab runs each cell and shows the output immediately below it
Every lab, checkpoint, midterm, and final in this course happens inside a Colab notebook — get comfortable here early


~2 min. Confirm everyone has a Google account and can reach colab.research.google.com before moving on — this is a hard blocker for Friday’s Lab 1 if not resolved today.

title: Introduction
text:
Colab Anatomy




Cells run top to bottom, but you can re-run any single cell out of order — this will bite you if you’re not careful (a variable from a deleted cell can still “exist” until you restart)
“Runtime → Restart runtime” clears everything and starts fresh — your escape hatch when things get weird


~3 min. Live-demo this on the projector rather than just showing the diagram — actually create a cell, run it, edit a markdown cell, and deliberately show the “stale variable” gotcha by running cells out of order.

title: Introduction
text:
Selecting a GPU Runtime




By default, a new Colab notebook runs on a CPU-only machine — you must explicitly request a GPU
Free-tier Colab gives you an NVIDIA T4 GPU, with usage limits that reset periodically
Changing runtime type disconnects and reconnects your notebook — any variables you had are lost, so save your work first

# The check every notebook should start with this semester:
import torch
print("GPU available:", torch.cuda.is_available())
print("GPU name:", torch.cuda.get_device_name(0) if torch.cuda.is_available() else "none")

~3 min. Live-demo selecting the GPU runtime and running this check cell. This exact check reappears as the opening cell of Lab 1 — make sure everyone sees it succeed once, live, before Friday.

The Weekly Rhythm




Monday and Wednesday: lecture (this room, this format)
Friday: lab session — guided, hands-on, graded on completion, no time pressure
The last ~20 minutes of most Friday labs: a checkpoint — timed, individually-seeded, auto-graded
Roughly every three weeks, a lecture opens with a 15-minute Blackboard quiz covering the previous module


~3 min. Students consistently confuse labs (relaxed, completion-graded) with checkpoints (timed, auto-graded, higher stakes) early in the semester — be explicit that they are different activities on the same day.

Engaged Learning: Beyond the Slides

Five short reflection assignments (EL-01 through EL-05) spread across the semester, ~1% of your grade each
Each pairs a short video or reading (10–30 min) with a ~250-word discussion board post
They’re not busywork — EL-01 (3Blue1Brown, due Sep 13) will make Session 3’s dot-product material click before we even get there

~2 min. Plant EL-01 now since it’s due before Quiz 1 (Sep 14) and directly supports Session 3’s dot product content — students who watch it early will have an easier time in the NumPy lecture.

title: Introduction
text:
This Week

Today (Mon): you’re here
Wed: Python for Java developers — bring your laptop, we’ll live-code
Fri: Lab 1 in Colab — first notebook submission, plus Checkpoint CK-1 in the last 20 minutes
Before Wednesday: make sure you can log into Colab and see a blank notebook — that’s the only prep needed


~2 min. End here. Confirm nobody’s blocked on a Google account before they leave the room — this is the single most common Week 1 support request.

title: NumPy Foundations
text:
The Goal of This Module

Everything we do for the rest of the semester operates on arrays — NumPy is the mental model, CUDA (Module 2 onward) is the execution engine that runs that same model on a GPU
If you can write fast, loop-free NumPy code today, you already think the way GPU programming requires
Today’s dot product example reappears, unchanged, on the very last day of this course


~2 min. Same framing as before but now delivered after students have Python fundamentals under their belt — reference Session 2’s “why loops are secretly expensive” teaser directly.

title: NumPy Foundations
section: The Array as the Unit of Work
text:
The Array as the Unit of Work

A Python list can hold anything, in any mix — flexible, but that flexibility is exactly what makes it slow at scale (Session 2’s “checking types every iteration” cost)
A NumPy array gives up that flexibility on purpose: one fixed type, laid out as one contiguous block of memory
In exchange, operations apply to the entire block at once — not element by element in a Python loop


import numpy as np
x = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], dtype=np.float32)
y = x * 2          # not a loop — one operation over the whole array

~3 min. Live-demo: type([1, "two", 3.0]) works fine, then np.array([1, "two", 3.0]) — show it silently converts everything to strings. This makes “one fixed type” concrete rather than abstract.

title: NumPy Foundations
text:
dtypes Matter



dtype
bytes
use case




float64
8
NumPy’s default, high precision


float32
4
GPU default, half the memory of float64


int32
4
indices, counts




Every element in an array shares one dtype — that’s the “give up flexibility” trade from the previous slide, made concrete
GPUs are built to move and compute on float32 efficiently; using float64 on a GPU can be noticeably slower and always uses twice the memory
We use float32 throughout this course, starting today — get in the habit now


~3 min. Ask: “if float32 uses half the memory, and a GPU’s speed is often limited by how fast it can move data (not compute), what does halving the memory do to speed?” Let students reason toward “roughly doubles throughput” themselves — this is a light preview of Module 3’s memory-bandwidth material, don’t over-formalize it now.

title: NumPy Foundations
text:
Shape, Reshape, Indexing
a = np.arange(24, dtype=np.float32)   # [0, 1, 2, ..., 23]  — shape (24,)
b = a.reshape(4, 6)                   # same 24 numbers, viewed as 4 rows × 6 cols
c = b[2, :]                           # row 2, all columns
d = b[:, 3]                           # all rows, column 3

reshape doesn’t move or copy any numbers — it just changes how the same block of memory is interpreted
Shape is always (rows, cols): b.shape == (4, 6)
Indexing syntax [row, col] and slicing [start:stop] are the exact patterns from Session 2’s list-slicing slide, now extended to two dimensions


~3 min. Callback explicitly to the list-slicing slide from Session 2 — “you already learned this syntax, we’re just adding a second dimension.”

title: NumPy Foundations
text:
Memory Layout



A 2D array’s rows are contiguous in memory — row 0’s six numbers sit right next to each other, then row 1’s six numbers, and so on (“row-major” order)
This means walking across a row is a straight walk through memory; walking down a column jumps around
File this away — it becomes the whole story behind memory coalescing, one of the most important GPU performance topics, in Module 3


~3 min. Don’t derive coalescing here — that requires GPU thread concepts they don’t have yet. The only goal today is: shape is a label on memory, not a rearrangement of it, and rows are the “straight walk.”

title: NumPy Foundations
text:
Reducing Along an Axis
grid = np.array([[1, 2, 3],
                  [4, 5, 6]], dtype=np.float32)   # shape (2, 3)

np.mean(grid, axis=0)   # [2.5, 3.5, 4.5]  — one value per COLUMN
np.mean(grid, axis=1)   # [2.0, 5.0]       — one value per ROW
np.mean(grid)           # 3.5              — one value, every element

axis=0 collapses rows together — you get one result per column
axis=1 collapses columns together — you get one result per row
Memory trick: the axis number you pass is the dimension that disappears from the shape after the reduction — (2, 3) with axis=0 leaves shape (3,)
np.sum, np.max, np.min, np.argmax all take this same axis parameter


~3 min. This is a notoriously confusing NumPy detail — most students initially guess axis=0 means “reduce along rows” (i.e. row-wise), when it actually means “collapse the row dimension,” producing one value per column. Have students predict np.mean(grid, axis=1) before revealing it. This exact skill is on Quiz 1 and gets hands-on practice in Lab 2’s last exercise.

title: NumPy Foundations
text:
Reducing Along an Axis, Visually



The arrows show which direction values get squashed together — not which direction you “read” the axis number
Same picture applies to np.sum, np.max, and every other axis-aware reduction


~2 min. Pair this directly with the mnemonic from the previous slide — seeing the arrows collapse in the opposite direction from what “axis=0” sounds like is what makes the rule stick.

title: NumPy Foundations
text:
Broadcasting Rules
a = np.ones((4, 6), dtype=np.float32)              # shape (4, 6)
b = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], dtype=np.float32) # shape (6,)

c = a + b   # b is stretched across every row — result shape (4, 6)

NumPy compares shapes right to left. Here: 6 matches 6 — compatible
A dimension of size 1 (or a missing dimension) is automatically stretched to match the other array — no data is actually copied
If shapes don’t line up this way, NumPy raises a shape-mismatch error rather than guessing what you meant


~3 min. This is consistently the single most-tripped-over NumPy concept in labs. Have students predict the shape of a + b before revealing the comment, then try a deliberately mismatched pair (e.g. shape (6,) against shape (4, 5)) live to show the error message.

title: NumPy Foundations
text:
Broadcasting, Visually



The stretching in the diagram is conceptual — NumPy never actually duplicates b in memory; it just reuses the same 6 numbers for every row
This “reuse without copying” trick is why broadcasting is fast, not just convenient


~3 min. Emphasize the “no copy happens” point explicitly — it’s easy to walk away thinking broadcasting is expensive because the mental picture looks like duplication.

title: NumPy Foundations
text:
Boolean Masking
scores = np.array([0.9, 0.3, 0.7, 0.1, 0.8], dtype=np.float32)
mask   = scores > 0.5           # [True, False, True, False, True]
high   = scores[mask]           # [0.9, 0.7, 0.8]

scores > 0.5 doesn’t compare once — it compares every element, producing a full array of True/False
Using that Boolean array as an index selects only the True positions — no loop, no if
This exact pattern (compare, then select) is used in Lab 2 and reappears constantly for the rest of the course


~3 min. Live-demo: build the mask, print it separately from the selection, so students see the intermediate Boolean array rather than the two steps blurring together.

title: NumPy Foundations
text:
Why Loops Are Slow

A Python for loop over an array processes one element at a time, and for every single element, Python re-checks the type, re-does bounds checking, and re-dispatches the operation — overhead paid 2,000,000 times for a 2,000,000-element array
NumPy’s vectorized operations hand the entire array to pre-compiled C code in one call — the type-checking and dispatch overhead is paid once, not once per element
Typical measured speedup on Colab: 50–200×, purely from removing per-element Python overhead — no algorithm changed, only how the same arithmetic gets executed


~4 min. This is the conceptual payoff of the whole module — connect it explicitly back to Session 2’s “why this matters for GPU programming” teaser slide. Note for later: Lab 3 / CK-3 (next module) has students measure this exact speedup themselves; today is intuition, next week is the number.

title: NumPy Foundations
text:
Not Everything Vectorizes
Vectorization works when every output element can be computed independently — NumPy doesn’t care what order it processes them in. Some computations don’t have that property.

# Fibonacci: each value depends on the two before it
fib = [0, 1]
for i in range(2, 10):
    fib.append(fib[i-1] + fib[i-2])   # MUST know fib[i-1] before computing fib[i]

There’s no single NumPy call that produces this — fib[i] cannot exist before fib[i-1] does
This is called a serial dependency: step i needs the result of step i-1, not just its position
Contrast with everything else today: x**2 + 1, boolean masks, dot products — every output element only needs the input values, never another output


~2 min. This is the one exception to “just vectorize it” that students need before Quiz 1 — ask them to spot the difference between this Fibonacci loop and the polynomial-evaluation loop from earlier: same syntax shape, but one has a dependency between iterations and one doesn’t. This same idea reappears in Module 1 as a reason GPUs specifically struggle with certain problems — today it’s just about NumPy.

title: NumPy Foundations
text:
The Dot Product

A dot product multiplies two same-length lists of numbers position by position, then adds up all the products
It shows up constantly: a weighted average is a dot product; a similarity score is a dot product; a full matrix multiply is just many dot products computed at once


\[
\mathbf{u} = [u_0, u_1, u_2, \cdots , u_{D-1}] \\
\mathbf{v} = [v_0, v_1, v_2, \cdots , v_{D-1}] \\ \\
\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = u_0 v_0 + u_1 v_1 + \cdots + u_{D-1} v_{D-1}
\]


u = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], dtype=np.float32)
v = np.array([4.0, 5.0, 6.0], dtype=np.float32)
np.dot(u, v)     # 1*4 + 2*5 + 3*6 = 32.0

~3 min. Keep the geometric meaning (angle, projection) out of this slide entirely — that’s EL-01’s job (3Blue1Brown). Here we want only the mechanical pattern: multiply pairs, sum the results. Work the 3-element example on the board before revealing the code.

title: NumPy Foundations
text:
Similarity via Dot Product
song_a = np.array([0.6, 0.8, 0.0], dtype=np.float32)  # "fingerprint" vector
song_b = np.array([0.8, 0.6, 0.0], dtype=np.float32)  # similar mood/tempo to a
song_c = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0], dtype=np.float32)  # totally different

print(np.dot(song_a, song_b))   # close to 1.0 — similar
print(np.dot(song_a, song_c))   # 0.0 — unrelated

When vectors are pre-normalized (length 1), their dot product lands between −1 and 1, and a value near 1 means “point in nearly the same direction” — which we’re using here as a stand-in for “sound similar”
This is the Session 1 capstone teaser, now with real, runnable code behind it


~3 min. Callback explicitly to the Session 1 “songs as numbers” slide — students should recognize this as the same example, now computable.

title: NumPy Foundations
section: Matrix Multiply as Batch Dot Products
text:
Matrix Multiply as Batch Dot Products
Q = np.random.randn(1000, 64).astype(np.float32)    # 1,000 query songs
D = np.random.randn(100_000, 64).astype(np.float32) # 100,000 database songs

sim = Q @ D.T   # sim[i, j] = dot product of query i with database song j
                # shape: (1000, 100_000)

One @ call computes 100 million individual multiply-and-add pairs — every query against every database song
NumPy hands this to a highly optimized library (BLAS) that’s already parallel across your CPU’s cores
We’ll do the same computation on a GPU’s thousands of cores in the capstone — same math, radically more parallelism


~3 min. Optional live-demo: time this cell on Colab CPU with %%time — it’s fast enough to look almost instant, which sets up the “and yet the GPU is still much faster” hook for later modules. If short on time, this slide can be trimmed to the code + first bullet only.

title: NumPy Foundations
text:
What NumPy Cannot Do

NumPy runs on the CPU. Q @ D.T above calls into parallel C code — but any Python for loop you write yourself still runs one instruction at a time on one core
A modern GPU has on the order of 10,000 arithmetic cores — NumPy alone has no way to address that many independent workers at once
The open question: if we want to run 100 billion dot products per second, how do we tell hardware to do all of them simultaneously? That question drives the next four modules


~2 min. This is deliberately unanswered — Module 1 starts answering it. Land the question and stop; don’t preview Module 1’s content here.

title: NumPy Foundations
text:

title: EL-01: The Shape of a Dot Product
text:
Engaged Learning · 1% of course grade



On the first day of class you heard: “Every song is described by 64 numbers. We measure how well two things match by multiplying those numbers together and adding up.” That operation is a dot product — and it is the computational heart of your capstone.
This assignment gives you the visual intuition that makes the math feel obvious rather than arbitrary. You will need it in Module 4 (tiled matrix multiply) and in the capstone.




3Blue1Brown — Essence of Linear Algebra (YouTube playlist: “Essence of linear algebra” by 3Blue1Brown)
Watch these three episodes in order — they are short (8–10 min each):

Episode 1 — “Vectors, what even are they?” What a vector is, how to picture it, why mathematicians and physicists define it differently.
Episode 3 — “Linear transformations and matrices” What it means to multiply a matrix by a vector. The visual that makes matrix math click.
Episode 9 — “Dot products and duality” The geometric meaning of the dot product: projection, alignment, and why a value near 1.0 means “pointing in the same direction.”

Total viewing time: approximately 30 minutes.





Write a 200–300 word reflection on Blackboard for EL-01. Address all three prompts — a sentence or two each is fine, but be specific:
1. The geometric picture. In your own words, what does a dot product measure geometrically? (Not the formula — the meaning. Use the word “direction” somewhere in your answer.)
2. The similarity connection. Suppose two songs both have 64-number embeddings and those vectors point in nearly the same direction. What does their dot product tell you about how similar the songs are? Why does normalising the vectors to unit length make this cleaner?
3. Your honest reaction. Did anything in the videos surprise you, change how you think about something, or clarify something that felt like magic before? If the videos were old news to you, describe one thing you noticed in the visualisations that you had not thought about that way before.

Today’s Plan

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
text:
Why This Course, Why Now

Every app you used this morning likely touched a GPU somewhere: the phone camera’s portrait mode, a voice assistant, a recommendation feed, a video call’s background blur
Large AI models (the kind behind ChatGPT, image generators, etc.) are trained and run almost entirely on GPUs — not CPUs
Five years ago, “GPU programming” was a niche graphics/gaming skill. Today it’s one of the most in-demand skills in computing, from finance to genomics to robotics
This course teaches you to think and program in the style that makes GPUs fast — not just to call a library


~3 min. Ask the room: “What app did you use this morning that was probably running on a GPU somewhere?” Let a few answers land before revealing the list above. The goal is to make “GPU” feel less like obscure hardware and more like the engine behind things they already use daily.

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
text:
The Question This Course Answers

You are given a problem and a chip with thousands of tiny processors. How do you split the problem into thousands of pieces that can all run at the same time, and keep those processors from sitting idle?


Every module this semester answers one piece of this question
By the end, you’ll write code that runs on real GPU hardware — not simulate it, not read about it, actually run it


~2 min. This is the organizing question of the whole course — plant it early, return to it at the start of every module going forward (module01 already references “the question for this course”).

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
section: The Capstone Teaser: Songs as Numbers
text:
The Capstone Teaser: Songs as Numbers

Imagine a music app with 100,000 songs. Each song is described by 64 numbers (a “fingerprint” capturing its tempo, mood, instrumentation, etc.)
To find songs similar to one you like, the app multiplies your song’s 64 numbers against every other song’s 64 numbers, and adds up the results — a dot product
Do that 100,000 times, for every user, in real time: that’s 100,000 × 64 multiply-and-add operations, repeated continuously — a textbook GPU workload
This exact computation is your semester-long capstone project


~3 min. Don’t explain the math of dot products yet — that’s Session 3 and EL-01 (3Blue1Brown). Here the point is purely motivational: a concrete, relatable, real system that needs exactly the kind of massive repeated arithmetic a GPU is built for.

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
text:
One Cashier vs. Twenty Lanes
[DIAGRAM] — Two side-by-side scenes. Left: a single, highly-skilled cashier serving one customer at a time from a long line, labeled “CPU: minimize time per customer.” Right: twenty ordinary cashiers, each serving one customer simultaneously from twenty short lines, labeled “GPU: maximize customers served per minute.” A clock icon on the left, a stopwatch-with-many-ticks icon on the right.

The single expert cashier is faster per customer — but the line is long
Twenty ordinary cashiers are each slower per customer — but together they clear the crowd faster
This is the entire CPU-vs-GPU design philosophy in one picture — Module 1 gives you the real numbers behind it


~4 min. This analogy will get reused (and made precise) in Module 1 — plant it now so it’s familiar vocabulary later. Deliberately avoid the word “throughput” here if it hasn’t landed yet; let the picture carry it, then attach the vocabulary word at the end.

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
section: From Graphics Card to Compute Engine
text:
From Graphics Card to Compute Engine

GPUs were originally built for one job: color millions of screen pixels, many times per second, for video games
Coloring a pixel is simple arithmetic, and every pixel’s color is independent of its neighbors — the same simple job, repeated millions of times, with no coordination needed
Around 2007, NVIDIA released tools (CUDA) letting programmers repurpose that pixel-coloring hardware for any problem shaped like “the same simple job, repeated millions of times” — not just pixels
Scientific simulation, finance, and eventually AI all turned out to be full of exactly that shape of problem


~3 min. Keep this brief — it’s context, not testable content. The full CUDA programming model (kernels, threads, grids) is Module 2’s job; here we only need the historical “why does a graphics chip do AI” hook.

Every notebook runs on a machine in Google’s data center, and that machine can include a real GPU
You write code in cells; Colab runs each cell and shows the output immediately below it
Every lab, checkpoint, midterm, and final in this course happens inside a Colab notebook — get comfortable here early
