Colab Anatomy
[DIAGRAM] — A labeled screenshot-style mockup of a Colab notebook window. Callouts pointing to: (1) a code cell with a “▶ Run” triangle to its left, (2) a text/markdown cell showing rendered formatted text, (3) the output area appearing directly below a code cell after running it, (4) the top toolbar’s “+ Code” / “+ Text” buttons for adding cells, (5) the Runtime menu in the top menu bar.

Cells run top to bottom, but you can re-run any single cell out of order — this will bite you if you’re not careful (a variable from a deleted cell can still “exist” until you restart)
“Runtime → Restart runtime” clears everything and starts fresh — your escape hatch when things get weird

Same Logic, Different Grammar

You already know how to program: variables, loops, conditionals, functions — that thinking transfers completely
What’s different is syntax — the words and punctuation Python expects instead of Java’s
Today is a translation exercise, not a “learn programming from scratch” lecture
Goal by the end of class: read any short Python snippet and know what it does, even before you’ve memorized every keyword


~2 min. Reassure the room explicitly — many students hearing “new language” panic unnecessarily. Frame this as vocabulary, not new concepts.

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
text:
No More Type Declarations


Java
int count = 5;
double price = 9.99;
String name = "Ada";
boolean done = false;

Python
count = 5
price = 9.99
name = "Ada"
done = False


Python infers the type from the value — you never write int, double, or String before a variable
The variable can even change type later (usually a bad idea, but Python allows it — Java does not)
Capitalization matters: Python’s True/False/None, not Java’s true/false/null


~3 min. Live-type this in a Colab cell rather than just showing it — run type(count), then reassign count = "five" and run type(count) again to make the “types are not fixed” point concrete.

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
text:
Dynamic Typing: The Grammar-Teacher Analogy

Java is a strict grammar teacher: before you say a sentence, you must announce what part of speech every word is going to be — noun, verb, adjective — and the teacher checks you announced correctly before you’re allowed to speak
Python assumes you know what you mean, and figures out the parts of speech from context as you go
Trade-off: Java catches certain mistakes before the program ever runs (compile-time). Python only discovers a mismatch when that line actually executes (run-time) — so Python programs can fail later and more unexpectedly than Java ones
This is why Python code tends to look shorter — but it also means you need to test what you write more carefully


~3 min. This analogy is worth landing well — it explains why Python looks so sparse compared to Java without requiring any compiler-theory vocabulary the students don’t have.

text:
Lists: Java’s ArrayList, Python’s list


Java
ArrayList<Integer> nums =
    new ArrayList<>();
nums.add(10);
nums.add(20);
nums.get(0);
nums.size();

Python
nums = [10, 20]
nums.append(30)
nums[0]
len(nums)


Python’s list is built into the language — no import, no <Integer> type parameter
A single Python list can hold mixed types ([1, "two", 3.0]) — Java’s ArrayList<Integer> cannot
len(nums) is a function call, not a method — this is a common early typo (nums.len() does not exist)


~3 min. The “mixed types allowed” point is worth a live demo — it looks alarming to a Java developer at first. Note explicitly that NumPy arrays (Session 3) are not like this — they go back to Java’s “one type only” discipline, for reasons we’ll cover then.

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
text:
List Slicing
nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

nums[1:3]     # [20, 30]   — index 1 up to (not including) index 3
nums[:2]      # [10, 20]   — from the start up to index 2
nums[3:]      # [40, 50]   — from index 3 to the end
nums[-1]      # 50         — negative index counts from the end
nums[::2]     # [10, 30, 50] — every 2nd element

Slicing has no Java equivalent — closest is manually looping and copying into a new array
The pattern [start:stop:step] — memorize this now, because NumPy array slicing (Session 3) uses exactly the same syntax


~3 min. Emphasize the last bullet strongly — this slide is deliberately positioned as direct setup for Session 3. Have students predict nums[1:-1] before revealing the answer.

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
text:
None vs. null, and Truthiness
result = None          # Python's "no value" — like Java's null

if result:              # careful: 0, "", [], and None are all "falsy"
    print("has a value")
else:
    print("nothing here")

None is Python’s null — same idea, different capitalization and spelling
Java only treats null itself as special in an if. Python additionally treats 0, 0.0, "" (empty string), and [] (empty list) as “falsy” in an if — this has no Java parallel and causes real bugs
Rule of thumb: if you mean “is this specifically None,” write if result is None:, not just if result:


~2 min. This is a genuine gotcha, not a style note — an empty list silently behaving like “false” surprises every Java developer at least once. Worth a quick live example: if []:  print("shown"); else: print("not shown").

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
text:
List Comprehensions: Thinking in Expressions


The loop way
squares = []
for x in range(10):
    squares.append(x ** 2)

The Pythonic way
squares = [x ** 2 for x in range(10)]


Both produce the exact same list — the second is Python’s idiomatic shorthand for “build a new list from a rule”
Read it right-to-left: “for x in range(10),” “compute x squared,” “collect into a list”
You’ll see this pattern constantly in other people’s Python code this semester — recognize it even if you don’t write it yet


~3 min. Don’t require fluency writing these yet — just reading comprehension. This slide is also a deliberate bridge: next session, NumPy will replace both versions above with x ** 2 on a whole array, no loop or comprehension at all.

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
section: Why This Matters for GPU Programming
text:
Why This Matters for GPU Programming

Python’s flexibility (no type declarations, quick to write) is exactly why we prototype in it
But that same flexibility has a cost: a Python for loop is checking and re-checking types on every single iteration — work a compiled Java loop never has to do
Next session, we’ll measure that cost, and meet the tool (NumPy) that removes it — which is also the first step toward the GPU way of thinking


~2 min. This is the bridge slide into Session 3 — plant “loops are secretly expensive” as a question, don’t answer it yet. Session 3 answers it with a real analogy and (in Lab 2/CK-2) real numbers.

text:
The Goal of This Module

Everything we do for the rest of the semester operates on arrays — NumPy is the mental model, CUDA (Module 2 onward) is the execution engine that runs that same model on a GPU
If you can write fast, loop-free NumPy code today, you already think the way GPU programming requires

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
section: The Array as the Unit of Work
text:
The Array as the Unit of Work

A Python list can hold anything, in any mix — flexible, but that flexibility is exactly what makes it slow at scale (Session 2’s “checking types every iteration” cost)
A NumPy array gives up that flexibility on purpose: one fixed type, laid out as one contiguous block of memory
In exchange, operations apply to the entire block at once — not element by element in a Python loop

import numpy as np
x = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], dtype=np.float32)
y = x * 2          # not a loop — one operation over the whole array

~3 min. Live-demo: type([1, "two", 3.0]) works fine, then np.array([1, "two", 3.0]) — show it silently converts everything to strings. This makes “one fixed type” concrete rather than abstract.

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
text:
dtypes Matter



dtype
bytes
use case




float64
8
NumPy’s default, high precision


float32
4
GPU default, half the memory of float64


int32
4
indices, counts




Every element in an array shares one dtype — that’s the “give up flexibility” trade from the previous slide, made concrete
GPUs are built to move and compute on float32 efficiently; using float64 on a GPU can be noticeably slower and always uses twice the memory
We use float32 throughout this course, starting today — get in the habit now


~3 min. Ask: “if float32 uses half the memory, and a GPU’s speed is often limited by how fast it can move data (not compute), what does halving the memory do to speed?” Let students reason toward “roughly doubles throughput” themselves — this is a light preview of Module 3’s memory-bandwidth material, don’t over-formalize it now.

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
text:
Shape, Reshape, Indexing
a = np.arange(24, dtype=np.float32)   # [0, 1, 2, ..., 23]  — shape (24,)
b = a.reshape(4, 6)                   # same 24 numbers, viewed as 4 rows × 6 cols
c = b[2, :]                           # row 2, all columns
d = b[:, 3]                           # all rows, column 3

reshape doesn’t move or copy any numbers — it just changes how the same block of memory is interpreted
Shape is always (rows, cols): b.shape == (4, 6)
Indexing syntax [row, col] and slicing [start:stop] are the exact patterns from Session 2’s list-slicing slide, now extended to two dimensions


~3 min. Callback explicitly to the list-slicing slide from Session 2 — “you already learned this syntax, we’re just adding a second dimension.”

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
section: Memory Layout — Why Shape Isn’t Free
text:
Memory Layout — Why Shape Isn’t Free
[DIAGRAM] — A single row of 24 numbered memory cells (addresses 0–23) drawn as a horizontal strip. Below it, the same 24 cells regrouped into a 4×6 grid, with color-coded bands showing that grid row 0 = memory addresses 0–5, row 1 = addresses 6–11, row 2 = addresses 12–17, row 3 = addresses 18–23. An arrow labeled “reshape — same memory, new labels” connects the strip to the grid.

A 2D array’s rows are contiguous in memory — row 0’s six numbers sit right next to each other, then row 1’s six numbers, and so on (“row-major” order)
This means walking across a row is a straight walk through memory; walking down a column jumps around
File this away — it becomes the whole story behind memory coalescing, one of the most important GPU performance topics, in Module 3


~3 min. Don’t derive coalescing here — that requires GPU thread concepts they don’t have yet. The only goal today is: shape is a label on memory, not a rearrangement of it, and rows are the “straight walk.”

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
text:
Reducing Along an Axis
grid = np.array([[1, 2, 3],
                  [4, 5, 6]], dtype=np.float32)   # shape (2, 3)

np.mean(grid, axis=0)   # [2.5, 3.5, 4.5]  — one value per COLUMN
np.mean(grid, axis=1)   # [2.0, 5.0]       — one value per ROW
np.mean(grid)           # 3.5              — one value, every element

axis=0 collapses rows together — you get one result per column
axis=1 collapses columns together — you get one result per row
Memory trick: the axis number you pass is the dimension that disappears from the shape after the reduction — (2, 3) with axis=0 leaves shape (3,)
np.sum, np.max, np.min, np.argmax all take this same axis parameter


~3 min. This is a notoriously confusing NumPy detail — most students initially guess axis=0 means “reduce along rows” (i.e. row-wise), when it actually means “collapse the row dimension,” producing one value per column. Have students predict np.mean(grid, axis=1) before revealing it. This exact skill is on Quiz 1 and gets hands-on practice in Lab 2’s last exercise.

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
text:
Reducing Along an Axis, Visually
[DIAGRAM] — A 2×3 grid of numbered cells (values 1-6 as in the code above). Left panel: downward arrows through each column labeled “axis=0 — collapse rows,” converging into a single row of 3 output cells below the grid reading 2.5, 3.5, 4.5. Right panel: the same grid with rightward arrows through each row labeled “axis=1 — collapse columns,” converging into a single column of 2 output cells beside the grid reading 2.0, 5.0.

The arrows show which direction values get squashed together — not which direction you “read” the axis number
Same picture applies to np.sum, np.max, and every other axis-aware reduction


~2 min. Pair this directly with the mnemonic from the previous slide — seeing the arrows collapse in the opposite direction from what “axis=0” sounds like is what makes the rule stick.

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
text:
Broadcasting Rules
a = np.ones((4, 6), dtype=np.float32)              # shape (4, 6)
b = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], dtype=np.float32) # shape (6,)

c = a + b   # b is stretched across every row — result shape (4, 6)

NumPy compares shapes right to left. Here: 6 matches 6 — compatible
A dimension of size 1 (or a missing dimension) is automatically stretched to match the other array — no data is actually copied
If shapes don’t line up this way, NumPy raises a shape-mismatch error rather than guessing what you meant


~3 min. This is consistently the single most-tripped-over NumPy concept in labs. Have students predict the shape of a + b before revealing the comment, then try a deliberately mismatched pair (e.g. shape (6,) against shape (4, 5)) live to show the error message.

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
text:
Broadcasting, Visually
[DIAGRAM] — A 4×6 grid of cells labeled a, all filled with the value 1. Beside it, a single row of 6 cells labeled b, with values 1 through 6. An animated-looking set of 4 faint copies of row b stacked to show it being “stretched” downward to align with each row of a, with a + symbol between the two stacks and a resulting 4×6 grid c where each row reads 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.

The stretching in the diagram is conceptual — NumPy never actually duplicates b in memory; it just reuses the same 6 numbers for every row
This “reuse without copying” trick is why broadcasting is fast, not just convenient


~3 min. Emphasize the “no copy happens” point explicitly — it’s easy to walk away thinking broadcasting is expensive because the mental picture looks like duplication.

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
text:
Boolean Masking
scores = np.array([0.9, 0.3, 0.7, 0.1, 0.8], dtype=np.float32)
mask   = scores > 0.5           # [True, False, True, False, True]
high   = scores[mask]           # [0.9, 0.7, 0.8]

scores > 0.5 doesn’t compare once — it compares every element, producing a full array of True/False
Using that Boolean array as an index selects only the True positions — no loop, no if
This exact pattern (compare, then select) is used in Lab 2 and reappears constantly for the rest of the course


~3 min. Live-demo: build the mask, print it separately from the selection, so students see the intermediate Boolean array rather than the two steps blurring together.

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
text:
Why Loops Are Slow
[DIAGRAM] — Two side-by-side panels. Left panel, “Python loop”: a single translator sitting at a desk, translating a document one word at a time — read a word, look it up, write it down, repeat — with a stack of 2,000,000 words waiting. Right panel, “NumPy vectorized”: the same document fed into a printing press that stamps every word at once in a single pass, with a stopwatch showing a dramatically shorter time.

A Python for loop over an array processes one element at a time, and for every single element, Python re-checks the type, re-does bounds checking, and re-dispatches the operation — overhead paid 2,000,000 times for a 2,000,000-element array
NumPy’s vectorized operations hand the entire array to pre-compiled C code in one call — the type-checking and dispatch overhead is paid once, not once per element
Typical measured speedup on Colab: 50–200×, purely from removing per-element Python overhead — no algorithm changed, only how the same arithmetic gets executed


~4 min. This is the conceptual payoff of the whole module — connect it explicitly back to Session 2’s “why this matters for GPU programming” teaser slide. Note for later: Lab 3 / CK-3 (next module) has students measure this exact speedup themselves; today is intuition, next week is the number.

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
text:
Not Everything Vectorizes
Vectorization works when every output element can be computed independently — NumPy doesn’t care what order it processes them in. Some computations don’t have that property.
# Fibonacci: each value depends on the two before it
fib = [0, 1]
for i in range(2, 10):
    fib.append(fib[i-1] + fib[i-2])   # MUST know fib[i-1] before computing fib[i]

There’s no single NumPy call that produces this — fib[i] cannot exist before fib[i-1] does
This is called a serial dependency: step i needs the result of step i-1, not just its position
Contrast with everything else today: x**2 + 1, boolean masks, dot products — every output element only needs the input values, never another output


~2 min. This is the one exception to “just vectorize it” that students need before Quiz 1 — ask them to spot the difference between this Fibonacci loop and the polynomial-evaluation loop from earlier: same syntax shape, but one has a dependency between iterations and one doesn’t. This same idea reappears in Module 1 as a reason GPUs specifically struggle with certain problems — today it’s just about NumPy.

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
text:
The Dot Product

A dot product multiplies two same-length lists of numbers position by position, then adds up all the products
It shows up constantly: a weighted average is a dot product; a similarity score is a dot product; a full matrix multiply is just many dot products computed at once

\[\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = u_0 v_0 + u_1 v_1 + \cdots + u_{D-1} v_{D-1}\]
u = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], dtype=np.float32)
v = np.array([4.0, 5.0, 6.0], dtype=np.float32)
np.dot(u, v)     # 1*4 + 2*5 + 3*6 = 32.0

~3 min. Keep the geometric meaning (angle, projection) out of this slide entirely — that’s EL-01’s job (3Blue1Brown). Here we want only the mechanical pattern: multiply pairs, sum the results. Work the 3-element example on the board before revealing the code.

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
text:
Similarity via Dot Product
song_a = np.array([0.6, 0.8, 0.0], dtype=np.float32)  # "fingerprint" vector
song_b = np.array([0.8, 0.6, 0.0], dtype=np.float32)  # similar mood/tempo to a
song_c = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0], dtype=np.float32)  # totally different

print(np.dot(song_a, song_b))   # close to 1.0 — similar
print(np.dot(song_a, song_c))   # 0.0 — unrelated

When vectors are pre-normalized (length 1), their dot product lands between −1 and 1, and a value near 1 means “point in nearly the same direction” — which we’re using here as a stand-in for “sound similar”
This is the Session 1 capstone teaser, now with real, runnable code behind it


~3 min. Callback explicitly to the Session 1 “songs as numbers” slide — students should recognize this as the same example, now computable.

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
section: Matrix Multiply as Batch Dot Products
text:
Matrix Multiply as Batch Dot Products
Q = np.random.randn(1000, 64).astype(np.float32)    # 1,000 query songs
D = np.random.randn(100_000, 64).astype(np.float32) # 100,000 database songs

sim = Q @ D.T   # sim[i, j] = dot product of query i with database song j
                # shape: (1000, 100_000)

One @ call computes 100 million individual multiply-and-add pairs — every query against every database song
NumPy hands this to a highly optimized library (BLAS) that’s already parallel across your CPU’s cores
We’ll do the same computation on a GPU’s thousands of cores in the capstone — same math, radically more parallelism


~3 min. Optional live-demo: time this cell on Colab CPU with %%time — it’s fast enough to look almost instant, which sets up the “and yet the GPU is still much faster” hook for later modules. If short on time, this slide can be trimmed to the code + first bullet only.

title: Module 0: Course Intro, Python & NumPy Foundations
text:
What NumPy Cannot Do

NumPy runs on the CPU. Q @ D.T above calls into parallel C code — but any Python for loop you write yourself still runs one instruction at a time on one core
A modern GPU has on the order of 10,000 arithmetic cores — NumPy alone has no way to address that many independent workers at once
The open question: if we want to run 100 billion dot products per second, how do we tell hardware to do all of them simultaneously? That question drives the next four modules


~2 min. This is deliberately unanswered — Module 1 starts answering it. Land the question and stop; don’t preview Module 1’s content here.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
Today’s Plan

What’s actually on a GPU chip: Streaming Multiprocessors and CUDA cores
How many cores a real GPU has, and how they’re grouped
Why “more cores activate as your problem grows” is a myth — the hardware is fixed, the work is what scales
How a block of threads gets assigned to run on that hardware


~1 min. Full 50-min session. This session is architecture-only — no code yet. Code starts Sep 23.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
section: From One Chip to Many Compute Units
text:
From One Chip to Many Compute Units

Module 1 compared CPU and GPU at the level of headline numbers (cores, clock, bandwidth) — today we open up the GPU chip itself
A GPU is not one big processor — it’s a chip subdivided into dozens of smaller, largely independent compute units
Each of those units is called a Streaming Multiprocessor, or SM
Understanding SMs is the prerequisite for understanding warps, occupancy, and divergence (Sep 30) — those are all properties of one SM


~2 min. Framing slide — connects back to Module 1’s CPU-vs-GPU table and forward to Sep 30’s content, so students see this as one continuous architectural story rather than isolated facts.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
The Streaming Multiprocessor (SM)
[DIAGRAM] — One SM drawn as a labeled box containing: a grid of small “CUDA core” ALU icons (dozens of them), a “register file” block, a “shared memory / L1 cache” block, and a “warp scheduler” block. Caption: “One SM — a self-contained compute unit with its own cores, fast on-chip memory, and scheduling logic.”

An SM bundles together: many CUDA cores (the ALUs that do arithmetic), a register file (fast per-thread storage), shared memory (fast per-block storage — full detail in Module 4), and warp schedulers (full detail Sep 30)
A GPU chip contains many SMs — tens of them on a typical GPU — all working independently on different pieces of your problem at once
Every thread block your kernel launches is assigned to run on exactly one SM


~3 min. This slide is the map for the rest of the module — registers, shared memory, and warp scheduling (upcoming sessions) all live inside the SM box drawn here. Point back to this diagram when those topics come up.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
CUDA Cores: The Actual ALUs

A CUDA core is one simple arithmetic unit — it can do one floating-point add or multiply per clock cycle, nothing more
Compare to a CPU core: a CUDA core has no branch predictor, no out-of-order execution, no deep pipeline — just an ALU and enough control to execute the instruction a warp scheduler hands it (Module 1’s die-anatomy diagram, made concrete)
Total CUDA cores on a chip = (number of SMs) × (cores per SM)
This total is a fixed, physical property of the chip — it does not change based on what code you run


~2 min. “Fixed physical property” is the setup for the myth-busting slide two slides from now — plant it explicitly here.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
section: How Many Cores? A Concrete Example
text:
How Many Cores? A Concrete Example
The GPU behind every lab and checkpoint this semester — Google Colab’s NVIDIA T4 — breaks down like this:
Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) : 40
CUDA cores per SM                : 64
Total CUDA cores                 : 40 × 64 = 2,560
Memory                            : 16 GB GDDR6
Memory bandwidth                  : ~320 GB/s

2,560 cores sounds enormous next to a CPU’s 8–32 — and it is — but it’s still a fixed number, not something that grows with your problem size
A data-center GPU (H100-class, Module 1’s “2,000 TFLOPS” chip) has far more SMs and cores than a T4 — the T4 is a modest, power-efficient GPU meant for exactly this kind of interactive/educational workload


~3 min. These are the real numbers behind every timing result students will produce all semester — worth memorizing “40 SMs, 2,560 cores” as their GPU’s identity. If students run !nvidia-smi in Colab they can confirm they have a T4 (occasionally Colab assigns something else — mention this as a heads-up, not a concern).

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
section: Myth: “The GPU Activates More Cores as N Grows”
text:
Myth: “The GPU Activates More Cores as N Grows”

A tempting but wrong intuition: launching a bigger problem makes the GPU “power up” more cores to match
What actually happens: the GPU always has the same 2,560 cores (for a T4). A bigger problem means more thread blocks are launched, and those blocks queue up to be scheduled onto the SMs that exist
If you launch more blocks than can run at once, extra blocks simply wait until an SM finishes its current block and becomes free — same hardware, more rounds of scheduling
This is why GPU speedup at small N is often worse than a CPU (fixed launch overhead dominates a tiny amount of work) but improves as N grows (fixed overhead gets amortized over far more useful work) — not because more silicon “turns on”


~3 min. This directly corrects a real exam distractor students encounter (Midterm D2 offers “the GPU activates progressively more CUDA cores as N grows” as a wrong answer) — say so explicitly, this is exactly the trap that question is testing.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
section: From Grid to Hardware: How Blocks Get Scheduled
text:
From Grid to Hardware: How Blocks Get Scheduled
[DIAGRAM] — A grid of 12 small labeled blocks (“Block 0” through “Block 11”) at the top, with arrows flowing down to a row of 4 SM boxes at the bottom. At the first moment in time, 4 arrows point from Blocks 0–3 into the 4 SMs (one block per SM), with Blocks 4–11 shown in a “waiting” queue off to the side. A second frame shows Block 0 finished and removed, replaced by an arrow from Block 4 now entering the freed SM.

Your kernel launch specifies a grid of blocks; the hardware decides which SM runs which block, and in what order
A block runs start-to-finish on a single SM — it never moves partway through, and it never splits across two SMs
An SM can often hold more than one resident block at a time if there’s room (this is exactly what occupancy, covered Sep 30, measures) — the diagram above simplifies to one block per SM for clarity
You don’t control this scheduling directly — you control it indirectly, through launch configuration (block size, grid size) — Sep 23 teaches you to write that configuration


~3 min. Keep this at “the hardware decides, you don’t” — the occupancy math (how many blocks actually fit per SM) is deliberately deferred to Sep 30, don’t get pulled into that calculation here.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
This Week

Session 2 (Wed, Sep 23): From architecture to code — writing and launching your first CUDA kernels. Quiz 2 (covers Module 1) opens that session.
Lab 04 (Fri, Sep 25): Your first Numba CUDA kernel — vector addition
Everything on today’s slides (SMs, cores, block scheduling) is background you’ll use starting Sep 23, not something graded on its own — but Quiz 3 (Oct 5) and both exams draw on it


~1 min. Quick pointer slide. Reassure students this session is conceptual grounding, not itself a checkpointed skill — the payoff is that Sep 23 onward will make a lot more sense.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
Today’s Plan

Quiz 2 first (15 min, Blackboard) — covers all of Module 1
Then: what a CUDA kernel actually is, and how to launch one
The thread/block/grid indexing hierarchy — in 1D, then 2D
Two worked example kernels, and a preview of the capstone’s kernel


~1 min. ~35 min of lecture time after the quiz, same structure as Module 1 Session 1. This is a dense, code-heavy session — keep momentum, save discussion for Lab 04.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
What a Kernel Is

A kernel is a function that runs on the GPU — you write it once, and the GPU runs that same code for every thread, simultaneously
Each thread automatically knows its own position in the grid of threads — that position is how a thread figures out which piece of data it’s responsible for
Marked with the @cuda.jit decorator, which compiles ordinary-looking Python into GPU machine code

from numba import cuda

@cuda.jit
def my_kernel(arr):
    i = cuda.grid(1)          # this thread's global index
    if i < arr.shape[0]:      # bounds guard — always required (next slide)
        arr[i] = arr[i] * 2.0

Three parts every kernel has: the decorator, a position calculation, and a bounds guard


~3 min. Students will forget the bounds guard constantly in early labs — flag it now as “always required” so it’s not a surprise two slides from now.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
The Thread Grid
[DIAGRAM] — A grid of 3 blocks in a row, each block containing 4 threads, drawn as a 3×4 array of small numbered boxes. Above the grid, label the whole structure “gridDim.x = 3” (number of blocks) and “blockDim.x = 4” (threads per block). Inside block 1, circle thread index 2 and label it “threadIdx.x = 2, blockIdx.x = 1”. Draw an arrow from that box to a computed value “global index = 1*4 + 2 = 6.”

blockIdx.x — which block is this thread in?
threadIdx.x — where is this thread within its block?
blockDim.x — how many threads are in each block?
Global index = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x — cuda.grid(1) computes exactly this in one call
This global index is what a thread uses to know which array element is “its” element


~4 min. This is the single mental model students need for the rest of the course — worth having them compute the global index for 2-3 different (blockIdx, threadIdx, blockDim) combinations out loud before moving on.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
Launching a Kernel
import numpy as np
from numba import cuda

N = 1_000_000
arr = np.ones(N, dtype=np.float32)
arr_gpu = cuda.to_device(arr)          # host → device transfer

THREADS = 256
BLOCKS  = (N + THREADS - 1) // THREADS   # ceiling division — see below

my_kernel[BLOCKS, THREADS](arr_gpu)    # launch: BLOCKS × THREADS total threads
cuda.synchronize()                     # wait for the GPU to finish

result = arr_gpu.copy_to_host()        # device → host transfer

(N + THREADS - 1) // THREADS is ceiling division — the standard way to compute “enough blocks to cover N, rounding up” using only integer arithmetic
You will write this exact five-line pattern (transfer, configure, launch, synchronize, transfer back) in nearly every lab this semester


~3 min. Walk through each line out loud. Ceiling division specifically is worth a plain-integer example: N=1000, THREADS=256 → (1000+255)//256 = 4 blocks = 1024 threads launched, 24 wasted (caught by the bounds guard).

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
The Bounds Guard
@cuda.jit
def my_kernel(arr):
    i = cuda.grid(1)
    # Without this line: threads with i >= arr.shape[0] write out of bounds
    if i < arr.shape[0]:
        arr[i] = arr[i] * 2.0

BLOCKS × THREADS is a ceiling, computed by rounding up — so there are almost always a few extra threads beyond the last real array element
Those extra threads still run the kernel body — without the guard, they read/write memory past the end of the array
Consequence: undefined behavior — sometimes a crash, sometimes silent data corruption that produces a wrong answer with no error message at all


~2 min. Silent corruption is the scarier failure mode to emphasize — a crash at least tells you something’s wrong. Lab 04 Exercise 4 has students remove the guard intentionally on a small array so they can see the effect directly.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
Module 2: CUDA Kernels
Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
Thread Count Intuition
[DIAGRAM] — Two small 1D grids stacked vertically. Top: N=12 elements, THREADS=4, BLOCKS=3 — exactly 12 threads drawn in 3 groups of 4, every thread mapped to exactly one element, no waste. Bottom: N=14 elements, same THREADS=4 — BLOCKS=4 (ceiling of 14/4), 16 threads drawn in 4 groups of 4; the last two threads (indices 14, 15) are colored gray/crossed-out and labeled “caught by bounds guard.”

Students who can draw this diagram from scratch can debug almost any 1D kernel launch-configuration bug
The gray/crossed-out threads in the N=14 case are exactly why the bounds guard exists — they’re real threads that ran, just with nothing valid to do


~2 min. Worth having students redraw this for N=13 themselves as a quick check before moving to 2D.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
From 1D to 2D

Images, matrices, and (soon) the capstone’s similarity table are inherently two-dimensional
Same idea as 1D, doubled: one thread per (row, col) pair instead of one thread per index
cuda.grid(2) returns a (row, col) tuple directly — you don’t need to compute it by hand from blockIdx/threadIdx (though you still can, next slide shows the underlying formula)

@cuda.jit
def add_matrices(A, B, C):
    row, col = cuda.grid(2)
    if row < C.shape[0] and col < C.shape[1]:
        C[row, col] = A[row, col] + B[row, col]

The bounds guard is now two conditions ANDed together — a thread must be in-bounds on both axes to do useful work


~3 min. cuda.grid(2) returning (row, col) directly is the convention used in every 2D checkpoint and lab this semester (CK-05, Lab 05) — always unpack it as row, col = cuda.grid(2), never reorder it.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
2D Launch Configuration
M, N = 300, 400     # matrix shape

THREADS = (16, 16)  # 256 threads per block — a 16×16 tile
BLOCKS  = (
    (M + THREADS[0] - 1) // THREADS[0],   # ceiling in the row dimension
    (N + THREADS[1] - 1) // THREADS[1],   # ceiling in the col dimension
)

add_matrices[BLOCKS, THREADS](A_gpu, B_gpu, C_gpu)
[DIAGRAM] — A 300×400 grid of cells overlaid with a coarser 16×16-cell block grid. Most blocks are full 16×16 tiles; the rightmost column of blocks and the bottom row of blocks are drawn as partial tiles (fewer than 16 cells wide/tall), shaded to show “extra threads here get caught by the bounds guard.”

16×16 = 256 threads per block is a common convention — a power-of-two total that divides evenly into full warps (32 threads each, from Sep 30’s content)
300 is not a multiple of 16 → the last block in each row/column has extra threads; the bounds guard filters them exactly as in 1D


~3 min. Point out the 256 = 8 warps connection explicitly if Sep 30 has already happened when this is taught in a future offering — for this semester’s ordering it’s a forward reference, mention it as “you’ll see exactly why 256 is a friendly number in a week and a half.”

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
Thread Index in 2D
[DIAGRAM] — A 2×2 array of 2×2 thread blocks (4 blocks total, 4 threads each, 16 threads shown). Block (0,0) contains threads labeled with their global (row,col): (0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1). Block (0,1) sits to its right and contains global indices (0,2),(0,3),(1,2),(1,3). Block (1,0) sits below the first and contains (2,0),(2,1),(3,0),(3,1). Block (1,1) contains (2,2),(2,3),(3,2),(3,3). Every box is labeled with its final (row,col) value.
global_row = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x
global_col = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y

This is the formula cuda.grid(2) computes internally — same ceiling-division logic as 1D, just applied on both axes independently
A thread that can correctly compute its own (row, col) here has mastered 2D kernels — everything else (2D bounds checks, 2D array indexing) follows directly


~3 min. Have students label the global index for a thread you point to at random in the diagram — this is the practical skill CK-05 tests directly.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
Looking Ahead

Lab 04 (Fri, Sep 25): Write three kernels — scalar multiply, array add, one of your own design. Observe what happens with a missing bounds guard.
Lab 05 (Fri, Oct 2): Naive matrix multiplication — implement, time, and verify against NumPy’s reference (2D kernel skills applied at full scale)

text:
Checkpoint Preview
Checkpoint CK-04 will ask you to:

Write a 1D kernel with a correct bounds guard, given a word description of the computation

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
Today’s Plan

Every kind of memory a GPU has, from fastest/smallest to slowest/largest
Where each kind physically lives, and what it costs to read or write it
The host↔︎device boundary — the slowest hop of all, and how to minimize crossing it


~1 min. Purely conceptual session — no new kernel syntax today. This sets up Module 3 (timing/profiling) and Module 4 (shared memory in practice).

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
section: Not All GPU Memory Is Equal
text:
Not All GPU Memory Is Equal
[DIAGRAM] — A pyramid diagram, narrow at top and wide at bottom, four tiers labeled top-to-bottom: “Registers” (smallest, fastest — inside the SM, right next to each ALU), “Shared Memory” (small, very fast — inside the SM, shared by one block), “Constant Memory (cached)” (small, fast when all threads read the same address — off-chip but cached), “Global Memory” (largest, slowest per-access — off-chip DRAM, visible to every thread on the GPU). A dotted line further below the pyramid, separated by a gap, is labeled “Host RAM (CPU side) — across PCIe, slower still.”

Just like a CPU has registers → L1 → L2 → L3 → RAM, a GPU has its own hierarchy — smaller and faster near the compute units, larger and slower further away
The core tradeoff is identical to any memory hierarchy: capacity and speed trade off against each other
Today: what each tier is for. Module 4 teaches you to use shared memory in a kernel; today is the map, not yet the tool


~3 min. Explicitly frame this as “the map, not the tool” — students shouldn’t leave today expecting to write cuda.shared.array yet, that’s Module 4’s job (C4.2). Today is purely “what exists and why.”

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
Registers: Fastest, Per-Thread

Every thread gets its own small set of registers — the fastest storage on the entire chip, physically adjacent to the ALU that uses them
Local variables in your kernel (like acc in the similarity-kernel preview from Sep 23) live in registers by default
Registers are a scarce, fixed resource per SM — the more registers each thread’s kernel needs, the fewer threads (and therefore fewer warps) can be resident on an SM at once
This is the direct link to occupancy (Sep 30): register usage per thread is one of the two things that can cap how many warps fit on an SM


~3 min. Forward-reference occupancy explicitly — this is exactly the “resource budget” idea Sep 30’s occupancy slides build on, just introduced here as one specific resource (registers) rather than the general concept.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
Shared Memory: Fast, Per-Block

Shared memory is a small, fast, on-chip scratchpad that every thread in the same block can read and write
Unlike registers (private to one thread) or global memory (visible to everyone but slow), shared memory is the middle ground: fast and shared, but only within a block
Threads use it as a manually-managed cache: copy a chunk of data from global memory into shared memory once, then have many threads reuse it without going back to global memory each time
Full syntax and a worked example (cuda.shared.array, cuda.syncthreads()) is Module 4’s subject — today, just know it exists and why it’s valuable


~2 min. Resist the urge to teach the syntax now — Module 4 (C4.2, C4.3) owns this material in full and has two dedicated lectures (Oct 26, Oct 28) for it. Today’s job is just motivating why it’s worth a whole module later.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
Constant Memory: Small, Cached, Broadcast-Friendly

Constant memory is a small (tens of KB), read-only region that’s aggressively cached
It shines in one specific pattern: every thread in a warp reading the same address at the same time — e.g., a shared coefficient or lookup-table value used identically by every thread
When that pattern holds, the read is effectively broadcast to all 32 threads in a warp from cache, instead of 32 separate trips to global memory
You won’t write to constant memory in this course’s kernels, but recognizing the pattern matters for reading exam questions about memory-access strategy


~2 min. Keep this brief — it’s the least-used tier in this course’s labs, but it appears as a plausible-sounding wrong answer on exam questions (e.g. “constant memory is broadcast-cached” is sometimes the correct answer, sometimes a tempting distractor depending on the scenario — students need the real definition to tell which).

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
section: Local Memory: A Trap in the Name
text:
Local Memory: A Trap in the Name

Local memory is per-thread scope, like registers — but it is not fast. It physically lives in the same off-chip DRAM as global memory, just addressed privately per thread
The compiler falls back to local memory when a thread’s data doesn’t fit in registers — large local arrays, or a kernel using more registers than the hardware budget allows (“register spilling”)
The name is the trap: “local” sounds like it should mean “close and fast,” but it means “private scope, global-memory speed”
Practical takeaway: keep per-thread working data small and simple, so the compiler keeps it in registers instead of spilling to local memory


~2 min. This is a favorite exam-distractor topic precisely because the name is misleading — spend a moment explicitly contrasting “local memory” (slow, despite the name) against “shared memory” (fast, despite being the more commonly-confused-as-slow-sounding one).

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
Global Memory: Largest, Slowest, Universal

Global memory is the GPU’s main pool — the 16 GB (T4) of GDDR6 from Sep 21’s specs. Every thread on the entire GPU can read and write it
It’s the slowest tier per access (hundreds of cycles of latency, same “memory wall” idea from Module 1) but by far the largest
cuda.to_device() copies your data here; every kernel argument you’ve written so far (arr, A, B, C, Q, D) lives in global memory unless you explicitly move it somewhere else
Module 3 teaches how the pattern of global-memory access (not just how much of it) affects performance — this is where “coalescing” comes from


~2 min. Tie back to Module 1’s memory-wall content explicitly — global memory latency is the concrete GPU-side instance of that general idea. Module 3 (starting Oct 5) picks up the access-pattern angle.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
The Memory Hierarchy, Summarized









Tier
Scope
Speed
Typical size




Registers
One thread
Fastest
A few KB per thread (shared across all resident threads on an SM)


Shared memory
One block
Very fast
~48–164 KB per SM (hardware-dependent)


Constant memory
Whole GPU (read-only)
Fast if all threads agree on the address
Tens of KB


Local memory
One thread
Slow (physically off-chip)
Spills only — not a size you allocate directly


Global memory
Whole GPU
Slowest per access
GBs (16 GB on a T4)




Reading this table top to bottom is reading the hierarchy from fastest/smallest to slowest/largest — the same shape as any CPU’s cache hierarchy, just with GPU-specific names and a crucial addition: scope (per-thread vs. per-block vs. whole-GPU) matters as much as speed


~2 min. Good slide to pause on for questions — this table is the single most exam-referenced fact in this session (it’s exactly what Midterm Q5’s register-vs-shared-vs-constant-vs-L2 question is testing).

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
section: Beyond the Chip: The Host↔︎Device Boundary
text:
Beyond the Chip: The Host↔︎Device Boundary
CPU (Host RAM) ←—[PCIe, ~16 GB/s]—→ GPU (Device global memory, ~320 GB/s on a T4)

Everything on the tiers above lives inside the GPU. Getting data onto the GPU in the first place — or back off it — crosses a much slower link: PCIe, connecting the GPU card to the rest of the computer
PCIe bandwidth (~16 GB/s) is roughly 20× slower than the T4’s own global-memory bandwidth (~320 GB/s), and dramatically slower than any on-chip tier
cuda.to_device() and .copy_to_host() both cross this boundary — every call is expensive relative to anything happening once your data is already on the GPU


~2 min. This is the widest gap in the entire memory hierarchy — wider than the gap between any two on-chip tiers. Worth saying explicitly: “the slowest step in your entire pipeline is very often not the kernel itself, it’s getting the data there and back.”

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
Minimizing Transfers
# Host → Device (before kernel launches)
arr_gpu = cuda.to_device(arr_host)

# Launch kernel(s) — all device-side, no PCIe traffic
my_kernel[blocks, threads](arr_gpu)
cuda.synchronize()

# Device → Host (only once, when you actually need the result)
result = arr_gpu.copy_to_host()

Rule of thumb: transfer data to the GPU once, do as much work as possible while it’s there, and transfer results back once — not on every iteration of a loop
A very common early-semester mistake: copying results back to the host inside a loop “just to check on them,” which turns a fast GPU computation into one bottlenecked by PCIe
Module 6 (CuPy) makes this pattern implicit — but understanding it explicitly now is what lets you recognize when a library is silently doing (or failing to do) this for you


~2 min. Flag this as an antipattern to watch for starting immediately — students will be tempted to add debug prints that copy_to_host() inside loops in upcoming labs. Naming the mistake now makes it easier to catch in code review.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
This Week

Sep 30 (next lecture): Warp scheduling, occupancy, and thread divergence — the last piece of the GPU-execution picture, and where the register/shared-memory scope facts from today become a hard resource budget
Quiz 3 (Oct 5): covers all of Module 2 — architecture (today, Sep 21), execution model (Sep 23), and warps/occupancy/divergence (Sep 30)


~1 min. Quick pointer slide before the Sep 30 content picks up.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
The Synchronized Swim Team

Picture a synchronized swim team of 32 swimmers: the coach calls out one move at a time — “kick,” then “arms out,” then “dive” — and every swimmer performs that exact move at that exact moment
No swimmer can be a move ahead or behind; they share one set of instructions
A GPU’s threads work the same way, in groups of exactly 32 — that group is called a warp
This is why a GPU doesn’t have “10,000 independent brains” — it has far fewer instruction streams, each one driving 32 lock-step threads


~3 min. This is the intuition to plant before the formal definition — students who’ve been thinking of every thread as fully independent (a reasonable takeaway from Module 1’s “10,000 cores” framing) need this corrected before Module 2’s kernel-writing content sticks.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
What Is a Warp?

A warp is a group of 32 threads that the hardware schedules and executes together, one instruction at a time, in lock-step
threadIdx.x values 0-31 form warp 0, values 32-63 form warp 1, and so on within a block
All 32 threads in a warp execute the same instruction on the same clock cycle — this is called SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads)
One instruction-fetch/decode unit serves all 32 lanes — that’s the hardware trade that makes thousands of simple cores possible (the “twenty ordinary cashiers” idea from Module 0, made concrete)


~3 min. Tie back explicitly to Module 0 Session 1’s cashier-lanes analogy and Module 1’s latency-vs-throughput table — this is the hardware mechanism behind “many simple cores.”

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
A Warp, Visually
[DIAGRAM] — A single instruction-fetch/decode unit box at the top, with 32 arrows fanning down to 32 small “ALU lane” boxes arranged in a 4×8 grid, each labeled with a thread index 0-31. All 32 lanes are shown executing the identical instruction arr[i] = arr[i] * 2.0 simultaneously, with a caption: “One instruction, 32 lanes, same clock cycle.”

If a block has 256 threads, that’s exactly 256 / 32 = 8 warps
Block sizes that aren’t multiples of 32 waste lanes — a block of 100 threads still occupies 4 warps (128 lanes), with the last warp’s 28 unused lanes doing nothing useful


~2 min. The “not a multiple of 32 wastes lanes” point is a direct, checkable fact — good candidate for a quick in-class poll (“how many warps does a 100-thread block need?”).

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
Hiding Latency: The Warp Scheduler

A memory read from global memory can take hundreds of clock cycles to come back — if the GPU just sat idle waiting, it would waste nearly all of its compute capacity
Instead, each Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) keeps many warps resident at once — often dozens — and a warp scheduler switches to a different ready warp the instant one warp stalls on a memory access
Analogy: a short-order cook working several dishes at once. While one dish is in the oven (a warp waiting on memory), the cook doesn’t stand and watch — they stir another pan (switch to a different warp) and come back later
This is why GPUs want so much parallelism: idle warps are what a scheduler needs on hand to keep the hardware busy


~4 min. This is the single most important idea in this session — it’s the mechanism behind why “give the GPU more work than it strictly needs” is good advice, not wasteful. Ask: “why would a GPU want MORE threads than it can run at once?” and let students reason toward “so there’s always a ready warp to switch to.”

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
Warp Scheduling, Visually
[DIAGRAM] — A timeline strip showing one SM’s execution slots over time. Warp A runs for 2 cycles, then hits a memory request (shown as a long gray “waiting” bar spanning ~8 cycles). During Warp A’s wait, Warp B and then Warp C run in the same slot. When Warp A’s data arrives, it resumes. Caption: “The SM is never idle — it always has another ready warp to run while others wait.”

The scheduler’s job is entirely about keeping some warp always running, not about running every warp faster
More resident warps = more chances to hide a stall — this is exactly what occupancy measures


~2 min. This diagram is the direct setup for the occupancy slide that follows — make sure the “always some warp running” idea has landed before moving on.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
section: Occupancy: How Many Warps Can Live Here
text:
Occupancy: How Many Warps Can Live Here

Occupancy = the number of warps actually resident on an SM, divided by the maximum the hardware could support
Higher occupancy generally means more scheduling flexibility to hide memory latency — but it isn’t free to achieve
Each resident thread needs its own registers, and each resident block needs its share of shared memory; an SM has a fixed budget of both
If your kernel’s threads use a lot of registers, fewer threads (fewer warps) fit at once — occupancy drops, even though nothing about your code is “wrong”


~3 min. Keep this at the definitional level — the full two-constraint (registers AND shared memory) calculation is Module 4’s job once shared memory exists as a concept. Here, the goal is: occupancy is a ratio, and resource usage per thread is what limits it.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
A Simple Occupancy Example
Suppose an SM supports a maximum of 1536 resident threads (a realistic hardware limit), and you launch blocks of 256 threads.
Max threads per SM        : 1536
Threads per block         : 256
Max blocks that fit by thread count : 1536 // 256 = 6 blocks
Resident threads          : 6 × 256 = 1536
Occupancy                 : 1536 / 1536 = 100%
Now suppose you instead launch blocks of 300 threads — an awkward, non-power-of-2 size:
Max blocks that fit       : 1536 // 300 = 5 blocks   (integer division!)
Resident threads          : 5 × 300 = 1500
Occupancy                 : 1500 / 1536 ≈ 97.7%

Block size interacts with occupancy in ways that aren’t always obvious — this is why launch configuration (Module 3) is worth experimenting with, not just guessing
Real kernels also have a register budget per SM, which can lower occupancy further — Module 4 picks this up once shared memory is in the picture


~3 min. Keep the arithmetic here purely about thread-count-per-block — do not introduce the register/shared-memory dual-constraint version yet, that’s explicitly Module 4 content (see checkpoint-competency-map.md’s C7.3 gap note). Have students compute the occupancy for a block size of 512 themselves as a check.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
How Divergence Is Handled: Predication

The hardware runs both branches, one after another, for the whole warp — on the “positive” pass, threads that fail the condition are masked off (they execute the instruction but discard the result); on the “negative” pass, the roles reverse
Total time for a divergent warp ≈ time for all branches taken combined, not just the one each thread needed
A warp where every thread takes the same branch pays no divergence penalty at all — the cost only appears when a single warp’s threads disagree

Warp with a divergent if/else:
  Pass 1 (if-branch):  active = threads where arr[i] > 0, others masked/idle
  Pass 2 (else-branch): active = threads where arr[i] <= 0, others masked/idle
  Total warp time ≈ time(if-branch) + time(else-branch)

~4 min. “Masked, not skipped” is the key correction to whatever intuition students walk in with — a masked thread still consumes a cycle, it just discards its result. This is exactly why “conditionals are expensive” on a GPU in a way they aren’t on a CPU.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
Divergence, Visually
[DIAGRAM] — A single warp of 32 lanes shown twice, stacked vertically as “Pass 1” and “Pass 2.” In Pass 1, roughly half the lanes are colored (active, running the if-branch) and the rest are grayed out (masked). In Pass 2, the coloring is inverted — the previously-grayed lanes are now active running the else-branch, and the previously-active lanes are now grayed out. A time axis underneath shows Pass 1 and Pass 2 as sequential (not overlapping) blocks, with a caption: “Total time = Pass 1 + Pass 2, even though each thread only needed one of them.”

Contrast with a warp where the condition is the same for all 32 threads (e.g., branching on blockIdx.x instead of arr[i]) — no masking needed, no penalty
Rule of thumb: conditionals on data (varies per thread) are the risky ones; conditionals on thread/block identity (same for a whole warp) are free


~2 min. The “conditionals on thread/block identity are free” distinction is the practical takeaway students should leave with — it’s what turns this from a scary warning into an actionable coding habit.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
section: Why This Matters for Your Code
text:
Why This Matters for Your Code

You will not be asked to eliminate every if statement — most real kernels need some
What matters: when a conditional’s outcome depends on data that varies across threads in the same warp, expect a real performance cost proportional to how many distinct branches get taken
A bounds guard (if i < n:) is usually cheap in practice — most warps are either fully in-bounds or fully out-of-bounds, so few warps actually diverge on it
Data-dependent branching inside the “hot” part of a kernel (like the classify example above) is where divergence bites hardest


~2 min. Reassure explicitly — students who’ve just written bounds guards in every Lab 4/5 kernel may worry they’ve been doing something expensive. Clarify why that specific pattern is usually fine.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
This Session: Recap

Warp = 32 threads executing in lock-step (SIMT) — the real unit of GPU scheduling, not the individual thread
Occupancy = resident warps ÷ maximum possible, limited by per-thread resource usage (registers, shared memory)
Divergence = the cost paid when threads in one warp disagree on which branch to take — paid in serialized passes, not parallel ones
These three ideas explain why GPU code that looks correct can still run far below its theoretical peak — Module 3’s profiling content picks up exactly this thread


~1 min. Land this as the transition into Module 3 (profiling/bottleneck identification) rather than a dead end — students should expect to come back to occupancy and divergence when they start reading profiler output.

title: Module 2: CUDA Kernels
text:
Module 2 Wrap-Up

Sep 21: GPUs are built from a fixed number of SMs, each with a fixed number of CUDA cores — bigger problems mean more scheduling rounds, not more silicon
Sep 23: Kernels are written once and run per-thread; cuda.grid() (1D or 2D) tells each thread its position, and every launch needs a bounds guard
Sep 28: Memory has a hierarchy (registers → shared → constant/global) with speed, scope, and physical location all varying together — and the host↔︎device PCIe hop is the slowest link in the whole chain
Sep 30: Threads execute in lock-step groups of 32 (warps); occupancy measures how many warps fit at once; divergence is the cost of threads in one warp disagreeing on a branch


~1 min. This slide is worth putting up again at the start of the Sep 30 recap slide’s follow-on, or just before Quiz 3 — it’s the full-module summary in one place.

title: Module 4: Shared Memory & Tiled Matrix Multiply
text:
Today’s Plan

Midterm debrief (quick — full discussion happens separately)
Why how threads access global memory matters as much as how much they access
Coalesced vs. strided access, in 1D and 2D
Why this sets up everything Module 4 does with shared memory


~2 min. This lecture follows the midterm (Oct 19) by two days — budget a few minutes for debrief/questions before diving in; the content below assumes a full ~45 min once that’s done.

title: Module 4: Shared Memory & Tiled Matrix Multiply
text:
Why Access Pattern Matters
[DIAGRAM] — 32 threads in a single warp, each about to read one float from global memory. Top scenario, “coalesced”: all 32 threads’ target addresses are drawn as 32 consecutive slots in one contiguous 128-byte memory block, with a single arrow labeled “1 memory transaction” pointing from the whole block to the warp. Bottom scenario, “strided”: the 32 threads’ target addresses are drawn scattered across a much wider span of memory (gaps between each), with 32 separate arrows each labeled “1 transaction,” captioned “32 transactions — 32× the bandwidth cost for the same 32 floats.”

The GPU doesn’t fetch memory one float at a time — it fetches in fixed-size blocks (transactions), and ideally serves an entire warp’s requests from as few transactions as possible
When 32 threads in a warp request 32 consecutive addresses, the hardware can often satisfy all of them with a single transaction — this is called coalesced access
When those same 32 threads request addresses scattered far apart, the hardware needs a separate transaction per address (or per small cluster) — up to 32× the memory traffic for the identical amount of useful data
This is the single most important hardware fact for writing fast kernels — every memory-access decision from here through the rest of the course traces back to this slide


~4 min. Worth pausing on: this isn’t about how much data a kernel reads — it’s purely about the pattern of addresses across threads in the same warp. Two kernels reading the identical set of bytes can differ by 32× in transaction count depending only on which thread reads which address.

title: Module 4: Shared Memory & Tiled Matrix Multiply
Module 4: Shared Memory & Tiled Matrix Multiply
text:
Strided Access
STRIDE = 128

@cuda.jit
def strided_kernel(arr, out):
    i = cuda.grid(1)
    idx = i * STRIDE
    if idx < arr.shape[0]:
        out[i] = arr[idx] * 2.0   # thread i reads element i*128

Thread 0 reads element 0, thread 1 reads element 128, thread 2 reads element 256, … — 32 consecutive threads, but addresses spread across 4,096 bytes
Each of those 32 reads typically needs its own memory transaction — roughly 32× the memory traffic of the coalesced version, for the exact same 32 useful values
Lab 8 has you time both versions directly and measure this ratio empirically — the slowdown is a hardware specification, not a fluke of one run


~3 min. Lab 08 Exercise 1 sweeps a range of stride values and has students interpret the resulting time-vs-stride curve — this slide is the theory that curve is confirming.

title: Module 4: Shared Memory & Tiled Matrix Multiply
Module 4: Shared Memory & Tiled Matrix Multiply
section: Why This Sets Up Shared Memory
text:
Why This Sets Up Shared Memory

Coalescing helps every global-memory read be as cheap as possible — but it doesn’t reduce how many reads happen
The tiled matrix multiply later in this module attacks a different problem: the same global-memory element gets read by many different threads (Lab 5’s naive matmul reads each row of A and column of B repeatedly, once per output element that needs it)
Shared memory (next section) lets a block load each needed element from global memory once, then have every thread in the block reuse that one load — cutting the number of global reads, not just making each one cheaper
Coalescing and shared-memory reuse are complementary, not competing, techniques — a well-tuned kernel uses both


~2 min. Bridge slide into the rest of the (not-yet-fully-promoted) deck below — makes explicit that “access pattern” (this session) and “reuse via shared memory” (rest of module) are two different levers on the same underlying memory-wall problem, not two separate topics.

title: Module 4: Shared Memory & Tiled Matrix Multiply
text:
Checkpoint Preview
Checkpoint CK-08 will ask you to:

Implement both a coalesced and a strided memory-access kernel
Time both and explain the performance difference in terms of memory transactions


~1 min. 20-minute timed, paired with Lab 08 (Oct 23). Note the date gap: this lecture is Oct 21 (Wed), but Lab 8/CK-8 land Oct 23 (Fri) — the same two-day lecture-then-lab rhythm as every other module.

title: Module 4: Shared Memory & Tiled Matrix Multiply
text:
Today’s Plan

Quiz 4 first (15 min, Blackboard) — covers Module 3 and Oct 21’s coalescing content
Then: why coalescing alone isn’t enough, and what shared memory buys you on top of it
Declaring and using shared memory in Numba, and the synchronization it requires
Shared memory banks and bank conflicts — the one subtlety that can silently undercut a shared-memory kernel


~1 min. ~35 min of lecture time after the quiz. This session sets up Oct 28’s tiled matmul directly — everything here is the “why” and “how” that tiling then applies to a real kernel.

title: Module 4: Shared Memory & Tiled Matrix Multiply
text:
Why Coalescing Alone Isn’t Enough

Global memory delivers roughly 2 TB/s of bandwidth on a modern GPU — but a single float32 is only 4 bytes, so that’s “only” on the order of 500 billion individual float reads per second at peak
ALUs can execute billions of FLOPs per second — often far more than 500 billion, if each one only needed one memory read to do its job
Arithmetic intensity (FLOPs performed per byte moved, previewed back in Module 1) is what determines whether you can actually reach that ALU speed, or whether memory bandwidth caps you first
Oct 21’s coalescing makes each individual memory transaction as cheap as possible — but it does nothing to reduce how many transactions a kernel needs. That’s the gap shared memory closes


~3 min. Explicit framing: coalescing (last session) and shared-memory reuse (this session) are two different levers on the same memory-wall problem — one makes each access cheaper, the other reduces the number of accesses needed at all.

title: Module 4: Shared Memory & Tiled Matrix Multiply
text:
The Roofline Intuition
[DIAGRAM] — A roofline chart: x-axis “arithmetic intensity (FLOPs/byte),” log scale; y-axis “achieved performance (FLOPs/s),” log scale. Two “roof” lines meeting at a corner: a rising diagonal line on the left labeled “memory bandwidth roof,” which transitions into a flat horizontal line on the right labeled “compute (peak FLOPS) roof.” Two points are plotted underneath the roofline: one labeled “naive matmul,” sitting low and to the left, close to the diagonal memory roof; another labeled “tiled matmul,” sitting further right and higher, closer to the flat compute roof.

Any kernel’s achieved performance is capped by whichever roof it’s under: if arithmetic intensity is low, the diagonal memory-bandwidth roof caps you regardless of how fast your ALUs are; if arithmetic intensity is high enough, the flat compute roof becomes the real limit
Naive matmul (Lab 5/Module 2) sits on the memory-bound side — Oct 7’s bottleneck diagnosis already established this: lots of global reads, little reuse per read
Tiled matmul (Oct 28) doesn’t add any new arithmetic — it does the same multiplications — but by reusing data out of shared memory instead of re-reading global memory, it raises effective arithmetic intensity and moves the achieved performance point up and to the right, toward the compute roof
We won’t formally derive this model (that’s beyond this course’s scope) — the picture is what matters: tiling’s entire purpose is to move a kernel’s dot rightward on this chart


~3 min. Students will confirm this empirically in Lab 9 — comparing naive vs. tiled matmul timings is exactly measuring these two points’ relative height. Keep the derivation at “picture level” — no formulas needed here.

title: Module 4: Shared Memory & Tiled Matrix Multiply
text:
Declaring Shared Memory
from numba import cuda
import numba

@cuda.jit
def demo_shared(arr):
    # Declare shared memory — size known at compile time
    s = cuda.shared.array(shape=256, dtype=numba.float32)

    i  = cuda.grid(1)
    ti = cuda.threadIdx.x       # local index within the block

    if i < arr.shape[0]:
        s[ti] = arr[i]          # load from global → shared
        cuda.syncthreads()      # all threads in block must reach here

        # Now every thread can read any element of s[]
        arr[i] = s[ti] * 2.0

Three new pieces of syntax here: cuda.shared.array (the declaration), a compile-time-fixed shape=, and cuda.syncthreads() (the barrier) — each explained on the next few slides


~2 min. Walk through the three new concepts by name before the rules slide formalizes them — students should recognize each one in the code above before moving on.

title: Module 4: Shared Memory & Tiled Matrix Multiply
text:
Rules of Shared Memory

Shared scope: visible to every thread in the same block — not visible to threads in other blocks, even ones running concurrently on the same SM
Size fixed at compile time: the shape= argument must be a literal or a module-level constant, never a variable computed at runtime
Lifetime: exists only for the block’s lifetime — allocated when the block starts, gone the moment the block finishes
Synchronization required: cuda.syncthreads() is a barrier — every thread in the block must reach it before any thread is allowed to continue past it


~3 min. The most common bug this session sets up for Lab 9: forgetting syncthreads() after writing to shared memory, so one thread reads a value before another thread has finished writing it — a race condition producing a silent wrong answer, no crash. Foreshadow this explicitly; Oct 28’s tiled kernel has two separate places this can go wrong.

title: Module 4: Shared Memory & Tiled Matrix Multiply
text:
cuda.syncthreads() — The Barrier
[DIAGRAM] — Four threads in a block, each drawn as a vertical timeline. Threads 0 and 1 write to shared memory first (short colored bars near the top of their timelines), while threads 2 and 3 are still busy with unrelated work (their timelines show a gap). A horizontal dashed line labeled “syncthreads() barrier” crosses all four timelines at the same height. Below the barrier line, all four threads’ timelines resume together at the same point, now reading from shared memory. A second, smaller diagram to the right shows the without case: thread 2’s read (an arrow reaching into thread 0’s write) happens before thread 0’s write completes, crossing into thread 0’s timeline before its write bar — labeled “race: read arrives too early.”

syncthreads() is a rendezvous, not a delay — every thread in the block must physically arrive at that line of code before the fastest thread is allowed to proceed past it
Without it: whichever thread happens to reach the read first gets whatever was in shared memory at that moment — sometimes correct, sometimes stale garbage, with no error raised either way
A subtle trap: calling syncthreads() inside an if branch that not every thread in the block takes causes a deadlock — the threads that skipped the branch never arrive at the barrier, so the threads waiting there wait forever. Rare in this course’s labs, but worth knowing exists


~3 min. The deadlock case is worth a brief mention but not a deep dive — students won’t hit it in this course’s structured exercises, but it’s a real failure mode in general CUDA code and a satisfying “why does my program just hang” answer if they ever encounter it later.

title: Module 4: Shared Memory & Tiled Matrix Multiply
Module 4: Shared Memory & Tiled Matrix Multiply
text:
Shared Memory Banks

Shared memory isn’t one monolithic block of storage — physically, it’s divided into equally-sized banks (32 banks is the standard width, matching warp size), and consecutive 4-byte words are assigned to consecutive banks in a round-robin pattern
Each bank can service exactly one memory request per cycle — but different banks can all be accessed simultaneously
When all 32 threads in a warp read from 32 different banks in the same cycle, every read happens in parallel — this is the fast case, and it’s what you get by default with straightforward, consecutive access patterns


~3 min. This is the shared-memory analogue of coalescing (Oct 21) — same underlying idea (parallel hardware wants parallel, non-overlapping requests), one level closer to the compute units.

title: Module 4: Shared Memory & Tiled Matrix Multiply
text:
Bank Conflicts
[DIAGRAM] — 8 shared-memory banks drawn as 8 numbered vertical columns (simplified from 32 for readability). Left scenario, “no conflict”: 8 threads, each with an arrow pointing to a different bank (thread 0 → bank 0, thread 1 → bank 1, … thread 7 → bank 7) — all 8 arrows land in parallel, captioned “8 requests, 1 cycle.” Right scenario, “conflict”: 8 threads all arrow into the same single bank (bank 3), captioned “8 requests, but only 1 can be served per cycle → 8 cycles, serialized.” A third, small callout shows one exception: all 8 arrows pointing to the same address within the same bank, captioned “broadcast — free, not a conflict.”

A bank conflict happens when two or more threads in the same warp request different addresses that happen to land in the same bank — those requests can’t be served simultaneously, so the hardware serializes them, one at a time
In the worst case, all 32 threads hit the same bank with different addresses: a 32-way conflict, taking roughly 32× as long as the conflict-free case for that one access
Exception: if every thread in the warp requests the same address (not just the same bank), the hardware broadcasts that one value to all of them in a single cycle — that’s not a conflict, it’s the best case
This typically shows up with strided access into a 2D shared-memory array — e.g., every thread reading a different row of the same column, when the array’s row length happens to be a multiple of the bank count


~3 min. Conceptual/awareness-level content — this course doesn’t checkpoint or quiz bank conflicts directly (schedule.md commits to teaching it here, but no lab exercise currently isolates it). Still worth teaching properly: it’s genuinely useful GPU knowledge, and it’s exactly the kind of subtlety that explains “why is my shared-memory kernel not as fast as I expected” once students start experimenting beyond the assigned labs.

title: Module 4: Shared Memory & Tiled Matrix Multiply
text:
Avoiding Bank Conflicts: Padding
# Conflict-prone: TILE columns, stride exactly matches the bank pattern
tile = cuda.shared.array((TILE, TILE), numba.float32)

# Padded: one extra column shifts the stride, breaking the alignment
tile_padded = cuda.shared.array((TILE, TILE + 1), numba.float32)

The classic fix for a systematic, stride-caused bank conflict: allocate the shared array with one extra column than the problem actually needs
That single extra column shifts every subsequent row’s starting bank by one position — which is usually enough to break the alignment that was causing threads to repeatedly collide on the same bank
The padding column itself is never used for real data — it’s pure overhead, traded deliberately for avoiding serialized access
You won’t be required to apply this technique in this course’s labs or checkpoints — it’s here so the option is in your toolkit if you ever profile a shared-memory kernel and find bank conflicts are the bottleneck


~2 min. Keep this at “here’s the standard trick” level — don’t derive exactly which access patterns in this course’s own tiled-matmul kernel would or wouldn’t benefit from padding; that’s a level of hardware-specific detail beyond this course’s scope, and worth saying so if a curious student asks.
